 I think I missed this one when it was originally published due to a personal King boycott right around that time -- I'd just gotten so very very tired of getting sooooo excited there was a new King book out, only to wade through yet another bloated, overwritten doorstop. 
 Having tried a few newer books by King lately, I decided to give some of those older books a try. Sadly, this one is pretty much what I feared it would be -- so many terrific ideas bogged down with the worst of out-of-control story telling. 
 Just an aside here -- what's up with King and portable toilets? I swear he's used these several times as doorways, right? Doesn't that seem odd to anyone besides myself? 
 Okay, so the gist of this one is pretty standard Stephen King -- a group or individual (here it's retiree, Ralph Roberts) stumbles upon hidden supernatural forces at work in (once again) Derry, Maine. The usual reluctant heroics and assorted nonsense ensues. 
 So it sounds like I really hated this one -- but no, actually I didn't. In fact, I might have really loved it if it had been edited down to about half the length, and some of the typical King-isms removed. 
 I get it, I really do -- King has an entire UNIVERSE that he seems compelled not only to explore, but to tie together. So in this fairly simple story about senior citizens battling the forces of evil, we have references to the Dark Tower and King's beloved ka-tet. 
 And it just makes me soooooooo tiiiiiiiired. 
 But the characters -- they're wonderful. Roberts is just a really lovely guy, and the interior voice of his late wife, Carolyn, is so believable. Lois, the lovely widow Roberts shares his adventure with -- while not as believable a character as some of the others -- is perfectly charming. Why oh why couldn't you have left it at that, Mr. King? 
 One aspect of this book that I have to comment on is the central conflict of the story -- the people of Derry are divided over the local Women's Center and the abortion debate. I checked the publication date on this, and it was released in 1994, TWENTY YEARS ago. I found it depressing that we are STILL fighting over this subject, so many years later. I did find it a difficult read at times due to this. 
 Despite all of this, there was a lot to like about this book -- when King wants to, he can really push your buttons and make you feel for his characters, and this book was no exception. (view spoiler)[When Roberts sacrifices his own life at the end of the book in order to save his dear friend's daughter, I bawled my eyes out. (hide spoiler)] 
 Probably for die hard King fans or completists only.

Evaline Stoker, supernaturally gifted vampire hunter and sister of aspiring author Bram, and Mina Holmes, niece of the famed detective and gifted with an (almost) equally brilliant analytical mind and eye for detail, have absolutely nothing in common other than being young women from exceptional families. Ordinarily, vivacious Evaline and loner Mina might never even have crossed paths. However, a series of deaths and disappearances among young women connected only by the discovery of an Egyptian style scarab at the scenes has led Irene Adler, secret agent in the service of the crown, to recruit these two unlikely partners to help solve the crimes. 
 Murder mystery, steampunk, conspiracies, a bit of time travel thrown in because whyever not - this was a fast-paced and entertaining read, although I found it a little light on the world building and the whole time travel storyline and everybody's almost entirely unquestioning acceptance of it seemed awfully convenient and ill-explained. I assume there'll be some further exploration of that in the next book. Minor annoyances aside, this was quite enjoyable lighthearted fun.

For some reason or another, it took me almost a month to read this book. I don't know if it was because I've been busy crafting, or if I'm lazy, or if the book just wasn't as good as I wanted it to be. Who knows. But aside from that: 
 I would suggest this one to mystery readers who loved The Thirteenth Tale. The writing style is eerily similar, and though the story is different, it has the same feel to it. I think this is especially due to the fact that an underlying theme is the love of books. 
 It gives a great sense of place with its description of Barcelona around the time of the Spanish Civil War. (My sense of history being what it is, I did not even know that such a thing existed.) 
 A good summary of the story was actually included as part of the story: "[It's] about accursed books, about the man who wrote them, about a character who broke out of the pages of a novel so that he could burn it, about a betrayal and a lost friendship. It's a story of love, of hatred, and of the dreams that live in the shadow of the wind." 
 Favorite Quotes: 
 I still remember the day my father took me to the Cemetery of Forgotten Books for the first time. It was the early summer of 1945, and we walked through the streets of a Barcelona trapped beneath ashen skies as dawn poured over Rambla de Santa Monica in a wreath of liquid copper. 
 [A] story is a letter the author writes to himself, to tell himself things that he would be unable to discover otherwise. 
 Books are mirrors: you only see in them what you already have inside you. 
 Sometimes we think people are like lottery tickets, that they're there to make our most absurd dreams come true. 
 Our world will not die as a result of the bomb, as the papers say, it will die of laughter, of banality, of making a joke of everything, and a lousy joke at that. 
 Disarmed, I realize how easily you can lose all animosity toward someone you've deemed your enemy as soon as that person stops behaving as such.
Best Magisterium book so far, almost matching Harry Potter.

You remember the movie The Sixth Sense, where a lot of people went back to see it a second time to try and pick how and where they were mislead. Well, this book's a lot like that. You think you've got everything worked out, and then all of a sudden Sarah Waters presents you with a rabbit from a hat, except you didn't even know there was a hat in the first place. Effectively, you just end up completely blindsided and thinking 'WHAT IS THIS SORCERY??!!' 
 (view spoiler)[I didn't like the end, but that's just me. It was a little bit too nice and fluffy, for such an otherwise twisted and treacherous little tale. Other than that, it was fantastic. I'm still going to give it five stars, because it was so much fun (hide spoiler)]

I am not a huge fan of short stories, often they come off as cynical and depressing, but Tenth of December is fantastic. It is utterly unique and unlike anything I have read before. Saunders believes in humanity. His stories are full of misfits desperate to fit in and become the heroes of their own lives. He captures their mental worlds so well. Although they're constrained by the painful circumstances of their lives, they strive to break free and rise to the occasion. Sometimes they succeed and sometimes . . . 
 In this age of disenchantment, it is refreshing to read someone who believes in human beings. Saunders saves his best story for last. The Tenth of December comes at the end and is the most emotionally powerful story of the bunch.

Once again, another book from Eve Langlais that I thoroughly enjoyed. I utterly loved Joe! He was so caring, sweet, and protective. Such as with the guard, getting shot at, whenever someone so much as made a comment about Chloe that he didn't like, and his reaction when they lost her. Chloe was so cute. She did what she had to do, and she truly cared about Joe. I felt so bad for what she went through. I thought Seth was funny, and I cracked up at Joe's reactions to his comments. I very highly recommend! <3

I enjoyed this more than I thought I would! Just when I think something completely predictable is going to happen, it catches me off guard a little. Out of the YA dystopian trilogies that have been popping up all over the place in the publishing world, I'm actually interested in the next one!

I'm getting more and more attached to the characters as the story goes on. It was a slow start for me, but now I'm hooked and I can't wait to find out what happens next. Is the guy in the dam a bad guy? Is Jeppard really evil? Is the scientist really evil? What's going to happen next I can't wait and that was such a cliffhanger! Also Gus's vision what was up with that, I'm going to have to get the next book ASAP.

I don't normally like to trash writers or their work; any work a writer creates is a labor of love, and I try to think of that when I assign my ratings for books. 
 But? 
 Two Words: EVIL. CHICKEN. 
 This book is the point at which I gave up on this entire series, despite not-minding ("Liking" is a strong word) the previous books in this series. (And this is from someone who slogged through the entire "Cerebus" comic book series.) 
 Don't believe me? 
 Check the [edited] snippet here: http://asoiaf.westeros.org/index.php/...

This book was won in a firstreads giveaway. 
 I didn't simply read this book, I devoured it. It became all I could think about, I even stayed up far too late last night not wanting to put it down. It's been a very long time since I've felt that way about a novel. Obsessed is an accurate word. 
 Did I enjoy this book? No. Could I stop reading it? No. Would I recommend it? 100% yes. 
 So why didn't I enjoy it? The subject matter of The Book of You is haunting, it's terrifying, it isn't something that can be enjoyed, yet it gripped me. It made me feel physically sick, it shocked me and it actually scared me. The writing was incredibly honest, Clarissa's thought process was well written, her diary entries were just brutal. I believed it, I was invested in her. I was scared for her. Kendal delved beneath the surface, into all the various feelings someone being stalked/threatened would feel, it was far deeper than I could have hoped. 
 The only downfall? The ending. 324 pages led to this, and it very quickly escalated and subsided in 40 pages. There were a lot of questions left unanswered and it was far less rounded off than I would like. Believe me, I don't want a happily ever after, but I want to know what happened to the characters I've invested in. The book/story/characters deserved a more thorough ending, and so does the reader. 
 Otherwise- scary, thrilling, incredible. 5*

Shades of Milk and Honey has a simple enough plot. Like any Jane Austen novel, there are young women eligible for marriage, young men of varying fortunes and recommendations that may or may not make good husbands, lots of balls and dinners to attend, and, in true Pride and Prejudice fashion, a nervous mother beside herself with worry that her daughters may never find a husband. The standard tropes were all there, only this time, there was a special ingredient: magic. 
 Read the full review here...

** spoiler alert ** 
 I LOVED the writing, the structure of the book, the whole creepy tone and layered meanings. I think I'd have given 5 stars, except for that fact, that all through the book I kept thinking of all the various possibilities for the increasingly weird happenings, and even though there was a resolution, I felt like there were just a few too many unanswered questions. Also, I was very bummed out that Owen didn't take on a bigger role. I thought he'd end up actually BEING someone, and instead he was left there hanging. But it IS the kind of book that makes you think more, and want to create your own version of the story, and THAT I do appreciate. 
 (Also, anyone like me, start reading the chapter titles consecutively, like they were going to provide some secrect clue to the mystery?)

"Is this what Chiss do? See a trap, and just walk into it?" 
 Good science fiction--albeit a space opera--not just good Star Wars fiction. The reader need not have any previous exposure to Star Wars nor Thrawn to enjoy this origins tale in which Zahn skillfully weaves the many threads of existing stories into a fresh, original story. 
 "There's no trust in politics. Never has been. Never will be." 
 Thrawn is there in all his glory, but he is also limited and occasionally tone deaf, so he's less superhuman. 
 "All Eli could see in his face was that maddening confidence of his." 
 The two primary threads interweave convincingly. Bad people see themselves as serving a greater good, just a good people are often blind to their own faults. Good Holmes-Watson interchanges. Understanding an opponent through his art is a constant with Thrawn. 
 "Military leadership is a journey, not a destination." 
 Quibble: Thrawn's voice, even his inner voice, is too childish. Don't care for the cover art; inconsistent with other portrayals of Thrawn. 
 "A warrior may retreat. He does not flee. He may lie in ambush. He does not hide. He may experience victory or defeat. He does not cease to serve."

I enjoyed The Namesake, but this book is just astounding. A very deserved Pulitzer Prize, the book is a collection of short stories. What makes them special is the incredible ability of the author of portraying the characters with few adroitly placed strokes. The characters are realistic, credible and, as a result, the short stories are powerful and touching. They have a way to work their way into the reader hearts, moving him or her to tears.

I've just finished reading this book , and ...Hmmmm ... God ! I kind of am disappointed ... 
 I do not know why , but I thought it would have a different ending .. 
 The title is misleading _in my opinion . 
 If someone told you Eve & Adam what will come in your mind ?! 
 It did not match my expectation _maybe that was the problem ... 
 The writing was good , and the plot was well narrated , yet somehow the characters did not stick in my mind . 
 I feel speechless , I have got mixed feelings about this book ,. 
 It is sad , because I really thought It would be one of my favorite ... 
 I am sorry to say that it was wasted my time =_=

I started reading this not knowing exactly what to expect. I've heard great things about the author, but that in itself doesn't mean much and I've been avoiding detailed reviews so as to not spoil the book for myself. In good and in bad I want to be able to make up my own mind when possible. 
 Alternatively snorting and giggling at the wonderful things Francesca or her family or her friends say, I'm still waiting for that aha moment that elevates one story above all others, but I'm not finding it. I prepare to finish the last few chapters expecting to rate this book with solid three stars when it hits me. The climax that elevates this book above most ya literature and ensures my interest in the authors other material. 
 It's not as dirty as it sounds. 
 Few things remain that I found improbable and those combined with 200 pages of waiting steal that final star from this book.

This story kept me entertained throughout. One nitpicky thing I have to say is that Eadlyn's speech at the end was a little off on my opinion. She didn't say enough about still working with her people. It was more about this is good for me and that is good for you. Also, I thought the ending and Eadlyn's realization of her heart were a little rushed.

Well, that was well worth the years of waiting for it to be published! I was complaining about how long it took for this book to come out, but if this is what Rothfuss creates in his own good time, then I'm willing to wait! 
 One of the best fantasies I've ever read. I could barely stand to put it down, and that's a problem when the book is 994 pages! But you know you're reading a great book, when you look up from the page and wonder for a moment where you're at. Reading this book was like being underwater, surfacing was always a little disconcerting. 
 I loved every story within the story, and I am still worrying at the clues to the overall puzzle even in my sleep. I will wait for the next installment, impatiently, but I will wait with great anticipation as I know if will be worth it!

I have ordered this. I will have it in my hands soon. I'm trying really hard to contain my excitement, but I just ... 
 Cannot. 
 Contain. 
 Excitement!!!!!!!

I was pleasantly surprised in this book because it started to really focus on one of the minor main characters. But was a little disappointed at the end because ultimately even though Maldonovo was given so much page time, I didn't even learn that much about him than I could found out from a secondary point of view. 
 We already know from other books that he's fond of clothes and women and tries to avoid direct responsibility, but is intelligent despite his foppish appearance. What did we learn more than that? Really not much. So this book did not do very much for his character development and that was a disappointment.

This book leaves me lost for words, what an amazing concept by an absolutely amazing author. This book had me from the blurb and left me glued to the pages for hours, gasping in suspense, my heart racing until the very last page which left me hungry for more. This book should be read by EVERYONE, and i mean everyone. Katniss is such a strong character and her story is amazing.

I've bee reading these Bond Novels by order of publication. This one of the best Bond novels as of yet! Although, I think the last one was somewhat better. Very easy and enjoyable read. Somewhat predictable but it is Bond so... nuff said?

A crafty book of tricks and traps about reading books and their tricks and traps. Don't be fooled by all the post-modern ninnies' gusto and fervor about this book's convolutedness: there is nothing secretive or innate here, rather it is a novel about reading, how we read, what we read, how what we read is written, and how to read things that are written. It is so carefully constructed that it'd be easy to flit through it and winnow it's internal and self-referential irreverence down into some stupid lit-crit miasma, but better to just read it for yourself, which is what Calvino would've wanted, and is probably the point. But who can tell? Reader judge!

My expectations were really high for this book, and I don't feel disappointed at all. Unfortunately, that makes this review terribly hard to write! So, I think I'll try a list format. 
 Things I loved: 
 The pacing - I never felt a minute of boredom 
 The emotions - Even though this is an action-packed book, Brown still pays attention to the emotions of Darrow and his friends 
 The shocks - I had a couple of moments where an event shocked me so much that I had to gasp 
 The characters - Everyone gets a fair shake, and even minor characters have their own opinions 
 The world-building - We got to learn some more about society in this book, and it was fascinating. 
 The uncertainty - You never know when a character is going to die, a plan be foiled, or a trust betrayed 
 Things I didn't love: 
 The cliffhanger? I'm just glad that I don't have to wait too long for book 3!

This is a book about the years leading up to World War II told by following the ambassador to Germany, William Dodd, and his family, intermingled with the general story of the rise of Hitler and his henchmen during that time period. The author does an outstanding job blending these two viewpoints together to give us a real feel for the events leading up to WWII. The book is filled with wonderful descriptions of the country and its people. 
 We are introduced to Martha Dodd, ambassador Dodd's daughter, a vivacious young girl who wants to believe that the new Germany will be good for all the people. She dates many prominent Germans. She slowly comes to the realization that things are not so great in the country. It is fascinating to read how the US also is unwilling to see the evidence of atrocities being committed. The people of the US had an isolationist attitude during this time which is hard to fathom looking back. By the end of the book we see the horrible changes that occur and get a good feel for how and why things fell apart. Highly recommended for anyone interested in world history.

If it had been a smidge longer, I probably would have given it five stars. 
 (view spoiler)[Full disclosure, I might well be biased as a few aspects of the book are semi-personal to me. But I was hooked before I knew about that. And the semi-personal bits weren't actually relevant to the story. (hide spoiler)] 
 Final Girls is intense. Every character is flawed - some more deeply than others - so every action is suspect. Much like protagonist Quincy Carpenter, readers won't know who to trust - including Quincy herself. I didn't especially like any of these people, but I found myself rooting for most of them at some point or another. Riley Sager made me care, even about the ones I sometimes thought deserved a punch or two on the nose. 
 Quincy's insecurities and repressed memories often result in poor decisions. Any confidence she displays rings false because it is false, and that's something she only discovers as her story progresses. Navigating the character's inner and outer worlds requires a reader's full attention, and Sager's writing commands exactly that. Filled with descriptions that engage all the senses, almost every paragraph felt like a physical experience. 
 Readers get a front row seat to Quincy's unraveling and an equally close view of her attempts to put herself back together. While I recognise that the latter isn't generally something emphasised in thrillers, I can't help but wish there had been more of it in this one. 
 But even though the end came much sooner than I preferred, Final Girls is still one of the best bools I've read this year.
Awesome artwork in here! I liked some of the stories better than others. And some were just too confusing but overall a very nice graphic novel. Now I want the rest of the volumes!
Good introduction to the series.

I've said it before and I'll say it again, Cassandra Clare is hands down my favorite author, and ANYTHING that she writes/co-writes I'll read. I haven't read anything by Holly Black, but I do have The Darkest Part of the Forest that I want to read ASAP. The Iron Trials was a really solid first book-the introduction of the worlds, characters, and magic system were done very well. I like how the information about the Mages, their world, their magic, and their past were distributed. It never felt like information dumping, but it didn't feel as if the authors were spoon feeding me the information either. I know a lot of people compare it to HP, but in my opinion, although there are some similarities I never thought that it was similar enough to cause so much speculation. 
 I love the cover of this book because by looking at it, you would think that the story would be about the golden boy in the center. You would think the boy to the left of him is just a side kick, so imagine my surprise when the entire story is told through Callum's point of view. I love that! I love that he's not the hero of the story, and that all eyes aren't on him, but he's the narrator which makes him special in his own way. Speaking of Callum, I really did like him although he did come off as immature and a bit stubborn at times-but he's 12 so what can you expect? The way he thinks/behaves is very much that of an average 12 year old boy-he wants to fit in, he wants to break the rules, and he wants to be accepted. I also liked Aaron and Tamara a lot, and they really brought a lot to the story. 
 I was a bit disappointed in the magic system because it wasn't as grand or as "cool" as I had hope it would be, but maybe in the next book, when they enter their second year, we will get to see more magic. 
 All in all, I enjoyed this book although at times it did feel a little slow. I can't wait to continue on with the series, especially after that crazy reveal at the end, which I of course didn't see coming. I can't wait for the kids to grow up and deal with their internal problems as well their magical ones!

Ahhhhh 10 billion stars please!!! I absolutely adored this! I loved the characters, the writing and pace, and I just loved reading about TJ and Brett falling in love. This had a great group of characters too, I loved Brett's scheming mother! 
 Sure, nothing groundbreaking or new, but this was just an incredibly well written romance - major, major romance - that I couldn't put it down. I really love that TJ and Brett took their time to make sure the emotions were there before they jumped into bed together, and the writing of some of the scenes where they first kiss, or when Brett first hugged TJ and kissed the back of his neck, were just incredibly sensual and hot. 
 I can't recommend this book enough...can't wait to read the sequel!
I am now (even more) terrified of having children.
Absolutely stunning and beautiful and breath-taking.

Loved this book! I think this might be Briggs' best yet! This book may have just pushed the entire series from "I really like this series." to "This is my favorite urban fantasy series!" I honestly loved this book too much to do it justice in my review. My mind keeps bouncing around with the nine million things that made it so fantastic. 
 The pacing was perfect! There's a fantastic amount of action and some great surprises. Mercy is amazingly kick butt. We get to see the entire pack and some of the great secondary characters. Stefan! Kyle! I was a little thrown with the switch to Adam's point of view, but it's not really that surprising with their bond playing such a large role in the story. I can't wait to see where Briggs takes Adam in the future books!

Don't kill me, reading friends, but I didn't like this one as much as I hoped to :( Jethro and Sienna meet when she comes into town to film a movie. They were cute together. Sweet and funny. Where I struggled is that I didn't really feel they got to know each other or develop their relationship. There weren't a lot of scenes together that I felt had depth. I also didn't feel they addressed their individual internal conflicts well. It felt almost like a fade to black then we're on the other side of it. Other than that, I liked Sienna's personality and Jethro's honesty and demeanor. They were good together and I think with a little more development I could have easily loved them as a couple. They were pretty sexy when they finally moved forward with that aspect of their relationship. Safety: No OW/OM/Sharing. There is a little drama with an ex of the h. No rape/abuse.
I get where Conrad is coming from but he is way too overdramatic and reserved.
Well JK Rowling, you certainly haven't lost your touch!

Wow if this is Kristen Proby's debut novel then I am blown away anticipating what her next book is going to be like, as this one was phenomenal.... 
 It was a great, flirty and fun read and I enjoyed every minute of it... Looking forward to the next book in January....

This is just an 'okay' book. Fast-pacing, yes. It doesn't excuse itself for the lack of world-building and characterization, though. Moreover, I have to agree to its bashers that June and Day were written as if they are the same person... I got to admit that I read this during one of the worst time of my life, I could not enjoy it so I stopped. I had to resume reading two weeks after. When I did, it got better towards the end. Maybe, I couldn't give this book a fair rating because of this. I will have to re-read it and see if it will have a more justified and favorable grade.

I am usually a fan of Josh Lanyon and this was no exception. From the opening scene watching Christopher try to get across the bridge, in the mud, ending up with his discovery of the dead body... it's funny and drew me in. The dialogue is good, the murder mystery is old fashioned but clever and the scenes with JX and Christopher are sexy. Sure the mystery is resolved a bit simply but I really enjoyed this and will definitely read book 2.

Listen, I love these books and I'm running out of ways to say that without gushing too much about it and showing my true trash queen colors to the world, so I'll just leave that at that. 
 Also, this next sentence outta super spoilery, but...dudes, the fact that T.J. was Thomas still managed to surprise me, but I TOTALLY CALLED IT when he was taking about his project. But it was still vague enough that I had dismissed the possibility by a certain point so, yeah!! Nice job, Jamie! Also, I loved how nicely the plot of this story played with the plot of Beautiful Disaster and Waking Disaster. That said, there was also a few scenes in A Beautiful Wedding that totally spoiled the outcome of this novel, thus removing certain points of tension throughout the timeline, but it didn't totally ruin the fun.
Fantasticles - loved it.

I have never read any Sherlock Holmes, but I imagine it would be amazing, and it's on my to do list. That being said, I didn't need to know anything in order to thoroughly enjoy this book. The characters are caustic, witty, and play off each other so well; maybe too well, but still darn awesome. I actually don't hate Charlotte, I begrudgingly love her because she's so tactless but observant. She's a Doctor Who, a Jackaby, a Sherlock. Watson is pretty endearing, as Charlotte notes, one of them should be kind, and I am glad it's Watson. I am not sure how I feel about a maybe relationship. I see how that could work based on how the characters have been built up in this first book, but at what cost to the professional relationship? 
 4 stars.

I loved this character. Kelsea is put in an incredibly difficult situation of assuming a throne she has never seen, and she's only nineteen. I was immediately impressed with her determination and strength. It would have been so easy to give up the throne and run away, yet that thought never crosses Kelsea's mind. I was also in love with the acute detail Johansen uses when writing this character. Her writing is incredibly skilled in that I got glimpses of the fear and insecurities that Kelsea has, yet they were just that - glimpses. These feelings are never dwelt upon, and Kelsea remains a vision of strength despite the inner glimpses given. I was never overwhelmed by Kelsea's feelings nor distracted by them, and I was so incredibly happy with the way Johansen managed this. 
 I also loved all the supporting characters. These are mainly the guards that were sent to protect Kelsea and her ascension of the throne. These guards were wonderful because they had varying levels of distrust and dislike for Kelsea that was visible. Over time they begin to trust her as they should trust a Queen, which as a reader made me trust Kelsea too. I loved that they weren't infatuated with her at the beginning, but rather over time, and even as they grew to like her it came in forms such as respect and honour, rather than infatuation or love. I think the supporting guards were very well done and really helped to support Kelsea's character. 
 The one aspect I thought may have been weak was the world history, which is given in pieces throughout the book. This world is actually a future dystopian version of our own world, but they have lost access to technology and a lot of human knowledge, thus reverting back to a feudal system. I actually don't mind that idea, and Johansen expressed it in an interesting way by giving Kelsea access to a few books that give her a distorted view of the past. While I understand that Kelsea herself only had a limited knowledge of her world history, I was frustrated by the lack of information of how humankind had gotten from our world into the Tearling, a completely separate world where magic is possible. There's really nothing to explain it, and while I like and can accept the idea of this world, I didn't quite see the connection being made to our own world in the story. 
 Overall, I love the story, the characters, and even with its flaws, the setting. There are a lot of little pieces that are working really well together in this story, and I thought it created a very nice, enjoyable, rounded story. This book is a great read for a strong female character, or those interested in kingdom politics or court life. I'm very much looking forward to the next book - I can't wait to find out what happens!

No, it's not the same, but Brandon Sanderson has done an amazing job with what he was given. Storylines are being wrapped up and you can feel the race towards the end now. Everything is lining up for an ending that readers have been waiting for for over 20 years and it has been written very well, even if the style is not an exact match to Robert Jordan. Kudos and thanks to everyone who worked to bring these final novels to completion.

A disclaimer here: I got the audiobooks for this series on impulse. I didnt know how to spell Cadogan House until I was well into the fourth book... in my mind, it was (and probably will always be) Cardigan Housewhich wasnt very glamorous. So, Im sorry about misspellings and possible typos. Now, on to the actual review: 
 What a promising start! Vamps are out of the closet, with all the glam and appeal you can imagine, and these ones have all the potential to draw me. 
 This is going to be a short review for several reasons, the most important being that this book has been around for ages and most of you already know about it... The next most important one being that, me being me, I went and kept reading the series before I reviewed and now I got a jumble of when a book ended and the next began in my head. 
 Ahem. Lets try to replicate the feelings I had when I finished listening to this audiobook for the first time, shall we? 
 Grad student of English Lit turns kick-ass heroine. I liked that. Specially because it didnt happen overnight: Merit had her work cut out for her, trying to keep up with her new life and new responsibilities. She also had a difficult time adjusting to her vampire existence, and I bought that. Her plans had just crumpled, after all, and while vamp existence is no longer a secret, its something fairly new and hard to reconcile with. That said, though, she was a bit whinny... There was a point where I thought suck it up and keep going already! Luckily, thats about the point where Merit herself decides to go the adult thing and accept her position as Cadogan vampire, so... All is well. 
 There seems to be a love triangle thingy going on. Cant say much about the deets, because itd spoil it all (as usual) but I like Morgan. Hes still boyish, even after immortality, and while his way to go about it might not be the best, hes genuinely interested. The other lead guy, Ethan, had his moments, but hes just too fixated on political capital and influence games for my taste... Well see how this plays out, though, because everything is very tenuous at this point. 
 The plot itself was interesting. The whole thing is around 9 hours in length; the first 2 were torture to work through without falling asleep but the last 4 went by in a single night. I guess thats the best way to sum it up: its slow to get going, but then it picks up momentum. The evil boss was a bit clich for my taste, in that the game she played was so obvious that it was insulting she thought itd work, but at the same time I had the feeling that she had been counting on it failing... and that it was actually part of the plan! So, no complains there. 
 All in all, a good series for anyone interested in urban fantasy. Id recommend it!

Ok, if you are looking for Alice in Wonderland meets The Walking Dead, Alice In Zombieland is not that book. The title is a bit misleading, as there are VERY few references to Lewis Carroll's beloved classic in this story. It is, however, chock full of zombies, so if you're into that kind of thing, this is the book for you! 
 After a horrible accident, Alice Bell is left an orphan trying to understand what she saw happen to her family. After years of not believing that her father truly did see monsters where no one else did, Ali begins to understand just what exactly he was seeing. Ali is forced to move in with her grandparents and begin attending a new high school, where she finds a group of rough students who see the same undead monsters she is now tormented by. She begins to trust, and maybe even fall for, bad boy Cole Holland, who has his own secrets. Together with their friends, they fight the zombies who took away everything Ali loved. 
 I thought this book was fantastic. It has a very different take on zombies, more than just the normal brain-dead, grave-escaping monsters that usually fill the pages of a book like this. Gena Showalter has created a completely original story(although the title is not so original) that is extremely fast paced and intense. It kept me addicted until the last page, and now I'm dying to get my hands on the sequel! 
 The characters are also very well written. Ladies, get ready to fall in love with Cole, because I don't think anyone can resist the descriptions of his violet eyes and his bad boy appeal. Really, all of the characters are well written. I didn't feel as though they felt into specific type-casts, the bad boys were bad boys but they also had sweet, honest sides, and the popular girls weren't fake but were relatable. It helped to make this story feel like it could really happen, minus the zombies. 
 My only complaint about the book was that I really was hoping to read Alice in Wonderland WITH ZOMBIES, and this is in no way that book. I was very pleasantly surprised though by the story I did get, and ended up falling in love with it by the end. Overall I give is 4/5 stars, and as I said earlier, I can't wait to read the other books in this series! 
 -Katie

First of all, I have to admit that I have high expectations for the book, probably because of all those glowing reviews out there and the mystifying cover. However, I find myself strangely disappointed by the book in some way. 
 The book is narrated through the two main protagonists - Waverly and Kieran. Ordinarily, I'd have loved to see the events unfolding through different POV. But this technique falls flat in Glow. Incidents are not told thoroughly enough and sometimes I feel as if I'd missed some parts of the story. Another thing I don't quite like is the building of character. Or lack thereof. Waverly seems to be pretty indecisive and fickle throughout the book while Kieran... Well, let's just say I can't figure out whether Kieran is the 'good guy' or not. In the first half of the book, we can see Kieran growing stronger and becoming a better leader. But the second half suddenly turns gears and Kieran is revealed to be slowly transforming into an idealistic cult leader. (shudder) This leaves me nonplussed and frustrated, especially since I was rooting for Kieran from the start. 
 Okay, enough with the bad stuff. Some may treat Glow as a mere science fiction, but when you look close enough, you can see that Glow actually explores deep, philosophical questions and the blurry line between good and evil. For example, what are you willing to do to ensure the survival of your crew? What lines are you willing to cross? And is posing as a representative of God a good thing if it gives your friends hope? Or is it just plain evil? Hm... Glow sure got me thinking about all these, leading me to explore the depths of humanity. (By the way, am I going too deep here?) 
 All in all, Glow is a nice enough book with enough twists to keep readers interested. Although the flow may not be smooth in all places, the way the book combines the darker and lighter elements of humans will leave readers pondering on the lengths we are willing to go to survive.

You know those compound German constructions, like schadenfreude, comprised of dissimilar single words? Well, I've got a new one that ought to exist if it doesn't already. It's schadenselbstungeduld, which translates roughly to "the sadness of your own impatience." Maybe you can guess why I'm bringing this up. I've had a bad case of it since last month when I joined the ranks of several Goodreads friends who have read all five of the David Mitchell books. We're now waiting long days, weeks, or, heaven forfend, even months for him to give us our next fix. 
 As a last high from the current stash, number9dream was a good one. And the ending, about which my keyboard remains silent, made me want more - no, in fact, more than that - more to the 9th power. The main character, Eiji, is a young man with problems. Parental abandonment is certainly part of it. A separate tragedy from his boyhood is always at the fore as well. He goes to Tokyo to resolve what he can, but he's not all that practical. In fact, his daydreams and fantasies often get in the way. They're a useful device for Mitchell, though, since they give his creative juices a chance to flow (if not gush) freely. As for Eiji's real life, it's a multifarious journey. His destination is sometimes diffuse, but seems to include acceptance of his situation, love, a sense of self, and whatever else coming of age stories are meant to bring. Along the way he meets some interesting people, drawn in Mitchell's customary way to a full human scale. Eiji also meets a few scum-of-the-earth types from warring yakuza gangs. The plot features plenty of action, some that seems as crazy as Eiji's dreams. (At one point it struck me as funny that it mattered so much to me to know if a scene was a made-up dream when, in fact, a work of fiction is itself made up. But you see where I was coming from - I wanted to know what was what for the integrity of the story (as opposed to the story within the story, nested like these parentheses.)) 
 The only points I took off for in this otherwise excellent book were for a few heinous crime sequences that I felt were over-the-top. I almost got the sense that Mitchell didn't feel the reality of them either (within the story, that is) since Eiji didn't seem as affected by them as a real, sentient person probably would be. The pyrotechnics are something I think Mitchell has always been drawn to, and he seems to have learned since how to modulate his use of them. Cloud Atlas, his next book after this one, provides all the evidence you need of his ultimate mastery. 
 Back to number9dream and its many positives: 
 -- The little narrative devices worked - lots of perspectives and styles including cyberpunk, crime drama (boiled good and hard), fantasy (a kid's story within the story about a goat who would sometimes unwittingly eat the pages he wrote), and military history (a moving tale in epistolary form of a suicide mission in WWII). 
 -- Eiji is a very likable character. You're happy for every small victory and anxious with every new threat. 
 -- The young lady he likes, the waitress with the beautiful neck and sublime musical talent, is wise beyond her years. She's given some thought-provoking lines. 
 -- Those of us who are big DM fans have always liked the way he writes. He has fun, he chooses his words well, and he's very creative with both structure and concept. That's all in evidence here. 
 -- People tell me that after DM, HM (Murakami) should be next. Is The Wind-up Bird Chronicle a good choice? 
 I'll end this with a personal note to David since he seems likely to respond to the pleas of his devoted fans. Will you please hurry up with that next one?! You don't seem like the type to revel in schadenfreude at our collective schadenselbstungeduld.

The novel begins with Allyson an 18 year recent high school graduate who is on a European tour for the summer. She is not really having a good time and looks forward to going home where she will begin to prepare herself for college. While in Stratford-upon-Avon, she goes with her tour group to see the RSC's production of Hamlet she meets Willem. Willem is a Dutch actor in a small independent acting group who tells Allyson that they will be performing Twelfth Night in a local park. Allyson goes and they have a few flirty moments such as catching each others eyes and he tosses her a coin at the end the performance. They each go their separate ways until they meet again on a train to London, and Willem nicknames her Lulu. When they reach London he is going back to Holland, and she to spend two more days in London, but he convinces her to go Paris for one day. They get to Paris and they have a day that imprints itself into Allyson's memory forever. The next morning Allyson goes back to London, but not after having a melt down because she wakes up and Willem is gone. The novel progresses from then onto to show the year after in which Allyson stars college and tries to understand what happened in Paris. 
 What I like about the novel was Pars. I' am a sucker for books that involve traveling. I have also been longing to back to Paris. Gayle Forman's writing is wonderful especially how she weaves Shakespearean plays into the novel very well. I am currently taking a Shakespeare class in college so it was cool to be able to understand the references to the plays. I liked how Forman wrote about college and how scary it can be, often time college gets overly glamorized in books and films and it isn't always like that for everyone. Dee was a fun character I want a friend like him. The uncertainty about Alyson's future and her career I felt were done really well 
 What I didn't like about the novel was Allyson. She was a downer from beginning to end and it bothers me that the one thing that convinced her to venture out of her comfort zone was a boy. I mean if I was lucky enough to get a paid European tour I would be eternally grateful to my parents forever and try to soak in every moment of it. Not mope around. As for her day in Pairs, I felt like it was was nice, but I think Allyson romanticized it too much. You can't fall in love with someone (who you don't even know their full name by the way) in one day. That is another thing that annoyed me the name thing. He doesn't even know her name and doesn't bother to learn it. They don't ask each other personal questions yet somehow they or she falls in love. Maybe I'm a bit cynical but there were so many moments when I seriously had to put the book down because I was cringing at how funny and ridiculous the situation was. Then instead of Allyson being a big girl and learning her tough life lesson she gets depressed. She doesn't care to make friends because she still can't get over one freaking day in Paris. Finally, when she semi snaps out her stupor it simply to get a job to go to Paris and find him. Ugh. I don't think Allyson learned about "self- discovery" One thing would have been if she decided to go to Paris because she wanted new memories of the place and to put everything behind her. The whole time instead of letting go and traveling she hunts down clues to find him. Then about four times she convinces herself to end the search and enjoy herself only to go back and start it again. I don't know I just didn't feel the connection here Willem doesn't sound that amazing. Someone she won't be able to replace or find someone better. In the end, we still aren't completely sure what happens because there is a sequel from Willem's point of view. This book wasn't terrible as I mentioned above it has it's good points. I like a good romance , but this one was a bit too cheesy for me. I will probably read the sequel, I am interested to see what happens.

For some reason, this book has readers in either the love it or hate it camp. I'm in neither, but I'm closer to the love it group than the hate it group. I found the book engaging and amusing, even though it was full of flaws. Here's a list of some: 
 *Follett struggles with keeping with the time period so that the book floats between the medieval and modern day in tone; 
 *There is excessive, graphic violence, and in particular against women and animals, that I wouldn't even label gratuitous - it's really superfluous and could have cut the book by 50 pages; and 
 *Some of the plotlines are a bit contrived but I credit Follett for trying to be thoughtful in how issues are resolved rather than simply working themselves out. 
 I own a number of Follett books, but I realized that I had not even read of one them until Pillars. But from what I know, historical fiction of an epic nature isn't really Follett's forte. He's more of a thriller-suspense kind of guy, which is why I think that he became in over his head trying to write something of this magnitude. 
 Nevertheless, I liked the book! It kept my interest. It's clear who the heroes and villians are and Follett was able to get me interested in a time in history where I will read more about it in the future. I didn't know anything about "the anarchy" period of England, and I'm looking forward to reading more. I'll also be reading more of Ken Follett in the future, including the sequel to Pillars, 
 . 
 I would recommend this book because it's one that all avid readers should read at one time or another.

This is really probably more like a 3.5* book, because while I really enjoyed it, there were things that absolutely drove me crazy. Mostly to do with the writing. Here is a sampling of what bothered me about Sarah's writing: the overuse of the em dash. Seriously, it's used like every other sentence and it breaks up the flow of the story. Next, overused phrases that don't even make sense, like when Feyre would "expose her teeth." That expression occured several times in the book and every time I kind of cracked up. I can't even imagine what that actually looks like in practice. Just try it, go look at yourself in a mirror and try to expose your teeth. Dumb. Also, there's a smattering of cursing in the book, which I'm not totally against in books, but when faeries say "shit" I don't buy it. That's a human swear word. I'm pretty sure faeries would be more creative with their curses. Oh, and this isn't really a writing critique, more a silly plot device, but the answer to the riddle at the end. Come. On. I won't say what it is because spoilers, but, based on my reaction I bet you can guess what it is. 
 HOWEVER. I loved the world of the Fae. I've never read a book about faeries before and I found it very engrossing. I want to read more faerie books! I liked Feyre SO much more than Celeana in the Throne of Glass. Feyre did make really, really stupid decisions time and time again, but at least she was likable while she made them. The story was also gripping. I was held captive probably partly because of the plot and also partly because of the romance. And hoooo boy was that romance steamy. 
 Like ToG, I think this series has potential. But it could be that I'm trying to force myself onto the Sarah J Maas bandwagon when she's just not for me? I don't know. I liked this book. I think I *could* have loved it but for the things I mentioned, because the world and plot almost made up for that. Those things were great.

This book made me so crabby at the beginning that I put it aside and almost didn't finish it. But in the end I'm glad I saw it through as the most interesting stuff was in the second half. 
 At first I was thinking I'd lost my taste for Card entirely. The three kids at the beginning (Bean & Petra's super bright and super tiny offspring) are setup as one peaceful brother, one violent brother, and an understanding sister stuck in the middle. Sound like Ender's family to anyone else? 
 There doesn't seem to be a lot of respect at first for the giant (their dad) who has been stuck in the cargo hold of the ship since he's now too big to fit anywhere else. (I had a hard time picturing all the sizes in this one and could have used some more clues earlier on.) The kids jockey for dominance and debate killing the giant and the girl whines a lot about not wanting to have her brothers' babies, even if they are supposed to be some sort of new species. Ugh. It's kinda like unhappy kids on their way to a really lame vacation picking on each other in the backseat of the station wagon with the dad too tired to stop it. 
 Little reference is made to what eventually happened with Petra and the normal babies left on earth. I know with the space travel they all would have died long ago, but to those on the ship it wouldn't have been so long, ya know? I liked Bean and Petra in the rest of the Shadow books and was sad to see it come to this. Also, the kids' names have been changed and are rehashes of other characters in the past books. What's up with that, Card? 
 Anyway, eventually the Bean family spaceship finds and intercepts a ship at a planet. It's a Formic (aka bugger) ship. It may or may not be empty. The planet below may or may not be habitable. What do you think will happen next? Bean extrapolates his plan for the kids to take over the ship and the world and to start their new species with the help of standalone wombs. (See, sis, no worries. The bros didn't want to make babies with you anyway.) At this point I paused, thinking that since the giant kindly told me what would happen next, why would I need to keep reading? 
 Picked it up again as the kids started exploring the ship, trying to figure out what had happened to it. I was half hoping the one murderous little sprout would get eaten by the "rabs" but alas, one of the other mini-beans made some knockout gas that doesn't affect small annoying children. 
 The stuff on the ship was the most interesting as Card has a good imagination and made the buggers' stuff seem really alien. I liked reading about them and was even kinda rooting for the obnoxious brats to help the poor creatures who were left. 
 In the end, there's hope for all the little legumes but not so much for the ginormous one. And there's some room left for the buggers also, as well as a chance for Ender to re-enter the story. I would probably be more excited about this if I had 1)read past Ender's Game to the sequels instead of just skipping to the Shadow books and/or 2)liked this extension of the story more.

I received this book from the author--I was surprised that it was an actual hardcover and not an ARC. I had wanted to read it because while the book's description was compelling, it also sounded very disturbing and possibly way too graphic for my library's YA collection--so I was happy to receive a free copy in order to review it without spending the money and possibly deciding not to put it in the collection. 
 This book is marketed as a YA title (the imprint is SimonSaysTEEN). While the story is about a girl who has been kidnapped and sexually (as well as emotionally & physically) abused for five years, it is not graphic. Most of the abuse scenes are left more to the imagination. That being said, there are references to rape and oral sex, as well as heavy profanity (that's just in the first 20 pages or so). 
 The story was gripping--I had to finish it before I went to bed, I couldn't stand not knowing the outcome. It was a fast enough read that this was possible. I think it is important, because it addresses the issue of how people think the victim of a crime like this should just run away or somehow get help, but how the abuse prevents them emotionally from being able to do so. It was disturbing and I would recommend it for older high school students. 
 I haven't read anything else by Elizabeth Scott, but I did order Bloom recently and hopefully I will get a chance to read it--I have a feeling that this book was a departure from her usual fare (which I have heard described as being similar to Sarah Dessen).

I must admit that I was hating this book when the twist was first introduced. I thought the twist was stupid and my eyes hurt from me rolling them so hard while trying to finish this book. I'm so glad that I kept reading. The final Coda is what moved this from a two star to a three star rating. The lessons of embracing your life and not wasting your opportunities was presented well by Samantha.

The last 150-200 pages were brilliant; interesting, arresting, a little challenging and utterly compelling. Clarke has created a wonderfully evocative and detailed world that feels as complete as any fantasy world ever written but it all feels rather flat (except for those last 150-200 pages). 
 Mr Norrell is a fussy, egotistical and rather priggish, and Jonathon, while initially more likeable, soon revels himself to be arrogant, egotistical and a bit of an asshole. I didn't really enjoy either character, and actively disliked them by the end, Strange even more than Norrell because his attitude to his wife is so awful. 
 The faux Victorian language and spelling was irritating although I did enjoy the sly humour. I must confess that I am completely flummoxed by the comparisons to Austen. Austen writes clear, clean prose and this writing is anything but. As for the footnotes, well sometimes they were helpful/funny/interesting but they became increasingly irrelevant, as if inserted just because hadn't been one for a while. The worst of the writing style was that it kept story at a distance and kept me - the reader - from being part of the world. 
 But while the story, the language and the main characters disappointed, the world and the side characters kept my interest. I would have gladly had less of Strange & Norrel and more of Stephen Black, Mrs Pole, Arabella Strange, Childermass and Viniculus; I longed (still long) to know more about them rather than more about the main characters. And would have loved more of John Uskglass. 
 My favourite parts were the initial acts of magic in the cathedral and the ships made of rain and those last couple of a hundred pages. 
 The 4 stars are for the world Clarke has created and for the side characters.

This seemed to go on way longer than 320 pages. Started a little too stilted and factual for me (I know it was needed, but still), but it got better as it went on and added more human elements to the story. Some of the side stories were completely a waste of time (I'm looking at your Ra al Ghul), but they started to find better footing with combing this sense of urgency with chaos and personal stories.

This is a very different Stephen King book. I do think it's much longer than it needs to be, but it is still an excellent book. Very different time travel "rules", and very interesting ones. It's also not a horror novel despite it's categorization as horror on many web sites and book stores. This is solely because it's a Stephen King book, not because of it's content. I'd say it's more of a Sci-Fi/Mystery/Suspense book, with some romance in there as well. It's a great book, I'd give it a 4.5/5 but Goodreads only goes in whole stars (why they don't go in halves is beyond me). This book definitely satisfied my craving for a great time travel read. I'd recommend this book to anyone, even if you hate King you'd like it. I think this is one of his more literary works, in many ways too.

Joshua Foer was covering the US memory championship, when he found out that the feats the mental athletes were doing could be done by anyone serious enough at giving it a go. He studied the fascinating techniques, practiced rigorously, and with the help of his mental gurus, won the event the very next year. 
 I wouldn't call this a self-help book, as the main focus is on the author's journey and not on how one can improve one's memory. This book contains a fair amount of science, psychology and neuroscience mainly, and therefore gives the reader a comprehensive education on the memory techniques. 
 Foer has a wonderful writing style, easy to understand, and exceptionally honest. I will definitely look out for more work by him in the future.

 This is the first book by Nalini Singh that isn't paranormal. I read 2 of her previous paranormal books and loved them. She has a way of telling a story that pulls you so far into it that you forget about everything around you. Who hasn't had a fantasy about a rock star? Well most of us have. Zachary Fox is the picture perfect rock star with the tattooed and pierced body that fantasies are made of. From the moment Molly and he lay eyes on each other their minds start to wander. Fox wants Molly and that is all that he can think about. She thinks it's one night and that she's just giving into a dream a crazy moment of lust. Fox knows differently and he is set on a quest to steal and capture her heart. 
 "Open for me, baby." He bit her lower lip as she'd bitten his, caught her startled whimper in a kiss. "I want in." 
 I fell hard for this honest, loyal and dirty talking rocker. I haven't enjoyed a rocker like this in a long time. He swept me away with his sweet talking and erotic persuasions. Zachary Fox had a way of making Molly feel like the most precious person in the world. 
 They had obstacles to overcome and these weren't the every day ordinary ones that most couples need to go through. Molly hates the lime light and Fox lives in it. His entire being screams PROTECT and that is what he is determined to do. 
 Touch by touch, kiss by kiss, he gentled her, seduced her, the raw sexual possessiveness he always felt when it came to Molly tempered by a vicious protectiveness. 
 I was captivated by every page and lost in the romance. I can't wait for the next installment and there are so many different stories to be told that I am going to be counting the days.

 I've been a fan of Nalini's for so long and yet I was so afraid to begin this series. I'm in love with Nalini's Psy/ changeling series and I thought if I read and hated this series then I'd stop reading any book by the author. But none of this thankfully happened. I can't say that I loved this series as much as I do the Psy/ Changeling or the Rock Kiss series but I definitely enjoyed it. 
 I've read a few books about angels and every book describes them differently. Nalini's angels were no different. Nalini has created this whole new world. Her angels were unique. They were human-like, very sexual creatures but they were also dark and sometimes even evil, they ruled the world. The angels were at the very top of the pyramid, while the vampires followed and at the bottom were the humans. If you actually consider it, it makes sense. The angels were always high up the sky, the humans were down to the earth while the vampires were in between. Not quite humans but not angels either. 
 Raphael, the archangel of New York, is in need of the best vampire hunter. So, who's better to do the job than Elena, a hunter with the ability to sense vampires? I really liked Elena. She was independent, strong, a survivor but above everything else she had a great sense of humor. She was very dedicated to her job and determined to see it through. On the other hand, Raphael was ruthless and as a member of the Cadre (a group of ten powerful archangels who ruled the world) he had to be. When he met Elena for the first time, he wasn't sure whether to keep her or kill her. But somehow he fell for her. All Raphael saw in Elena was a strong warrior and a woman who hid behind a mask. A mask that Raphael wanted to remove. He wanted to see the real Elena, the person she never let anyone see. 
 I loved this couple. 
 The author managed to take their attraction to the next level and show us what they can become. They were so many twists and turns and the end was an unexpected one. I never saw it coming. Thankfully the second book is already out so we don't have to wait to see what's going to happen next. 
 Totally recommended!

The fourth book in this series wraps up all the main plot points from the previous books. It looks like there is a fifth book after this one, but it appears to follow a minor character who was only introduced in this (4th) book, and even then only mentioned very occasionally. It felt like a pretty obvious set up to have an excuse to write something else set in this world, and I don't find myself terribly compelled to go on after this point. 
 I mentioned in my previous reviews that the first book seemed like kind of retrograde fantasy with a few interesting elements, the second showed some more action and promise, and then the third dropped off in interest. This fourth book puts me solidly back in my first position that this is pretty retrograde series overall. This is what I mean by that: 
 1. As I was reading, it gradually dawned on my that this series, which was published in 2006/2007, has zero people of color in it. Zero. Not just among the main characters, but in the entire country that Shinn has created. Every random shopkeeper, soldier, farmer, bar patron, you name it, was some shade of white (if they were described at all). I think of this as a phenomenon in fantasy that was common (and unremarkable) when I was much younger, reading stuff from the 1960s, 70s, and 80s, but even by the 90s, it was relatively common to have at least a token acknowledgement that non-white people might exist in a fantasy world, although they were rarely more than background or side characters, even then. In contrast, this setting seems like straight-up white-washed faux medieval Europe, which is a historically inaccurate view of that time/place in any event. 
 2. I was also struck by the odd social/sexual politics and customs. Odd, in that they were not internally consistent. On the surface, the society is set up as, again, a fairly standard/retrograde patriarchal feudal fantasy society, where women are not supposed to be alone with men they are not married/related to, and are supposed to be virgins until marriage, and no one is supposed to marry outside their class. In practice, our main characters pay lip service to these ideas, professing to be shocked that they are considering traveling in mixed company and having sex outside of marriage and then marrying people of wildly different social spheres (or applauding themselves for being so "different" and open-minded about these things), but in reality, it doesn't seem to disquiet them for very long or much at all. And more than this - there seem to be no actual social repercussions for breaking these supposed taboos at all. It's one thing for a character to break with strong social taboos and then face the consequences as a result - that can make for a very compelling story. But to be told that "oh, gosh, this will be so shocking to society, but I'll do it anyway" and then have there be zero social repercussions at all is just...not good storytelling. There's no real tension where there's no real danger. Even in the most extreme mismatched pairing, (view spoiler)[when the common mystic Cammon and the princess-then-queen of the country decide they want to get married, people say "we are shocked! Impossible!" for about 5 minutes, and then calmly decide that, well, it is possible, we'll just lie and say that the orphaned Cammon was secretly a bastard minor noble all along. Problem solved. (hide spoiler)] It just doesn't seem internally realistic for everyone to be so casual about it. 
 3. The writing was sometimes clunky, doing the kind of thing that was parodied in the movie "Anchorman" at one point, where Will Ferrell narrates along as he and his friends are laughing at a dumb joke together: 
 Ron Burgundy: We are laughing and we are very good friends. Good buddies sharing a special moment... 
 Brian Fantana: Don't say anything Ron and just let it happen. 
 Ron Burgundy: ...laughing and enjoying our friendship, and someday we'll look back on this with much fondness. 
 Brian Fantana: Yeah, yeah. 
 Only all the characters in this book are Ron Burgundy, telling each other and themselves how very special their friendship is, and laughing for hours over things that are not really even funny (in the middle of battles!) And then all of the plot and tension in the last few chapters relied on the characters falling for obvious tricks and forgetting half the things they spent all the books up until now learning before triumphing with no major losses to anyone they really care about (i.e. anyone in the group of main characters - they kill off a few outsiders who are theoretically-but-not-really close to our insiders, and neither the main characters' grief for friends or relief for their own survival seem all that intense or real). 
 So, to sum up, it was OK, as far as retrograde fantasy goes, but there's so much better and more interesting stuff out there. I wouldn't invest the time in this series if you haven't already.

 Dai Sijie tells a literary jewel of story, just a short book, well worth the effort. I remember what the young men I grew up were like. I loved their ideas and their brawn. I remember who I was a young woman and what path to empowerment I took. All so usual at one level. All so dangerous at this time and place in which the story is told.

I had a weird experience with this book. When I was reading it I would be frustrated with the characters or bored with the story. However, when I stopped reading the book and just thought about it - I liked it way more. I found the characters to be complex, the mysteries engaging, and a strong promise for book 2. Like I said, it was a weird experience, but I did end up enjoying the book. 
 Things I Liked 
 : 
 -Main Characters. Now, I didn't actually like either Charlotte or James. In fact, I found them both to be rather unlikeable - but that's the reason I liked them. They were flawed and damaged and arrogant and selfish. Charlotte is manipulative and secretive about her past and her methods. She doesn't trust easily and only slowly begins to accept James in her life. James is rash and quick to anger. He has idealized Charlotte from a young age and seen her as a figure - not a person. Though I didn't personally connect with the characters, I can clearly see their personalities and growth through the story. 
 -Mysteries. I really loved that the cases Charlotte and James were working on were recreations of famous Sherlock stories. Though I have never read any of Sir Conan Doyle's stories, I felt more connected to the story because there was a life force from the Sherlock mythology. I also thought each reveal was believable and built the story, adding tension and character development. (view spoiler)[Their relatives involvement in bringing them together really showed their families personalities and their relationships to their resective family members (James' father and Charlotte's uncle). Nurse Bryony's ultimate reveal was satisfying and further highlighted Charlotte as a character, giving her a backstory and showing her manipulative and resourceful nature (hide spoiler)]. 
 -Sequel. I am actually really excited for the next instalment in the series. Primarily because I LOVED everything about August Moriarty. He might have been the only character I connected to in the story and he was only mentioned by others. I can't wait to get more background information on him, his family, his relationship with Charlotte, and what he's been doing since the public fallout. 
 -Epilogue. I loved that the epilogue was Charlotte making noted on Watson's version of the story (which we just read). I actually found Charlotte to be likeable and have personality. I felt more connected to her here, than in the rest of the story. I hope we get more from her POV in the next one. 
 Things I Didn't Like 
 : 
 -Long Chapters. This is a personal preference. I find that books with longer chapters (more than 15 pages consistently) usually feel LONG to me. They can get a bit draggy and boring. This was probably the BIGGEST reason I was bored when I was actually reading the story. 
 -Character Elevation. I felt like Charlotte Holmes wasn't particularly gifted or exceptional, everyone else around her was just kind of inferior or bumbling. The other students and even the police officers working the cases didn't seem like they were that competent or capable, simply to contrast with Charlotte's superior genius. I found the secondary characters to be a bit flat and forgettable, because they were used to mainly prop up Charlotte. 
 This was a truly unique reading experience for me. With the story ending on a high note, I am hopeful that I will like The Last of August even better and have a more consistent experience while reading the story.

 "Baby girl, if that's all it takes to make you swoon, then you just wait 'til you see what I do with my hands." 
 Man, did I enjoy this book. It was full of innuendos, smoking hot sexy times, great dialogue, intriguing character, some CRAZY action and plot twists. I loved Ana Belle. I could relate to her dissatisfaction in small-town life. Until, you know, the walking-talking sex god Elijah walked through the door to her pie shop and shook things up. Elijah. Just wow. Hot. Awkward. Sexy. Dangerous. Far from perfect, but somehow wonderful because of that. He and Ana had fantastic chemistry right off the bat and I just knew it was only a matter of time before they gave in and got it on. I was right. And when they did? Day-yum. It was more than just lust, though. I cheered for them to get together and wanted to yell when they (inevitably) found a way to screw it up. 
 "With all the shit I've done, the hurt I've caused people, some I barely knew and others I knew too well, for all the worthless hours I've spent wandering through this mess I call a life, looking at this girl before me - who is so perfect and innocent, and downright trusting in every way - I know that, somewhere along the line, I must have done something right for her to want to let me in." 
 Don't get me wrong, this book isn't all sweet and hot sexy times. The plot took some pretty interesting - and serious - twists that I didn't expect at ALL. Some scenes were downright disturbing and more than a little uncomfortable, but somehow I still found myself unable to look away. The author's writing, my connection to the characters and the twists and turns kept me fully engaged until the end. Even then, it left me wanting more. 
 "Come on, Ana, would it really kill you to go out with Mr I'm So Freaking Hot Even My Mother Would Sell Her Soul to Get a Piece of This? Would it kill you to have a little fun for once?" 
 Welcome to Sugartown does a really good job portraying life in a small town: the gossip, the scandals and the characters who were just quirky enough to be interesting without being unbelievable. Ana's best friend Holly was always good for a laugh or advice. Sometimes both. Her little brother Sammy was absolutely freaking adorable and I loved the relationship between them. Ana's dad is a trip, too. I loved him. It was particularly fun to read his interactions with Elijah. Not all the characters were good. You'll find that out for yourself. 
 If I'm being honest, this book wasn't AT ALL what I was expecting, but that is far from a bad thing. I thought it would be a sexy, fluffy story with a HEA. It was sexy. I'm not telling you anything about the ending. :) But damn, the action in this book. Mind-blowing. It was exhausting - in the best way possible! I laughed, I swooned, I cried, I freaked the hell out. 
 What a ride. I can't wait to see what happens in the next book, Enjoy Your Stay. It's Holly's story. :)
