Originally, I gave this book 5 stars after marathoning it in one day & loving it so much. After consideration and further discussion, I'm dropping my rating to 4 stars. 
 I did really love Flame In The Mist. The story was entertaining, had some thrilling scenes, and was all around really enjoyable. As always, I love Renee Adhieh's writing. She has the most delectable prose that is unlike any other YA author out there. Once you get used to it, it's very easy to get lost in her flowery writing style, and I always love that about her books. 
 I really loved Mariko as a main character. I especially liked how she's not a typical Mary Sue - she's an inexperienced fighter and struggles through training, like you would expect someone who has lived a privileged life to do. Though that does not mean she is not a TOTAL BADASS and definitely makes her way through tough moments her own way. I think she's an admirable character and I really enjoyed her story arc. 
 Despite how much I enjoyed reading the story, I quickly realized I retained almost NOTHING about this world and where the storyline is going. Could it be because I read it so fast? Absolutely. But, this is a recurring theme with Rene Adhieh's books for me. I love them so so much in the moment as I'm reading, and the next day I can't remember any specific details. I don't know if I can fully attribute that lack of retention to my fast reading because it's happened to me with her past two books, physical and audiobook formats. I think it's just a case of her ABSOLUTELY BEAUTIFUL WRITING STYLE not always matching up with me as a reader. 
 I also wasn't a huge fan of the romance. While I do enjoy the way the characters come to complement each other, I think their development was rushed. It felt as if there was no chemistry, and then nothing but chemistry after a certain course of events that just felt unnatural. I would have loved some more time for these characters to grow together as opposed to going from strangers/enemies to acquaintances to immediately lovers. 
 I feel similarly about the magic system, it was presented to in the beginning, but the ending EXPLODED with magic. I initially went into this story expecting a fictionalized feudal Japan and came out with a bit of a fantasy headache. I felt like I didn't have enough time to grasp how the magic system works because all of the rules/future of the magic system was super saturated in the last handful of chapters. I wish it had been more spread out so that it could have been more easily comprehendible. More magic throughout the story also would have probably sped up a few of the slower scenes. 
 I also want to add a TW for suicide in the first 5 pages of the book. Given, it is a ritualistic suicide which some may view as different, but it's still very graphic and could be potentially triggering. Honestly, you could skip to page 6 or so and you would not have missed anything from the story at all. 
 Despite my small critiques, I really did enjoy this story. It was fun, enjoyable and had interesting character dynamics with beautiful writing. I would recommend it, but I do think you need to be in the mood for a high fantasy with lavish writing & stay really focused throughout. All in all, I'm anticipating book two!

 It looks like this book and I had a major case of "babe, it's not you, it's me". As a result, I feel like a complete asshat. 
 The thing is, I started losing my interest in the series somewhere in the middle of Clockwork Prince. No wonder then that I slowly lost my anticipation of its sequel. It got so out of hand that I had to force myself to read Clockwork Princess. And maybe that was the biggest mistake of all. Because I felt absolutely nothing while reading it. No happiness at the happy ending, no sorrow at heartbreaks, no adrenaline rush at action. Nothing. 
 Worst of all, I lost my love for these wonderful characters. I didn't care about Tessa and her heartache. I didn't care about Jem and his health. And I most definitely didn't care about Mortmain and his evil plans. I just didn't. I tried, but the only characters that I managed to truly enjoy are the Lightwormwood brothers and Magnus. And, of course, Will, because apparently no matter how I feel about the book itself, I just keep on unconditionally loving this broken boy. His sufferings most definitely tugged at my heart, even if not as much as I expected. And surprisingly, it wasn't about the romance at all. It was about Will himself, and that I loved. But even he was not enough. 
 Maybe my problem is that this book is not heartbreaking enough. I'm not kidding. Maybe my heart is an icicle, but I just did not feel a thing when Jem "died". Maybe because it was pretty damn obvious that Jem did not, in fact, die. Because there is just no way Clare would kill one of her major characters, one so loved by everyone, one who has already suffered enough. There's just no way. So I felt nothing and I continue feeling nothing. Except major disappointment. 
 Only during the epilogue did the tears come. When I saw the date, I was expecting a bittersweet meeting. What I got was Will's life. Naturally, I wept. Like a baby. And I do not know it those tears were ones of happiness or of sorrow. I'm glad Will and Tessa did not get an eternal HEA. Although I wish Tessa had aged and died together with Will, I knew she wouldn't and that's okay. I was prepared for Will's death, Tessa's immortality and Jem's joyless future. Left like this, it would've made a beautiful, sad ending. I'm a sucker for those. But then Jem happened and I became so damn frustrated. I felt and still feel cheated. Clare tortured us with this complicated love triangle for three books only to give Tessa both boys. Miss Gray didn't even have to make a choice, the boys, in a way, did it for her. So excuse me if I'm a bit bitter that Will died and Jem has a whole future ahead of him. I just can't help myself. But even if I wasn't in love with Will, I would've still felt cheated. It has nothing to do with the fact that I feel like Jem and Tessa don't click as lovers, that they see the world differently, that they don't belong together, that Jem deserves someone different, better. No, the thing is, the ending is too perfect. There is no sacrifice. Tessa enjoyed a beautful life with Will and now she has a beautiful future with Jem ahead of her. I understand that she loves them both and I accept it. I think "Tessa and her boys" is a very beautiful thing. But just because it is, it doesn't mean it has to end on a perfectly happy note. No HEA can happen without sacrifices, and in this book, I see none. And this is why I can't help wishing the book ended with the last chapter and the epilogue consisted of only a bittersweet hopeless reunion of old friends, with no mention of the past. I just can't. 
 Somewhere deep inside, I see that this is a wonderful conclusion to a wonderful series. But it just did not work for me. Who knows, maybe one day, I'll give it another try and fall in love. Maybe... Someday...

 When Lainey Taylor takes a job at Starr Media, she finds herself with a rule book filled with things that absolutely aren't allowed. Among those though are don't call your boss the Antichrist and definitely don't fall for him no matter how hot he may be. But the more Lainey gets to know Brogan Starr, the more she finds herself struggling to follow his many rules. But with Lainey needing to help support her sick mom she knows that she needs to do whatever it takes to keep her job, even if that means fighting the growing connection between her and Brogan. 
 I liked Brogan and Lainey a lot. They had so much chemistry right away, and I really enjoyed their banter. This story was witty and funny, and I loved the interactions between these two. Brogan had a ton of rules and at first he was sort of hard to warm up to, but as the story continued I really liked seeing how he and Lainey got to know one another and grew closer. I liked Lainey and I really admired her taking care of her mother. You could tell how close they were and I liked that family was so important to her. While I liked these two, I will say that I did wish that there had more steam. There was a lot of chemistry and tension, yet there wasn't a lot of follow through. 
 The other thing that I will say is that while this one was witty and funny, there were times that it came off a bit choppy. It sort of took me out of the story and romance a bit, even though I did enjoy most of it. I think that this book is one that NA and Contemporary fans will enjoy though, and if you are enjoy rom-coms, this is definitely one worth checking out. I know I will read more from Jennifer Blackwood in the future, and I look forward to seeing what she writes next.

4.5 "Feminist Mulan in Japan" Stars 
 This book is ridiculously good. I almost hate how good it is because I knew it'd end at some point and I just didn't want it to. I don't want to let go of the characters. I want them with me. Right now. Stay, please. 
 The first thing I'll say about this is: Renee Ahdieh can't disappoint. She simply doesn't have it in her to write a crappy book that isn't made out of beautiful words and likable characters and OTP material. After having read three books by her set in two completely different worlds, I can officially say she's made it to my favorite authors' list. 
 Like The Wrath & The Dawn and its sequel, Renee Ahdieh created a story that balances history and fantasy, which that hint of magic and retelling that makes everything much more interesting. 
 Flame in the Mist is Mulan is Feudal Japan (and in case you didn't know, Mulan was Chinese and no, they're NOT interchangeable) with a strong feminist arc and a romance that will melt you heart, you soul and your pants. It'll melt everything because it's OTP material. More on that later. 
 Our Mulan-inspired character is Mariko. I love Mariko. I loved Mariko from moment on, so I don't know how to say anything other than Mariko kicks ass and Mariko and I are friends, so don't speak ill of her in front of me. Mariko holds power in her hands and her mind. She's smart AF and she knows it. But Mariko doesn't know what to do with her power--not until the end of the book, and that's Mariko's journey. A beautiful, touching, make-you-heart-happy journey. 
 Mariko's feminist arc is beautiful because it goes from her resenting being a woman to embracing that. As the daughter of a powerful, but somewhat cruel man who only wants more influence, she was promised to the son of the Emperor. What did Mariko do when her father "sold" her as a possession to marry a man she didn't know without even asking her for it? Oh, she found a cute boy and slept with him because her body belonged to her. 
 I love Mariko. 
 When she's traveling to the imperial city, Mariko is attacked. Everyone dies but her. She hears her attackers saying they were sent to eliminate her and she identifies them as the Black Clan, a group of bandits. Mariko escapes and comes up with a plan: she'll pretend to be a boy, infiltrate the Black Clan and find out who ordered her murder. Then, she'll eliminate the Black Clan and reappear with the truth. I told you, Mariko is kickass. 
 The things Mariko learn about herself and about embracing the power of being who she is warmed my heart. It was a beautiful journey. She learned so much from the beginning to the end of this book that I was proud of her. Proud of how far she came. Proud of how much she learned. 
 Mariko also learned things about other people. She learned things about her family and the life she used to live, but mostly, she learned things about the people she vowed to destroy, about the members of the Black Clan. When she joined them in her quest for truth and vengeance, Mariko didn't expect to find in the Black Clan her true home. True friends. People she'd learn to care about. She definitely didn't expect to find love. 
 I won't talk about the love part just yet, because once I start I doubt I'll be able to stop. 
 So, let me talk about friends and the Black Clan. 
 I've come to learn something about myself as a reader: a book will become special to me if it has a group of well-developed friends as part of the story. And the Black Clan was that beyond everything else. Those people didn't have to stay together. They weren't forced there. They weren't born in that circumstance. They chose to get together and fight for something they believed in. They chose to form the Black Clan and protect each other. So I chose to love them for it. 
 I absolutely fell in love with all of them. From strong, mysterious, loyal Ranmaru to creepy, funny Ren. From smart, warm and fatherly Yoshi to brave, kickass, feminist, perfect Okami. Yes, perfect, because how else would you explain him? Even Yumi, a minor character, enchanted me. 
 I enjoyed every scene with those boys. Every time they looked after each other, teased each other and even mocked each other. Like Mariko, I wanted to be a part of the Black Clan. And I got really emotional when she finally became one of them. 
 Speaking of side characters, I also liked Mariko's twin. I loved how complex he was portrayed. A brother who would stop at nothing to find his missing sister, but who was also blind in his loyalty to the emperor. A young man who loved a servant, but was afraid of standing up to his own father even though he knew the old man wasn't walking down the right path. 
 Having said that, while I enjoyed getting to know him, I wished there had been less chapters from his POV. And less chapters following the emperor, his wife and his concubine. But that's mostly because I couldn't get enough of Mariko, Okami and the Black Clan. 
 Oh, Okami, my love. *sighs* 
 Fair warning, this is when I start talking about the romance, so there'll be a lot of fangirling happening from now on. 
 The romance was everything. Everything. No, I mean it. 
 In the beginning, I wasn't sure if my heart would betray me. I thought the love interest would be one because of how the story started (with a boy seeing his honorable dead executed), but my heart had been claimed by another. Then, fortunately, Renee Ahdieh didn't make me suffer. She gave me exactly what I was hoping for. She gave me Mariko and Okami. She gave me life. 
 OTP life, which, in case you don't know, is the best kind of life for a shipper heart. 
 Mariko and Okami started with the kind of hate-to-love trope that kills me and brings me back to life. It makes me swoon and smile and tear up because I can't handle the feels. The angst was there. The want, the desire, the sexiness. I love how Renee Ahdieh isn't afraid to write sexy in YA in a tasteful way. 
 Okami held my heart in his fists from the moment he stepped into the story, long hair loose. He continued to charm me with his smart words, his loyalty, his strength. He intrigued me with his mysterious powers. He had me cheering when he showed himself as a true feminist. He completely destroyed me when he gave in to his feelings for her. 
 I simply couldn't look at any other boy as a love interest for Mariko. I wanted those two together. I waited for it to happen and I savored every single moment of it. It was, like I said, everything. 
 "To me, you are magic." 
 So, thank you, Renee. Thank you for giving me another OTP. 
 Thank you for giving me a story about girls learning how powerful we are, about how much we can change the world by being us and by being strong and by loving, hurting and fighting. I love this book. I truly love this book.

 The reason this book wasn't rated as high by as many people is because, to be honest, this book didn't have much substance. There was a plot, and a romance side plot, but that really was it. 
 I understand that not all realistic fiction books must be emotional. But I felt like this would should have been; not just to copy On the Jellicoe Road, but because Dan (the love interest) actually hinted at an emotional life. A depressed mother, absent father, beaten up sister, and more. He had character. If he had been the narrator, this book could have taken a whole new turn. 
 I also thought all of the issues were sort of straight in-and-out. There was an issue, there was dwelling on that issue, and then it was resolved. No complications whatsoever. 
 I guess you could call this a guilty pleasure. Even with these issues, I still rated it four stars because I thoroughly enjoyed it. (And I really did like Dan. Sigh...)

The seventh son of a seventh son is highly regarded for his magical ability. When Lan is born as a double-seven, there is rejoicing until his twin sister Eff follows as the thirteenth child--a birthplace regarded as evil. Eff's life is miserable as she is tormented by children and persecuted by adults. To give her a chance at a better life, Eff's family moves to the wild frontier where no one needs to know that she is a thirteenth child, as the adult children choose to remain behind. 
 An unexpected twist on the magical fantasy sets Eff's family in an alternate United States in the pioneering years of the Wild West. Growing up in what was the Wild West, I especially enjoyed the take on pioneer magic. 
 When I looked over reviews to see what I wanted to read next, I was surprised to see that Thirteenth Child was embroiled in a controversy: Wrede hadn't included Indians in her alternate take. This offended a great many people, but I imagine they would have been offended no matter how she had handled the situation. If she had included Indians as adversaries, that would have been problematic; if she had included them as part of the communities, there would be screams of revisionist history. As far as I'm concerned, my Indian ancestors wouldn't be offended by being omitted from a fictional account of an alternate universe that featured steam dragons, mirror bugs, and magic.

Perhaps I'm not smart enough for this book. Or perhaps I shouldn't have read it right after reading and loving The Gate. I found myself waiting for things to happen that never did. Also, the shifts from one section to another of the narrative were too abrupt; characters who were very important in one section vanish and take their issues with them, with no resolution or continuation. I found neither of the main characters very sympathetic. The narrator with his immature hero-worship of the man he calls "Sensei" (teacher, in the "disciple" sense of the word)through which he projects all sorts of character traits on someone who doesn't posess them or want his admiration; the "Sensei" character who is withdrawn and cold, due to a past traumatic experience that controls his life and isolates him from everyone around him, and particularly those who love him best. Both men have very low opinions of women in general--our intelligence, capabilities and empathy if any always seem to come as a surprise to these two. Typical of the early 20th century Japanese male of the upper classes, perhaps. Admirable, not really, in men who are educated and supposedly intelligent. Both have had the best opportunities available in their place and time for higher education; neither of them really uses those opportunities to advantage to grow as people or participate in the world around them, preferring to spend (waste) time and resources doing desultory "reading". Somehow they manage to live their entire lives without doing a single day's work, in spite of being done out of large parts of their inherited income by others. Well, as the old jazz tune says, "Nice work if you can get it." Both men see themselves as victims, but seem incapable of doing anything for themselves except to take the easy way out of any given situation. Neither one seems to learn anything from their experiences, in spite of their much-vaunted intellectualism and introspection. They don't spend time thinking, so much as obsessing on their wrongs, real or percieved. Sensei's "trauma" could have been avoided if he had simply spoken out, been honest with himself and others; he prefers to temporise, and later to speak of his supposedly dear friend as a "devil", conveniently forgetting that said friend hadn't asked for any of the "help" that the young Sensei thrust upon him. Sensei sees himself as "rescuing" this friend, but the rescue ends very badly. 
 The Introduction, though plagued as usual with spoilers for anyone who hasn't read the book yet, does provide enough context to lend understanding to the story, but I found the much-vaunted structure dissatisfying. The "story within a story" given by Sensei's letter simply comes to an abrupt end, without any reaction on the part of the narrator or winding up of the tale. Yes, I know, life is like that. There's always some unfinished business. But I had expected something rather more complete and satisfying. 
 One thing I can say for Soseki, the texture of each of his novels is totally different from any of the others, though he deals with many of the same themes: emotional immaturity and isolation, misfits, the overwhelming need for a "perfect" affection that never comes (because affection comes from other, fallible, human beings). The essential paranoia, paralysis and mistrust of both main characters is well drawn and realistic, but it doesn't make for pleasant reading. Kokoro may be about "the heart" but it's a torn heart. 
 Kokoro is a cautionary tale about the meaning of true integrity and honesty, with oneself as well as with others, and about not projecting our expectations onto those around us.

WARNING>>>UNHIDDEN SPOILERS AND SIGNIFICANT DOG-LOVER CRAZINESS AHEAD 
 The story is about a dog, who is so much more than a dog that he deserves a different pronoun than I would normally grace a canine: Who. The Art of Racing in the Rain by Garth Stein focuses around the narration of Enzo, who will tell you up front, that he is a "philosopher with a nearly human soul." Good thing Stein uses "nearly" from the get-go. This choice word justifies the enormous amount of teeter-tottering in this book on whether Enzo is a regular dog, or an advanced dog. 
 First off, lest you think otherwise, I love dogs. But the reason I did not enjoy this book had everything to do with the portrayal of an advanced dog. Ask anyone who knows me personally, and they will tell you that I love my dogs like they are my children. Because they are like my kids, key word being like. Dogs are not human beings. 
 I'm sure I'm not the first to say this, but I can only attribute this book's success to our secret desire that animals are really akin to humans, that they have the capacity to think deep philosophical thoughts like Enzo does. I hate to break it to you, they do not. And I'm perfectly comfortable with that. It's not that I think animals incapable of understanding and affection. From experience I know that dogs can be highly intelligent and even perceptive (see the recent mini-documentary on YouTube entitled A Boy and His Dog), but not to the degree of this fictional character Enzo. 
 And that's all well and good. In this story, the narrator is a dog, and he also is just like a human. I read fantasy -- I can go with it. That point was not contentious for me. What I disliked, and ruined the story for me, was the utter self-loathing Enzo has about being a dog, for having no thumbs. Enzo insists at the fore that he can control his more primal dog side, but he doesn't always. When he is stressed, he acts like a dog, and he hates himself for it. 
 I devoured the squirrel. I had to do it. I missed Eve so much I couldn't be a human anymore and feel the pain that humans feel. I had to be an animal again. I devoured, I gorged, I gulped, I did all the things I shouldn't have done. My trying to live to human standards had done nothing for Eve; I ate the squirrel for Eve. 
 Stein doesn't waste any time trying to explain dog behavior in realistic terms. He makes sure we know that Enzo hates that part of what he is. And if that wasn't bad enough, Enzo also allows humans more leeway than he does himself. In some context for the following quote, one of Enzo's owners leaves him alone for three days without food or water. What he does while she is gone is pee and poop so politely in one spot, and also destroy a whole lot of dolls and stuffed animals. His master, and best companion, treats him thus: 
 Denny was so angry that his anger filled up the entire room, the entire house. Nothing was as large as Denny's anger. He reared up and roared, and with his great hand, he struck me on the side of the head. I toppled over with a yelp, hunkering as close to the ground as possible. 'Bad dog!' he bellowed and he raised his hand to hit me again. 
 I'm sorry, but now I have lost all compassion for Denny. His thoughtless wife leaves his dog ALONE WITH NO FOOD OR WATER and he hits the dog with the intent to continue because he destroyed replaceable stuff? And what does Enzo do but completely forgive his owner like nothing ever happened because it wasn't truly him, he was acting out. I'm sorry, are you worthy of this dog? Because my entire being says no. 
 One day before my husband and I were on our way to the store, we tied up the kitchen trash bag to take to the bin in our garage. Upon returning home, there was trash everywhere in our house, containers and plastic licked clean, unopened yet expired yogurts devoured whole. In our rush to get out the door, we had forgotten to take the bag with us to the garage. My husband was peeved at first, but I could only laugh. It was totally our fault. We set our dogs up in these situations. You wouldn't expect a child to resist cookies on a platter in front of them would you? What dog could resist wickedly smelling leftovers and wrappers in a neatly tied package sitting out on the floor just for them? 
 Do not treat your dog like a person, and do not put the same expectations on them as you would a human being. Treat them like a dog, and you will understand them a whole lot better. Expect them to behave like an adult, able to avoid temptation because it's "wrong," and you will be disappointed time and again. You are responsible for their well-being, own up to it and train them better if there is a trait you don't like. Too lazy to train them? Then stop punishing them when they do something you deem wrong. Most of the time I bet it is something you did that set them up to fail (like leaving garbage on the floor or locking them alone without nourishment for three days). 
 I will let that self-righteous dog owner rant be over, now. 
 Back to the book. I wanted to see the true dog side explained, but what we are delivered is human thoughts implanted on an unreliable narrator who is limited in his scope. Enzo is physically a dog, so he can't go to the courtroom when his owner is on trial for accused rape of a minor (I will go absolutely off-the-walls if I have to remark on how false rape was lumped on as part of this contrived plot), or any scene where dogs cannot go. This means Enzo does a lot of telling, relaying what he heard to us in a informational dump sort of way. And, to boot, the deus ex machina reigns supreme in this book. A man who feels complete sympathy for Denny offers him his dream job, helping him escape from crushing destitution. You know, because that is a fairly realistic portrayal of life. 
 The novel's main message is somewhere along the lines of, If you keep going forward, you will get what you want/everything will work out. Enzo is able to express this metaphorically through F1 racing. Besides racing not appealing to me, I'm also highly cynical and a realist (check the tag name at the bottom). I'll just leave this point as, I don't really buy into that. There were aspects that I enjoyed -- like every time Enzo acts like a dog without feeling guilty about it, and when he takes a dump on a nice rug because the people deserved it. 
 And one final thought on this book. I knew going in I was going to cry. Why? Because it is set up very early on that the dog is old and going to die soon. So, when I reached the end, and he died, you bet I cried. I don't know if you can tell by this point, but I LOVE my dogs. I get misty eyed thinking about them not being around one day. I really wanted to read about a real dog, with real doggy thoughts (I feel ridiculous even typing that), not a dog with a severe case of disliking who he is. I like my dogs to be dog-like, running like mad, and wrestling and barking and carefree. Not trying to determine how life works or the meaning of our existence. Keep it simple, dogs. I like you just the way you are.

 Before I get into this review I feel it is necessary for everyone to take a moment and admire that cover. It's not very intricate, it is actually quite simple, but I love it all the same. Okay, moving on to what is behind the cover. I am so monumentally glad that I finally picked this book up, because it is absolutely without a doubt worth your time. The story has a pretty original feel to it even if it does contain some of the elements typically found in a Young Adult novel. 
 One thing I truly loved about this book is the writing style. Storm is written in the third person, which is something I find to be few and far between lately. So this style was not only refreshing but truly enjoyable. I was not stuck in one characters head for the entire book and I liked that a lot. The reader will see events going on in numerous places simultaneously and see how different characters react to these events. It was the perfect way to portray the events that occur in Storm and it gave depth to the story that first person perspectives sometimes lack. 
 Our heroine Becca is a feisty one, so naturally I could appreciate her. Becca has had it rough the last couple of weeks due to some vicious rumors circulating. However, I admire her because she does her best to not let it bother her and even when it does she tries not to let others see that. It showed that she was strong just by simply enduring the ridicule. She is also strong because she does not back down. The reader can pick this up in the first chapter. Becca gets involved in the whole elemental mess when she saves Chris Merrick from two guys who were attacking him. 
 Speaking of Chris, he is a character that it is easy to love, even if you want to smack him at times. Chris is the kind of character that goes from being incredibly sweet to protective to funny to a complete jerk. However, Chris has his reasons and he genuinely thought he was doing the right thing, so I couldn't stay too mad at him. Chris is the kind of character that comes through when you need him to the most. Along with Chris we have his brothers Gabriel, Nick, and Michael. Each and every one has something to offer to the book with their distinct personalities. I also need to mention Hunter, who I was never a big fan of, but he even brought something to the storyline. 
 The paranormal aspect to this book is something that has not been overdone. These brothers can control elements; each has the ability to control a different one. This was a twist, for me at least. It was unlike anything I have ever read and it was simply cool to see the brothers in action. However, I liked that it was not safe and the author made that abundantly clear. It very easy to lose control of the elements and then things can get out of hand. Naturally things do get out of hand and that is what makes for this wonderful story. 
 There was one thing that drove me bananas. At one point, shortly after Becca meets the Merrick brothers and learns the truth about their abilities, someone pops in and makes her doubt what she has been told. Now the person who tells her is not trustworthy, or at least I wouldn't consider them trustworthy. However, for some reason Becca decides to believe this person. For someone who has been the victim of lies and rumors, I just thought she was a bit quick to jump to conclusions. It was not something I would normally attribute to a character that has dealt with those kinds of circumstances. 
 Despite my one tiny grumble, I would highly recommend Storm. It is the perfect book for paranormal fans who are looking to get away from all the vampires and werewolves. It is fast paced and has twists and turns throughout. It will keep you engrossed up until the very last page.

As a fan of the apocalyptic genre, I'm drawn to titles like this book in much the same way a zombie is drawn to the living. Paul Jones spins a decent end of civilisation as we know it tale, but with a nice twist. There are no zombies in this story, no rampant screaming crowds, or constant masses of blood and gore. Instead the focus centres on a journalist, Emily Baxter, a New York journalist, who seems unaffected by the mysterious red rain that infects the rest of the population. 
 The story has good and not so good points, and I'm reluctant to say bad points as I couldn't really see anything that stuck out as bad, or enough to leave me with a bad feeling after reading. 
 First, the good stuff: 
 Paul Jones captures the loneliness of a city suddenly devoid of human life incredibly well. The humdrum noise of daily activity we take for granted, from crowds of commuters to the drone of vehicles plodding the streets. The eerie silence is unsettling. The story isn't rushed either, Paul Jones takes his time to give the reader insights into Emily's life; her thoughts, feelings and emotions come across well. 
 The unique twist isn't exactly original, in that despite there being aliens, they're presented in a different more subtle way, rather than an obvious "conquer the planet and destroy all life" plan, these new life forms inhabit Earth without a plan or a hive mind driving their actions. They behave as any other organism entering a new ecosystem might, like fungus or moss growing in new places, exploiting a new previously unvisited habitat. 
 The pace was pretty good, enough to keep me turning the page, although I would have preferred to see the tense/action scenes broken up a little more instead of overly long paragraphs. An interesting thing is that there's very little dialogue, and you might expect more given the nature of the plot. However, this doesn't hinder the story or slow it down as the visuals are enough to keep the story ticking along at a decent rate. 
 The scenes in total darkness were gripping, as were the noises, that tap-tap-tap following Emily up the stair well was unnerving to say the least, as was the elevator doors pinging open and shut. The description of the aliens was spot on, just enough for my imagination to fill in the blanks. And the alien trees gave me enough information to ask more questions than there going to be answers for, I quite enjoyed that. 
 Now for the not so good stuff: 
 First thing that struck me as odd (few spoilers here folks!) is the death of Emily's boyfriend. Whilst obviously traumatic, she seemed to cope with it remarkably well. And when the aliens begin to emerge she gives more thought to the baby in the apartment above changing into something alien than her boyfriends own metamorphosis. 
 On the subject of the bike and supplies. I don't read reviews before choosing a book but I do have a quick read before writing my own review, and I have to agree with a couple of other comments about the sheer amount of supplies Emily gathers. At times it felt like severe overkill and I'm sure the story wouldn't suffer if the vast shopping list was considerably reduced. The reader didn't need to know every single item Emily put in her panniers. 
 The bike issue niggled me because it felt wrong. Emily comes across as pretty resourceful, but not that much. It didn't feel right for a New York journalist to suddenly turn into a doomsday prepper and survivalist, though I guess in that situation some people can surprise by giving such forward planning a lot of thought. 
 I suspect the author has read his share of apocalypse stories and is keen to give his own slant on what survival means and how his character reacts. The problem is that the reader is told all humans have vanished. There's been very little widespread looting of grocery stores that you might see in a zombie plot for example. Therefore Emily, also knowing there's plenty of food left, should know that stocking up is a good idea but not to the extent of overloading her bike with food and water to last months. 
 I felt the plot gears grinding with the bike issue and since Emily couldn't drive she figured the safest way out of the city would be on a bike. And the rest of plot hinged somewhat on that fact. I question her reaction to not want to try and learn how to drive. Surely it wouldn't take more than a day to figure out the basics and travel safely out of the city in a car? It's not like she had anything better to do in those first few days is it? It really isn't that difficult to learn, certainly not for a character who comes across as intelligent as Emily. 
 At least she could have attempted it and come up against a barrier like being scared after crashing a car or clogged streets leaving no room to navigate a route out of the city. It felt too easy for her to simply decide not to bother in order for the rest of the story to be played out on the basis of a bike journey leading the reader through the alien forest etc. 
 From her background story the reader knows that Emily had once learnt how to use fire arms. Nothing wrong with that. And it made sense for her to equip herself with a gun. However, it felt a little unrealistic that she was able to master the use of the shotgun so proficiently given her limited training. Again the plot gears were put in place in order for the showdown with the creatures in the forest to carry any sense of tenseness and action. 
 Whilst I found Emily's plan to trek north to find the scientists kind of plausible, I felt her decision was made a little too easily. Not much thought, if any as far as I can remember, was given to travelling to find her parents. I can't recall if they had already died or not. 
 In the first few days of the event taking place, Emily makes a list of things to do, but it seemed to take her forever to start searching the internet for survivors. These days I'd have thought this would be one of the first things to do. After all wouldn't a journalist make best use of the tools of trade? 
 Conclusion: 
 A thoroughly enjoyable read, and whilst I may point out some niggling issues they're in no way bad points at all. The arrival of Thor is a huge relief. Despite Emily's contact with the scientists, I was hoping she'd find another human along the way at some point. Thor's description and mannerisms are well portrayed, and as with any furry companion in such stories I hope he doesn't come to a bad end. 
 My over riding issue with this story is that it wasn't long enough, which is both a good and bad thing. I wanted more. Good thing. I didn't get it. Bad thing. But I am pleased to see there is a follow up. So, yay! A good thing. I'm looking forward to that. I read this book in 3 sittings, and was reluctant to put it down and go to sleep. 
 Paul Jones has given me some much needed respect for writers who publish eBooks. I've read plenty of junk from writers who shouldn't write at all, and honestly I was started to wonder if I'd ever find a writer who had the ability to tell a good story, put together a decent plot, create good characters and not have page after page of spelling, punctuation and grammatical errors. 
 Extinction Point isn't perfect, but what it lacks in niggling little things it more than makes up for it in the best way - being a page turner.

It has been awhile since I have felt this passionate about a book. I love my romances with the steamy smex, but I also am a huge fan of urban fantasy. I love the altered worlds, kick ass heroines, the sexual tension, and great action. Three Days to Dead has it all, written so well there were times I had to make myself take a deep breath so I could get through the page. I laughed out loud and at one point I had to read with one eye open because of the awful things that were being done. This book also brought back my bad habit of sneaking peeks ahead. Yes, I'm a peeker and it is this book's fault. There were two occasions where I absolutely had to take a quick look to make sure a certain character was coming back. The reason I had to look is because Kelly Meding doesn't write a perfect world. Innocents die, bad things happen to characters you like, Evy doesn't always succeed in what she is trying to do. So as the reader, you are left on the edge of your seat without being able to guess what the outcome is going to be. Although the world has supernatural rules, it felt real. Bad things happen, and that makes a great book. 
 There are about two hundred things I want to talk about, but I knew nothing of this book when I started it and I think it greatly enhanced my reading experience, so I am not going to go heavy into the plot. The book has one of the best beginnings I have read this year. Evy opens her eyes and she is in a morgue and in a different body, but she has retained her mind and memories - at least all of her memories except for the past few days - those detailing how and why she died. After scanning the charts, she discovers her new name is Challice. Desperate for clothes, money and transportation, she goes to Challice's address. Her plans become somewhat mottled when she runs into Alex, Challice's roommate who discovered Challice dead and identified her at the morgue. Think he is a bit freaked out to see her now? 
 The world Evy lives in is full of magic, although most people don't even realize it. Most are oblivious because Evy has spent the past four years working in a secret organization. She is a bounty hunter that protects the innocent humans from the dregs - otherwise known as the vampires, goblins, shifters, etc. She works in what is called a triad, with two other team members. All triads have a handler that send them out on their mission. It can be a very violent job, and Evy has lived quite a hard life, but she likes it. Her triad is elite with more kills than any other. She likes to think of imaginative ways to kill the rogue supernaturals, she lives for that high. 
 When Evy awakes in the morgue, she knows someone must have performed a spell to put her spirit in another body. But she has no idea who, nor why. She can't remember the past couple of days. She has no idea how or why she died. The last of her memories are of her teammates being killed, her being blamed for it, and innocent shifters being slaughtered. 
 The only person that is alive that she can trust is her handler, Wyatt. After literally running into him and convincing him that it is actually her in another's body, they must figure out who set up Evy to die. Wyatt knows Evy was captured and tortured, but why is the big question. The twist is, the spell performed to bring Evy back lasts only three days. She has 72 hours to live, to bring justice to those murdered, and to try to remember the past few days before she is dead, forever. 
 There were a few times where I thought Evy may have forgotten she only had three days to live, where she seemed a little too nonchalant about the situation. However, the desperation starts to seep into her as the clock ticks and towards the end it becomes a full out race. To put it plain and simple, Evy is kind of bitchy but that is not necessarily a deterrent for liking her character. She doesn't take crap from anyone, and to say she is enraged that someone set her up, is an understatement. The funny thing is, she isn't really that upset that she is dead. She is more angry that innocent shifters that were trying to protect her were killed. She is angry that she was deceived by people she thought were trustworthy. And she is angry that Wyatt has been dragged into this. Ultimately, I found her to be extremely unselfish and because of that, she becomes a very likable heroine. 
 In these three days, Evy has a monumental task of figuring out how she dies and why, and coming to terms with her feelings for Wyatt. Wyatt and her have a history, and as her memories come back from her final days, although her physical body is healed, her emotional memories are dark, and hurtful. Her relationship with Wyatt is very complex and this definitely becomes Evy's weakness. Wyatt tells Evy three simple words, and with everything going on in her life, these three words become the most difficult for her to deal with: 
 "You've got me" 
 She does. He is her base. He is not only her mentor, her friend, but he becomes so much more. And if you look from his perspective, he loves this girl that he only has three days left with. He has to be strong for her, be the rock, give her space when her emotions topple. For as strong as she is, he holds it together for them.

 5 Favorite Books on Goodreads - 2016 
 The School for Good and Evil

 Asking for It 
 This book is a tough read but masterfully done. It's about two beautiful yet broken people doing relationship in the most healthy way I've ever seen in fiction. More an emerging adult bildungsroman than erotica, BDSM is gestalt therapy in this amazing novel. 
 Ember 
 It takes so much skill to cover a classic song, remake an iconic movie, or rewrite a fairy tale. 
 Instead of cinders, there are red hot embers in this erotic interpretation of the Cinderella story. I'd almost call it a deconstruction.. If there really were magic, what would she really wish for? What are the consequences of being undeniably a Prince Charming? 
 Regardless, it's thoroughly enjoyable and highly recommended. 
 More Than Magic 
 More than Magic is contemporary romance with a dash of classic 90s thriller at its heart. 
 What makes it stand out is the setting of the Appalachian mountains, a setting that is a character in and of itself. It's enough to make a born & bred city girl want to hike the 1,200+ mile Appalachian trail to experience a bit of the magic for myself! 
 Never Sweeter 
 There are many bully to lover romances, but none like this. 
 This book takes it's time with the characters, allowing an understandably fragile relationship to develop convincingly in a very satisfying way. With a less noble hero guided by a less talented author, the heroine's flower petal heart would seem a spoiled brown mess. Instead we get an artfully pressed bloom, the scent and bright colors linger & warm the senses. 
 It's honesty and care make it a refreshing, palatable representative of the New Adult genre.

While I have never actually been a fan of Dan Brown's Langdon series I have read them all out the sheer enjoyment of picking out the flaws. It may be a petty thing to do, but Brown got paid his nickel for the book and I get some enjoyment from it. Books 1 -4 were bad, Origins was horrible. 
 i won't provide a synopsis for this book, if you want to know what happens read it and suffer as I have. I will comment on a few of the aspects that I really had a hard time with:

 1. Robert Langdon is absolutely the most inconsistent and vapid protagonist I have ever read. The man supposedly is a swimmer and a scholar yet he repeatedly out maneuvers assassins, police and military in all throughout this series. This book has him actually performing a WWE-style dropkick on an armed assassin then quite literally backflipping across a 3 foot wide 100 foot drop of spiral staircase, while essentially suplexing the aforementioned assassin to his death. All this while wearing his formal tails and Mickey Mouse watch. Is he a Harvard professor with tenure and a Harris Tweed suit or Jackie Chan. Make up your mind Mr. Brown. Horrible and unbelievable. 
 2. The plot is incredibly formulaic, but so has every one of the novels since Angel & Demons. Long preamble where Langdon is in a city full of art history for some mysterious or unknown reason. He meets an exceptionally beautiful and intelligent woman who conveniently has incredibly important significance to the entire upcoming plot. There is a crazed or deluded religious fanatical assassin or agency after Langdon who instead of simply just killing him, allow him just enough time to find a secret passage or decipher a text. 
 3. There was noticeable advertising in this novel that wasn't present before. Lots of brand names dropped that felt unnecessary. Tesla and FedEx are the prime one, but there are more. Also the little clip art doodles and images are very obvious and distracting. Did I really need a 3/4 page graph of the evolution of man skulls? 
 4. The long-winded descriptions of every single piece of art or architecture in Spain was exceptionally boring this time. I know it is Brown's niche to go into details about this stuff, but the 100 page intro of modern art before the actual plot started seemed a bit excessive. Honestly, the better part of the first 100 pages had nothing to do with the upcoming plot, except to vaguely- and I do mean vaguely- introduce some of the secondary characters. 
 5. There was a disappointingly few riddles in this book. Basically there was the 47 character password hidden in a poem. Other than that a few obscure references to Winston Churchill and a painting done by an AI. Some of the revelations that Langdom comes to seem to be very thin and stretched, even for a character with his handy eidetic memory and years of skill. Hint: "&" typed in a different font... 
 6. The red herring was incredibly obvious. I won't say what it was. I trust if you have read anything by Brown before you will notice it. 
 7. The length of this book was unrealistic. I like long books, I have read longer and shorter. The good ones fill the pages with character and plot. They make the words count and the paragraphs all come together to tell the story. This one seems like Brown was trying to meet a minimum word count. There were parts where it was laborious to read and there was little to no importance. Again I will reference the 100 page modern art descriptions, also the epilogue was just plain unnecessary. 
 8. The female lead was less important than ever. She contributed nothing other than her relationship to both Julian and Edmond. Her role seems to be to feign indecision about whether to marry Julian, repeat everything that Langdon says and to conveniently know some unknowable facet of a private billionaire's personal life when it suits the plot. WHY WOULD KIRSH GIVE HER OF ALL PEOPLE A CLUE TO THE PASSWORD TO THE SUPERCOMPUTER THAT HOUSED HIS GREATEST ACCOMPLISHMENT? Honestly she was arm-candy who facilitated a venue. 
 9. The murders of the religious leaders. One was cursory the other way too detailed for the significance to the plot. I guess it added to the Herring bit I alluded to above, but not much. 
 10. I think Langdon has ADHD. Seriously no matter the situation he gets distracted by something. Is there a man with a gun chasing you? Oh look that 18th century architectural anomaly needs explaining. The entire secret plot of the whole novel is about to be revealed in less than 30 seconds? Better check out that weird test tube on the dark shelf in the corner and explain what it is, directly before the goddamn revelation is revealed 2 pages later......!!!!!! (sorry Brown's writing style has really irritated me this time) 
 (hide spoiler)] 
 On a positive note there was a tiny bit of character development on Mr Langdon's part. After thousands of pages we now know he not only wears Harris Tweed and a Mickey Mouse watch, he has also a fucking coat of tails and a Mickey Mouse watch. Seriously Dan Brown, why the fuck would he be wearing tails, even if he grabbed the wrong suit by mistake in his rush, he easily could have gone and bought or rented a tux in Spain so he didn't look like an imbecile. 
 While I do normally enjoy roasting these books, there was no actual enjoyment of in this one. Perhaps this is where I throw in the towel on this pass-time. This one felt like work to read, which is the exact opposite of why I enjoy reading.

 Stanton and Jenny are childhood best friends. They're also childhood sweethearts, and have been in each other's lives more than anyone else they know - other than family, of course. Being each other's first best friends, first loves, first everythings, they end up having their first child together who they name Presley. 
 Stanton, at this point, is my love. His support and genuine love for Jenny was so lovely to follow along with and I just wanted one of him for myself - because, let's be honest, don't we wish we had a few book boyfriends. But anyways, he's admitted to wanting to drop all of his future plans and marry the girl of his dreams, sealing his perfect family together with a happy little bow (or a diamond ring on Jenny's finger - whichever sounds nicer right?) But Jenny will not be the reason that he stays behind and forgets the dreams he's worked so hard to prepare for. She loves Stanton and his decision but she wants to see him grow into the incredible man she knows he is, so after a nice talking to, and a lot of refusal, she gets him to agree on going to law school and doing everything he's dreamed of doing. 
 2 months after Presley was born he's out of their small town, and into the big city. After pledging, he has made his home within one of the fraternities on campus, and one of his brothers, who later ends up being his best friend, convinces him that he should be taking advantage of this open relationship that he and Jenny have agreed on. Stanton is missing his daughter's first birthday, so anything sounds better than sitting in his dorm room sulking at this point. With a little convincing, he's out the door and has had his first lay since Jenny, and also the first girl he's been with that wasn't Jenny. 
 So all this is going down and he ends up going home to visit, and comes clean to Jenny - who is heartbroken because she never really wanted to know in the first place. 
 - At this point, I would just like to point out that OPEN RELATIONSHIPS DON'T REALLY HELP ANYONE, LET'S BE REAL. But to each their own. If that's what you think you can handle, then who am I to tell you not to try it out? But I'm too emotional for that shit. Anyways - 
 Fast forward 10 years later, Presley is 11, Jenny is at home taking care of hurt, but has found a job within the local hospital, and Stanton is still doing his think in another state. He's now part of a law firm and his partner Sofia is sitting alongside him in the court room. You find out that she is his partner in more than one way with their smutty little note passing. That's right, Sofia is his "one of the guys" girlfriends who is nothing but a friend, who is a girl, who he also has sex with regularly. 
 Then, like we all knew was coming, Jenny sends Stanton an invitation to her wedding. WEDDING????? BUT STANTON WAS COMING HOM- no. Jenny had every right to move on. She'd only been dating James Dean (I know right? What a name) for a little bit, but when you know.. you know. (I'm 20, what do I really know). Stanton obviously loses his mind, packs up what he can, and is on his way home to get his girl back with no real plan but that's what Sofia is for. That's right, he brought back his friend with benefits who has feelings for him, poor girl, and wants her to help him keep his head on straight so he can get Jenny back. 
 So all this time Sofia never really understood how close Stanton and Jenny were, but in a matter of a few hours is smacked in the face with it and can do nothing much but smile and accept it - not that she wants to. 
 I love Emma Chase, and I love her writing, but my annoyance with Stanton's character kind of pushed this one into my only going to read once pile of books. One of my favourite parts was seeing Drew show up again. (If you don't know who Drew is, please read her books. I'll leave you to a nice surprise). 
 Stanton expected way too much from both girls. He went home to get his girl back, after leaving her for the bigger half of almost 11 years, and expected her to be there waiting when he returned - IF he returned. That was something that bugged me more than I can tell you. And THEN WHILE HE'S HOME TRYING TO GET JENNY BACK, HE CONTINUES TO HAVE SEX WITH SOFIA. Honestly, I saw a shit show ready to be released, but fortunately nothing too bad happened. 
 Honestly, I was just bothered by that whole scenario and it kind of ruined the book as a whole for me. The girls were wonderful and Presley was adorable, but I wanted to kick Stanton's ass half of the time. 
 Let me know if you felt the same and please don't hate me if you disagree with what I felt completely

 Review: I must say that I honestly didn't know what to expect when I started reading this book. I knew I loved Trisha's writing from what I read in her short story Unveiled, but this was my first time reading a steampunk novel. But as soon as I started reading, all my worries flew away. Destiny's Fire grabbed me on page 1. Literally, and if you've read the book, you know why! Immediately in the story we meet Dez and the triplets - Jace, Lana, and Nick. We learn about their world in 2040 where the Narcolym are coming to start mingling with the Shythe. No one really likes this idea, especially Jace. Dez and the triplets train for a battle they feel will be inevitable. 
 As I mentioned, steampunk is new to me and I thought I would be completely confused by the terms. I should have factored in Trisha's fabulousness. She made it exciting! She completely described this foreign world to me in a way that helped me truly visualize it. It all made sense! 
 Dez was incredible. She was such a strong character and she really cared about her friends. This is all tested when Reese, a Narcolym, pushes his way into the picture. Jace and Reese do not get along, at all! Due to all of this conflict, Jace finally stars showing his feelings for Dez and she tries to see what is stronger, her feelings for her best friend or her best friend's new enemy. Drama! Reese is more than he seems though, and he shows Dez a part of her past that she didn't know existed. 
 Jace or Reese, Jace or Reese. It's like picking cake or ice cream. Trisha created the type of love triangle I adore. I could see the pull for each guy and they both did have a downside. No one was perfect and between Jace's temper and Reese's secrets, I could see the conflict Dez had between them. 
 The plot and action Trisha created in this story was also an unexpected turn. There was a great back-story, a lot of manipulation, and a powerful Council that both races had to deal with. I felt like I was thrown headfirst into this intense battle and I loved every minute of it! Dealing with all the craziness really helped Dez grow as a person. It was as if she was 3 years older by the end of the book. 
 I was very satisfied with how everything wrapped up but I gotta have book 2 soon!! Who can resist reading more of a wonderful story with a sizzling romantic love triangle? Not me! 
 Destiny's Fire gave me a taste of something new and I'm hooked! I can't wait to read more from Trisha Wolfe and see where she takes these characters next. 
 Recommended: Paranormal/steampunk readers or anyone who wants a taste of steampunk. Also, anyone who just loves a lot of drama, action, and hotness.

Given the whole girl-goes-to-assassin-school vibe of the blurb, I had originally thought this book might be YA. You'd think the "assassin" part of "assassin school" would have tipped me off. Still, by the end of the first chapter I knew very well that Nevernight wouldn't be for younger readers. Jay Kristoff doesn't pull his punches. 
 The book is violent, and doesn't make any excuses for that. There are sex scenes that are just shy of erotica in their level of detail, though I never found them gratuitous. And in the opening chapter we actually get both, the scene flipping back and forward in time between a sex scene and a stabbing, highlighting the, erm, rather obvious parallels. 
 There are a lot of flashbacks in Nevernight, especially early in the book. The main storyline picks up when Mia is 16 and seeking to be accepted into the Red Church (said assassin school), but we get glimpses into the formative events of her past. I found the flashbacks interesting, but they were presented in italics to differentiate them from the main story, and I found them harder to read as a result (physically harder; large blocks of italics are painful. Maybe I'm just getting old!). 
 The other stylistic quirks of Nevernight are the use of footnotes, where the narrator provides extra detail about the world -- generally amusing anecdotes and trivia that don't really have a place in the main story but give a glimpse into the narrator's personality. The other quirk is that we don't actually know who the narrator is, just that it's not Mia herself. (My money is on her shadow companion, Mister Kindly.) 
 There is magic in the world of Nevernight, which is a lush combination of Ancient Rome and slightly less ancient Venice, but it's the sort of magic that imposes a cost on the user. I really liked that as a mechanic; it stopped the various magic-users from being completely overpowered and silly. 
 As far as the characters go, Mia is -- unsurprisingly -- hard as nails. But there's an empathetic side to her that is rather out of place in a school of murderers, and as a result she makes herself some good friends and snags a sort-of boyfriend among the other novices. Of course, there's the obligatory mean girl (who has a very good reason for hating Mia, so she's not your typical shallow archetype) and the Snape-like teacher (though he makes Snape look soft and cuddly). And the classroom politics and scheming tends to wind up with people dead. 
 Story-wise I won't say too much, except to say that there's a plot twist I didn't see coming and all sorts of other awesomeness in there. I did have one head-scratching moment over Mia's apparent inability to remember one particular event in her past -- I wasn't clear on the reasons for that, though maybe I missed something. 
 I'd recommend this book for people who like their fantasy gritty, their prose rich with metaphor and their heroines stabby. 4.5 stars.

 Why can't I be happy to be alive instead of afraid of living. 
 Sadly, this is the world that we live in. Morgan lives in fear each day. Trapped in the prison of both her mind and her apartment, she can't even muscle up the courage to step outside. All because of that one faithful day. That one day at school where everything changed. A student came in with a gun. 
 We've all seen the stories on the news and one of the first things that rums through my mind is 'those poor people'. Well here, Reichardt gives us a glimpse of what happens after. How do people rebuild after their world is shattered? Can they rebuild? Can they survive? 
 This book was hard to read in some ways because there were a lot of times where I just wanted to shake Morgan. To wake her up from this stupor that she's been living in for months. But then I would pause and remember what she went through or the author would throw in another memory of that day that had me reassessing my opinion of her. Everyone deals in their own way. Morgan constantly saw how other people who were also there that day were able to move on and continue living, but she just couldn't. All because of one secret that she was holding onto. You know that old saying secrets kill? Well, this one was slowly killing her. 
 It turned out I wasn't dying on the outside. I was only dying on the inside, where nobody could see. 
 Luckily she had people in her corner who wanted to help. Her mother, brother, therapist, and the new boy next door. Her brother was the cutest thing in the world and all he wanted was for his sister to come see him in his school play. A little request that most would think nothing of, but to Morgan it gave her purpose but also crippling fear. I had little issues with the love interest, Evan. He was extremely pushy knowing her situation and would ignore her when things didn't go his way with her which I thought was extremely childish but he was a teenage boy so maybe that's normal? 
 The reason for the three stars was that this book moves extremely slow. At times it was a little boring and the only thing that kept me reading was to find out her secret. But aside from that, I think the mental state was well represented here. I went to an author signing with Reichardt and she talked a little about the research she did and how she spoke with therapists about the aftermath of this kind of trauma and that shows. So while it was a slow read, it wasn't a bad read.

The first in my online book club challenge books of my list for 2016, I finally got to take The Weird Sisters off my "to-read" list. I've owned the paperback for more than a year, but finally located it in my library's audiobook section, and it was actually nice to have both versions, tracking back and forth, as I enjoyed tracking down the many and various Shakespeare quotes mentioned in this book. Not a surprise, in a book named after a Shakespeare quote, about three sisters, named Rosalind (Rose), Bianca (Bean), and Cordelia (Cordy), the daughters of an esteemed English professor at a small college in an equally small Ohio town. 
 I've read several other books in the past several months featuring sets of three sisters. I adored the sisters of Girl Waits with Gun, and I stare in fascinated horror at the dynamics of the adolescent three sisters in the Flavia de Luce series of books (starting with The Sweetness at the Bottom of the Pie). Sisters are a foreign entity to me, as I'm a middle child between brothers, so I always treat these long descriptions in literature like the setting of a fantasy universe. Who are these strange people and why do they treat each other like that? Oh, how odd. 
 These sisters fall somewhere in the middle of the universe of fictional sisterhood. They all seem to completely embody a stereotype based on their birth order. I feel the closest to oldest daughter Rose, the long suffering martyr who has been taking care of everyone and everything for 33 years now. I think this role was somewhat thrust upon her as their mother was portrayed from their childhood as a flighty bird who gets so lost in a book she would forget to cook dinner for her young children (or forget that she had something on the stove and nearly burn the place down). I'm reminded of that saying "You had one job . . . " 
 Less sympathetic are particularly middle child Bean and somewhat annoying (27 year old) baby Cordy. They do seem rather human, however, and do seem to have interesting lives and conversations. I loved how much this whole family loved to read. And not just The Bard, though he is prominent. I loved their comparisons of poorly acted adaptations, and recollections of their shared childhood. 
 Probably the most interesting aspect, and at some points distracting, but I can see why the author took this approach, is the "collective first person" perspective narrator. The narrator is a "we" speaking on behalf of all three daughters collectively. However, the narrator also shifts around to discuss on of the sisters, and then speaks from the perspective of the other two sisters (even when they are not in a scene). This perspective is constant, and until I figured out what was going on, I thought that one of them was mentally ill. But then I realized what was going on and it made sense. By not wanting to give the perspective of just one of these three sisters, the narrator gives us this odd "collective" perspective which allows any two to opine about the third sister, and does so often, and then also have all three share memories and perspectives of their parents and the other characters. 
 Once I got down to it, this was a quick and enjoyable read. It's a freestanding novel, and other than the epilogue, I think we saw pretty much everything they had to offer, but it was a satisfying read. Everything ended up tied up perhaps a little too neatly with a bow, but for a freestanding novel, it is what you'd expect. So, nothing earth shattering, but a nice story with a ton of sister-dynamics and Shakespeare quotes.

One of my bookish resolutions for this year is to read more contemporary books and I'm so happy I started with Awkward. This book is funny, sweet and highly entertaining. In other words, it's my type of contemporary YA book. 
 Mackenzie is a girl with issues. Her father cheated on her mother when Mackenzie was a kid and she blames herself for the divorce and her dad's subsequent abandonment. As a result, she does not trust men, rely on anyone or allow others to pay her way. Ever. Because of an embarrassing and traumatic childhood incident, Mackenzie goes through great lengths to not attract attention in school, to be invisible. 
 Mackenzie's character is, as the title of the book implies, very awkward but she is also very funny. She does not really filter her thoughts, says whatever comes to mind and when she gets nervous, she babbles random facts. Her faux pas are cringe worthy and funny at the same time, especially the entire incident that gets her on YouTube. 
 While fame propels Mackenzie into unfamiliar situations, she tries to handle them with grace and sometimes fails (with hilarious results) but that's a part of the beauty of this book. I love that Mackenzie is a smart girl that prioritizes her grades and her relationship with her family and friends even after she becomes famous. 
 While Awkward is about an ordinary girl who sky rockets to fame overnight, it's also about self-esteem, perception and about Mackenzie getting over her hang-ups stemming from her father leaving the family. There is also a sweet, well developed romance in the book that I absolutely love. 
 While I thought some of the secondary characters, especially Mackenzie's friend Corey, were a bit cliche, it did not take away from the story. Awkward is a funny and modern contemporary romance that will appeal to both teens and adults. While the book appears to be a standalone novel, Invisible, a book set in the same world as Awkward is scheduled to be released next year. I'm looking forward to it.

She would be strong. 
 She would reclaim her rightful throne. 
 She would be Queen. 
 I'm on an emotional rollercoaster that only goes up, my friend. 
 Falling Kingdoms took all my expectations, chewed them up, and then spat them at my feet. It was beautiful, heart-shattering, and astounding in its character and plot development. When people compare this to Game of Thrones, they aren't kidding - it has the same feel, emotion, and drive as those books do. This novel was everything that was promised to me and more, and I couldn't be happier. 
 "Even paradise could become a prison if one had enough time to take notice of the walls." 
 Writing: This book was a stunning compilation of action, romance, tragedy, murder, politics, and general ass-kicking. Falling Kingdoms reminds me so much of The Assassin's Blade inasmuch as it feels like an origin story. These characters change so much throughout the novel so that, in the end, you are left with entirely new voices. They each start so wide-eyed and with a thousand possibilities laid out in front of them - and then, suddenly, they are each brutally introduced into a harsh, cruel world that will consume each of them if they don't become stronger, colder people. I didn't like half of the characters in the beginning, but by that last chapter I'd fallen in love with each of them for a multitude of different reasons. 
 The complexity of this book was astounding, and I have to praise Morgan Rhodes for weaving such a beautiful plot together in such a remarkable way. At the start of this novel I had no idea how it could possibly go anywhere, but all of the sudden I was taken away in a whirlwind of political rivalry, war, and brutality. Looking back at the beginning from where I am now, I can see a sharp contrast in the world the characters begin in and the world they are opened up to by the end. The veil is slowly lifted for each character, and it's heart-breaking each time it happens. 
 "Even in the darkest and most cruel person, there is still a kernel of good. And within the most perfect champion, there is darkness. The question is, will one give in to the dark or the light?" 
 Characters: Falling Kingdoms is a multi-point-of-view novel that follows four characters and takes place in a continent called Mytica, which consists of three kingdoms: Limeros, Paelsia, and Auranos. Our main characters are Cleo, Magnus, Jonas, and Lucia, and - in all honestly - they all need a hug. 
 We have main characters who each walk such a morally-grey line, and anybody who knows me knows that I love my characters ambiguous. We have heroes and heroines both on the moral and immoral sides of this war, and I loved dipping into their different perspectives. We also get to watch as characters fall into the sides of good and evil, and Rhodes does a perfect job at voicing these character's falls from grace. No matter what side a character is on, however, you can't help but want them to achieve their goals - no matter how dark it is. Rhodes knows how to make you love or hate whichever character she chooses, and this subtle manipulation on her part is just one of the many things I love about her writing. 
 Cleo: 
 Cleo starts the book as quite a spoilt, stubborn princess but by the end of Falling Kingdoms she becomes my everything. She is loyal and passionate with a pure heart and rock-solid convictions. By the last chapter, she has the fate of the world on her shoulders and she is determined to rise to the occasion and become what her nation and family needs her to be. Cleo Bellos is the Queen of my heart and I can't wait for her to slay everyone in Rebel Spring. 
 Magnus: 
 Magnus Damora has stolen my soul with his tormented, dark self. I'm so in love with this bucket of sins that it isn't even funny. If I'm going to be honest, the only reason I started reading this series was because of all the praise I've heard about his character. And, my friends, you were all so very right. Magnus is raised by the Blood King, and is expected to be brutal, cold, and calculating - and, by the end of the book, he certainly doesn't disappoint his father on this front. From the very beginning, Magnus is quite a dark character - but he has one thing that keeps him from turning to ice. What happens to him the moment that his tether gets ripped away from him I hear you ask? Well, just be ready to welcome the Prince of Blood. (Also, when do I get Magneo?) 
 Jonas: 
 Oh, my sweet Rebel, I did not like you at first. Jonas took a little while to learn to love, but by the last chapter I found myself grinning like a maniac when I saw him. I can't wait for my troublemaker to stir the new order up - and then promptly destroy it all. If you're a fan of Bellamy Blake from The 100, I think you'll definitely enjoy Jonas as a character. 
 Lucia: 
 Lucia is the character I have the most complicated relationship with inasmuch as I don't feel much of a connection to her. She starts out as an innocent, adorable, albeit naive character, and doesn't really lose this personality throughout the novel. Lucia is manipulated quite well by her father, though, and I can tell in future novels she's going to become extremely powerful. I think in Rebel Springs Lucia's going to have to face the repercussions of her actions and power and I think this is going to be what starts her on her character arc. I'm really hoping I'll start to care for her more in the next book. 
 Also, I have one addition thing I need to cry about: Theon. 
 "Then his heart, now broken into a thousand pieces, slowly began to turn to ice." 
 Overall: Despite its slow start, Falling Kingdoms is a wonderfully crafted novel that is action-packed, heart-stopping, romantic, tragic, and earth-shattering. I recommend this book purely for the characters alone, who aren't wholly good or evil, but simply trying to do what is best for themselves and the people they care for. You will find yourself rooting for people you thought you could never love, and ultimately you will just give up any moral convictions you have and just route for everyone. This book is addictive, tear-jerking, and thrilling. 
 And, once you're done, you can join all of us trashlings in the Magnus Damora Sin Bucket!

 The Accidental Duchess is book 4 in Madeline Hunter's Fairbourne Quartet Series. These are not stand alone books, in my opinion. There is an underlying plot that is in each story that builds until the conclusion. 
 Lydia is an Earl's sister who never wants to get married. Penthurst is a Duke who has been too busy with his duties to want/find a wife. The two have been at odds with each other for years. There is gambling, blackmail and a wedding.
