There's nothing worse than a good story poorly told, unless it's a mostly good story mostly poorly told. I'm not sure which this book is, but either way it's bad news. 
 I've seen Rothfuss and his work ballyhooed for some years now and was really looking forward to the chance to get into the first book of "The Kingkiller Chronicles." By all accounts, it seemed to be a genre-mover, an epochal work that moves the boundaries of fantasy forward while paying homage to the best of what came before. I was intrigued by the promise of a frame narrative, of a famous man mysteriously brought low, and of a creeping, misunderstood, demonic threat. There seemed to be echoes of my loves, "The Wheel of Time" and "A Song of Ice and Fire" in the promised themes of real-world events turning to legend and myth before our eyes and of the meaning made by stories determined by the skewed perspectives of the individuals through whose eyes the stories are experienced. It all sounds so good! 
 Sadly the book does not deliver. Or it only delivers up to a point, which makes it supremely frustrating rather than just bad. 
 First of all, Rothfuss' work needs to come with a trigger warning for grammar-lovers. Seriously, how did this book get past first draft like this? Who is this guy's editor? He or she should be canned immediately. Small but noticeable problems abound, the most frequent being an inconsistent and maddening lack of facility with the conventions of dialogue and tags. "'I think,' he said. 'That you are pretty.'"--that is NEVER RIGHT. (Okay, it's right if your character hesitates and makes the statement into two sentences. But if that's the case you should let us know that that is happening. And I know, Patrick Rothfuss, that you were just doing it wrong, because you did it 50-75% of the time.) 
 Sorry. I feel strongly that writers should know how to write. 
 The next big problem: the main character, Kvothe, is a baaaad example of whatever the male equivalent of a Mary Sue would be called. Let's say a Marvin Sue. (Oh, I guess some people say 'Gary Stu.' I like mine better.) The point is. Kvothe is perfect perfect perfect, he was better at everything as an 8 year old than you will ever be at your one passion in life at age 30, he runs rings around the authorities, and everything bad in his life is inflicted upon him by his enemies and/or his cruel destiny, boo-hoo for Kvothe, but wait, thanks to his daring and cunning, he always gets his way in the end! This human being is SO. DAMN. FRUSTRATING. And yes, he's charming, and occasionally shows some sensitivity, just enough to get you to want to follow his story and feel bad for him. But his entire personality is so much revenge porn for the downtrodden nerdlings of the real world, and, speaking as one of them, I feel like we deserve better than that kind of pandering in our fiction. 
 (To say nothing of Kvothe's supposedly rapier-sharp wit. Seriously, he talks like the picked-on kid in the schoolyard who hasn't yet come up with any better coping mechanisms. But Kvothe is rewarded with gales of laughter at every turn. Sigh.) 
 Then there's this authorial tendency throughout the text to seem tragically holier-than-thou compared to all that *snooty voice* run of the mill fantasy. We're constantly reminded how real life isn't like the stories and Kvothe has to work so much harder than the heroes of his world's folklore and mythology because god damn it there is no God or Narrator who's just going to hand us a win. Rothfuss makes such a point of it that it's obvious we're supposed to perceive Kvothe's story as this somehow rarefied, uber-realistic version of fantasy that, aside from magical metaphysics, abides by real-world laws of cause & effect and rationality and whatnot. At one point, he says something very much like, "I wasn't going to find their plans written out on an accidentally-discarded piece of paper!" 
 A few pages later, enter the convenient plot swineherd. He only travels this remote area once in a while, but he happens to be here at the same time as Our Hero, with not only the info Kvothe's looking for but also additional intelligence to propel the plot forward. 
 Look, I'm all for dissecting fantasy tropes and realism now and then. But don't preach about it and then substitute the deus ex machina you just had your character basically decry as lazy writing with another one that you hope your audience won't notice (or perhaps that you, yourself, did not notice). 
 The sanctimonious attitude gets old, and it extends to Kvothe's rhapsodizing about music, about how non-musicians just can't understand beauty and love and perfection. Oh, God's body, get over yourself, Patrick Rothfuss, you overgrown damaged adolescent. 
 And yeah, now I'm reading book 2. That's the most frustrating part. I almost feel as though Rothfuss structured his story as cynically as possible, knowing that no matter how disagreeable readers find the first volume, they will want the full story on all the hints and clues and intriguing bits seeded throughout. I feel manipulated, and I'm 7% in and grinding my teeth at the same old usage errors, but I'm not stopping. 
 And yet this book is as highly-rated as I've seen anywhere. I don't get it. I honestly don't. I'm usually fine letting people have their taste and enjoy their enjoyment ("I don't want to yuck your yum"), but this book violates the various laws and maxims and pet peeves that I've seen cited by numerous readers complain about OTHER books. (Poorly written--check. Mary Sue--check. Sanctimonious underpinnings--check. Manipulative--check.) And everyone is eating it up. I am saddened. 
 Maybe this will convince you to trash this book: Rothfuss writes "make do" as "make due." Twice. 
 *cheery smile* I hate what you've done to us, Patrick Rothfuss.

 There are two problems with me mentioning what happened in this book and it has something to do with having read it a while ago and wanting to actually put the book out of my mind. What I can say is that the book continues from where the last book finished where the main Christian characters decide to form some elite commando group called the Tribulation Force to go and tell as many people the gospel of Jesus as possible. A noble idea and something that we should consider doing ourselves, except that while the gospel should be first and foremost in our lives, we should learn to balance our relationships with others so that we do not drive them away with them thinking that we are fundamentalist jerks. 
 I have known people that base their relationships purely on their success of sharing the gospel with others. A friend of mine once said that he met somebody in his university course whom he became friends with however as soon as this person discovered he was a Christian, she no longer wanted to have anything to do with him, and this person was a Christian. Others make friends and immediately launch into a gospel presentation, and when that person rejects the presentation, they simply dump that person and move on to a new person. I can understand some of the reasoning of the second person (though not the first) however I have always preferred to develop the friendship alongside my love of Christ so that while they know that I am a Christian, they can also see my Christianity in action and respond appropriately. I have had rabidly anti-Christians come to me and tell me that I am one of the best Christians that they have known, and with that, I feel that my role in their understanding of the gospel has been successful. Remember, sharing our faith does not come down to runs on the board, but rather our living relationships with others, both Christian and non-Christian. 
 Now, I will speak about the idea of pre-millennialism. This is the theory that there is a period in the future (usually the near future) in which all Christians will be taken from the Earth (the rapture) which will herald in a period known as the last days, or the Tribulation. During this period things will go from bad to very bad, namely because the moderating force of Christianity is no longer present. This period usually lasts for seven years, at which time Christ will return and rule for 1000 years. At the end of that thousand years the final battle between God and Satan will be fought with God being the ultimate victor. 
 I used to subscribe to this idea, but not any more as I feel that there are a number of problems with this theology. First of all, where do all the bad people go for the millenium? They suggest that they are still present, only they are under the authority of God no matter how much they hate it. The second is that there is a focus on the rapture that could happen at any time, so we need to be prepared. Graeme Goldsworthy supports my view on this in that whatever the idea of the rapture, we must remember that we could die at anytime, and the fact that I could walk out onto High Street and get hit by a bus sort of makes the idea of the rapture a moot point. Yes, the rapture could occur, but then so could my cold blooded murder. I think we need to be aware of the fact that we all die more than the belief that all Christians could suddenly vanish. If that is the case, at least we get a second chance. There is no second chance where death is involved. 
 Another problem is Jesus' warnings about calculating times and dates. He specifically says that we should avoid trying to pinpoint a time when he is coming. As he says, he will come like a thief in the night, suddenly and unexpected, and that we should actually avoid those people that try to tell us when he is coming, or even pointing to events and saying that these events say that he is coming soon. Of course he is coming soon, he told us that when he was on Earth, and he has been coming soon for the last two thousand years. Time to God is not time to us. God is patient, and to God a thousand years is a day and a day is a thousand years. We should be aware, just like death, Jesus could come at anytime, and there is no actual event that will signal this, beyond his death and resurrection. 
 It is also interesting that in one of the epistles (I cannot remember which one) we are warned against focusing on times and dates as it is distracting. It seems that even as far back as the early church people were caught up with times and dates, whether it be when he would return, or the exact age of the church, or whether God created the world in a literal or figurative seven days. We are told that this is not only irrelevant, it is also very distracting. It takes us away from the centrality of Christ's death and resurrection, and gets us caught up in fringe arguments that have nothing to do with our salvation.

Right from the start, you know ILLUMINAE is going to be a unique book; the storytelling is done completely through documents like emails, online journals, combat reports, surveillance footage, Im's, schematics, and the creepy log of an AI. 
 So basically, our two heroes, Kady and Ezra (Kady's ex), were living pretty boring lives on this mining planet, when suddenly, this company called BeiTech attacks them (the planet, not Kady and Ezra specifically). A few thousand people survive on ships with the help of AIDAN, the AI in charge of the battleship Alexander Ezra is on. Kady is stuck on the Hypatia, a science vessel, while her mother is transferred to the Copernicus, to study a new disease that BeiTech brought with their attack. Suddenly, this disease is more than just a simple problem of quarantine and treat; it's victims are going insane and brutally murdering everyone in their path. And if that's not enough, BeiTech is still after them. Even worse, AIDAN, the AI charged with protecting the fleet, begins having less than protective ideas. 
 I won't lie, I wasn't sure I was going to like this book. I love this kind of Sci-Fi (it's very reminiscent plot-wise of shows like Battlestar Galactica and Firefly), but I wasn't sure I would like the storytelling. It took a little to get into, and the first third or so moved pretty slowly, but once all hell broke loose around the midway point, I couldn't put it down. Everything became so ridiculously intense. I seriously thought everyone was going to die. Or be eaten by psychotic cannibals. Which I guess is still dying. 
 This book is action packed, which was another fascinating thing because of the style of storytelling. 
 There were times, especially early on that I wasn't sure what was going on or which characters were involved in the conversations. This is probably due to the style of storytelling, and it's hard to get a good sense of a character by reading an email. But as the book goes along, you figure out who is important and who maybe isn't as important. They make it pretty clear. 
 [image error] 
 There's an entire section about AIDAN, the AI, and that is creepy as all get out. It's like 2001: A Space Odyssey all over again. I mean, seriously. Destroy that thing now. 
 One of the best parts was that I wasn't expecting the ending. At all. I'll say the same thing for the twists. There were some fantastic twists that completely blindsided me. This book will certainly keep you guessing and on the edge of your seat up until the very last page. 
 I would love to get my hands on a hard copy of this book, since there are some really interesting and gorgeous illustrated pages that the ebook just doesn't do justice. They were still super cool to look at, but I can't wait to see them physically. 
 This book is a fight for survival from page one up until the last chapter. And it's a bleak, ridiculous, terrifying, thrilling ride. There's really even a sweet romance that helps give some humanity to the main characters, and is the real connection that you hold onto during all the killing and insanity and hopelessness. If you're a fan of Sci-Fi, you must get your hands on this book.

I had a hard time rating "Winter" because while I really enjoyed reading it, I also recognize that it has some pretty severe--and hard to forgive--flaws. 
 I started reading this series way back when "Cinder" was first published. At the time I found the concept of a cyborg Cinderella fun and interesting, but wasn't really sure how the rest of the series would shape up. I ended up really liking Meyer's use of a different fairy tale as the frame of each book. The fairy tale aspect is one area where "Winter" continues to shine. Despite the fact that this is the fourth and final book of the series, and that therefore there are a ton of characters and plot threads that need to be tied up, the fairy tale frame still works. The main elements of Snow White are all still recognizably here, pretty cleverly woven into the larger story and re-done for a sci-fi setting. The way that the fairy tale tropes are woven through the entire series is actually my favorite thing about it, and I loved that each book was able to build on the others while still focusing on a particular well known story. 
 "Winter" brings us the end of Cinder's revolution against Queen Levana. We all know that this is what has to happen, and it would be a relatively satisfying final conclusion except for one thing. (view spoiler)[Cinder defeats Levana mainly by revealing her actual un-glamoured appearance to everyone. Levana was permanently disfigured in a pretty horrific attack/accident involving fire when she was a child. Her face is scarred and "ugly" from this incident. We are supposed to be totally behind Cinder showing this off to everyone with the message basically being "look! She's so ugly! You can't possibly want her to be your Queen because she is SO UGLY!!" Levana has done a lot of truly horrific things. She has murdered children. She has enslaved people. She has forced genetic modifications on people. She has engineered a lethal disease and purposely released it on Earth. Cinder could have found proof of any of these things and used it to turn the people against Levana and shake her confidence in her rule, and yet what she finally uses is an attack on Levana's appearance. I'm not really sure what Meyer was trying to do with this, but it comes off as a pretty cheap attack that actually made me more sympathetic of the villain instead of less. (hide spoiler)] 
 I have never been as invested in the romantic relationships in the series as I was in the political storyline, so I was happy to see that romance is not ultimately a main thread in this book. The various couples all have their moments, and while some are more satisfying then others (seriously, when exactly are we supposed to believe that Cress and Thorne became a viable couple?), I was not displeased with how any of them worked out. My major complaint with this book (aside from the previously listed one about Levana) is that although I really liked Winter, she was not nearly as well used as she could be. Winter is an interesting character. She refuses to use her Lunar mind control gift, and in doing so has sacrificed a good portion of her sanity. I spent most of the book waiting for Winter to do something, and for her storyline to pay off, and in the end I was disappointed. Winter doesn't do nearly enough here to justify the book being named for her, or to really do justice to the character herself. In the end we don't even really get to see what happens to Winter, whether she ultimately regains her sanity, or what she chooses to do with her life. I wanted more from the character then we were given. 
 Despite the complaints, I mostly enjoyed "Winter" as a conclusion to the Lunar Chronicles. I think part of this is due to the fact that while I read and enjoyed "Cinder" and "Scarlet" I was only halfway sold on the series. I like it and I respect Meyer's cleverness in adapting these fairy tales for a sci-fi setting, but I was never that heavily invested, and so I think I was able to enjoy this ending without the flaws bothering me all that much. This is a fun YA series that doesn't rely nearly as much on romance as many others. The fairy tale frames are well used, and by the end I was impressed with how nicely all of the stories connected. Overall I think that the Lunar Chronicles are flawed, ambitious, but overall fun. 
 For people who enjoyed this mashing up of traditional fairy tales and science fiction I'd highly recommend Joan Vinge's "The Snow Queen."

From the start she is immune to poison, furthermore she sees the death marques on people apparently signifying how she is supposed to kill her (although that is not a rule (view spoiler)[ see Duval's mother (hide spoiler)] and can communicate with souls of dead people. She gets magic eye-drops that sharpen her senses or even "cast them out". And of course, a magic misericorde, even though only full initiates are supposed to carry them and she is still a mere novice. 
 None of the above is either anchored in the world-building or explained plot-wise, which brings us straight to point 2. 
 2. We are set in medieval Brittany albeit with the magic twist. I have two issues with this setting. Firstly, the historical is medieval in appearance but utterly modern in spirit (take the nationalist thinking about one's 'country' that was born in the 18th century the earliest!). Secondly, the magical is just dumped whenever convenient without any explanations: how is it that the death marques appear? in what way the abbess communicates with Death? what is the role of the Seer? Why is the Death itself concerned with the well-being of one piece of Earth (Brittany) and does not care about another (France)? We know nothing; the world of the novel is sketched only in perfunctory strokes in order to get the ball rolling. 
 3. The rolling ball, i.e. the plot, is, in fact, the strongest point of the book (hence my two stars). The Duchess of Brittany, indeed the whole "country" is in grave danger and therefore our heroine is sent forth on the mission to unveil the conspiracy and protect the young ruler. To complicate things further, she is not sent alone but in a company of a young, handsome male whom the abbess suspects to be the traitor but who appears to be the duchess' staunchest ally. 
 That is the quintessence of what I loathe about certain YA novels: They are very "young" (read shallow and naive) when it comes to character development, world-building, and plot-intricacies (or sometimes plausibility) but extremely "adult" in the romance department. Do not get me wrong, I like (strike that), I relish a good bodice-ripper but not at the expense of everything else and not when a book pretends to be something else than a paranormal historical romance. 
 Surely, there is some potential, some avenues for future development hopefully explored in the next instalments. You can give it a try. I don't think I am ready yet. 
 Edit: I have decided to discontinue the series and this in itself is a disrecommendation.

Killers of the Flower Moon offers a look at Osage Murders and the conspiracy behind what happened, and the process that investigators went through to find out who was behind it all. 
 David Grann takes the reader on a wild ride as her chronicles the events leading up to the first murder of an Osage woman, and the horrendous and mysterious slayings of several others over time. The fact that this is not a part of American consciousness is indicative of the erasure of the histories of Native Americans. With the plot thickening and no solution in sight, J. Edgar Hoover tasks some agents with investigating these mysterious events. Thus, the FBI was born. This is non-fiction that reads just like any great piece of fiction, except the implications have real world consequences. 
 Narratively, the story of the murders and the birth of the FBI reads quite well. It's easy for a reader to get into it, and if you're a fan of true crime, this might do it for you. Grann does more than simply tell the story up until the final reveal; by inserting himself into the narrative and thus the investigation. He searches for closure for the descendants, and makes some startling discoveries. 
 For an exciting true crime story, check out Killers of the Flower Moon.

Though with our heroin I have her a bit of slack in some area where she seemed to change from strong and determined to...well something completely different but a boy and love was involved so I let it slide on the acceptance that estrogen is a hardcore thing that makes the best of us crazy at one time or another. 
 The pacing of the story does jump around, some moments its very slow then right after an event it just ahead. The book covers a full year as his Novice and she has to pass the final test in order to pass and secure her families souls which Grim is holding onto. She learns that this may not have been random and she may have been destined to be part of something much larger. She has questions but the answers seem to be held just out of reach for her. Can she save souls? An entire race? Her family and friends?

IQ "Saba used to say there was a difference between bravery and courage. Bravery was doing something dangerous without thinking. Courage was walking into danger, knowing full well the risks." Willem, pg. 133

I also like this book for avoiding sappiness, it is about a romance but it is not about finding a romance. Rather, the story used the romance as a jumping off point and then expanded to become a story about family and fate vs. luck, acting and double happiness. Willem is 21 and I hope authors continue to focus on college-aged or true 'young adults' because their stories are fascinating and it's more believable when they act independently (as opposed to in actual YA). This is a different kind of romance and travel tale and I am appreciative of that fact, Willem's family has a great backstory and it is a surprisingly complex book.

Especially when the prize of the reality show is being the President's son's prom date! 
 Addy has no desire to participate. She finally agrees when his uncle states that God may have other plan for her. The first thing in her mind is to get kicked out of the show as soon as possible though. She is the ninety-seventh contestant called to get a shot of her being welcomed by First Son to her new house, The Mansion. Addy knows from the information packet that only thirty girls will be chosen from the initial one hundred, and she is determined to be in the majority. 
 Addy marched back to the bus, then walked over to the president's son and shook his hand. "Hello, Jonathon. My name is Addy Davidson. I have no desire to be part of this 'competition,' and I suggest my name be the very first you take off the list." 
 It's a good luck, or bad luck for Addy, that America loves that attitude. They start cheering for Addy and that makes other girls angry. It's also not easy to play difficult in front of the First Son, Jonathon Jackson. It's even harder to speak something smart, or even think a coherent thought when she is looking at his eyes. His perfect teeth. His masculine scent. Jonathon Jackson is the best-looking Addy has ever seen, and it doesn't make anything simpler. 
 Addy will have to stop being stubborn, or she will lose her only friend in this competiton, the president's son who seems attracted to her, and her composure state. She has to learn to accept and forgive the death of her parents, and accept that maybe God has other plan to her... 
 First Date is a light read and I liked it. This is a Christian YA but it's not overly infused with Christian belief. I think you'll enjoy it even if you're not a Christian. Addy is a wonderful character and I really like her. She's really nice and she has strong faith to God. Jonathon is also a loveable character. He's very kind to other girls, and even when Addy is being difficult, Jonathon is nothing but patient. He's a portrait of perfect First Son. Kara may be my favorite character here aside from Jonathon. She's full of life and fun. I won't mind to have her as my bestfriend. However, this book is too fast-paced for me and sometimes I don't quiet grasp the animosity in some scenes in the books. I love the characters and the ending though. Very sweet. 
 This reality show doesn't only change Addy's life, but also her view of things. She learns to forgive and love her enemies. Because love is the answer, not hate. 
 Special recommendation for Christian moms. I really think that this book is a perfect gift to a young girl struggling with her growing-up. This book is a very clean one, there's no any sexual things or cursing act. You have my promise that this book is very safe if you want to buy it for your daughter. :)

 Lucia Alvarez is at the beach with her little brother, Frankie, when she notices a loud rumble. She's surprised to see a parade of large trucks, loaded with soldiers. Their small town of Puerto Mujares, Cuba has never seen such a military movement. But it is 1961 and the Revolution is changing everything in Cuba. Before long she'll no longer be anticipating her quinceanera party, but wondering how her best friend could have turned on her, and worrying how she and her family will get through this. When her parents make the difficult decision to send Lucia and seven-year-old Frankie to the United States, Lucia must grow up quickly and take on the responsibility of keeping herself and her brother safe. 
 This children's novel is a very good work of historical fiction. Lucia narration shows her growth from an innocent young girl, to a responsible young lady. The reader sees how she chafes against what she sees as her parent's unnecessary restrictions, and lets her own teen-aged desires begin to lead her away from them. The effects of peer pressure are all too evident, as are the dangers of misplaced trust and fascination with adventure. But Gonzalez gives us a heroine who is able to think and decide on her own what path to follow. Lucia is intelligent, sensitive, kind and courageous. While she embraces the new life in America, she continues to recall the life lessons imparted by her mother and father. Chiefly she remembers her mother's large red umbrella, which becomes a symbol for strength of family. 
 There's a fair amount of Spanish used, but context will explain almost all of those words and phrases, and the book includes a glossary with translations. I think some of the situations - parents held at gunpoint, a hanging - are pretty heavy, but would definitely recommend it for middle-school readers.

Then enter Reagan's hot bi-sexual ex lover and roommate. But can Trey stick to chicks only - or will he find him self craving his own private cherry sucker of his own? But why does someone as sexy as Trey have to pick one team to play for? 
 This book pushed some of the sexual bounds for me - although I found most of it extremely erotic. These books bring fantasy to life - sometimes the taboo or just pushing you to your limits. There are plenty of woman who fantasize about 2 men at once - this book gives you full on lady boner full of them. 
 I am drooling in anticipation for the next book to get a bit of an inside peek at Jace and his submissive ways. They have left such a blank slate for him in these books that you still have no idea about what is going on in that pretty little bottle-blonde head of his. 
 Olivia Cunning does it again and pulls off one hell of a book and continued look into the bedroom (Tour bus, dressing rooms, public places, closets, hotels....) of The Sinners. I suddenly have an urge to get tickets to the next rock show in town and never look back.

The novelty has worn a bit; Scarlet didn't bring anything especially new to the story nor did Wolf. There wasn't time to explore world-building as much, and we only get a handful of scenes with Kai.

Spoiler free: As much as I love Harry Potter I wasn't really sure we needed this story and I was nervous about it, especially since I don't really like reading plays - they are meant to be seen after all. But...I really really liked this. 
 Except that I am now going to have to rename my cat now that we know Moaning Myrtle's full name. We named her Myrtle because she was meowing outside our house whilst we were watching HP and we took her in. Could definitely have done without that bit. 
 It was weird adjusting to a perspective that wasn't Harry's, but I think that's also what made this work. It's not the 8th HP book - it's the next generation. Thinking of it like that helped me just enjoy it. I connected with it enough that it made me cry due to nostalgia and also because I may have a wee crush on Neville. Which feels less gross here since it's more clear that they are my age. :) I was born two days after the fight in Godric's Hollow. 
 I liked that this showed the more positive side of Slytherin, considering that is the house Pottermore sorted me into (even though I'm obviously a Ravenclaw). 
 I liked that the next generation weren't just duplicates of their parents. I liked that Harry was flawed. I liked seeing life go on. I liked Harry struggling with parenting because he had no good example of parenting. I liked the plot but won't give any details. :) I liked the format - this isn't Harry's story and that made it feel different. I hope I get to see it performed at some point, although I do think it would be hard seeing different actors in the roles. I have seen some people say it was poorly written and I didn't feel that way. It's just different from the novels because it's all dialogue, which isn't as rich as what we got in the novels. I also don't think calling it fan fiction is fair since Rowling came up with the story and worked with the playwright - it's not like she wasn't involved. Is it as magical as the novels? Nope. But it's still an enthralling story and a new chapter in the HP universe and it made me happy.

I was really disappointed by Eleanor and Park, and this book has completely redeemed Rainbow Rowell. I noticed that after I finished Attachments, the next day I started reading another book. It was more of a book about a situation. For example in Attachments, Lincoln has a job to read people's emails. So in the book, you read the emails, and you read a bit about Lincolns life. But lets face it. Lincoln doesn't have what you would call an interesting life. He isn't the kind of person who reads emails by night and fights of firey dragons by day. His life is really mundane. This book was so thoroughly entertaining. It had be laughing through the entire thing, even when I didn't want to be. I didn't know what to expect from this book since I went into it without knowing much, but I SOOO fell in love with Ryan Dean and Annie.

Hannah's mother is getting married and claims she's leaving the planning to her girls but every time they suggest something, she changes her mind. Dolores is also upset that the local newspaper editor put a story about the Swenson ladies knack for finding dead bodies on the front page, It's been months since any of them found a body and Hannah and her sisters can take a joke. When Lisa's car breaks down and Hannah goes to get her they get caught in a thunder storm on the way home. While swerving to avoid hitting a large branch, Hannah hits something. That something turns out to be a someone- an unknown man by the side of the road. Unfortunately this incident causes Hannah to be arrested. Mike and Andrea's loyalties are tested and Hannah feels just horrible about the whole thing. She worries a lot about the man's identity and who might be missing him. When they figure out his identity, it's not what they expected and Hannah follows the clues back to Lake Eden and another mystery. 
 This story is a lot different from the others. First there's the lame accident. If Hannah shut the windows, her truck would have been the safest place regardless of whether they were under the trees or not. Second, the man's injuries don't seem like they're consistent with the speed Hannah was traveling and the force she hit him with so arresting her for vehicular manslaughter doesn't make much sense. Howie explains the politics of it all to Hannah and that does make a little more sense but it's all rather stupid. The plot first meanders into a local mystery which seems random and then the clues are dropped and I connected the events a lot faster than Hannah did. The plot takes a dark and gritty turn with prostitutes, pimps and other unsavory characters. At first the ending seems a little too nice but then it picks up to a surprising thriller scene. I'd like to know how that person knew where to find Hannah unless they followed Hannah, which in Hannah's case was stupid and careless to do what she did. The subplot about Moishe's new hobby was cute but repetitive. Though Dolores is writing a new novel, she stopped speaking in Regency language which I always found charming and funny. She's incredibly annoying with her indecision about her wedding and that plot got tired after awhile. There's also too much inane conversation going on in this book, as usual. 
 The only new characters are Loretta, Connor and Jennifer. Loretta is really nice and sounds like she's an excellent baker as well. She's apparently as good at judging character as Dolores has been but she seems to have maybe found the right man. Connor has secrets and I didn't fully trust him. Jennifer is the big mystery in the story. Is she really Jennifer who ran away 16 years ago? I wasn't sure until the clues fell into place and then I knew one way or another. She seems like a nice young lady at the moment despite running away as a teen. 
 Hannah is still such a prude, even her mother calls her on it. It's not her place to tell Michelle to change. I'd just tell my sister she looked like a 'ho and mom would be mad but it's her choice. Hannah is still somewhat technophobic. Yes Hannah, your phone does text if you have text messages included in your plan. Even my MOM knows how to text. I don't because I have a flip phone and it's a pain to type with but I know HOW! At least Hannah uses her computer now. 
 Unfortunately for me, there was only ONE recipe I want to try! The Blackberry Pie sounds good and almost identical to my family's famous blueberry pie. Blackberries are WAY to expensive to make into a pie. I would try the Airy Berry cookies, the chocolate orange crisps and the Butterscotch Brickle cookies if Hannah made them for me. I would love to make the Triple Chocolate Cookies but I would have to make the alternative version because I don't keep dark cocoa powder or bittersweet chocolate on hand.

 I loved the plotline of this novel, but several other things severely irritated me. (DO NOT READ THE FOLLOWING IF YOU DO NOT WANT TO READ SPOILERS). I was irritated that Jane left Edward because I do not feel she had reason enough to do so. Upon finishing the novel, I realized that Jane tended to love anything damaged, nothing pristine. Mr. Rochester could have been saved from a damaged body. She claimed herself that now, Mr. Rochester NEEDED her due to his disability -- what sort of love is that? She loved him through and through, yet she ignored it because she could not handle jewelry, riches, and attention. She asked too much of him, and the consequence was unneeded pain and suffering upon Mr. Rochester's person. 
 I also believe that Jane claims so much to be an independent person, but it cannot be because her school impounded so much religion into her. She was a slave to Christianity throughout the whole novel. 
 In summary, it was a wonderful book to read, but the sufferings of Jane Eyre were brought upon her own melodramatic self, and she caused much pain upon those she met.

I was utterly enthralled 
 Sci-fi stories were my favorite reading choice for a very long time starting in high school. I devoured Heinlein, Clarke and Asimov, among others. So, of course I had to read this when I saw it and I'm so glad I did. 
 This is not an ordinary romance, and for the majority of the book, our MC's are connected only by voice. Curt, now 40, is the mission commander of the Hermes 1. He's NASA's bad-boy: hot-tempered, hard-drinking, brash and an unapologetic straight talker. He was a wunderkind and the youngest astronaut to go into space. Patrick is a 27 yr old engineer, brought in to handle communications through the system he developed, between Houston and the spacecraft. He monitors information and talks with crew members frequently. He's that voice you hear on news reports, waking the crew and piping in music. Patrick can see Curt on monitors, but Curt can only hear him. Patrick can tell when BP and heart rates show Curt is awake during sleep schedules and they begin to converse, as it's also how the crew stays connected with "home". This is how their romance begins, through exchanges of information, both personal and professional. Their exchanges range from describing cheeseburgers and take-out orders from space, to the feelings they share about star-gazing and the lure of space. 
 I wasn't sure if I was going to like a day by day narrative, but Kay Simone did a great job of keeping it flowing and interesting. There's a news interview interspersed through part of it, detailing how Curt was the catalyst that revived NASA's manned space program, after the 2012 budget cuts. I do think the political reasons were oversimplified here (but that's just me). There are very thinly veiled celebrity names used in the interviews, that I thought were quite amusing. The premise is highly improbable but I loved that the crew was so diverse. Patrick had come out as bisexual in the 90's, two members are a lesbian couple, one of whom is trans, the pilot is female and pansexual and there's one token straight guy! 
 There's almost no sex in this book and the couple doesn't even meet until about 75%. But their first kiss is just awesome! There isn't a great deal of technical jargon but much of the story does include activities on the ship, of the crew and ground crew. Mostly though, it's about people and the strange intimacy that develops between the crew members themselves and between them and those on the ground, who they depend upon to get them there and back. There are wonderful secondary characters and their friendships and support develop beautifully. 
 I didn't buy the rather quick way they both decided they loved each other. This was after only two weeks, although they didn't say it to each other. I could accept a strong connection and attraction through conversation alone but "love" was too much to believe. It was pretty damned romantic though. Reader thoughts: I was so disappointed! The first book (and short story) were so much fun. Alas, this one was not. 
 The plot: being an apprentice mage is hard. It takes four years. Sometimes raiders attack (two or three times). 
 That's the summary of the total plot. But Ry's main concern will be whether she likes Ian (who is kind and funny) or Darren (who treats her like scum half the time and passionately kisses her the other half). She waffles back and forth between them. She tells Ian she loves him, and then she'll tell Darren she loves him, and repeat. She kisses both, sometimes the same night. This is the worst love triangle I have ever read. 
 So, Darren. He tells Ry he's going to break off his engagement with Priscilla so that he can marry her, and then he breaks his promise and tells Ry that he never loved her, that he hates her, and that he was only pretending in order to have sex with her (which, thankfully, never actually happened). She later admits she cried herself to sleep for two years. Why does she still "love" him? It's not like she actually likes anything he does. She just likes his kisses! Seriously. When she tries to describe her feelings for him, it's all about how he makes her feel, tingly and warm and bubbly and like she can't look away. Anytime he talks or walks into the room, she is transfixed, despite hating everything else about him. 
 Why in the world do Ian and Darren both want Ry? She is mean enough to keep pitting them against each other. She is immature enough to keep kissing them both. She has little personality except for a short temper. I guess she must be a good kisser? Is that really worth fighting over for three years? 
 Ry was not cool in this book. She used to be determined and hardworking and struggle just to make 6th place out of 5. Now? She's just angsty and more concerned about her love life than her training. Her late nights are spent eavesdropping on Darren or kissing him (or Ian) intead of training/studying. She is constantly mad at someone, her brother, her best friend, Ian, Darren, the master, or the situation. 
 How does it end? Worse. (view spoiler)[ Darren stands in front of his father's court and breaks off his engagement to Priscilla and announces that he is marrying Ry. This is after basically not speaking to her for two years and her hating him. He has no right! She should tell him no! 
 How does he "win" her heart? He tells her that he never stopped loving her. What? How could anyone be that mean to someone they love? He made her cry herself to sleep for two years. I don't believe it. I'm pretty sure he means "lust" not "love." 
 He says he was mean to try to get her to leave him alone because it would be bad for the kingdom if he married her. He was trying to do his duty to his kingdom by crushing her heart and feeding her to the wolves. Why did he not just tell her? Surely he could have explained that it was in his kingdom's best interest for him to marry someone with a large dowry? Surely he respected her enough to know she would understand his reasons? 
 Here's their last conversation. 
 Darren says something like, "I couldn't stop loving you" and gives his reasons for pushing her away and being a jerk. 
 Ry: "I never stopped (loving you). I wanted to. I hated myself that I couldn't." (And another sentence or two like this.) 
 Darren: "Who would've thought that the girl who tried to get me kicked out of the academy ... this girl who tried to light me on fire, this lowborn girl I absolutely couldn't stand ...." 
 Ry: "You insulted me, mocked me, tricked me, lied to me!" 
 Darren: "Let me finish, love. That this one person would be the one person I am hopelessly, madly drawn to against my will, possibly even my better judgment." 
 Ry: "I don't think either of us had a choice in the matter." 
 Didn't have a choice? Ry should never marry him. Why does she still like him anyway, after all he did to her? She can't trust him. I guess he's a good kisser or something. That's a dumb (really REALLY dumb) reason to marry. (hide spoiler)] 
 I didn't understand which were the mentors and which were the mentees. Ry was a mentee the first year, but then she was a mentee her second year, and then in her third year, she called Ian her mentor. What? Other third year apprentices were mentors, why does she need to have her own mentor? Plus, in her first year, her mentor was Ian's girlfriend (who is conveniently not mentioned in the last two-thirds of the book, but I might have missed it). 
 Writer thoughts: I'm curious about the blurb. It mentions the master Ry hates. The combat mage apprentice trainer guy apprently dislikes women and picks on Ry, but she gets overly dramatic and upset about it all. Didn't I mention she has a short temper? 
 Also, the blurb doesn't even mention Ian and barely seems to mention Darren. When 95% of Ry's focus and energy are in this love triangle, it might have been nice to mention these in the blurb. All The Missing Girls is one of the best thrillers/books IaEUR(tm)ve read this year. It has a unique presentation, interesting characters, and so many twists and turns that I honestly was unsure of what to expect throughout the entire book. 
 The presentation of this book is its biggest asset. The investigation told in this story is told backwards, readers start on the final day when the police are pulling up to the house of our MC, Nicolette, and she asks the haunting question What did you do? 
 On our journey back through the investigation we see answers to questions that we have not yet thought to ask. We see people making judgements based off of evidence that we have not yet seen. We see results before we see actions. While this can be a bit confusing at times, it lets the readers pay close attention to small details that we may have not thought to focus on. We see how devastating rumors can be in these situations, considering that we see the consequences of these rumors before we see why they were started, we are able to better understand why things happen and how ridiculous it is for people to assume something else. The backwards story lets us, as readers, view the evidence presented in a way different from the norm which allows us to make conclusions that are different from those that the investigators quickly come too. 
 While this story focuses on the investigation of a missing girl, Annaliese, it allows our characters to revisit the investigation that took place years earlier of their mutual friend, Corinne. The investigation of CorinneaEUR(tm)s disappearance was left inconclusive, there was no clear explanation as to what happened the night that she disappeared, so naturally when a second girl goes missing from the town, who also has ties to the same friend group, questions of the CorinneaEUR(tm)s disappearance are brought back into light. This is really interesting because it just adds more depth to the story rather than just being about one investigation. I canaEUR(tm)t really go into this anymore without starting down a slippery slope full of spoilers but itaEUR(tm)s just really interesting to see the similarities of the two disappearances and trying to figure out what the link is between the two disappearances (or if there is one at all). 
 Along with the unique presentation of this story we have some pretty great characters. They are all presented in a way that suggests that they have something to hide, but as the story develops and we travel back these things are slowly explained to us and we are left to decide if (and how) they are important to the investigations or not. Some things are minor and unimportant, other things feel minor but end up being super significant, and of course others feel super significant and end up being not at all important. I can say that without giving anything away because there is so much revealed throughout the story that I donaEUR(tm)t think any of that gives anything away. 
 Individually the characters are interesting and deep, but together their dynamic is electric. I love watching these relationships be explored and explained. I love watching them grow and deteriorate, sometimes at the same time since the characters relieve their past throughout the current investigation. ItaEUR(tm)s just so amazing to see not only how the details of the investigation are important but also how the characters interactions with one another are important. 
 Everything about this story is incredible. There are so many layers to be explored, so many details that need to be picked up on, and somehow everything falls into place so perfectly. It all seems to make sense in so many different ways, it feels like there are so many different explanations to this story, that when the ending is finally revealed it is equal parts messy and satisfying. This book was everything I could have hoped for, and then some.

There were many, many things that drove me crazy about this book: 
 1) So they're historians. Polly going back to study the first week of the Blitz and peoples' reactions as a department store clerk; Mike as a US reporter to interview people coming back from Dunkirk in his (somewhat juvenile) ordinary people becoming heroes research; Eileen to record children evacuees from the Blitz as a maid in the country. But...these WW2 specialist historians didn't know about Dunkirk, Bletchley Park, Agatha Christie, and most egregiously of all that MEN WORE HATS in the 1940s (was a man who didn't realize this). Not only didn't they seem non-nerdy or academic, they didn't even seem particularly observant. 
 Okay they're from 2060, so the war was a 120 years ago. But no excuse. You don't really see them do any historical research either. Shouldn't they be taking notes? Surreptitiously recording or taping people? Doing you know...something besides fretting about skirts, train schedules, children, and newspapers? I feel like if I was whisked away to 1940 now, I'd be better prepared and with more of a plan than any of the characters. Even if they can't take their notes back to the future, they could always get a safety deposit box or maybe bury them somewhere--I don't know, but something. At the very least, in the St. Mary book I read earlier, they were actually recording and taking measurements. Even in To Say Nothing of the Dog, there was an actual plan--read a journal and give the cat back. I am just not seeing an actual plan by any of the characters that couldn't also be solved by reading a bunch of old 1940s newspapers (or they could just get an implant), except for maybe history tourism. If I could advise main characters it would be: "Watch Mrs. Miniver--there, research completed. " 
 2) Most of the action seems belabored. The skirt thing drove me crazy. They gave her way too much money anyways--and why do they need to get a job immediately when they arrive? Take a day or two to get your bearings and buy a suitable work outfit and clothing. I'd rather read that than 40 pages about skirt issues. Once they actually get trapped in the past, okay, then start panicking and working hard. Actually taking your time in preparation would have solved 100% of all the problems in this book. The time travel department seems so frazzled and out of it, all under one man, Mr. Dunworthy, who has all sorts of meaningless rules to protect the time traveling historians, but all the rules seem to do is to send folks back completely unprepared (and not knowing vital things like major events of the war taking place at the same time you plan on arriving). Why no backup drop point? Why shouldn't you know the identities and locations of all the fellow time travelers in your vicinity? Seems like all of that would be helpful memos. 
 Ignoring the fact that a great majority of the book is like watching 3 clueless bugs trapped in a bottle trying to find a way out--I still actually liked it. I liked Alf and Binnie (though the plot of measles seemed an awful lot like Auntie Mame, but maybe being trapped with a bunch of bratty British children refugees under quarantine is too fun to pass up)--and I thought Eileen had the strongest of them all. Mike's story bored me a bit--isn't it granted that interacting with the past at all is going to change some history? Especially visiting during war--chatting with someone or asking someone the time during the Blitz could save lives every day, just by freak randomness. I didn't really care for any of the Polly storylines--I liked her fellow shelter folks, but I didn't like...(view spoiler)[ when she finally got reunited with Eileen and Mike after hundreds of pages, only to freak out because she didn't tell her shelter buddies that she'd miss practice, even though she had an understudy, and could easily lose everyone again in the crowd...ugh..and I semi rolled eyes as her relationship with the old Shakespearean actor got a bit too much mind meldly and clingy (hide spoiler)] 
 I like Trot and Spitfire as girls' names now, and I hear that All Clear is amazing and it really was intended as one book--so maybe not fair to Blackout to be judged ENTIRELY on its own merits. Really, if the time travel part was removed entirely and the book was about a maid, a clerk, and a reporter, it might have been a lot better. And I plan on reading the second--which is next in my stack, along with Doomsday Book. So this is an odd book in a way--I don't regret reading it, enjoyed chunks even though I was exasperated with much of it, wouldn't necessarily recommend it, but plan on reading more, which makes it fall into almost a special category.

Both surprisingly enjoyable and unsettlingly creepy, Maybe This Time is one of the most intelligently told and enjoyable ghost stories I've come across. Set in the nineties, Andromeda "Andie" Archer does a favor for her ex-husband, to go to "the wilds of southern Ohio" to a haunted house and domesticate the two children living there. Of course there's old history ("ghosts" if you'll excuse the horrible pun) from her past relationship with North complicating an already entangled mess. 
 Andie is likable, capable and above all, warm. She's funny, with a dry wit and little to no tolerance for bullshit. She changes from a very independent woman who is constantly looking for something/somewhere new into a devoted and loving mother-figure for the two tormented children. 
 Alice, the younger child, is the more obviously affected by the ghosts. One in particular is possessive of her and violent towards any interference. Alice was, either intentionally or unintentionally, the funniest person in the novel. She's often "outraged" in the way only a child can be when they realize they don't always get what they want. She's a very emotional and vulnerable little girl, so it makes sense that she's very attached to her brother Carter, and eventually Andie. 
 Carter himself is a cipher most of the novel. He's been through so much anguish and internal pain since the death of his mother, then his father, his aunt and a nanny that he has almost completely withdrawn from verbal communication besides Alice. He's utterly devoted and protective towards her, and I was always curious to know more about the hidden undercurrents going on around him. 
 The pacing is wonderful and builds like a ghost story should be retold. At first there's hints and vague movements but as it get creepier and the multiple ghosts more malevolent, the pages fly by and the plot races on to a very riveting conclusion. Highly enjoyable.

 An interesting novel which shows that one person's life is someone else's fiction as the narrative progresses from story to story. We begin with a journal kept by an American in the Pacific during the 19th century before moving to letters written by a composer who is the son of a wealthy English family. From him, we see the adventures of a journalist who wants to live up to the stories her father broke. The story of Timothy Cavendish running from people to whom he owes money after publishing a surprisingly successful story is next, after which a tale of consumerism and corporation in the future. Finally we end up in a post-civilisation world, before exploring the end of each of the stories that Mitchell has introduced us to. 
 I found several parts of this novel fascinating, but firstly I want to talk a little about the progression and the logic of the shells (the six different stories). We first meet a fairly wealthy American named Adam Ewing sailing the Pacific and interacting with slaves as well as colonists. From him, we gradually progress to people that have less and less wealth and social standing until we arrive at a man from a culture with almost nothing left except for superstition, and who must do his best to survive in that context. It's interesting that Mitchell places a woman who was a cloned slave in a corporate world before the savage at the centre of the tale, if he is intentionally moving from most wealthy to least; is the wealth of civilisation really outweighing the problems caused by the lack of freedom that accompanies it? 
 Some of the novel annoyed me a little. The birthmark that recurs throughout the novel is never really touched upon or explained, and the hint that the main characters are somehow linked by destiny seems a little heavy-handed to me now that I have finished the book. Similarly, in places the shells do not obviously have much to connect them; there are clear connections between two pairs of shells but the others are harder to connect with the narrative. 
 Ultimately, it's that annoyance that means I don't give this novel five stars, but it's definitely a terrific book. Each new story proves more fascinating than the last. Particularly given the intelligence of the Sonmi-451 chapter, which very subtly deals with the evolution of language ('-ight' replaced with '-ite', 'ex-' replaced with 'x-') and has a terrorist organisation called 'Union' amongst the corporate world on show. As a work of literary fiction it's extremely accomplished, but it also brings a lot to the table as a work of science fiction.

 One was eye-opening when it came to conjoined twins, and the reality they face while living through life. The fact is, along with stares and being judged by others, they have very low life expectancy and may never experience romantic love. What is a very stark and difficult life came through the beautiful souls of Tippi and Grace, who start school for the first time and experience friendship, love, and loss. 
 Twins already share a close bond with one another, and Tippi and Grace are closer than most. While they have different heads, hands and hearts, they both share the bottom half. It was interesting how these sisters would have to go everywhere together, from showering together, to sleeping, and everything else. They sacrifice a lot of what they want to do - romance, resting, adventure for the other. While I haven't particularly thought much about conjoined twins before, it was definitely interesting to learn about it in One. 
 The whole book is written in poetic phrases, and while it was readable and fitting to the beauty of the story, it jumped around at times. I found it was difficult to connect to the characters because of this, you'll see glimpses of the things they were experiencing, such as not being able to fall in love or the struggles their parents were facing. While One felt realistic and touched upon multiple issues, such as financial distress, parental conflict, alcoholism, mental health and segregation, it doesn't really explore anything too deeply. Some of these things felt unresolved, and included for the sake of it. 
 One is a beautiful, poetic book that raises awareness about a rare condition, about two twins who share a body. Their experience is raw, touching and eye-opening, although it doesn't explore anything else other than being joined too deeply.

I did not think much of "The Prince of Thorns" when I read it the first time and had no interest in reading books 2 or 3. But recently one of my Goodreads groups selected this series and I had an opportunity to give it another chance. 
 I found Book 2 of The Broken Kingdom Trilogy, "The King of Thorns", to be a stronger story than the first book but I still have too many problems with this science fiction novel disguised as a fantasy novel to ever consider the series one of my favorites. (At least now, I can say that I finished reading them.) 
 Lawrence does do a much better job of fleshing out both his world and his characters this time around. However, if you expect to know what post-apocalyptic Europe looks/smells/feels like, you will be disappointed. There just aren't any details. How does the coast of Italy differ from our Italy of today? I couldn't tell you...I just know a female pope is in control of the church in "Roma". His home kingdom of Ancrath is in France and his mother's family is from the Cote d'Azur - but does the book let me see if his grandfather's kingdom is 
 "one of those nice little smaller cities, pushed into the water like a seashell, fed fish and sea air and producing sailors... It feels of fishing and flaming tar, brine and hull boats. It shows, on the cobblestone streets, shining like pearls, flaked sardines, and along the harbor walls lame people and paralyzed old sailors warm in the sun on the stone benches. .." 
 No (The above is Guy de Maupassant's description of arriving in Saint-Tropez). Instead, all I get is "Castle Morrow bakes in the southern sun much of the year. The winters can be ferocious but are rarely cold...". I can create a mental image of Jorg's world only because I know my geography well and I have played all the Fallout/ Fallout 2 video games. The same holds true for characters: what does Fexler Brews look like? The answer is "an old man. ...in looks he could have been brother to Sword-master Shimon." OK...so what does Shimon look like? "He looked as old as tutor Lunquist, with the same long white hair". How is the reader supposed to visualize the places and characters of this story if the author can't even describe them? 
 Plot-wise the book follows two time frames: the present and 4 years earlier. In the present Jorg is 18 and is king in his own right of the Kingdom of Renar (after having defeated his uncle in book 1). The "4 years earlier" section directly follows the events of the first book. Also Interspersed between these time-jump chapters were entries from Katherine's Journal and are a view on the earlier events from her perspective. I know Lawrence did this to try and hide the plot "surprises", but it really creates a narrative tangle for the reader. Sometimes, narrative exposition works as well as flash forward/ flash back and this is one of those times. There was not a "surprise" hidden in the tangle that would have been diminished by a linear narrative. We, the readers, already know Jorg is going to survive. How he survives is the story. 
 I still have a problem with the "magic" of this world, although Lawrence finally gives us a token explanation: the builder's technology altered the fabric of reality. We know the events of Jorg's life take place 1000-1200 years after a nuclear /technological holocaust. What things have survived and what has been lost is very inconsistent. Jorg knows the song "American Pie", knows that Hannibal crossed the Alps with Elephants, and can quote Shakespeare- but the history of the Builders is gone? There are no trains or other powered transportation systems - but the 1200 year-old gunpowder/primer in colt .45 cartridges still works ...and if center-fire cartridge handguns were still being used at the time of the Builder's collapse and are still working, why is everyone in the lands of the Broken Empire using swords? Even Fexler Brews' holographic ghost admits that Jorg's world could rebuild itself in 50 years- there is that much surviving tech laying around. This makes everything left by the Builders a literal deus ex mechina to solve each and every one of Jorg's problems. 
 So, why give this book four stars when it has so many problems? Because there are times Lawrence is a joy to read, as with my favorite quote: 
 "The blatter-pipe, a local Highlands specialty, is to music what warthogs are to mathematics. Largely unconnected."

I was first attracted Acne, Asthma and OtherSigns You Might be a Half Dragon by the lovely cover; the title then "sealed the deal" for me. I was looking for some light fun reading and hoped that based on the title I'd get that and hopefully some sassy, quirky one-liners as well. 
 Rochford's book did provide all that - it was fun and a bit sassy, though there were parts that I felt needed to be fleshed out a little more. 
 The protagonist of Rochford's novel, Allyson, has never known her father and her mother moves them around the country a great deal with each new job offer and promotion. She's always the new kid and outsider, without many friends. 
 In the town she currently lives in she has finally made a friend - Beth. Allyson dreads hearing that her mother will move them yet again. Events rapidly unfold that make this the least of Allyson's worries. She discovers an entire supernatural community lives around her and that her recurrent acne is really one of the signs that she is a half dragon - everybody else seems to know what's going on except Allyson. Allyson and Beth get caught up in territorial wars between various supernatural races and find themselves prey to those involved in an evil plot which they must try and foil. 
 What I loved about this book was that the unicorns were not squeaky clean - they were just as prone to hatred and the desire for revenge as any other race. They had suffered years of persecution only to adopt a "shoot first" policy in their dealings with others. Also the political intrigue between races was rife in this novel and I felt the world building and history in this regard was good. The pace was generally excellent. 
 I would like to have seen this story fleshed out a little more, particularly in terms of the initial set up. The book immersed the reader straight into the action, but at the expense of setting up the main character. It was clear from the title that Allyson was going to discover she was a dragon, that's not the type of set up I'm referring to. Rochford revealed too little about Allyson's character, her desires and her past early on. We learnt more about this as the story progressed, but the result was that I didn't empathise with or care about Allyson until over half way through the book. I did, however, like her best friend from the beginning. 
 Overall I really enjoyed it. I'd definitely read the next one. So if you're after a light fun read give this one a try.

I honestly don't know what drew me to this because I've ranted before that I'm not the biggest fan of shirtless man covers but I am so glad I didn't let that stop me because THIS BOOK! All the FEELS! It was just so beautiful and real and sweet and yup there I go, I'm in a mini flail. Pull yourself together, Dani! 
 WORTH THE FALL tells the story of Abby and Matt, two souls in desperate need of a connection. Abby has spent her life, feeling forgotten and unloved by the people who should protect her the most and Matt has spent his life, putting his country and fellow SEALs before everything else. When they meet, it's not a story of star-crossed lovers who can abandon everything and give into their passions. 
 Matt is grieving the loss of his best friend, killed in action and escapes to the beach to figure out his life and begins to realise that a wife and kids is something his heart wants despite his head telling him that the guilt he feels at his best friend's death can only be appeased by a life of being the dutiful man at arms. 
 Abby, an orphan, who has embraced the feeling of abandonment as inevitable, is dealing with the recent death of her husband and the harsh reality of a life raising four young children with another one on the way. 
 They only have a week at the beach but as the days pass, their easy friendship blossoms. As Abby watches Matt embrace her children and her unusual circumstances with no hesitation and Matt opens up to the possibility that maybe he can have the one thing his heart wants the most, the two realise that maybe a week isn't enough... 
 I get butterflies in my stomach just thinking back at all the emotional moments in this book. Abby and Matt were two amazing characters who instantly garnered sympathy with their respective backgrounds and their all-round awesomeness. Having spent her life, being the one who wasn't noticed, Abby is determined that her children never feel that way. Never balking at the prospect of being both a mom and a dad to her kids, her courageous and loving nature ensures she has everything handled. Almost everything... 
 Despite the love and fulfilment she gets from being a mom there's still something missing. Her marriage wasn't perfect and now her husband is another in a long list of people she has lost. When she meets Matt, Abby has to open her heart to the possibility that it's okay to let some of those balls drop, because there are people out there who are more than willing to catch them. She just has to decide if it's "worth the fall ". 
 As for Matt... 
 BOOM! That's the sound of my ovaries, ladies! He was such an interesting character and I loved learning about his time in the navy and his family. His interaction with the kids was so sweet and I loved how hard he worked at earning their trust, he genuinely cared for them before his feelings for Abby deepened, it was never just a cheap ploy to seduce her. 
 At times I grew frustrated at Abby's attempts to distance herself but it was completely understandable given her past. The development of their relationship was handled really well. When I read the blurb and saw "the week" part I was wary of insta-love but that is so far from the case. Abby and Matt are two adults, who have lived through a lot of pain and heartbreak and can recognise when something good comes along. The children were the star of the show for me, they never came across as a plot device but were given their own little personalities that stole my heart and made me want to volunteer to babysit so Abby and Matt could get it on *cue Marvin Gaye*. 
 WORTH THE FALL was simply a gorgeous story that will make you experience the full gamut of emotions as you read it. Full of love, sacrifice and belief in happiness no matter what, I highly recommend you too fall for Matt and Abby, it's definitely worth it!

Unravel Me was much the same as Shatter Me, to be honest. Both books were beautifully written with stunning imagery and the use of techniques that made them very engaging. Both had relatively similar plotlines of people wanting to use Juliette and her wondering about whether she should listen to them or the other side. Both, while very good, still left me wanting more. As much as I'm enjoying this series, something isn't clicking with me. It's not hitting me in the heart as much as it should be. It doesn't make me laugh or cry or gasp. So while I can't fault the writing style or much of the characterisation, something seems to be lacking here and that's why I'm unable to give 5 stars. 
 There are lots of possible combinations as to why I'm not feeling this series. Is it because Juliette is a narrator who wallows in her own self pity? Is it because Adam is a boring character and an even more boring love interest? Is it because the prettiness of the writing takes away the hard-hitting edge of war? I'm not sure, especially since every bad thing about this book seemed to be countered with a good thing. When reading Shatter Me, I didn't understand why so many readers seemed so in love with Warner's character, but I definitely understand it now. Warner is by far the most interesting and developed character in the series. He isn't my favourite yet, but I'm definitely starting to see the attraction. My favourite character would be Kenji, mainly because he brings a little bit of light between Juliette's self-pity and Adam's desperation. Kenji was the only character to criticise Juliette for her 'oh poor me I'm a monster' act, and I really don't think I'd have enjoyed the book half as much if she'd carried on any longer. People who read my reviews will know that I don't like whiny narrators so I'm very glad that Juliette didn't turn into one. I hope to see her grow even stronger in the last book. 
 Overall, I did really like it. I read it quickly and I liked a lot of the plots and I do like most of the characters. Juliette may have her whiny moments, but she's learning and improving and that's what I like to see in a character. The only character I really dislike is Adam because he's even more whiny than Juliette is and it makes him seem pathetic. I've really lost interest in him since the first book. So, there are good bits and bad bits. It isn't giving me the gut-wrenching feeling that a 5 star book should give but I wasn't disappointed with it either. Therefore, this series to me is good, but not great.

Wow!! Who is Fisher Amelie? One of my new favorite authors!! I immediately have to read everything she has written. 
 This book was not what I expected and the description does not due the book justice. 
 Sophie price is a young socialite. She is rich, one of the beautiful people, and Queen Bee of her entourage. 
 "I rule the roost because I'm the most wanted by all the guys, and all the girls want to be my friend because of it." 
 She snorts cocaine, parties every weekend and sleeps around. She does this to belong but also fill a void. 
 "That was my secret weakness. Rejection. Rejection of any kind, in fact. I hated it more than anything." 
 She is crude...a true mean girl. She let's everyone know that they are beneath her. 
 "My lingerie probably costs more than your entire wardrobe," 
 At the beginning of the book, Sophie gets caught with cocaine for the second time. Her punishment...to work 6 months in an orphanage in Uganda. Her whole world has fallen apart. 
 "I suppose the choices you make really are what define you." 
 This trip makes her reassess herself... 
 "That girl was the real me. Frightened. Worthless. A terrible friend. Terrible daughter. Well educated but so limited in ideas worth having. Beautiful yet repulsive...and finally honest." 
 When she steps off the plane...the first person she meets is the young man she is going to be working with for six months...Ian. Ian is a HOT South African and Sophie is immediately drawn to him... 
 "It was like my body knew instantly that he was mine and that I was his." 
 There is one problem. Ian hates her!! 
 "Girl, you are the epitome of spoiled. I can smell it in your expensive perfume, in the quality of your ridiculous clothing, in the bracelet wrapped 'round that delicate wrist...You won't last out here. You'll stay blind to the environment that surrounds you. You'll live in your clean, perfect bubble and return to your posh life come six months. You are...you. I know your kind. I've seen it all before. You will never wake up. Not really." 
 When Sophie gets to the orphanage...she is appalled by what she sees. I was heartbroken by what I read. I fell in love with all of the characters that worked at this orphanage. I fell in love with all of the children. I couldn't understand how they made the orphanage work... 
 "We just do. Lot's of faith, my love. It always works out in the end. Somehow. Somehow we turn thirty beds into sixty. Somehow we stretch our food to impossible measures. Somehow we survive on our impossibly meager income. Somehow we love them all equally. Somehow." 
 While working together, day in and day out...Sophie found Ian irresistible... 
 "How can someone bug the shit out of you so much yet simultaneously cause you to want to know them intimately with your tongue?" 
 Ian still found Sophie to be a spoiled brat... 
 "Every single soul here is present because they want to be. You're only serving a sentence." 
 But time gives them a change. Slowly but surely...Sophie begins to change...Ian begins to see it...but how will it work, she is supposed to go back to America in 6 months?? 
 This is really a great non-typical story. I shed tears. I laughed. I felt. I would recommend this book to everyone.

The Lightning Thief is kind of a cross between Harry Potter and 
 American Gods 
 . 
 Greek gods haven't gone anywhere in the past several thousand years. They've been around the whole time and still up to their same old business mingling with mortals and spawning demigods. Luckily, there's a special summer camp for these demigods. When they're middle-schoolers and monsters start coming after them (sounds like middle school to me), they get the option of heading out to summer camp on Long Island, where they canoe and practice archery and run footraces and learn sword fighting and practice battling monsters. 
 My seven-year-old came in to say goodnight to me while I was reading it, and she read over my shoulder for a little while. 
 "It's about Greek gods," she said. I was impressed that she'd noticed the names and placed them so quickly. 
 She started asking more questions about the things she was reading where I had the book open, but I deflected her. 
 "It's kind of confusing when you've not been reading the whole story," I explained. "It will make more sense when we read it together." 
 I'm not sure how long it will be before I think she's ready for this series, though. This first book, at least, is pretty good, but it's also pretty violent. There's betrayal and swordplay and monsters and other scary stuff. And there's this sense of mortals being stupid and oafish and the world being a dangerous and scary place, which I'm not sure is the best message for a child rather prone to anxiety anyway. Of course, she's currently reading a kid version of Beowulf, so she'd probably be fine with that kind of thing. And she might really enjoy the idea of satyrs and centaurs and being able to talk with animals. 
 In addition, it feels maybe a little basic. Defeating the monsters seemed a little too easy and the schemes of the immortals a little too simple for my taste and, even worse, the characters seem a little flat. Their actions didn't always seem to match what Riordan was saying their personality was. Their motives were difficult to figure out. I suppose I ought to cut the book a little slack since it's meant for kids and I'm a jaded grown-up, but I don't think that fact that it's intended for children is a good excuse for flat characters. 
 But it's better than the Magic Treehouse series, and I'm letting her read those. Maybe we'll start on these sooner rather than later and see how it goes. I'm sure her dad would love to read these stories with her.
