Seldom have I approached a book with such large baggage. I have tackled literary classics with less expectation or prejudice than I did when I decided to read this novel. In fact I had almost convinced myself that I wouldn't read this because of my feelings about Child's advocacy of brown haired 5'7" Tom Cruise playing the blond haired 6'5" Jack Reacher in the movie adaptation of One Shot. 
 But is was there, in the world and although i wouldn't pay top dollar for it, I guess I always knew that I would pick it up at some point. As it happens, Audible had a sale and I got if for a very reasonable price and I thought what the hell. 
 I guess to balance some of that i should say that my first Reacher novel was The Enemy which like this was a prequel novel dealing with Reachers time in the Army. I was keen to find out what event precipitated him leaving the Army, therefore I was drawn to find out more of Reacher's back-story. I guess I was pre-disposed to like this story as a result. 
 Well, I've managed to write three paragraphs without touching on the actual novel. Maybe i should get on and review the actual book. Having got all of my baggage into the open, the questions which should be answered are; 'did i enjoy it' and 'is it a worthy edition to the series?' 
 The answer to those questions are 'maybe' and 'maybe'. I'll explain... 
 When it comes to these many parted series featuring one main protagonist, i am of the opinion that more is more. I generally like it when an author goes back to formative events in the characters past and in the case of Reacher i became hooked on Child's books by (inadvertently) reading what, chronologically, would be the first book in the series (but was actually the 8th novel) featuring the character while he was still in the Army, so when i found out that we were going to get the event which resulted in Reacher leaving the army i was excited. And that story is a decent one. The mystery was interesting enough keep me engaged and the mis-directions were not so obvious and clumsy as they have been in some of the more recent Reacher installments. 
 What spoilt this for me was the excessive use of 'knowing nods' and foreshadowing of the future. I suppose it is an easy trap to fall into when writing about the backstory of a character. This books is chock full of references to 'how Reacher would handle leaving the army', how he felt ambivalent about settling down in one place, with a home and normal job. He tours the army PX and picks up his trusty travel toothbrush. He goes undercover and determines his attitude to carrying a bag and washing clothes. He is advised to set up a bank near Washington and he muses about setting up a password so he can access his account from anywhere. He gets 'the postcard' from his brother telling him he is going to Margrave, etc.... 
 A few such references would have been a sly nod from the author to his long term readers because they were all in on the joke. But fully a quarter of the book seems to be taken up with these knowing self references, to the extent that it moved from an amusing aside to a smug 'see what i did there' jab in the ribs each time one occurred. Maybe my annoyance with the author coloured my judgement in this respect but as they piled up i became less enamored with this device. 
 In one particular respect i found so jarring it literally threw me out of the story each time it happened. The narrative, as always, is in the first person told in Reachers voice and from his perspective and i thought in real time, so i believed that the story was being told in 1997 by Reacher, not recounted from memory. The way the other references were made reinforced this view, they aren't knowing from the characters point of view, only the authors and readers, but then wham like a sledgehammer the author 'through Reacher' makes comparison to the differences between the security at the Army Base or the pentagon before and after the events of 9/11. It's just seems sloppy from Child, dislodged me from the story and wound me up no end.

I've read a few horrors in my time, and this book is scarier than any of them simply because of how easily our own world could turn into a situation such as the one described by Offred, a Handmaid who is placed within a family because of her capacity to breed. This or similar is the world we could live in, if we stop valuing people's diversity; something that seems to be happening at a staggering rate in a variety of contexts in our current political contexts. 
 In this book the details matter and there are a lot of them. This leads to some moments that are fairly explicit, both in terms of violence and sexuality. But it is because, not despite of this, that I feel this should be a necessary read to share with the mature young women in our lives, combined with in depth discussion of the things that somehow seem more possible in the world's current climate than less than they did twenty years ago. Things like religion, sex, conformity, education, authority, government intervention, feminism, patriarchies... the list goes on. 
 I recently read an article of Atwood's reflecting on this book and she said "Back in 1984 the main premise seemed--even to me--fairly outrageous. Would I be able to persuade readers that the United States had suffered a coup that had transformed an erstwhile liberal democracy into a literal-minded theocratic dictatorship?" In 2017, with a simple-minded, authoritarian President holding the reins of government in Washington, DC, and all manner of intolerant extremists in the wings, that premise no longer seems preposterous. 
 Atwood's prose, is impeccable. She writes with urgency, purpose, and humanity--and delivers an ending more brilliant and deliberate than I thought was coming. Then finally in a post script, we zoom out to a place of academia, where the calm eye of history in review sees Offred story as a blip, or an inconvenience as "She could have told us much about the workings of the Gileadean empire, had she had the instincts of a reporter or a spy." Offred's tale of captivity is reduced to how much information she gave about her male captor. How often do we do this already? Looking at first hand accounts of atrocities that have happened in our own history with no empathy for the victim, but rather bemoaning the details we aren't able to glean in the name of research? How easy is it to forget the faces we even now see every night on the news, victims of atrocities being carried out in our own back yards? 
 This novel is too powerful and relevant to dismiss because of the more unpleasant aspects portrayed within its pages. Instead it is a startling prediction about the direction our lives could be taking. It challenged and startled me as I was reading it, and I suspect it will continue to do so in years to come.

Updated September 6, 2014: Ugh, trying to write about each successive Rainbow Rowell novel gets more and more difficult. How many different ways are there to say THIS WAS SO GOOD. HER WORDS ARE SO GOOD. HER CHARACTERS SO GOOD. EVERYTHING GOOD. RELATE SO MUCH. HELP. 
 That's pretty much all I feel like saying, because even over a month later, my feelings about this book are so jumbly wumbly it's hard to get them to sit still long enough to make them cohesive enough to write about. 
 Granted, having never been married and never had a serious vocation like our main character Georgie McCool does, I don't relate quite as much to this book as I have in her previous efforts (Fangirl and Attachments in particular). But there's just something about the way Rainbow Rowell writes about emotions that makes me instantly think YES I RECOGNIZE THAT. It's like her books are the story versions of falling in love or making an instant connection with a person. Like, those rare instances where you meet someone and you just instantly KNOW them. I've only had that happen a couple of times in my life, which is probably part of why I love reading her so much. 
 Just completely disregard the silly sounding plot with the time traveling phone. It's not important. It's just another way to explore the dynamics between people we care about, and how relationships can change and evolve, how we lose and find each other over and over again, how we have to commit to the relationships that are important to us. (Although, honestly, I think that kind of silly shit is incredibly cool.) 
 Definitely glad I own this in hardcover, and I'm sure I will be revisiting it over and over in years to come, just like I plan to do with all her other books. 
 Rainbow Rowell, why can't I quit you!?!? (Also, please don't stop writing these wonderful books. Please don't ever stop.)

 Nothing makes me one-click a book faster then one that includes a forbidden relationship between step-siblings. I like to blame this specifically after reading Rival by Penelope Douglas because that book rocked my world. So to say my hopes were high for Stepbrother Dearest is an understatement and more than likely the reason was I was left underwhelmed and unsatisfied. 
 "I have no desire to sit on your dirty bed." 
 "Is that because you'd rather sit on my dirty face?" 
 Stepbrother Dearest has all the trimmings of what could be a delectable story. First you have Elec, a cocky asshole with a sharp tongue and good looks. Second you have Greta, the virgin stepsister that secretly covets an attraction to Elec. The angst and illicitness to be had by all would be great if it was there. But mainly my issue with this story is all the wasted potential. Greta is a forgettable character. All she does is fawn over Elec despite how rude and demeaning he is to her. Elec had a little more personality but I never felt warm towards him even when he showed vulnerability and true emotion. And the two of them together? Well it felt like the attraction and lust was forced. You know that saying about showing and not telling? I feel like I was told how in lust and connected the two of them were instead of drawing those emotions on my own. 
 "I know I'm not supposed to care. But when it comes to you, what I'm supposed to be feeling has never seemed to matter." 
 Again, I hate to compare this to Rival but I can't help it. Rival succeeded with strong characters that stood apart from one another but had the ability to ignite together. It also was able to give a backstory in just a few flashbacks that really touched on the forbidden and set up the foundation for the rest of the book. With Stepbrother Dearest the potential is there but it's just potential.

 The story begins with a young woman waking up in a cave, seriously injured and desperately hungry. She can't remember anything whatsoever of her past, but instinct kicks in. Her intuition leads her to begin a relationship by biting a man...and drinking his blood. She and her new human companion establish that she is more or less like the vampires of human legend, though her dark skin provides some protection from the burning daytime sun. As they begin to learn more about her nature, the science behind it, and how she came to be separated from others of her kind, things turn more and more suspenseful. Danger and discovery lurk around every corner, and the vampire girl (called Renee, at least at first) has to make her way through an uncertain world while protecting those she comes to care about. 
 That's the basic starting point for the plot, but there's a lot more going on in the book beyond the action. Some of the relationships between characters seem designed to make the reader highly uncomfortable, but...keep reading. This book reminds me a lot of things I read in college/grad school because it challenges you to continually reevaluate assumptions about power and relationships. It's a book in which immediate needs and decisions have lasting effects, and the reader is constantly rethinking things along with Renee. Characters are varied and memorable, which adds a lot of depth to the story. 
 Science fiction often has a message or messages, and here several ideas revolving around difference and interpersonal relationships come through clearly. These themes come about organically and are treated with subtlety and respect for the reader's intelligence, which I appreciated. I think that overall, the book has a hopeful tone about the possibility of overcoming certain current and historical issues. The vampire perspective is unusual and adds to the perspective-challenging quality of the book. I thought it was a very worthwhile read, and the immediacy of the main character's situation made it quite compelling as well.

One Tiny Lie is the sequel to "Ten Tiny Breaths" and this sequel is about the Kacey's little sister Livie. I liked Livie's character in "Ten Tiny Breaths" but I enjoyed her character even more in this sequel. She really broke out of her shy shell and really showed us what she's all about. In this sequel she goes to college and not only does she get her education on but she also falls in love. And she makes us fall in love too. 
 In One Tiny Lie, the author introduces you to a few characters. These characters brought so much to this book. You meet Reagan, her roomie in college. Now every one should have a roommate like her. She made me laughs so many times. With a roommate like her, your college experience will never be dull. I would really love to read a book about her. That's how interesting I found her character. 
 Then of course you meet the loves interests. They're both very interesting. But of course one is the good one, the one your parents want for you. Then you have the bad one, the one that excites you to no end. Which is the one your parents warned you about. And of course it always comes down to who wins? The heart or the mind? And almost 100% of the time the heart wins. And that's where Livie gets in trouble. She's dating Connor but can't stay away from Ashton. The chemistry between Ashton and her is real. I have had an Ashton in my life and it's intoxicating. 
 I really enjoy the banter, the chemistry between Ashton and Livie. It's almost like an addiction, that no matter how hard she tried to resist, she couldn't. Connor didn't do it for Livie and he certainly didn't do it for me either. Ms. Tucker also gave us some time with Kacey. Who happens to be hilarious! I love her and her sarcastic ways. She's come a long way from her book. It was nice to see how well she's recovered. Then you have Dr. Stayner whose unorthodox ways made his page time interesting. He's one doctor that I actually like. His unethical behavior is funny yet comforting. He played his position well and really helped Livie. 
 "One Tiny Lie" was an enjoyable read. I'm glad that Livie got her own book and that she didn't make her a goody two shoes. She broke out of her shell in this book and I loved it. The only thing I have to say about this book is that, in comparison to the first, it didnt' have that huge climax like "Ten Tiny Breaths" did. "Ten Tiny Breaths" was much more raw for me. But I still loved "One Tiny Lie". I really love Livie's character. I like her personality and her relationships with all characters. 
 I give One Tiny Lie 4 stars and it's definite a Good Choice for Reading!

 Cheater's Regret is the second book in the curious liaisons series. This is Austen and Thatch's story. I may be going against the popular vote here when I say that Cheater's Regret is my favorite book in this series. There was something about Thatch and Austen's situation that felt real. I connected with the characters more in this novel than the last. 
 We were first introduced to Austen and Thatch in the first book of this series 'Cheater'. Austen is Avery's best friend and Thatch is Lucas's main bro. 
 It was only supposed to be a one night stand between the two, however, it quickly started to evolve into a relationship that neither one was expecting. Thatch has never been able to commit to a woman given his home life wasn't always so loving while growing up, when he starts to connect on a deeper level with Austen it scares him and he decides to cut the strings and let her loose by doing the one thing that he knew would change her views on the type of man he is. He cheated. 
 Austen has dealt with cheater's in the past. So with the help of her best friend Avery the two devise a plan of payback or as some may ball it revenge. But that plan quickly comes to a halt when Austen is failing a class and needs the help of a certain plastic surgeon to boost her score back up. 
 I loved the back and forth banter Thatch and Austen had going on, I was cringing at one moment and then laughing so hard the next moment. Austen's one line moments were hilarious. She is such a random person and I related to her character the most. 
 Not going to lie Thatch was a douche canoe in the beginning but don't give up on him. He's a sweetie! 
 Overall, Cheater's Regret was amazing and I highly HIGHLY recommend it to anyone looking for a hilarious romance novel with a touch of angst. I hope you love it as much as I did, I hope you feel the emotions as I felt them and I hope Thatch and Austen touch the soft spot in your heart as they did mine.

 The fourth book in Erin Watt's dramatic and humorous YA family saga (The Royals) deals with essentially the middle child-Easton. This seemingly happy go lucky man child has some serious demons riding him from a drug and alcohol problem to unresolved guilt over his mother's suicide. When a little afternoon delight brings a new girl to his attention, Easton finds himself intrigued with the only person at Aston Prep to ever tell him no. As nothing is ever easy in the Royal Family, Easton finds himself desperate to play knight in shining armor for his new love Hartley only to discover that he needs to fix himself before he can fix anyone else. Unfortunately, it may take a tragedy to hammer that point home. 
 Erin Watt's really opens up with Easton, taking us from your average everyday sex fueled melodrama YA to a serious coming of age story that addresses love-both romantic and familial -along with loss, redemption, hope, and acceptance. Alone now that both his older brothers are gone and his younger brothers (twins) stay to themselves, I couldn't help but feel a large part of the book kept us poised on the edge, waiting for the huge cliffhanger at the end. While Easton opens and grows in here, thanks largely in part to his POV, I really felt we missed having a true connection with Hartley as well. As with any YA, there's some whining, some bad girls, some stupid decisions, and a whole lot of innuendos. :) Regardless, I am looking forward to book two as I must see how on earth Watt's plans to resolve this mess.

I loved adding the boys to this one. The Gallagher Girls, save one, haven't really had any contact with the male persuasion their own age. As Cammie learned in the last book, it isn't so easy to assimilate when you have no idea what to do when it comes to something you've never dealt with before. 
 Zach was great. He's a great character. I really enjoyed Cammie and Zach and their very interesting dealings with each other. And not just them, but the other girls as they fight for the attentions of the other boys. What I liked about this was we don't really get the full picture when it comes to the boys. There was a few lingering questions (at least for me) even after the book was done about the boys. 
 So far, this series has been fun. I love how while this isn't a typical young adult series, there isn't anything in here that could never happen. I love paranormal romance, a lot, but there is just something about a book/series that takes place in our world that I could actually imagine happening.

I first read this book last year. I don't know why, but ending left me confused and little bit disappointed back then. Maybe it was the outcome of the story and promise of another war (which I don't like in fantasy books, because they seem all the same to me) I didn't like, I don't know anymore. 
 The point is - I remember how I loved this book and how I kept talking about it to my friend - how she has to read it, how amazing it is. So I read it again. And I fell in love with it again. 
 Characters in DoS&B are just amazing. So likable and real. I really would love to have friends like Karou and Zuzana. And I would really love to punch Kaz - on behalf of the humanity. 
 I don't actually like it when the characters are overly perfect - too beautiful, too smart, too everything. But here I didn't mind. I loved Karou because she was independent. She wasn't naive, she knew how to take care of herself, but she wasn't arrogant either. She was caring and loyal. Her decisions and thoughts actually made sense (which isn't very commong in YA fantasy). She was real. 
 And what got me most (after the writing, of course) - is probably that it wasn't the same old "I am a normal (lonely) girl which falls in love with supernatural amazing (arrogant) guy". Karou was living supernatural her whole life. And she wasn't even hiding it (too much) or making big deal out of it. It was her life and even though it got on her nerves time to time, she loved it and enjoyed it. 
 Almost as much as I enjoyed reading this book. :) 
 Favorite quotes: 
 " 'All you need in this life is ignorance and confidence; then success is sure.' Mark Twain, you know. He had a fine mustache. Men of wisdom so often do." 
 "Have you ever asked yourself - do monster make war or does was make mosters?" 
 (This one actually got me thinking a lot.) 
 "I don't know many rules to live by. But here's one. It's simple. Don't put anything unnecessary into yourself. No poisons or chemicals, no fumes or smoke or alcohol, no sharp objects, no inessential needles--drug or tattoo--and...no inessential penises either." 
 And the one that made me fall in love with the series in the first place (even though almost EVERY sentence in this book is amazing): 
 "Once upon a time, an angel and a devil fell in love. 
 It did not end well."

This book reads a lot more like a Jack Reacher book than a Harry Bosch book. I found it read a little more like a spy novel than a mystery. 
 It also seems to inspire readers to love it or hate it. When I read the reviews they seem to be raves or roasts. I guess I come down on the side of the rave even though it is a bit of a departure from the normal Bosch I love so much. This book has big twists and surprises that I will not spoil but those twists are part of the reason I love this book so much. I felt those events in this book helped develop Harry's character more than many of the others and that is my weakness in books. I am a lover of character driven stories. While I love a good plot, a huge cliffhanger, a tender story, a twisted antagonist ... what I am most enchanted by is a well-developed hero with lots of flaws. This book gave me that in spades. 
 I have one big complaint about the Bosch character -- he is growing old and one of these days Connelly is going to have to leave him behind. That day will be one on which I grieve the loss of my arrogant, grumpy, stubborn friend. 
 Unlike many other reviewers, I like Cariou's approach to Bosch. He reads with a subtle approach and allows me to find Bosch more likable. When other narrators put more vehemence behind Bosch's dialogue I find him to be less appealing. Bosch is written with many failings -- which I like, but it is easy to tip the balance and have him come off as conceited instead of driven, angry instead of scarred. For me, Cariou allows Bosch to be slightly tender and soft as well as a tough, and motivated detective.
Had its moments, but overall I don't get the appeal.

 This book has been on my shelf for months, and this weekend I decided it was time to just finish it. And honestly, I liked what I saw. For the first two-thirds of the book, I'd been considering what my rating would be, and now that I've finished it, I have to say I liked the book a lot more than I expected to. This is truly a book that must be read in full, though I know some people find that hard (including me, for a while, considering it took me such a long time to read it), in order to really see the whole picture. 
 I was surprised by how graphic the book is, especially sexually, and to be perfectly honest, I wasn't sure it needed that much. It did really put us into Celeste's mind, which was absolutely necessary for the book as a whole, but it's obviously a turn-off to many readers. This is a book that does an amazing job of taking you out of your comfort zone (or mine, at least), which is essential for well-rounded reading, but sometimes it felt like Nutting was pushing for that at the expense of her own work. 
 The premise never really settled quite right with me, which I think is part of the point, but the last 50 pages or so really bring it all home. I was less than surprised by what happened at the end, but at the same time, I think that's the way this book should have ended. I wouldn't say the end brings about a sense of vindication (though for some, it might), but more of an extended understanding of the characters and the situation. 
 (view spoiler)[Honestly, I am glad that Celeste took the plea bargain and didn't wind up in jail. If she had, this would have been more of a morality play and less of a layered, nuanced novel. This is a topic that doesn't get much attention, and I think Nutting really nailed it. For Celeste, things are black and white, but Nutting does an incredible job of writing it so that we can get a look at Celeste's perception of things while still maintaining our understanding of how things should or shouldn't be. Obviously, Celeste is troubled, but Nutting masterfully explains that while keeping her in character the entire time. (hide spoiler)]

Spinning Out really grabbed my attention. The synopsis really had a good hook. The story as a whole has a good hook. There are parts I enjoyed, parts I didn't enjoy. Overall though it was a good read. One of the many things I love about Lexi Ryan is her ability to create complex, deeply emotional, relatable characters. I'm always amazed that her love triangles work for me. What I mean is, I can never decide who I want the characters to end up with. I end up loving everyone and wanting them all happy. She really makes me think differently about romantic obstacles. 
 This story is Mia and Arrow's, and boy is it super depressing. There is no light in this book. No fun. No laughing. It's just sadness, depression, grief, guilt, angst. I don't mind really. Especially if the story warrants it and I think this one does. There's really nothing to be happy about. Both Mia and Arrow are broken and just plain sad. Again it's warranted. But it gets heavy fast. 
 Told in past and present Lexi attempts to reveal everyone's truths, however the added dual pov's made it sometimes confusing and honestly I think it took away from what she was trying to build. There ended up being too much of everything and not enough oomph. What it lacked, in my opinion, was the added complexity of developed characters and the investment in their relationships. Which in the end made it harder to commit to the actual relationship between Mia and Arrow. 
 The plot though is where the meat is. Lexi Ryan is a master at whodunnit. It keeps you intrigued, guessing, flipping page after page longing for the answers. That's what keeps me coming back book after book. Her writing style is engaging and dynamic. I'm looking forward to reading more from this series.

Billy Lynn's Long Halftime Walk is set in the early aughts, when Bush was still in office, the war in Iraq was still front page news and popular support was high (at least in Texas where most of the action in the book takes place). Billy is 19, a soldier who is part of a stateside two week "victory tour" following his squadron's successful fire fight with Iraqi insurgents that just happened to be caught on camera by Fox News. The culminating stop on the tour is an appearance at a Dallas Cowboys half time show, which takes on a nightmarish quality as the soldiers are glad-handed by the public, courted by Hollywood and generally treated a like performing seals. The book levels plenty of criticism at the Bush administration, the jingoistic, dimwitted American public, the absurdity of war, etc. I just don't know that Fountain brought anything new to the table with this novel.
Not bad. Characters didn't have much of an arc and though the story tried to avoid being a cliche, it didn't manage to.

 I can admit it... I haven't really read a lot of time travel books, so I was a bit leery going into this. I don't know what I was thinking. I absolutely loved it. 
 Anna lives in 1995 in Chicago. 
 Bennett lives in 2012 in San Francisco. 
 They were never supposed to meet. 
 Bennett has an incredible ability to travel through time. There are a few catches to the whole process, but as long as he stays within the years he's been alive, he's never had any trouble, and I thought this was a wonderful twist to the story. 
 He shows up in Chicago in 1995, seemingly out of nowhere. Anna first encounters him on the bleachers while she runs one morning, only Bennett says it wasn't him. The bulk of the story takes place during this time period and it was wonderful to relive all the things that were going on back then... the music references and concerts! 
 After something happens that forces Bennett to spill his secrets to Anna, they grow closer. I couldn't help but feel nervous for these two, simply because Bennett was somewhere he wasn't supposed to be and Anna was falling for him completely. 
 I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with this information. Tell him to leave? Tell him to stay? But I don't have time to consider any other alternatives, because he scoots in closer and brings his hands to my face, and I fall back into the bookcase as he kisses me with this intensity-like he wants to be here, and if he kisses me just long enough, deeply enough, none of what he just said will actually be true. And as much as I know it's all true and that it's incredibly stupid to feel this way about someone who doesn't belong here-who, when he leaves, will hardly be a plane ride away-my hands leave the Berber carpet, find his back, and pull him toward me until I'm flat against the shelves. Because he's here now. And because I'm pretty certain I don't want this to stop. Ever. 
 After something happens and both Bennett and Anna test his abilities by changing the past and breaking his personal rules for his ability, I swear I read with a ball of nerves resting in my stomach, waiting for something to happen. I mean, they are messing with fate and I've seen that movie The Butterfly Effect. Just saying. 
 I really enjoyed the characters - definitely Anna, while I found myself a bit angry with her a few times, I thought she was written really well. I did find myself emotionally attached to her and her feelings so she obviously worked for me. 
 Bennett, once we got to know him was sweet and protective and caring and while their relationship wasn't born of the normal, he made the effort to try and give her the normal as well as the spectacularly grand and unbelievable. 
 One thing I would have liked to know more about is the manifestation of his ability. We get a brief explanation, which works for the book, but being naturally curious you wonder if there is anyone else like him, who has this talent as well ... where did it come from, why him... those kinds of things. I myself would have a hard time accepting the ability without doing tons of digging and trying to find out why me. 
 I also would have liked to know what happened with Anna in her previous life... why in the prologue does she give him the letter and what made her first choice not the right one for her. 
 I think what is most intriguing about this book is the idea of time travel itself and changing history... 'what if' ... what if you could have made a different choice in life, what if you could change the outcome of an event. All these things are intriguing and can't help but make you as a reader think of the way things might be different in your life if only... 
 Once I started this book it was hard to put down, like I said, I turned page after page nervous for these two while reading. If you're looking for a sweet contemporary YA romance than this is just the thing for you.

I'm not sure what I was expecting when I started reading this, but I was pleasantly surprised. Although it's evident J.K. Rowling didn't write this book, it almost feels like she did. G. Norman Lippert does a very good job of paying homage to not only Rowling's writing style, but her Potterverse in general. 
 Lippert included scientific-esque explanations of some of the magic the characters use and encounter. This is definitely unique, as Rowling never explained how magic worked in her books. They were handled quite well; neither overly expository, nor too long. 
 Overall, a very enjoyable book. If you enjoyed the Harry Potter series, you'll enjoy these.

It's like reading a good book. The kind where you don't want to skip pages to see what happens at the end. Each moment is a story in itself. 
 You know that feeling when you don't really expect all that much out of something and it turns out to be this wonderful, precious gem and you wonder how on earth you could have ever been indifferent towards it? Yeah... pretty much me right now. 
 Last night I went to bed thinking I would just read a couple of chapters of a new book to take my mind off another book I hadn't really liked. I picked up Swear on This Life on a whim. I was in need of something light and fun. Surprisingly, things went a whole lot differently than I had anticipated. 
 From the very first page the book had me hooked. After three chapters I knew I couldn't just put the book away and go to sleep. There was no way I could stop, I was way too invested. So I ended up reading the whole thing in one sitting. For five hours straight I let myself get lost in the world of Em and Jase, only occasionally stopping to throw an uncomfortable glance at the clock. My head was screaming to get a grip and give up already, but I couldn't until the very last page. I finished at about four am, knowing very well I was going to pay the price in the morning. Having had about two and a half hours of sleep, of course I was a complete wreck at work the next day. I barely kept myself from falling asleep at my desk and I constantly tuned out my colleagues' conversations. But I tell you - it was totally worth it! 
 I have read a book by Renee Carlino once before. Before We Were Strangers was light and fun and also completely different from this one. Swear on This Life is strangely tragic and heartwarming at the same time. It was a lot deeper and more intense than I think anyone would expect it to be. 
 In real life we have a hard time recognizing serendipitous moments because we're not making the story up as we go along. It's not a lie--it's really happening to us, and we have no idea how it will end. Some of us will look back on our lives and recall events that were a bit too perfect, but until you know the whole story, it's impossible to see the universe at work, or even admit that there is something bigger than us, making sure everything that should happen does happen. If you can surrender to the idea that there might be a plan, instead of reducing every magical moment to a coincidence, then love will find you. 
 This is the story of Jason and Emiline, childhood neighbours who grew up having no one and nothing but each other. Both victims of terrible circumstances and even worse parenting. In their desperation for an escape from life and in search for some affection, they clung to each other and created a bond unlike any other. As the years passed, their bonding only got more intense and less likely to ever break. But life kept throwing impossible challenges at them. Obstacles and difficulties so cruel that in the end the choice to spend the rest of their miserable lives together was no longer theirs to make. They are brutally torn apart and forced to spend the following years separately, pretending to be okay. 
 That's when Em finds 'the book'. The book that somehow tells her own life's story. It brings up the past that she has been fighting so hard to leave behind. There is only one person in the entire world who could have possibly known what she went through as a child. Jase wrote the book, the most demanding question is why? Why bring up something that terrible? 
 This could be the best thing for us, after it stops being the worst. 
 I loved this concept. At least half of Swear on This Life is told through the narrative of 'the book'. We simultaneously learn about the past and the present. And that past is particularly dark. Reading the first chapters I never would have guessed what I was signing myself up for. What Em had gone through before. We get to know her and Jase through Jase's writing and I absolutely loved that. We were in the main character's head, but it was through someone else's eyes that we somehow learned who she was. Or had been. The characters in the book were Em and Jase but they also weren't. It was so beautifully done! I'm completely impressed. 
 There aren't all that many characters, but they were multi-layered, relatable and well-developed. I got really invested in their stories. The feelings were honest, conflicted and compelling. The plot was split in two, past and present, and both were equally captivating. I liked the writing, the easy flow of the words and the building of the story. I think it's been clear from the very beginning of this post just how much I needed to know how it was all going to unfold. And while everything slowly started to become clear, there was still the big plot twist in 'the book' that was constantly foreshadowed and hinted at, but didn't become clear until the very end. And I desperately needed to know how it ended (hence the read-all-night policy). 
 What struck me as remarkable, though, was that Em and Jase somehow seemed younger in the present than they did in the past. I'm not entirely sure if this was a conscious decision or even intentional, but to me it made perfect sense. Their ugly childhoods had always denied them to really be children. They had been forced to grow up very early and now (in the present) it's as if being released from the burden of the past finally gave them the freedom to act a little wild and impulsive for once. Their new lives allowed them to find back some innocence and a chance to start over. 
 I don't know much about fate, but I know something brought me back there. Maybe I fought that force for too long, or maybe everything happened exactly the way it was supposed to. 
 Yes, I loved this. But I read it in the middle of the night and I'm well aware that these circumstances may have had an influence on my judgement. Yet even now that I'm no longer dead tired and once again fully functional, I still find it hard to point out flaws. I'm not saying there aren't any, but they can't have been all that bothering or important because they didn't really leave an impression on me. Is the book life changing? Nah, not really. But I haven't quite been able to leave it behind these last couple of days and that really ought to count for something. 
 And.. holy crap. Jase writing 'the book' for Em the way he did.. No matter how tragic it may have been, it is the kind of romantic gesture I would gladly sell my soul for. Seriously, where is that King of Hell when you need him. ;)

It's been awhile since I've read one of April's books, so I was delightfully surprised when I entered back into the creepy dreaminess of her fictional world(s). 
 But with that being said, Wink Poppy Midnight is definitely one of those books where actually doing a traditional review would spoil the story (and the experience!) of reading, so I'm going to keep this a bit short and a bit vague. 
 Wink Poppy Midnight is narrated by Wink, Poppy and Midnight, who are both outcasts and standouts within their small town. They each have their respective hangups, desires and issues, and Tucholke brilliantly explores them, by using first-person narration and alternating between each of their voices. 
 While a number of the trio's problems seem like fairly standard teenaged fare - e.g. Midnight has an unrequited love for Poppy, and Poppy doesn't hesitate to exploit that fact - there are elements of the story that are also classic Tucholke. She incorporates elements of the supernatural and whimsical into the trio's interactions, and interweaves them in a way that makes their struggles and tribulations feel beautifully removed from the real world. 
 Though the characters each developed organically as the story progressed, I was especially fond of Midnight's growth. Without giving spoilers away, he comes to the realization that it IS important to live is life and value what he has, verses chasing a seemingly impossible dream. It's a nice lesson, which I think will resound strongly with other readers. 
 Bottom line: Though the book is unusual, it's a worthwhile reading experience. Tucholke transforms readers into a world where lines blur between the real and hints of the fantastic, and it's an interesting, beautiful result.

 When I first began The Daughter of Smoke and Bone I had a look at the sequel on goodreads too. And what I generally found were that ratings for this book were higher than its predecessor - and on reflection I can see why. 
 Admittedly, the title is slightly misleading as it contains words other than 'blood' which should be a trade description breach because blood is a defining characteristic of this book. Yes, this book is hard going. There are scenes of war and retaliation, both from chimaera and seraphim, to the degree that my alliances were thrown away and I came to the stark realisation that I didn't really support either side. I think it would be truly impossible to wholeheartedly agree with the actions of either. 
 Which is the nature of war I suppose. 
 But Taylor did something which, until I read Insurgent, I had thought was impossible. She wrote a middle-trilogy book well. Which was not in existence merely as a first half of the last book, but an amazing standalone accomplishment. Nevertheless, I would say that there was some pacing issues, particularly in the first half, but these had very little impact on my overall enjoyment of the book. 
 Something I was amazed by again, even more so in this book I think, is the humanity of these characters. Karou and Akiva surpass their fantasy forms and become remarkably relatable as they rebel against the causes of their respective sides and find common ground. Though their romance was toned down (read: nonexistent) throughout the majority of the novel, their undeniable connection as well as the discovery of more of their memories I really loved. 
 However, all this book could ever be was a build up to the climax (to come in 2014?!) but it was remarkably good at it. I loved the discovery of Eretz and of course, I couldn't finish without mentioning her, the wonder-character that is Zuzana. There is nothing quite like Zuzana nor will there ever be. Walking into the deserts of Northern Africa in some zebra-printed trainers whilst remaining hilarious is a sight to behold and something Karou, and me, LOVES. So the cliff-hanger leaves you thinking 'WHAT. YOU FINISH THERE?!' but I was so immersed in the world by the end of the book that I didn't realise how much I was enjoying it until I finished - when I realised I needed the sequel in front of me immediately.

Tattoo artist Ash has trouble trusting people. A life that started in foster care and ended on the streets taught him to be self-reliant. Which is why even he is surprised when he starts to fall for his paramedic roommate, Pete, and the feelings seem to be mutual. What he finds with Pete helps to keep his demons at bay, and he thinks he may just be able to make it. But it can take quite a bit to exorcise the ghosts that haunt us. And a series of unexpected events and miscommunications send everything crashing down for Pete and Ash, leaving them unsure if they will be able to piece everything back together... 
 Sometimes it is easy to forget that bring able to trust someone, to give them your heart and really mean it, can be a scary and difficult prospect. And that's not just for those who have experienced heartbreak, abuse, or violence in their past. But those experiences certainly complicate matters in ways that we can't always understand. By recognizing this and understanding that everyone brings things to a relationship that are beyond their control, perhaps we can be a bit easier on ourselves and give ourselves permission to love freely, to trust another person, and to really engage. Some deep themes here in what is a well-written story of acknowledging and confronting the past rather than simply hoping it will go away.

I realized upon reading The Iron King that I was NOT into Tinkerbell and whatnot. The first 16 chapters were painful to read. I litterally had to force myself to go on. But, let's be clear, it had nothing to do with the story or the writing, it had everything to do with me. I was simply not into it. 
 Since I was never a huge fan of Narnia and deeply hated Alice in Wonderland and The Iron King reminded me of those books in some ways, it was really hard to connect to it. At first, I thought the writing was good and simple, easy breathy and to the point. Then, things got heavy. But it was probably the language barrier. I mean, I had a hard time focusing on one thing and trying to imagine it when so much was going on, the first time for Meghan in the woods. It may have been just me. 
 For me, Meghan lacked a little attitude. I expected her to be more colorful. I surely didn't expect her to go through all this so easily. She didn't seem too phased about discovering the nevernever and who she really was. Okay, she may have seen strange things before but come on.... Meghan is too ZZzzzz. There wasn't enough empathise on the "freaking out" part of her journey. Then, her best friend forever Robbie turns out to be the infamous Puck. We go from two peas in a pod to two strangers. I guess it was wanted from the author since it is how Meghan felt about Robbie when she found out her BFF wasn't who she thought he was. But, still, it felt strange to "read" Robbie as a stranger to her all of a sudden instead of her long-time sidekick. The feel of him was diminished. I had difficulty to get attached to him and care for his fate. Apparently, Meghan did too. She was worried....sometimes. But, not that much really. 
 Meghan learns a great deal along her journey. She has a king fey for a father but she leaves the Seelie court as quick as she came and we don't get to see a lot of bonding. He's still a total stranger. Then, there's Ethan. At first, I was like "what bring the kid into this? why not just take her and get on with it?" Fortunately, by the end of the book, the author connects the dots and explains it all. I was reassured. In fact, everything is connected. Maybe a little too much. She is into computers...will this come in handy later in the story? I don't know, but it can't be a coincidence. She's a half breed so she can't be hurt by iron. Lucky her, the ennemy is the iron king! And so on... Convenient, isn't it? 
 I think it became interesting for me by the 17th chapter when it's just Meghan, Puck and Ash (I love that name!). Oh and Grim, the talking cat. The story finally takes off. We don't really get a chance to see Meghan sort out her feelings for Ash. Turns out he's gorgeous, she is attracted and OMG! he's into her as well!!!!! How that for luck? They just mesh after a while. He pulls the hot and cold bullshit and finally gives in. There's definitely potential here for a great romance but it lacks passion, opportunity and pace. It happens fast and doesn't take a lot to either... It was too...high school musical for me. Meaning: too nice, too puppy love, too easy. Boring, in a nutshell. 
 The good thing is it was okay enough for me to want to read the sequel. Let's just hope it gets better. I hate starting a series knowing that I cannot not see it through and waste my time in the meantime because I won't like it. I had no prejudice towards faeries and I don't want to. Let's just hope I'll get over it and hump up on the hype train that is Kagawa's new series.

Rewriting Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None to appeal to the Pretty Little Liars crowd is a genius move. Genius! 
 Ten cleverly adapts and updates the original book -- in which ten strangers are lured to a deserted island house to be murdered one by one as punishment for past crimes -- with a scenario in which a group of Seattle-area teenagers with loosely interconnected social lives are invited to a house party by a popular cheerleader. Like the movie Scream, Ten features characters who are well-versed in the conventions of teen horror films. 
 Regular blog readers know that I'm a huge mystery fan, and I loved the fact that Ten is a true mystery, with all the clues laid out for sharp-eyed readers to find. While I guessed a major plot twist -- possibly because I remembered the original book -- I missed one crucial clue and had my eye on the wrong person as the killer. 
 I'm pretty sure the original book had no romance, so I was happy that as poor Meg tries to keep herself alive, she's distracted to be spending the weekend with a classmate she has a huge crush on -- a guy she ditched as her homecoming date so as not to make Minnie jealous. Minnie and Meg have one of those weird girl frenemy relationships going, which also added a bit of depth to this fast-paced plot. 
 Ten is a fun, fast-paced read that should keep you guessing up until the end!

 The best scenes in this story are when Kate and Anthony are sparring. It's when we see Anthony coming alive and Kate's spunk. I'm finding I like the heroines in this series as much as their male partners, if not more. He showed real depth when he could see in Kate what everyone else seemed to miss. I loved their chemistry as it was based on their compatibility more so than an instant physical connection. We got a chance to see a romance develop in a much more exciting way because they challenged each other. 
 There were times when I worried that Anthony would treat Kate cruelly and he came close a few times. It would have been easy for Quinn to go that route and the story was strengthened because she did not. It was also realistic for Kate and Edwina to have a healthy sibling relationship in spite of the differences in physical attributes and for Mary to be a loving stepmother. I found it refreshing. 
 This is a good story that plodded along at times but the great scenes made up for those lapses. I'm still enjoying the series and look forward to the next book.

 I am with Ky in not trusting The Rising. In my opinion, they have way too many similarities to The Society. 1) The members of The Rising, can only know about what they are assigned to. 2) People are still sorted. Also, it is clear that they were the ones to wipe out the Farmers. They are no better than The Society and I do not trust them. Also, I think it was The Rising who put Ky into the matching pool, because they somehow knew that Cassia would get him to join with them. 
 Also, as much as I hate to say it, I don't know if I really trust Xander, as much as I want to. There were a couple of moments where I doubted his intentions. I really hope I am wrong. However, for someone who knew a lot about the red and green pills, he should have known what the blue pills really do. 
 The long distance love triangle is probably the most annoying part of the book. Cassia just fled her society, and risked her life for Ky, but she is still thinking about Xander. I mean, come on, everything Cassia has done will have been for nothing if she all of a sudden decides Xander is the one for her. Her feelings for Xander feel very forced, especially since Xander is practically nonexistent. 
 One thing I did enjoy about this book, was Ky's point of view. I feel like I understand his character much better now, although I still feel that there is a lot to be learned. Ky really needs to learn how to open up. I like Ky, but he is far from one of my favorite fictional characters. 
 All in all, Crossed is just alright. It is no Delirium or Divergent, but if you are a big fan of dystopians, you will probably enjoy this.

 An Unnatural Vice is a wonderful and engrossing enemies-to-lovers story! It introduces new characters, but follows some of the events in the first installment of this series, An Unseen Attraction. It has an added element of mystery that keeps you on your toes, some paranormal shenanigans, and complex and developed characters. 
 K.J. Charles continues to deliver entertaining and fast-paced novels. This one is action packed, and a great mixture of mystery and romance. It has some steamy and sweet scenes to counterbalance the dangerous ones, and keeps you flipping pages the entire time to figure out what's going on. 
 Once again, K.J. Charles gives us well-developed and complex characters, one of which has a unique profession. Justin's work is super interesting to read about, especially with the way it ties together with the plot and last installment's mystery arc. It gives him an edge as a character, especially as you struggle to empathise with him and his line of work. 
 The conflict in this novel is also really engrossing and well-thought it. Like mentioned above, it brings up things from An Unseen Attraction. This book also reveals and adds to the main mystery left over from the previous installment - the Godfrey kids, while also providing new twists and obstacles for Nathaniel and Justin to face. It's such a delight to read about their relationship and feelings changing as they get to know each other, and makes the romance rather sweet at the end. 
 In the end, An Unnatural Vice is a great addition to this series. It's a fun book with an intriguing mystery, and definitely worth a read if you enjoy historical mysteries with a dash of romance.

Then we have her love interest Sergeant Amarok, I love him so much! He is very patient, strong, protective and loyal. I just loved reading about them. Picked this one up for a bit of light fun, which it provided. I'm not sure about the comparisons to Gail Carriger's books -- sure, the period is roughly the same and the covers have some commonalities, but Alexia is a lady and India is a mercenary whore (and I mean that literally, not pejoratively). The kind of humour is different -- sharper, less light, often relying on India's bitter attitude toward, well, almost everyone. Carriger does have Alexia being more intelligent than a lot of people, but she also has more interaction with other intelligent characters (including other women). The emphasis on romance is entirely lacking in India Black, too. 
 Still, as a quick romp with a bit of spy/thriller/mystery stuff going on, it's quite fun. It's in first person from the point of view of India herself, and she's pretty sharp and cutting about the world, and knowing about the way things are. That gives her a pretty fun voice. 
 In terms of the plot... it's not too tight, with a fair amount of coincidence and people just being stupid. It's not bad for a light bit of fun, though.

Fair Warning : This review has not been made directly after finishing the book. I read These Broken Stars around last month, with a whole bunch of books wedged between then and now. 
 I really, really, really enjoyed this book. There was just so much to love- the writing style, the unique characters, the plot, everything. 
 Characters 
 After reading YA books on a regular basis, you begin to notice a pattern consisting of cliche characters- we have the female protagonist who starts off as meek, unaware of her great beauty/power, and the male protagonist/love interest who captures our heroine's attention with his gorgeous face and body and helps our gal realize what an incredible person she is. 
 For These Broken Stars, this was not the case. I love how Lilac and Tarver knew exactly who they are. Their confidence, their character background, and their personality really shine through. 
 Due to their being shipwrecked, Lilac goes through the natural (but brief) damsel-in-distress mode but she pulls her shite together and (view spoiler)[ even ends up being the one to take care of Tarver for a bit! Since I already warned you about spoilers, I might as well throw in the fact that she was the one to bravely light the explosives (though that didn't exactly work to her advantage) Anyways, I'm glad that at the end, we find that she wasn't going crazy (See? More points for our strong Lilac) and that she was in fact right about the voices (hide spoiler)] 
 We were introduced to Tarver as him being the strong, tough characters who's so bad-ashe and can take care of himself. There are scenes in which he cracks and we see his beautiful vulnerability, (view spoiler)[ the scene where Lilac dies and his grief following it (hide spoiler)] and that for me highlighted his change. 
 Setting & Plot 
 I loved how well Amie Kaufman described Icarus and the foreign planet in which they are later stranded on. These Broken Stars is that type of book where you don't just want to know what happened, you want to take your time and soak up all the details and imagine the setting the characters are in. 
 I love love loved the plot. I love the connection that Lilac is revealed to have with the planet, I love the sweet scenes between Lilac and Tarver so much that I kept going back just to read them again. I loved all the little twist and shocking moments. I'm not even going to bother spoiling these for you- you just have to read the scenes yourself. 
 Writing Style 
 I was intrigued by the dual POVs, and honestly of all the books I read, I think These Broken Stars really nailed this. Through their separate perspectives, we were able to see how they both coped with their struggle to stay alive, and also their affections for one another. 
 I seriously urge you to grab a copy NOW. The only reason I haven't given this book a full 5 stars is because the book was a little light for my taste. Other than that, it was pretty much excellent. 
 Happy reading! :)

 "And we believe you why?" asks Tattoo. He's found a letter opener from somewhere and is checking out the edge. 
 "Because I'm a human being and so are you. That puts us on the same team, like it or not." 
 I've been so disappointed with sequels of late. The Infinite Sea and Mortal Gods all let me down horribly and I loved the heck out of their predecessors. 
 Then this brilliant miracle dropped into my lap. 
 "He glares at me as if he already hates it. "What is it?" I consider lying but what's the point? I clear my throat. "Pooky Bear." 
 He's silent for so long I'm beginning to think he didn't hear me when he finally says, "Pooky. Bear." 
 "It was just a little joke. I didn't know." 
 "I've mentioned that names have power, right? Do you realize that when she fights battles, she's going to have to announce herself to the opposing sword? She'll be forced to say something ridiculous like, 'I am Pooky Bear, from an ancient line of archangel swords.' Or, 'Bow down to me, Pooky Bear, who has only two other equals in all the worlds.' " He shakes his head. "How is she going to get any respect?" 
 The first half is tedious, I admit. Last book, we saw Raffe bringing a seemingly dead Penryn back to her family and after she wakes up, she explores the Resistance. There's a distinct whiff of Second Book Syndrome since nothing essential happens. She runs around, stumbles onto bits of information, and internally monologues. 
 The good thing is she doesn't dwell on Raffe excessively. I was scared she would because World After used the infamous male-lead-leaves-in-the-second-book cliche. 
 New Moon, Crescendo, Days of Blood & Starlight, anyone? 
 Penryn gets shit done. She takes care of her sister, whom was kidnapped in the first book and returned a scarred, monstrous sight. She takes care of her mentally ill mom, who used their food tokens for rotten eggs to ward bad spirits. 
 She gets sword-fighting lessons from Raffe's sword, which is semi-sentient, and it's really cool except for the obvious fan service element. She gets to see Raffe's thoughts, including when they first met and or him wrapping her sleeping form in his arms for warmth. 
 "Her voice is insistent but melodic. It's a good sound to die to." 
 Look at that and tell me it's not direct-to-reader pandering. 
 I can't help but feel World After would've been so much better if Paige had her own POV. Before, she was sweet, defenseless Prim 2.0. Here, she's the creepy little girl that crawls out of a TV screen. 
 "She's powerful enough to seriously challenge them and give them a real fight. On this uneven terrain, she might be able to throw them off balance and make them fall. 
 Instead she struggles ineffectively. 
 Just enough the ropes cut into her. Just enough to hurt in punishment. Just enough so no one gets hurts." 
 She's the anti-heroine The Young Elites wishes it had. Feared, shunned and misunderstood. A vegetarian animal-lover at heart yet hungers for raw meat. Penryn is boring in comparison to that goldmine of character development. 
 Still pretty awesome though. And so is this book.

 Rag and Bone is a mix of Regency, fantasy, and mystery, and while some parts were stronger than others, the two heroes and the rapidly developing plot kept me reading for hours longer than I intended. 
 Before I get into what I liked about this story, I want to give you a heads up about its location in a larger world, and in a series. This book is part of the Charm of Magpies world, and I haven't read any of the other books in the series. I'm pretty sure I met some past characters, or maybe future characters, in this book, and their presence didn't detract from the story for me. There is also a prequel novella to this story, A Queer Trade, which I haven't read, and I don't think you need to read it to understand this book. That said, the romance elements might have been more developed or more pronounced in this book if I'd read the prior novella, which details how Ned and Crispin met. 
 The mix of mystery, fantasy, and romance worked really well for me. I read this book in one sitting, which isn't difficult given that it's about 145 pages, but I didn't want to stop reading. I liked that the relationship started in what I would call the late-beginning/early-middle stage, where both men knew and liked one another, but weren't sure how to make a permanent connection work emotionally or logistically. I really liked Crispin's magical talent and would eagerly read a whole series just about graphomancy and how writing can create magic. The dialogue was also intensely layered, because each character was trying to communicate clearly, but they misread one another's motivations, and a lot of the time ended up talking at cross-purposes. Their understanding of each other was hampered by their insecurities, and they couldn't bring themselves to be honest about those feelings until closer to the end of the story. 
 I wish there had been more space for both Ned and Crispin's characters to have been developed and explored; there was just enough backstory for each man to make their actions and decisions logical and credible, but I wanted more, in part because I liked reading about them so much. For a shorter story in a world I haven't read before, I found this book to be rich and enjoyable, with a good balance of emotional complications that seemed logical within that world, and a mystery that had real stakes for both the world and the individual protagonists.

Seriously. Where did this book come from? Or maybe the better question is what the hell have I been doing the past few years that this was out, and I was reading much less impressive books? 
 I am going to keep this review short and sweet...much like this book. 
 Mia gets in an accident very early on in the book. The remainder of the book is her watching the events post-accident unfold (mostly in the hospital) and memories of her life. This could have gone south for me very quickly. It sounded a bit too much like The Lovely Bones, which I detested. So what was so superb about this one that I gave it five stars and bumped it over to my favorites list? 
 1. The MC, Mia, is not an annoying, cliche Mary Sue. She has a best friend who is as wonderful as she is. I often find in these books that the best friend is either much cooler than the MC. But these two truly act like best friends. As equals. She has a boyfriend and doesn't act like a total wet blanket around him. She isn't full of teen angst and actually loves and respects her parents (which would be hard not to because they are exceptionally cool parents). She doesn't talk about how irritating her little brother is but instead how funny he is. I have a younger brother who is ten years younger than I am (the same age gap between Mia and her brother) and felt a familiar tug when she described their relationship. 
 2. The other characters. The best friend, boyfriend, parents, grandparents, little brother. They felt very real to me. 
 The best friend, Kim, is everything you would want in a best friend. She is honest, comical, supportive. The boyfriend, Adam, is everything you would want in a boyfriend. Loving, romantic, accepting. What makes this work is that they are not without their flaws and still have normal arguments with the Mia that you would really have with your best friend or boyfriend. It didn't feel fake or forced. 
 Mia's family is amazing. They are the family I think I will have with my children minus the punk hair and leather (I have a strong fear of leather pants after the episode where Ross wore them on Friends). Even her grandparents are amazing. 
 I am pretty sure I feel in love with Mia's mother after this line (stated while in labor): 
 Don't be scared, she'd whisper. Women can handle the worst kind of pain. You'll find out one day. Then she'd scream fuck again. 
 3. The story is never boring. I read this in one day. I couldn't put it down even though it was only available on the computer, and I had to lug my laptop around with me everywhere - the laundry room, the bathroom, the kitchen...you get the idea. There was a lot of talk about music. There was a lot about Mia and her cello and her love of classical music. Let me tell you right now: 
 I FUCKING HATE WHEN A MAIN CHARACTER IN A YOUNG ADULT BOOK RECOGNIZES RANDOM CLASSICAL MUSIC PLAYING IN AN ELEVATOR/WAITING ROOM/'93 BUICK CENTURY EVEN THOUGH THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NOTHING TO INDICATE HOW OR WHY THEY WOULD KNOW THIS. 
 However, Mia's love for classical music actually made sense. It was supported by an actual background that would make her appreciate this type of music. Gayle Forman, I cannot thank you enough for doing this. 
 4. This book made me cry. Several times. At one point, I was doing the ugly sob with my hand clamped over my mouth. Here's the deal. A couple months ago, I went on some fun meds because of some super fun things called depression and anxiety (winter bums me out, yo. This medication can make me feel like a robot, which is usually better than feeling like I am on the verge of having an anxiety attack every two seconds. I am the big baby cry face in our family who hasn't teared up since going on this medication. This book completely messed me up and broke through my medicinal no-feelings wall. And I was actually relieved to feel again. And then I got a little freaked out thinking what a wreck I would have been had I read this a few months ago! 
 This book is beautiful. It is very well written, flowing so well with no awkward sentences. It immersed me in fictional Mia's life and made me stop and think about my own (very real) life. I cannot wait to read the next book. 
 Bravo!

These novels are not quite as bad as I remember, now that I'm reading them all back-to-back instead of waiting years to read each one, but they're still not as good as the earlier examples in the series. I can tell now what Jordan was trying to accomplish with the way he stretched out the story a bit thinner over the next few books, but I don't really like the end result. 
 The biggest problem is the pacing. There's a lot of space spent on things I didn't particularly find interesting--Mat's affair with Tylin, Rand running from place to place like a hamster on speed, endless descriptions of how hot it is and how much people are sweating and what they're wearing--and the things that I did want know about are compressed by everything else. The invasion of Illian, which has been in the background for two books, is dealt with by a snap decision from Rand, Traveling, and Sammael getting punked. The Sea Folk searching for their Coramoor is resolved by Rand showing up, saying, "I'm the Dragon Reborn, kneel, now," and then pushing any further negotiations onto the Aes Sedai that serve him. Egwene and the Salidar rebels are only briefly in a viewpoint chapter, Loial vanishes for something like four books after this based on one line from Rand, and Perrin is barely there at all. 
 Oh, and Cadsuane Melaidhrin, who will play an important part from this point on, the oldest known living Aes Sedai, a woman who, if you hear the sisters talk, walked across the Erinin to get to the White Tower, demanded that the Amyrlin Seat let her write her name in the novice book, ate lunch, then passed the tests for Accepted and for the shawl back to back, a woman so legendary Aes Sedai barely dare to whisper her name...appears out of nowhere for the first time. You'd figure that if she were so amazingly important, someone would have mentioned her before. 
 Another problem is that A Crown of Swords doesn't really have any self-contained plot. In The Eye of the World, plenty of other stuff happens, but they have to find the Eye, and by the end of the book, they do. In The Great Hunt, the Horn of Valere is stolen at the beginning of the book, and they go through difficulties and travel far, but by the end, they've recovered it. 
 There's nothing like that in A Crown of Swords. Basically every plot here began in a previous book--the Bowl of the Winds, the Seanchan invasion, the Shaido running around and causing trouble, the invasion of Illian, hunting the Black Ajah, the sea Folk embassy, etc.--or begins here but isn't resolved. One of the big things that struck me about the series when Brandon Sanderson took over was that the novels became self-contained again. Of course they drew on the ongoing plot, but each novel had its own narrative arc that didn't rely on the novels on either side of it to actually provide structure. 
 I think the best action would have been to combine Lord of Chaos and A Crown of Swords into a single book. Cutting out the irrelevant description of the embroidery on people's clothes would probably provide plenty of space, and it'd be a stronger narrative arc. You'd see all of Sammael and Graendal's attempts to manipulate the Shaido, the midpoint would be Rand's capture, transportation, and then Dumai's Wells, and it'd lead to the planning of the invasion, the invasion of Illian, and Sammael going down like a chump, all of this interwoven with trimmed versions of the other plotlines. It'd be a much more satisfying novel, and would avoid a lot of the tendencies of the next few novels where reading the prologue, the first chapter, and the last chapter provides you with basically all of the important plot developments. 
 On the positive side, one benefit of all the time spent on characterization is that we do finally get a point of view from Aviendha that helps flesh her out to more than just the Aiel tsundere, and the differing viewpoints from Mat and from Elayne and Nynaeve do a very good job of showing why a lot of the characters don't communicate very well. From Mat's viewpoint, Elayne and Nynaeve are horribly stuck-up, ungrateful prigs whose entire mission in life is to give him tons of work, waste his time, complain about his choice of leisure activities, and make his life miserable. From Elayne and Nynaeve's viewpoints, Mat is an inveterate rogue and wastrel who has become degenerate since leaving the Two Rivers, is so full of himself it's amazing that he doesn't float away, and keeps doing stupid things that just require Elayne and Nynaeve to fix instead of doing what they say like he should. The points where they break out of the characterization that the other has set for them, and the differing contrasts between their viewpoints, are one of the things that makes all the descriptions of people's bosoms and the patterns of their clothing and the color of the hair worthwhile reading. 
 In reference to my previous rant about Taim, Moridin refers to "these so-called Aiel" at one point. In reference to my rant about linguistics, the last page talks about something being translated into the "vulgar tongue," but it's dated 300 years after the Breaking. I figured the Old Tongue had lasted longer than that, since Mat has memories of it at least through to Hawkwing's time, but the use of vulgar tongue means it's obviously supposed to parallel the way Classical Latin and Vulgar Latin separated, which makes it even more bizarre that there's still one common language after 3000 years. A common language in a post-scarcity technomagical utopia that already has a common culture and a unified government makes sense. In an inexplicably socially and technologically static pseudo-medieval world, it makes a lot less sense. 
 That does lead into a major complaint I have, not specifically about this book, but about the series as a whole up to this point. No one can deny that destiny occupies an enormous amount of thematic space in the Wheel of Time series, and with all the talk about the past, and all the "The Wheel weaves as the Wheel wills," you'll realize it at the end of the first book. The problem is that as the series goes on, more and more stuff seems to be happening just because of destiny!! 
 Take Egwene rediscovering Traveling. She learns how to travel physically in the World of Dreams from the Aiel, and then when Moghedien talks about Traveling, her response is just, "Like this, right?" and she weaves a gateway. Or in A Crown of Swords, Moridin's mention of all the stuff that Aes Sedai can do in the Third Age that they couldn't do in the Second, like unpicking weaves, healing severing, or the Warder bond. This despite that the Age of Legends had actual research universities devoted to studying the One Power. Hundreds of Collam Daan researchers outdone by Nynaeve randomly shoving Fire and Spirit into Logain's head until he can channel again. 
 The problem with predestination is that it removes agency. Who cares whether Elayne, Egwene, and Nynaeve made all these discoveries, since it was fated by the Wheel anyway that they be available for the next Age, just as their loss in the Breaking was probably fated and the 3000 years of nothing happening but the Trolloc Wars and the War of the Hundred Years was also fated. Rand winning is fated, as is his losing a hand, Mat's losing an eye is fated, etc. Min's viewings make everything worse, really, because it's stated multiple times that they always come true. None of this would be so much of a problem if the story was tighter and faster-paced, but when there's a lot of meandering and sniffing and pulling of braids, it comes to the fore a lot more strongly. Jordan weaves as Jordan wills, I guess, and he wills that we spend thousands of words on people's clothing and how hot the weather is. 
 Oh, one final thing on the subject of unfortunate implications--there are no trans people in the Wheel of Time, and not only that, they are cosmologically banned by the rules of the universe. You can tell because of Aran'gar. Aran'gar, nee Balthamel, can still use saidin even though he's currently in a woman's body. This implies that the ability to touch the True Source is a property of the soul, not the body (despite that The World of Robert Jordan's The Wheel of Time claims it's genetic)), and furthermore implies that souls have genders. Assuming that, and that in WoTland a trans person would have a mismatched soul and body, presumably at some point in the last 3000 years there would have been at least one apparently female channeler who went made and rotted while alive, or one apparently male channeler who the Aes Sedai would have been very interested in studying. Not only that, but Moghedien also seems astonished to see Aran'gar using saidin, which implies that this kind of thing was unknown even in the Age of Legends, when there was a standardized testing system for all children so that anyone who could channel was properly trained. 
 So, yeah. Stuff like this is why the gender portrayal in Wheel of Time is even more problematic than your normal variety of Men->Mars/Women->Venus idiocy, and I haven't even talked about how in any circle greater than 13 men have to have control, or how men are almost always stronger in the Power than women, etc., etc. I'm pretty sure anyone who's read the series up to this point could not have failed to miss those. At this point, it's not enough to ruin the book for me, but I'm definitely noticing this kind of thing more and more as I go through the series.
