Spider-Woman Vol 1: Spider-Verse written by Dennis Hopeless and illustrated by Greg Land contains issues #1-4 of the latest (Marvel Now) Spider-Woman comics and an origin story issue from 1971 to bulk it out. I previously posted a short review of Issue #1. 
 I feel a bit bad for Spider-Woman on this run because it's very much squeezed between two events (if you consider that Vol 2 leads into Last Days). This volume deals with some of Spider-Woman's adventures during the Spider-Verse event, which also involve Silk (pictured on the cover), Spider-Gwen (who is great) and Spider-Girl (Anya, briefly). The Spider-Verse event (which I thought was explained sufficiently within the comic -- a nice change) centres around a bunch of bad guys who want to eat all the spider-people. It kind of reminded me of the Family of Blood from Doctor Who. The story in this volume starts of focusing on Spider-Woman and other protecting Silk, who seems to strongly attract bad guys. The mission takes them across universes and past doppelgangers until the day is more or less saved (something which obviously involves story lines in other books) and the event winds up. 
 The fourth issue winds up the most recent chapter of Jessica Drew's life and sets her up to get a new costume (spoiler) in the following issue, which will be in Volume 2. It was a one-shot story involving Carol Danvers and Steve Rogers (Captains Marvel and America) a small bad to fight, and of course many quips. 
 The last issue, from 1971, which was bundled into this volume, tells yet another origin story of Spider-Woman. Honestly, it's not that terrible, although it is that ridiculous. It starts with Spider-Woman as a Hydra agent and,via an encounter with Nick Fury (disappointingly white), ends with her questioning everything she'd been lead to believe. It was a bit melodramatic, but on the scale of weird old comics I've read, really not as offensive as it could've been. But overall, meh. 
 It's interesting to see that Spider-Woman's costume hasn't changed since the 70s (except for maybe her hair) and that makes her recent update all the more exciting. Her costume isn't the worst ever since it at least covers her, but it does tend to be drawn with unrealistically clingy fabric. And so, while I enjoyed the story in this volume, there were a few slightly icky art moments. Nothing too egregious, but boobs that were too big -- which bothered me most on Spider-Gwen, for whatever reason -- and a few weird poses. This is the series that had the particularly anatomically incorrect cover for issue #1, so perhaps I shouldn't be too surprised. It's disappointing, but on the other hand, I was pleased to see that cover wasn't included in the cover gallery at the back or anywhere else in the volume. 
 I am looking forward to the next volume of Spider-Woman (out next year :-/ ) and I enjoyed this volume. I'm not sure whether I would recommend it to readers who aren't already fans of Spider-Woman or Silk (or at a stretch Spider-Gwen). I don't think it stands alone that well and I suspect the next volume will actually be a better jumping on point (although I say that without having read any of it). On the other hand, this made me even more eager to read Spider-Gwen (I'm waiting for the trade) and has also made me interested in Silk, about whom I didn't know much before. 
 4 / 5 stars

 After the big shocker in the last book, Kate and Curran have left the pack to allow Kate's dear old dad, Roland, to say he "punished" them for Kate claiming the city. Now Curran is patrolling the 'burbs in beast form and scaring all the busybody neighbors out of their wits. And they also sit down to dinner with Roland... at Applebee's. So is he a super bad guy, is he a doting dad, or what? I am on the fence about this one... I think I know which way it's gonna go, but I still hold out a little hope for Kate and Roland to develop some kind of fluffy bunny familial tie. (I'm delusional, I know.) 
 Though Kate and Curran have left the pack, the pack hasn't really left them. They constantly have pack members (or former pack members) coming to them for help, showing up at their breakfast table, and even moving in next door. In just one situation, they discover that Eduardo (the werebison) is missing after taking on gigs at the Mercenary Guild. Their investigation into Eduardo's whereabouts puts them on the path of killer zombies, odd shapeshifters that don't die, and an ancient evil newly awakened. Although the action in this series is always good, this one was not quite as up to par for me as the books with Roland and Hugh d'Ambray and Hera. However, like previous books, the Andrews' writing team continues to weave wonderful aspects of mythology into the story, and we get to experience some Arabic mythology in this latest installment. I really enjoy these aspects of the story. 
 I love seeing Kate and Curran's domestic life, and I think the community and family they are building outside of the pack is going to have a really special dynamic. Though it does seem weird referring to Jim as the Beast Lord - that will always be Curran for me. We get another great bathtub scene in this book, which harkens me back to the days of Coronas and a hot tub during the Games. I wish I could elaborate on it a little more but I am writing this review almost a month after I listened to the audiobook. (Procrastination, thy name is Jen.)

Reamde starts out as the story of Richard Forthrast, a black sheep of his family of sorts, living in a Schloss and seemingly quite wealthy. The story starts at a family reunion, where he notices a niece that he hasn't seen in a while, and decides to arrange for a job for her. 
 Four months later, she's working for his company (though he is retired), visiting him with a somewhat dodgy boyfriend, and about to embark on a high tech thriller type adventure. I won't give away the plot (if you want to read a review that mercilessly reveals almost every important thing that happens in the 1000 pages, look no further than The Guardian: http://www.guardian.co.uk/books/2011/...). But let's just say it starts out as a near future, Cory Doctorow-esque story about a computer game and a virus (and the future of MMPOG economics), and then loses its way as mafia and terrorists start appearing... 
 The most striking thing about Reamde is that it really only has one character type - or at least, the author only ever chooses to follow one character type around in his close third person narration. That character type is eminently competent, resourceful, uber-smart, constantly alert to psychological implications of each and every interaction with others, and with a certain amount of wit and humour. It does not matter whether the character is male, female, black, white, Asian, Russian, a goodie, a baddie, an Osama Bin Laden wannabe... they are all the same people, just having different intentions. It's like a chess game with a handful of queens on one side, a bunch of pawns and a queen on the other. (The pawns being the non-starring incompetent characters of the story - so interchaengeable that many of them remain nameless). 
 Once you get used to reading about this veritable army of Mary Sues (for, let's face it, that's what they appear to be), you'll probably start noticing that there are really only three gears in this story: 
 Gear 1: Infodump explanations and exposition. Like Cory Doctorow, this author loves to explain every detail of the world that he knows about to his readers. 
 Gear 2: Slightly witty dialogue or slightly witty narration. 
 Gear 3: Bullet-time action. Seriously, you may read two pages about a series of actions that takes less than half a second - the author likes to zoom in to every detail, where each foot is, what's in each hand, what the character is thinking and evaluating (and my, do they evaluate. Seriously, sometimes they seem to have an essay's worth of thoughts, mid-fall from a walk to the ground)... 
 At some point, this runs into a problem: the more time we spend with an antagonist, the more he gets to be quipping and charming and interesting to be around. That takes away a lot of their ability to be scary - and so the author runs away from that problem by not really giving us many talky scenes with the antagonist(s) after a certain point. 
 I started reading this book, expecting something of average length, with a bit of scifi, and an interesting perspective. Instead, I got a really long book, with minimal scifi, and some vague insights into possible futures for MMPOGs. The length would not be a problem, if the plot and the characters warranted it. Unfortunately, the plot and characters could just as easily have been found in a Michael Crighton novel. 1000 pages of Michael Crighton style plots and characters is a bit much... 
 There is enough stuff happening for the book to feel like a thriller, but ultimately, it's a bit boring. Gunfights and explosions are simply more impressive in movies, and by the fiftieth time a character wonders whether they will be psychologically scarred by something, or psychologically analysis a short conversation with their antagonist, or deduces actual events, Sherlock Holmes style, from minor clues... well, I sort of did not really like anyone in this book any more, because no one in here came across as a believable human being...

 This was such a fun book to read and quickly became one of my favorite YA series. Seventeen-year-old Gwen Frost is new to the Mythos Academy in her small hometown. A Gypsy with the gift of psychometry, the ability to touch an object or person and get a feeling of the emotions attached to it (which also allows her to start a lucrative side business of locating lost objects), Gwen was recruited by a teacher at the school, Professor Metis, six months earlier, shortly after the death of her mother. While Gwen's gift makes her different in the regular world, at Mythos she's seemingly below average, as every student is descended from mythological warriors including Spartans, Valkyries, Romans, Ninjas and so on. At Mythos they're being trained to be warriors in the war against Chaos, started by Loki, who's now imprisoned for the second time, and continued by his Reapers of Chaos who are also trying to free their god. 
 After a popular student is killed in the library and an ancient artifact that could help Loki's cause goes missing, Gwen decides it's time to use her gift to find out who really murdered the student and why. 
 Gwen was such a real character, her thoughts and actions seemed like such a normal teenager, despite her gift, which didn't make her all-knowing or super powerful, though there is more to her than meets the eye or else she wouldn't be at a school filled to the brim with fighters, particularly since she isn't one, or attractive to every living male at the school. She's actually looked down upon by most of the students at the school who also don't understand why someone who isn't a fighter is at Mythos. However, she does attract the attention of Logan Quinn, the hottest Spartan in school, who seems to be hiding something as well, which will hopefully be revealed in the next book. I loved Logan as a romantic interest for Gwen, despite the fact that at the end of the book I wanted to backhand him until he was spitting Chiclets. She is attracted to him almost immediately (but seriously, who doesn't feel an immediate attraction to someone they find smoking hot?) but not only doesn't let me him know how she feels but gives him crap about flirting with her. Additionally, their relationship does move fairly slowly and they do become friends before any hint of romance beyond flirtation appears. 
 Daphne was a terrific character. She starts out as your typical one-dimensional, social butterfly, mean girl antagonist but slowly becomes more of a well-rounded character with more depth to her than previously thought. She turns out to be the perfect ally for Gwen as she tries to solve the murder. 
 Jennifer Estep has written a fast-paced book with a good plot, nice world-building and intriguing characters. She's also added a lot of humor to it; every time Gwen called Logan a man-whore, which was fairly often, I cracked up. And her first conversation with him? Hilarious. 
 I'm so glad that the students study at Mythos Academy until they're twenty-one, that means more books can be set at the school well beyond the usual age of seventeen for other YA books that take place during high school. And I recently read that Estep is under contract for a total of six books. If they continue to be as terrific as Touch of Frost, I'll keep reading. 
 I really can't wait to start the second book in the series, Kiss of Frost.

 But the story is still told in 1st person POV of Emma and in the 3rd person POV of Galen. I usually don't complain when a book is in alternate POVs of the main characters, but I feel that here, the story didn't really flow smoothly. (Probably due to the fact that one chapter was written in the first person, then the next would be in the third person?) But then again, I was really okay with the alternate POVs because Emma and Galen didn't really get to spend a lot of quality time together. So with the alternate POVs, the reader won't miss Galen at all! 
 Speaking of Galen... 
 Hot syrena prince anyone? I think Galen is a great male lead because he is fiercely protective of all those he loves, not only Emma. He is willing to do anything for their safety. He's intelligent and very gifted as you will find out.

 Six of Crows by Leigh Bardugo 
 Book One of the Six of Crows series 
 Publisher: Henry Holt and Company 
 Publication Date: September 29, 2015 
 Rating: 4 stars 
 Source: ARC gifted (thank you, Kel!) 
 Summary (from Goodreads): 
 Ketterdam: a bustling hub of international trade where anything can be had for the right price--and no one knows that better than criminal prodigy Kaz Brekker. Kaz is offered a chance at a deadly heist that could make him rich beyond his wildest dreams. But he can't pull it off alone... 
 A convict with a thirst for revenge. 
 A sharpshooter who can't walk away from a wager. 
 A runaway with a privileged past. 
 A spy known as the Wraith. 
 A Heartrender using her magic to survive the slums. 
 A thief with a gift for unlikely escapes. 
 Six dangerous outcasts. One impossible heist. Kaz's crew is the only thing that might stand between the world and destruction--if they don't kill each other first. 
 What I Liked: 
 Okay, fine. The hype for this book is totally justified. Whether you read Bardugo's Grisha trilogy or not, whether you enjoyed it or not, you could easily fall in love with Six of Crows. On that note, you do not need to have read - or even liked - the Grisha trilogy. It's not necessary at all! The Grisha references are the setting, the locations and places. No characters make cameos (that I remember - but I'm shaky on my Grisha knowledge sometimes), nothing dire you needed to know from the Grisha trilogy. Set in the same world, but in totally different places, with totally different characters. 
 Kaz Brekker is the most dangerous person in the Barrel, in Ketterdam. He is a gifted thief with an insatiable desire for money, and for solving puzzles and having all the tricks. He always has the drop on everyone, and he takes very risky risks that always seem to work in his favor. When Kaz is presented an opportunity with a large payout and even great risks, he has no other choice but to take it. He and five other unique individuals embark on a job, an impossible heist, to capture one thing and bring it back. But getting into the Ice Court is suicide, and getting there might prove even more perilous before the job has even begun. 
 I think the thing that I liked the most about this book is that the tone of the book isn't gloom and doom, save the world, martyr or die trying kind of tone, like in Shadow and Bone/Siege and Storm/Ruin and Rising. It's not Alina fighting within herself on whether or not she should obtain all the amplifiers to defeat the Darkling. It's not all about destroying something. No, the tone of this book was so much more... adventurous than Bardugo's previous trilogy. I wouldn't necessarily say more "fun", because there is no way I'd describe this book as fun like it's some lighthearted adventure novel, but it is certainly more reader-friendly, with less heartache and gloom and doom, and more laugh-out-loud, head-spinning action. 
 I absolutely adore the cast of characters. Kaz is definitely my favorite, but all six protagonists get their fair share of page time. This book is written in third-person perspectives, each chapter written in a different character's perspective. Kaz is my favorite, because he is so tricksy and smart, mysterious and surprising, unpredictable and more caring than he would ever let on. I personally think he is the most fleshed-out character, and the most likable. There is something about him that is cold and hard, and it's really appealing. He is also HILARIOUS, with a great sense of dry humor. But then he is deadly and quite the murderous thief. We see so many sides of him, and I love and/or am intrigued by all of them. 
 The other characters are equally as interesting! Inej is the Wraith, able to move basically without being heard. She is light on her feet and quick. Kaz saved her years ago, and she has worked with him since. The same with Jesper - he's worked with Kaz for years, and is basically Kaz's second-in-command. Jesper is such a flirt! And I love him. He is all about his guns, whereas Inej is all about her knives. Next is Nina, a Healer/Heartrender, who has been trying to have her former friend Matthias freed from prison for years. Matthias is the fifth person, a convict who is out for Nina's blood. He used to hunt Grisha before he was thrown in prison, but he especially wants to strangle Nina because she is the one who put him in prison. Lucky for himself, he is from the area that the Ice Court is located, so he is useful to Kaz, and Kaz springs him. Lastly is Wylan, the son of the merchant who wants the thing from the Ice Court brought back. Wylan is seen as weak, but he proves himself to be quite clever and useful. He is so cute! 
 I know what you all are thinking - SIX characters?! Six perspectives?! Third person, which is cool, but SIX?! Sounds like a recipe for disaster, like in Legacy of Kings by Eleanor Herman. However, not so! Since the six characters in Six of Crows are basically always with each other (once they're gathered), it's not like there are six plots happening. It's one, with six cars on the road, instead of six lanes or six exits or merging areas or something. You all love my analogies, I know! But really, there isn't six different plots and six different locations and six different schemes happening. It's one, with six different brains and hearts. Very different from Legacy of Kings, which was confusing with all of its perspectives and plots. 
 There are so many action-packed scenes! There is no shortage of crazy action and high stakes. You'll hold your breath during so many scenes, hoping and praying and crossing your fingers that Kaz doesn't screw things up (and really, he always has a plan). Bardugo did an amazing thing, in which she wrote the book from third person, so we are not privy to any of the characters' inner thoughts at all times. Hence why Kaz can pull off all that craziness and surprising the readers! My heart stopped several times, hoping there was another way that Kaz considered. He is so clever! 
 Like I said above, I really liked the change in tone of this new series by Bardugo. Don't get me wrong, things get very "everyone-is-going-to-die-if-we-don't-do-something", but it's more like a "hold-on-we're-in-for-a-crazy-ride" kind of thing. The story is very intriguing, and the 400+ pages fly by. I will say that the first 50 pages took me a bit to get into, but once I was in, I was hooked. 
 ROMANCE. Well. There are six people in the group... and, as you might guess, there are three pairs. No love triangles AT ALL. Three linear relationships. And the other nice thing - the romances in this book are barely there. Sure, the author does an amazing job of hinting more-than-friendships, or when a character is acting really friendly with another, or just plain old hints. But there are no steamy romance scenes or even passing romantic scenes. I really like this, because it's Bardugo's way of giving the romances time to grow. There are three sets of romances, on their own wavelengths. Different starts to each romance. Each can develop in books two and three! 
 Overall, I really enjoyed this book. I was wary, because the Grisha trilogy was just "okay" for me, and the hype for this book was/is pretty crazy. HOWEVER. I liked it and I personally think the hype is warranted. This book is so different from the Grisha trilogy! In great ways! 
 What I Did Not Like: 
 Like I said before, the beginning of this book was a bit slow, and it took me a while to really get invested. About 50 pages or so. Basically, once the six of them are actually gathered together, THEN things start to get really good. This might have been closer to around 100 pages in, but you get the idea. 
 Would I Recommend It: 
 For anyone looking for an adventure (yay Bilbo), definitely give this book a chance! Make it your first Bardugo read. I personally think it's Bardugo's best book to date, but I know others really, really enjoyed the Grisha trilogy. Shadow and Bone was my favorite of that series, but I think Six of Crows is better. It's a fantasy novel with a lot of action, high stakes, developed and fun characters, and well-placed humor! 
 Rating: 
 4 stars. A huge thanks to Kel from Booked Til Tuesday for passing her ARC to me. If you all get a chance, give this book a shot! If anything, the cover is gorgeous and would look great on your bookshelf!

I picked up Uprooted because it's considered a top contender for a Hugo award nomination this year, and I'm trying to stay on top of them. It's not a book I'd have been likely to pick up otherwise, mostly just because of the girly YA vibe it gives off from its cover, description and reviews. 
 That isn't really fair, though. I think the book largely deserves its acclaim. 
 Uprooted isn't entirely sure which genre it wants to be, and doesn't really care. It starts out Young Adult, but abandons that genre halfway through. It has just enough Romance to be tagged "Romance", but for much of the book the romance is out of the picture entirely. The magic and creatures and politics are clearly High Fantasy, but at the same time it's Historical Fantasy in disguise ((view spoiler)[the "fictional" kingdom of Polonya is literally Poland, though I only suspected that while reading and had to Google it later (hide spoiler)]). 
 I wasn't consistently enthusiastic about it. I wasn't always feeling the characters. Agnieszka is sympathetic enough for the most part, but I found her hard to relate to for much of the book. Her behavior and personal crises during the first half of the book weren't very plausible to me, though this could just be because she's not much of a critical thinker. Or maybe I just have difficulty empathizing with a 17-year old girl due to being a 31-year-old man myself, but I don't think that's it. 
 As a result the first half of the book engaged me only periodically. A few gripping segments were just enough to keep me going through the boring parts. 
 The romance in this book did not do anything for me at all. I don't really see it as romance so much as... shared fantasizing between the author and some hypothetical female reader. It's almost pornographic in that sense: not in terms of content, but in terms of the substance (or lack thereof) of the relationship. Obviously 31-year-old men are not normally part of the target demographic of YA fantasy romance, but that's never prevented me from appreciating romance in other works of fiction, in the context of more realistic relationships. 
 But about halfway through, the plot got started for real and didn't stop again until the very end. The second half of the book is a roller-coaster of action and suspense and drama and a little bit of intrigue. It kept me up past my bedtime more than once, which I suppose is as good a litmus test as any for a good book. 
 Combine that with a rich and unique setting with excellent world building rooted in eastern European folklore for a very enjoyable novel overall. 
 3 stars for the first half, 5 stars for the second. If you're thinking of giving up before the halfway point, hold on a little while longer.

I don't even know why I bother reviewing Stiefvater's books anymore. 
 Did you love it? Yes. 
 Did it give you feels? Yes. 
 Did you do that thing where you hold the book against your chest when you were done and sighed? Yes. 
 Do you know HOW to tell us why you love this book so much? Nope. 
 The thing that struck me about this Stiefvater title in particular, aside from her flawless writing style, monologue that shows she is definitely inside my brain, and otherworldly character development, was the novel's primary theme -- the LA music scene. I have read plenty of books on the subject, but none very good. It doesn't seem that it is as natural to write about music than it is to write about real life. A Visit From the Goon Squad is really the only quality "punk" book I have read on the LA music scene other than this one. I didn't even know that this is what Sinner's focus would be -- let's face it, if Stiefvater has a new book, I just buy it -- but it delivered anyway. 
 It takes a special type of wordsmith to make you think one thing throughout the entire book, and then make you realize that you were thinking the wrong thing, all because she made you think that thing, and you really just want to be her, sometimes. This may be a writer thing only, but I definitely want to be Maggie Stiefvater when I grow up.

Sweet YA romance with an authentic-sounding teenage male voice. Some angst, but overall a happy book. 
 Sixteen-year-old Simon Spier has a secret. He's in love with Blue, a fellow student at his high school. Except, he's never actually met Blue. Simon and Blue only know each other through a long-running email exchange. Both have kept their identities secret. Both are gay, and neither have formally come out to family or friends. 
 Simon's secret is safe until Martin, a classmate, stumbles on Simon and Blue's email exchange, and uses it to blackmail Simon. Martin has a crush on Abby, one of Simon's friends. If Simon doesn't help Martin get to know Abby better, Martin will out Simon. 
 Which, of course, means Martin is a huge douche canoe. 
 Meanwhile, Simon is falling more and more in love with Blue and is desperate to figure out who he is. This mystery, not the blackmail, is the driving force in the novel. Homophobia is alive and well in Simon's comfortably middle-class high school, but it isn't the virulent, violent thing of days gone by. (Or perhaps, other schools.) The tone of the story is sweet, with realistic depictions of the ups and downs of teenage friendship, platonic and otherwise. There are no deep themes, but in this case the result is kind of uplifting, rather than fluffy. 
 This is also the novel's weakness. It's happy, but not memorable. About a week after finishing it, I find myself struggling to remember details. It's a delightful read, especially after some of the tedious dreck I've DNFed, but lacks enough emotional oomph to really stay with me. Hence, four rather than five stars.

My husband kept asking me if I'd read this book and finally I picked it up and started reading. It hooked me pretty easily -- global conspiracies, future tech, medical advances, an ornery central character ripe for redemption, and a library at the core of the action. The story moved ahead at a steady pace and there were times it was difficult to put down. 
 Robert Gu spent most of his life pushing people away but after his Alzheimer's is reversed, he finds himself starting over in a world he doesn't recognize. Worse, still, he's no longer the man he was before. He is forced to go back to school but soon receives a mysterious offer he cannot refuse. How far will he go to get back what he had? Gu makes uneasy alliances and further alienates his family while the reader is left to guess who exactly is steering the action behind the scenes. 
 Almost nothing about the tech advances seemed out of sync with current global trends; the wearable hyper-connected (and still vulnerable) gesture-driven future could be around the corner. I was not as convinced by the medical advances, although I did appreciate Vinge's position that there would be no single magic bullet and that the cure that worked for one person might not have similar results for others. 
 There was a deeper connection for me personally, though. One of the main subplots is about mass digitization and how libraries evolve once the "real books" are gone. I work in an academic library, more specifically, I work in the digitization unit. The library described in Rainbows End is my "worst case scenario" and the description is a bit more horror than sci-fi to me. 
 I loved so much about this book; it is going to be one of those stories that sits with me a long time because the concepts and images are clear and so in line with our current reality that they seem almost inevitable. Except maybe the library part; I really hope that future remains fictional.

I wanted to read When We Collided because I really like the sound of the two main characters. Plus, I really have thoroughly enjoyed her other two books, and hoped for more of the same. Vivi sounded like a girl with a lot of energy and someone so bubbly and such a charismatic personality Jonah is kind of the opposite he is very responsible taking care of his younger siblings along with his two older because his dad died and his mom has been pretty depressed.  Not that far in the you begin to realize that Vivi has some issues of her owN. she described it as she got really low and then she got really high as far as her moods go awhile back. Then she had a conversation with her mom about the fact that she had lost some weight and that made her mom suspicious that she wasn't taking her medicine like she needs to be, since side effects for psych meds can cause weight gain. Mental illness is an issue that is very important to me because I deal with bipolar with hypomania and anxiety and I've been on all kinds of medication for it and I was able to relate with her on all new levels. I began to a suspect that's what she struggled with. she was bubbly and friendly and anything because she was experiencing her high/manic part of the disease she's very talkative and friendly and all those things could have just been her personalities but we also see her throwing out her medication and the synopsis also talks about her descent into risky behavior and that sounds like the beginnings of the swings from manic to depressive. 
 I love the scenes where Jonah and Vivi were getting to know each other it's so sweet. Vivi brings a intensity to everything, for example of she believes in reincarnation and she told things about her past life and how it relates to who she is today. The things she said about Jonah totally makes sense to his personality she said that he was a tree in a previous life and that is why he's so steady and how he wants to shelter the little ones. 
 The scenes with Jonah's sibling are so well written. It is so realistic how they still bicker and give each other a hard time but at the end of the day they're really there for each other. I love that he treats his younger siblings with respect and he plays with them and sacrifices things to help them with their homework and take care of them. They all look up to him and love him for it. I love seeing vivi with the youngest Leah, she was able to bring out this younger part of herself to really understand and she really give her time to her, she listens to her and really enjoys playing with her. this brought out a good side of Leah because she had been pretty withdrawn and not talking much and Jonah and the rest of the siblings love to see her just kind of blossom under the attention of Vivi. Leah began to talk and light up again. 
 Even though with a synopsis and knowing her history with mental illness when Vivi started going downhill it was hard To read. I have grown to care about her a lot and seeing so much of myself and some of her manic behavior was difficult. Its been a battle for me to stay on my meds and I knew that she wasn't staying on her on her mood stabilizers so I knew it was going to go downhill. and even though I have hypo-mania which means that my highs aren't quite as high and my impulsiveness and rashness and talk a mile a minute isn't as bad as someone with full out bipolar disorder like Vivi, it was an emotional train wreck I couldn't stop watching. Even knowing how much it upset Jonah because he had no clue about the manic depression. He must have had a clue with the way she acted around Jonahs mom and the understanding of how she might be feeling that she's dealt with mental illness but Jonah didn't know about her other side. She was danger seeking, in full out creative mode.and it hurt Jonah's feelings when he tried to talk to her about what he was going through and she couldn't focus on him or what he was saying. 
 I could tell as the book was coming to a close that the ending was going to be hard but I really respected it. I don't want to give any spoilers but I love that VIVI made decisions for herself and for her mental health and based on what she really needed even though it was a very hard choice to make. she knew that she was giving up a lot but looking forward to gaining a lot. 
 I like the way that it shows that mental illness doesn't have to have some huge tragic and that there are good days and there are bad days there are good decisions and then there's a very bad decisions and sometimes you get hurt sometimes the people around you get hurt. I like seeing slow and gradual change and jones mom and her eventual of decisions. I like with Vivi how she had to come to accept what was going on with her and that she eventually decided that other people can come to her that they could see that she's dealing with a mental illness but still love her and still see the good parts in her and forgive her for when things go wrong. 
 One of the messages that I took away from this book is that mental illness needs to be talked about more. That those who are suffering should look around them and see who is holding out of hand or who has offered to help and accept that help. for those who are suffering to also give that whenever they aren't the ones having a hard time that they can look for someone else who is struggling because they've been there they know the signs. and for those who are not struggling with the mental illness to realize that it is a disease that there's going to be relapses that there's going to be hard days but the treasure of the good days and to be there for other people.

I felt really conflicted about how to rate this book. On the one hand I flew through reading this book, especially the last third of the book. Things were constantly happening! I was definitely never bored. The story always held my attention and kept me engaged and for that it deserves at least 4 stars. 
 On the other hand, I felt there were too many"shocking" moments. Those moments definitely keep you engaged with the story, but some of those moments felt forced, like they were just put there for shock value. That's my major complaint with the series so far- not enough depth. And so many shocking moments that as a reader you get so used to looking for the next one that it doesn't really come that much of a shock anymore. 
 I feel Rhodes did a good job with developing some of the other characters though, especially Magnus. He's really grown on me. I really can't wait to follow his story line in the next book! 
 I really enjoy all the shifts in character perspectives, something that is a strength with this series, but I'm ending this book feeling like Rhodes has only scratch the surface with character development, motivation and depth. This book is often compared to the A Song of Ice and Fire series, which I agree with as far as the large cast of characters and shifting character perspectives, but this series is greatly lacking compared to that one. 
 I guess maybe it's an unfair to compare these two series since one is adult and the other young adult, but I don't think just because a book is YA that it should lack in character complexity. There are quite a few shocking moments in A Song of Ice and Fire, but those book are really long- usually over 1,000 pages. Those shocking moments made much more sense to me because the readers had much more time to get inside each character's head and more time to create a complex plot. They didn't come just 30-40 pages after the previous shocking moments. 
 But.....that said I still am very excited to move on to the next book. I'm just sad that I can't jump right in and read the 3rd book right away. I know I'm going to receive it as a Christmas present and have to wait until next week now :(

Bared to You is very much like 50 Shades in all of the ways that people will like (if you're into that sort of thing) without so many of the things that make 50 Shades the worst book on the planet. Bared to You is another billionaire suit-and-tie romance with dark edges and a ton of sex, but without the lip biting idiocy of Anastasia Steele and terrible writing. For what it is, Bared to You wasn't badly written at all. Yes, there are moments where the plot makes no sense, but I find that with ANY rich guy and plain girl romance these days and I don't think people read these in order to have their brains exposed to rich storytelling. I think most people lean towards historical and paranormal romance for that. 
 I actually liked Eva for much of the book because she actually said no, had no problems walking away from Gideon multiple times, and wasn't afraid to tell him that she wasn't a tool to be used. At the beginning, Eva shocked me by being so adamant about not sleeping with someone she was so incredibly attracted to. I'm used to my heroines in these books turning into puddles that still somehow bite their lips. 
 I liked Gideon, too. Sure, he was all polished and perfect, but as soon as Eva walked out on him, he wasn't afraid to be sensitive and emotional and beg her for another chance and apologize for fucking up. I'm used to the billionaires being gigantic assholes nearly all of the novel, so that was a nice change of pace. 
 Honestly, despite the fast paced, jumping-into-bed, lust = love kind of plot, Bared to You was kind of refreshing at first. But then the constant issues started. Jealousy, sexual abuse, miscommunication, unnecessary drama, other women, etc.. it was so much in a very short amount of time. Towards the end, I started to feel like they needed to just get over themselves. Eva once impressed me by walking away, but then that became her thing and then Gideon kept getting all upset about how he fucked up again and they both just got on my nerves. 
 I think if you read these books often and like them, Bared to You is one of the better ones. But as good as it was, it wasn't good enough to redeem the genre.

How can my food taste the same after reading this? Or, how can I eat in excess after reading this book? How can I ignore the monsters that live deep inside all of us, sedated, but still there, waiting for our morals to fade? As the book suggests, it does fade away sometimes, replaced by delusions of grandeur. Or does it happen the other way around? 
 Anyway. Monsters. We should acknowledge them. We should drive them away when they rise up and demand respect. Burning babies, killing mothers, fine-tuning death machines, that are what these monsters do. Driving them away takes humanity. 
 Elie Wiesel had the chance to know these monsters rather intimately, as he, and his family had been under their custody until the time they were liberated by the Allied forces. These NaziMonsters had the goal to eliminate every living Jew there was, even after the war was lost for them. Just before the end of WWII, Elie's village was sent packing to Germany, to the bowels of Auschwitz. I'm not sure what happened to his mother and sister, but his father had made the journey with him when inside the camp. Elie described the horror around him quite matter-of-factly, then admitted that no words can ever describe the things he had seen, the things he (and his family) had experienced. Yet, I shiver upon reading his words. How powerful his words are. How it makes me bitter and misanthropic to the bone. 
 It's a great thing that the book is often required reading for high school students. After all, show a [becoming] man (or woman) the inherent weaknesses of human nature, and s/he will take them into consideration when making future decisions. Why the Nazi's did what they did? What can we, the future generations learn from their nature? How do their nature complement to that of our neighbors', or the one staring back at us from our bathroom mirror. These questions need to be pondered, and we must not forget the holocaust and six million Elies 150 years from now.

 Although Julia's Quinn's Bridgerton series is written with great undertones of humor, this book seemed more broadly funny than any other books of hers that I can remember. 
 It starts off with Daniel Smythe-Smith drunkenly and accidentally winning a hand of cards. Accidentally, because Daniel is an indifferent card player whereas his opponent, Hugh, can count cards and is sure that Daniel could only have won if he'd cheated. This leads to pistols at dawn where Daniel again, accidentally shoots Hugh in the leg (he meant to delope). Hugh's father is a mean, vengeful man who vows to destroy Daniel causing him to flee the country in fear. 
 Despite the seriousness of events that occur, the prologue is written quite humorously. Daniel's befuddlement at how events spiral out of control is very entertaining. 
 After three years running always looking over his shoulder, Hugh tracks Daniel down and assures him that his father has ended the vendetta. Daniel can come home. 
 He does right in time for the annual, infamous Smythe-Smith musicale where he sets eyes on and becomes immediately smitten with Anne Wynter, the governess of his young cousins. 
 But Anne isn't what she seems and has some big secrets of her own. Daniel determinedly pursues Anne, despite her (feeble) protestations. She is determined to keep her job with the family and is aware that a dalliance with Daniel is a very dangerous proposition. Even more so that a spectre from her past has resurfaced and is threatening her current comfortable life. 
 JQ has gotten some great mileage out of the Smythe-Smith family and their dreadful musical ambitions and this book adds to that. As governess to a branch of the family, Anne has a first row seat to the madness. Much of the humor of the story stems from Anne's high-spirited charges and the witty, flirty back and forth between Anne and Daniel. 
 The drama comes from the revelation of the mystery of Anne's past. To the author's credit she doesn't draw it out until the bitter end. Fairly early in the story we get treated to a flashback that fills in the details of Anne's history. So I spent a lot of the story in anticipation of Daniel learning the truth as well. When it all comes to a head, it is very satisfying. 
 I only gave it 3.5 stars because there were points early in the story that I thought it dragged a bit. But it rebounds well. And Hugh makes for a great breakout character. Hope he gets his own story. 
 Recommended.

I started the year with Backman's A Man Called Ove, and now I'll (nearly) finish it with his My Grandmother Asked Me to Tell You She's Sorry. I loved them both! My Grandmother continues discussing the theme Backman began examining in Ove of family. What is a family? Backman seems to be showing us that we aren't just born into families, we can make our own by gathering those around us into our circle and learning how to love them--despite their rough exteriors and complicated interiors. In Ove, we get to see an assembled family and how they ultimately become the most intimate and fulfilling relationships for each of the characters. The relationships are transformative. While Grandmother also explores this idea, we begin to understand that blood relationships are not to be disregarded. On the contrary, disaster can result when blood relationships are allowed to go wrong. But, through acts of kindness and forgiveness, family relationships can have the same and possibly even greater power. They force us to see people with whom we have a past with new eyes. Compassion for those who have wronged us is difficult, it may feel impossible, but it improves us as humans more than probably anything else. 
 The other thing that Backman seems to understand really well is that the power of literature is not when you can see yourself in the story, but when the story and characters allow you to see the world in new ways. Today we get so caught up in the idea that only the things we read and watch and do that reflect us back to ourselves are enjoyable and beneficial. We forget that the primary function of literature is to expand our world and make us bigger. Granny's stories do just that. They are not about Elsa; they are for her benefit. They help her understand her Granny, the people around her, and ultimately herself and her place in the world. They inspire empathy and compassion. They help forge bonds of love and friendship. They bring about healing. They do just what stories ought to do. I love this about Backman's work. He helps us see others for who they truly are--flawed people wanting to be loved for who they are, seen, understood. 
 If you are just entering the world from Fredrick Backman's point of view, I am truly jealous! Dive in and enjoy the swim! You're going to wish it would never end!

I'm still not totally sure how to categorize this book. It is definitely one of the strangest and most confusing books I've ever read- but by far one of the most unique, and Mieville's prose is incredible. 
 It's hard to describe Embassytown at all, but it is essentially about the relationship that humans have on a specific planet, Arieka, with the native species, the Ariekei or "Hosts." The Hosts speak a certain "Language" where there are no signs or signifieds- everything they say is true and literal. They also speak with two mouths simultaneously and cannot comprehend artificial forms of Language, so the only way humans can communicate with them is with Ambassadors, sets of twins that can communicate simultaneously with one sentient mind. Kind of. 
 I have to commend Mieville for writing something so unbelievably difficult. The kind of creativity involved in crafting a story like this seems almost impossible, and his writing style is perfect to tell it. It was fascinating to read a sci-fi book entirely centered on language and semiotic theories, and to try to imagine the linguistic concepts he mentions. 
 My main problem with Embassytown is that it felt like the author was trying to shoehorn in a ton of interesting, but extremely confusing, concepts that weren't really relevant to the story. For example, the immer, which is a sort of universe that's been consistent throughout all three iterations of the universe where Arieka and Embassytown are located. Cool, but insanely hard to comprehend and not all that relevant to the story. The same goes for Ehrsul and the Turingware, "floaking," and other concepts. They play a tangential role in the story, but they mostly just distract from the plot itself, which is confusing enough on its own! 
 I would probably give this 3.5 stars- closer to 4 for complete originality and ingenuity, closer to 3 because the book felt very jumbled, which made it even more difficult to read and understand.

I've read some of Charlotte Bronte's work before, but I'd never read Anne, and even after only one story, I can truly say that Anne is the more poignant, truthful, and vivacious author. There were times that this story literally had me shaking with anger and the wrongs done to women during the Victorian era. They had absolutely no recourse for relief from their own husbands (a divorce required an act of parliament, and you would lose your children). 
 It's said that this is one of the first feminist novels, and at the time of its publication some people, including Charlotte Bronte, tried to have it banned. It was too dark, too vicious, for the public. What I find disturbing, is that everyone had to know this sort of thing was happening, but they clung so desperately to a hope of naivete in the general populous. Indiscretions of family members were not discussed, so perhaps when one suffered, they truly thought they suffered alone? 
 Anne was clearly before her time, and her introduction to the second publication of the novel is so revealing about her personal strength of character. She refused to apologize for shining light where so many refused to look saying, "I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it." Good for you Anne. It is such a shame you were claimed so young. 
 This is an absolutely stand-out Victorian novel. While it is veiled with optimism, it is checked by reality, something that is often missing in the other Brontes' works. I highly encourage everyone to read this novel.

 I don't know where to start with this one, I have so many thoughts and they are all racing to get out. I will say first of all, that I don't know what I expected coming into this book, but I didn't expect to love it as much as I do. This book is the perfect blend of romance and historical fiction, I don't know what I enjoyed reading more Tatiana and Alexander's love story or the backdrop of the war between Russia and Germany. This book is very atmospheric, and certain times I felt as if I was there in the story. There is something about a romance that takes place in a war that is beyond compelling and well...romantic. I don't know if it's because I can't think of anything more attractive than a man in a suit, or if it's because during times of war the next day is never guarantee, but I get really invested in these relationships because I want them to beat the odds so bad. 
 Let's start with our first lead: Tatiana wasn't someone I thought I would like at first because when the book opens up, she's 16 but she acts as if she's 9. Her family can't trust her to go to the market and bring some food home because she wanders off and forgets what she has to buy. She's also extremely passive, and she allows people to take advantage of her. She doesn't know where to draw the line between being helpful and being taken advantage of. There are times where I understand why she is the way that she is, her family is beyond lazy and useless and they make her feel as if she is lazy and useless so she will do more for them. Yet, her character development, at least in this field, didn't improve much even by the end of the book. Yet, it still did improve and I like that she is spending her time as a nurse helping people who actually appreciate her efforts. 
 Alexander- I can't say anything else without saying that I think he is so so so SO SEXY. I love how brave he is, how honest he is, how he keeps his promise, how he's witty and funny, and how much he loves Tatiana. He cares about her so much, and all the times she made him promise to be with Dasha broke my heart. I know a lot of people say that it's wrong of them to get together, and normally I would agree but it wasn't as if he was in love with Dasha, she was just some girl he was spending time with for the time being. Tatiana was the one he fell for, and it just really sucked (sorry couldn't think of a word more fitting) that she had to be related to Dasha. His backstory with his parents was so devastating, and it just proves what a great person he is. He could be sullen, selfish, and cruel but he chooses not to be, he chooses to better and I think that's more attractive than if he just came from a privilege background. 
 Like I mentioned before, I love their relationship despite all the high and lows (the many lows) that they dragged me through. So many times I wanted to shake Tatiana for being so stupid, or Alexander for being so clueless (men *smh*) but overall I just root for them till no end. I NEED the next book, but at the same time I think my brain and my heart need a breather. You can't just marathon this trilogy, you just can't.

I adored this. A generational story spanning about 300 years, it almost reads like a prequel to something like a Pern novel. Forty Thousand in Gehenna is part of the lengthy Alliance/Union universe series, but does not itself appear to have a direct sequel: if it does I would love to be introduced to it, since I want more of Cherryh's aggressively nonverbal dragons. 
 Between this, Rider at the Gate, and the Foreigner series I'm on a bit of a Cherryh kick, but her stories of first contact (and unsuccessful second, and violent third, and weirdly comradely fourth) haven't become repetitive yet. They aren't exactly a repudiation of stories where humans tame or become symbiotic creatures, although Rider at the Gate contained elements of that - instead they're stark, realistic bio-mysteries, monster stories with hard science fiction explorations of alien senses and alien perspectives. The calibans are violent, hierarchical, and capricious, (view spoiler)[although at the end there is a neatly packaged glimpse at a more stable partnership (hide spoiler)]. 
 At times, the politics of the book seemed a bit muddled: a matriarchal, casually monogamous society is portrayed much more positively than a patriarchal one which treats women as bargaining chips and second class-workers, but gang rapes are treated with calm acceptance by several protagonists, as long as they are committed by a certain sect of characters. 
 Sexual politics aside, Gehenna was a compelling, rich world as odd and puzzle-intricate as any of Cherryh's. I have a feeling I won't be tired of her aliens for a long time.

 This book really is not FOR adults per se but it without a doubt is, adult. Alcoholism, drug use, and sex is fairly rampant. 
 I didn't like Quentin at all at first but after getting further in the book I felt he became a very relatable character (minus the magic) as far as his feelings of being lost, not truly believing that things he was witnessing were real, long lost loves and rampant drug use coupled with no motivation. After awhile I started to care not only for Quentin but for his relationship with Alice as well as the rest of the Physical Kids. 
 This is a human story, where magic is real but isn't really magical. At least in the traditional fantasy tropes. Yes he goes to magic school, yes there is a magical fantasy land behind a portal. But non of that crap matters. Imagine yourself trying to get into a college but instead of getting a regular interview your thrown into a crime scene and happen upon a school where you must take completely ridiculous tests in a seemingly regular environment only to be told your a magician and magic actually exists. Couple that with a fantasy land of your favorite childhood book series being an actually reality as well, only not at all what you dream about and is far more violent and frightening then you ever imagined. How would you deal with it? Most people when given the opportunity to rise up and do great things... Fail, matter-of-fact. And I loved this book for the way things wrapped up. Its an incredibly human story told with a side story of magic. 
 Any book that you can get drunk in a fantasy world bar with a magic talking bear, a birch tree and a monkey looking dude serving you beer is a story worth knowing in my opinion.

I became aware of this book at BEA, but it wasn't until I saw it available for audiobook review that I decided to pick it up. There had been mixed reviews from the bloggers I follow, so I wasn't sure what to expect. 
 You guys know by now my love for audiobooks, so let's start there. I think listening to Hunter gave it an added quality that I probably wouldn't have gotten from reading the book. I've looked at the actual book itself before, and the text and format weren't all that inviting to me. I thought Amy Landon did a good job with the narration, though I kept thinking I knew her voice from somewhere else (I've looked, this is apparently my first narration of hers). Her voice fit the character of Joy really well, which is important because the book is told from Joy's point of view. There were a couple of times in the beginning where I was taken back by how she pronounced a few things (I can't remember the word now, but there was one instance in particular that I remember thinking "Who says that word like that?!"), but things seemed to smooth out as you got deeper into the book. I did think, however, that her male voices all sounded the same, which could have been a problem if there were more than a few scenes that had multiple male characters involved. Still, overall, I enjoyed the audio version, and I'm really glad I requested it for review. 
 I found the story of Hunter to be fascinating. At the surface, it seems very broad, but then it begins to twist and turn and you realize that there's more going on here. It's very dystopian, but with a fantastical twist, which I thought was unique. Honestly, I truly enjoyed it. Also, the plot can really be taken a million different ways at this point, and I think that's key in keeping a series going. 
 I liked Joy a lot. She has insane respect for other people, and is a truly humble person. She puts others before herself, which is what makes her such a great Hunter. I also thought it was cute how she had to overcome all these social norm issues, because of being isolated on the mountain. 
 I loved the idea of the Hounds and how they work together with the Hunters. I wanted more info on how this all came about. I struggled to keep all the other fantastical creatures separate in my mind though, as it seemed like some were very casually mentioned and others we got full details of. I was also disappointed by the utter lack of DRAGONS in the story. If you're going to put one on the cover, THERE SHOULD BE ONE IN THE STORY. Just saying. 
 What really brought this book down for me though was the writing style. In the beginning, I was seriously considering DNFing, because DEAR GOD it was just page after page AFTER PAGE of info-dumping. I really prefer the "show, don't tell" method of world building, and Lackey didn't manage to capture that at all. The info-dumping continues throughout the book, which was frustrating, but the action later on at least kept it from becoming overwhelming. I also found it very weird that there are several points where Joy is literally talking to the reader. It would have been one thing if Hunter was told from the perspective of "this has all already happened, let me tell you my story", but that's not what this book is. It's supposed to be happening in real time, so I found it odd that the main character would do such a thing. 
 Okay, so after all that, you're probably wondering why I still gave Hunter a 3 out of 5. Well, let me remind you once again that my ratings are entirely subjective. Frankly, despite all it's missteps, I still enjoyed the story... and I want to know what happens next. I think that's the biggest reason why I've given this book 3 stars - the fact that I most definitely want to pick up the 2nd book of the series. Additionally, like I said, I think the audio really lent itself to the story, and I'm not sure I would have finished the book if I had been reading it. I'm also keeping my fingers crossed that Lackey's writing skills improve with the 2nd book, and that there will be less info-dumping now that the world has been created. 
 All in all, if you're interested in this book, I would definitely recommend the audio version. Be aware that you will have to wade through a ton of info dumping, but try to enjoy the fantastical dystopian that is this story. 
 This review was originally posted on Books Are My Thing

Here it is - a re-read of IT, one of the most haunting and popular horror books of our time. It does deserve this honor, it really does, for King does talented things here - he takes a small town in the grip of its own horrors, its own secrets, and lays at the heart of the town a monster that has no true face, but that does have true intent, intent to feed on the fear and the lives of its towns residents. People in the town belong to IT as the monster itself belongs, in a way, to them through their own creepy makings and acceptances. 
 I never realized until reading a review recently (duh is me) that King started this book with two prologue introductions to both time pieces. They avoided doing this in the movie, opening with made-for-film scenes, but keeping the ultra-disturbing Georgie boat opening. Here it opens for the adults too in the form of what happened to the tragic homosexual couple by the disturbed and ignorant townsfolk who, through their homophobic violence, joined in without their knowledge with the clown. 
 It was clever for King to begin the book with two openings - one for the adult stage of life, one for the childhood stage. From there it keeps mixing and going back and forth, flashback to reality, reality back to memory. 
 Some stories were more interesting than others and the first half of the book, after the initial two openings, is consumed by the current adults getting that epic phone call, only to start on their journey back, accompanied by returning memories of past horrors faced. At times I think it grew too long in duration and at times I grew impatient with it, but overall it was an effective opening with the book and helped explain not only the characters as adults, but the characters as children and how they came together. 
 King always had a great talent with writing childhood, friends, and the magic of youth and coming of age. One does have to raise an eyebrow with the weird way to escape the tunnel with Beverly and all the boys - didn't make much sense to include that to me - but overall the children's interactions is believable and is the heart of the story. As adults they're interesting but they lack the magic of their relationship as compared to when they were kids. 
 The clown is just creepy - he is one of the eeriest monsters invented. There were some genuinely disturbing scenes in the book that make this stand in a sobering reality. What always comes to mind when I think of creepy scenes are small flashbacks rather than the events as they happen - for instance, 
 (view spoiler)[ 
 when in the police station the man is recounting the tale of the clown dragging the body, looking up at him, and then appearing to bite into the guy's armpit. That was mega creepy. 
 And the other horrible story is told from Mike as adult, of the 2 year old being murdered and the mother hearing the sounds from downstairs, the maniacal laughing and the toilet flushing, to come and find her child drowned and his back broken. Terrifying stuff. 
 (hide spoiler)] 
 And of course the story of Georgie is just disturbing and sad. I got teary eyed when it happened, teary whenever it was brought through with memory. I think Georgie is the trademark of the both the novel and the movie version for how horrible it all really is. 
 My favorite character is Ben. He was fascinating as a child, struggling with his weight and pining for a girl he never thought he would have, spending the best moments of his childhood in the library, devouring books and losing himself in their worlds. It's suiting he grew up to be an architect, a builder of worlds. 
 King puts the main character, or at least the strongest leader, in Bill. I did like Bill but he wasn't my favorite; I found him lackluster when compared to the rest. I also didn't feel much for Eddie, who I found whiny and weak but cared more toward him as a child. The same can be said for Richie, who could get annoying with the voices - really. Beverly was interesting to read about as a child but, unlike the others, came alive more as an adult. Stan wasn't delved into much for obvious reasons, nothing was told through his viewpoint, even when he hears the news at the beginning; it's told through his wife's POV. Mike is another big favorite with his love of books, history, the group, the town, and his depth. 
 So King wins with creating a truly unique and disturbing villain, injecting some disturbing scenes, some truly eerie ones. He wins with character formation and giving each child a sense of isolation because of parental abuse, parental absence, or their own psychological limitations. The town of Derry is so strongly formed it becomes a character in its own right. 
 I don't give it a perfect rating, however. As with many of King's works, I think the book would have been better with more trimming. The story's complex and a lot goes on, but not enough for this duration. One of the flashback stories Mike hears from his father took several pages for that story alone. 
 Also, I didn't care for the ending. I don't like how IT ended up being explained (some of it I dug, some of it I didn't.) Just like in the Shining, I think King made a mistake by (view spoiler)[ giving the villain an internal monologue voice at the end. It ruined a lot of the mystery and horror of IT to me and didn't feel convincing. (hide spoiler)]Frankly, I do find the ending weak for many reasons - the strength of the fight with Bill and others, the lack of tragedy, the explanation and dealings with the monster. 
 The character of Tom a bit weak and unconvincing as well. The other human villains, as the bullies, were particularly fascinating in the story and King excelled with writing Henry and the gang. However, I hated the two cycles of animal deaths or cruelty *shudders* 
 Finally, I really disliked the memories starting to change again. Felt cheated by that. I can understand the first time, but not the second. The second makes little sense to me. 
 Overall IT is an epic, excellent book that any horror fan should read. It's awesome in its scope of terror, it's inventive, original, shattering, and captures the strength of youth being forced to come together to fight something that seems bigger than themselves. Perhaps a bit too long and rambling, perhaps a tad weak at the end, but it shines with its beginning and it shines with its content.

Twelve years after the conclusion of Tricked, Atticus O'Sullivan--the last living Druid--is ready to begin the ceremony to make his apprentice, Granuaile, a full-fledged druid in her own right. This happy moment is interrupted when several extremely irate Greek gods see through the clever fake death Atticus constructed, and realize that he is still alive. So begins a race around the world while various divinities try to kill Atticus, Atticus tries to finish Granuaile's ceremony, and Oberon the telepathic dog provides a running commentary. For all of the linguistic laymen out there, Hearne has once again included a glossary of tricky names (and, let's face it, every character in this book has an unpronounceable name). 
 The charm of this series, for me, is primarily Hearne's creative weaving together of multiple mythologies. The plot and characterization are light, but humorous.

But Cal is fairly certain those needs are special and seeks help from one of James's ex-rentboys, Nick, who is known for being a sexual sadist. 
 This story is told from Callum's point of view as he is learning to become a Dom and fulfill James's needs. Cal is believable as a new Dom, instinctive enough to make it work for James, but still insecure about reading his cues and getting it right, not losing control of himself in the scenes. These guys are private, so they're bedroom/home scenes, not dungeon scenes. 
 But what makes this story special is the navigation of their employer/employee relationship outside of sex. Because the sex is instinctual and natural between them. Figuring out how to act around each other the rest of the time is the hard part for James and Cal. By the end, you get the feeling that they'll manage to navigate the rocky patches and come out strong together. 
 Not my absolute favorite of the series, but a very strong addition to it. I love the rentboys, so I'm hoping there are more stories to come.

 "Dirty Talk" introduces us to Vegas West, a man searching for himself in New York while working for a sex chat line called Black Vanilla. We're privy to Vegas's everyday life with the other men of Black Vanilla and his constant struggle to reconcile with the heartbreak of his past. When Vegas receives a threatening call during one of his shifts, the story takes a dark and frightening turn. 
 First let me say this novel was extremely interesting and unique and I appreciate the work the author put into such a story. There are both positive and negative elements that shaped my reading experience. 
 The negatives: 
 POV whiplash - the POV changed often and sometimes without warning. The tendency to head-hop, especially in the first half of the book was confusing and unnecessary. 
 Slow pacing - the first half dragged on due to some serious information dumps and backstory 
 Editing issues - I found many repetitious descriptions and dialogue, plus numerous typos 
 Character naming conventions - The majority of the characters were named after cities, places, etc. I felt like I was left out of some weird inside joke. I kept waiting for this to be explained, but it never was. 
 Inconsistent characters - At times I felt some of the characters' actions were only motivated by plot, not their true natures... 
 As for what I liked: 
 Awesome handling of the thriller/suspense aspect of the book - I was absolutely terrified along with Vegas. When the pacing picked up, I was hooked. Well done! 
 Hot sex - despite my disappointment over the lack of actual "dirty talk" outside of the calls Vegas receives at work, the sex was hot and steamy. I wanted more. 
 Masterful plot - the weaving of character and plot twists kept me turning the pages. 
 Intriguing ending - I'm still not sure how I feel about the ending, but I consider it a win since I'm still puzzled and thinking about it. 
 Despite its short-comings, I would recommend this book for those who enjoy erotic thrillers.

When I found out that three of my favorite adult romance authors in the world were releasing an anthology of historical romance novellas about couples connected to Alexander Hamilton, I was excited. But when I actually started reading it, I was blown away. These novellas are FANTASTIC. 
 Rose Lerner's "Promised Land" is about a married couple who run into each other by surprise in the middle of the war - which is particularly surprising to the husband, Nathan, as he'd thought his wife Rachel was dead, but he has now been arrested by her (a soldier in men's clothing, serving in Hamilton's battalion) because she suspects him of being a British spy. Their story is brilliantly funny and smart and fiercely romantic as they battle to reconcile their real love for each other with their competing dreams. Rose Lerner writes some of the smartest, sharpest historical romances I've ever read, and this is my favorite of all of her stories so far. 
 Alyssa Cole's "That Could Be Enough" is just gorgeously romantic in the most swoonworthy way. It's absolutely overflowing with deeply-felt emotion - even as the central heroine fights to restrain her own emotions, having been hurt so terribly in the past that she gave up love AND the poetry-writing that was her vocation. But in the course of serving as Eliza Hamilton's secretary, she meets another woman who opens up all the emotions she's been bottling up for years. Their letters to each other are just astonishingly lovely, and I cried at the happy ending, in the best possible way. 
 And Courtney Milan's novella is so delightfully, hilariously funny - a romantic comedy road trip with deeply serious underpinnings (as it's also a love story between a formerly-enslaved black American soldier and a white British officer on the run, and their respective issues are explored in detail). Those emotional underpinnings - and the grave inequalities between the two men - are strongly felt, but the dialogue itself, as they banter their way into love despite everything, was so deliciously witty that I laughed out loud again and again. (The Cheese of Doom! It's just delightful.) 
 All in all, this is my favorite adult romance anthology I can ever remember reading. Very highly recommended!

 Ravka: fantasy Russia, with magic. This country's only access to the sea is cut off by the Shadow Fold, a stretch of land full of darkness and demon-like creatures, so the Ravkans are landlocked and stuck in a decades-long war with their neighbours. Their economy sucks and their politicians are all idiots. Or evil. Or both. But, hey, at least unemployment is down because the army's always looking for fresh recruits. Our protagonist Alina is a trainee mapmaker in the army, and the story starts with Alina and her team preparing to cross the Fold. I liked that. There's one obviously interesting place on the map, where I as a reader know that some interesting action will take place, and we're already starting from here instead of taking a long boring journey from the protagonist's home town. 
 ...Obviously my hopes were dashed: they take two steps into the Fold and then realize that Alina has magic, so she's sent back for training in the boring part of the map. The middle of the book was very stagnant, with the usual plot of the protagonist trying to control her powers, but I thought starting the book near the Fold was cool because it gave me a taste of what was outside the Little Palace and made me eager to read on and see what would happen when Alina finally went back. What also kept me interested was that the book subverted many of my expectations. I literally groaned when I saw the signs of an impending romance, and even considered giving up on the book because it felt like the author was just throwing a love triangle in to be like every other YA writer (between a childhood friend and a tall dark stranger, to boot!) but in the end I stuck with it. I'm glad I did: the resolution of the love triangle was very satisfying and not at all what I expected. I'd say more, but I think this book is more enjoyable to read with a minimal amount of spoilers. 
 As a protagonist, Alina was okay. I got very frustrated with her during the middle of the book because at first she scoffs at the ostentation displayed at the Little Palace, but then she wastes almost a whole chapter describing how she got ready for the ball, and her new clothes, and how her hair was all pretty, to the point that she didn't seem the same person any more. But later on Alina herself recognizes that she'd been dazzled by life at court, so it's okay Alina, I forgive you. I don't mind characters fucking up and having some serious flaws, as long as that's acknowledged, and in that respect Shadow and Bone was very good. It also does a good job of walking the line between Alina feeling guilty because she doesn't have the power to vanquish the Shadow Fold and Alina knowing that she shouldn't feel guilty about that because it's kind of a tall order for someone who only just found out about her powers. What I didn't like about Alina was that she spends most of the book being ordered around: she almost never decides what to do for herself, and when she does she's only choosing between what one person told her or what someone else told her. She only truly makes her own choices in the last couple of chapters, and then she kicks ass, so I'm really hoping she'll do more thinking for herself in the sequel. 
 My only real quibble with the book is that the secondary characters were very secondary. We don't get much about Mal, Genya, or the Darkling, and as for everyone else there might as well be cardboard cutouts instead of people living in the Little Palace. The short story The Tailor (spoilery, read after the book) delves a little into Genya's backstory, but there's still little depth to the characters. Even Alina is not as fleshed out as she could be. Did everyone at the orphanage join the army, or did she join because Mal was going to? Why become a mapmaker in particular? This is never expanded upon. The setting also feels bland: the characters are dressed in keftas and fur hats, they drink tea and kvas, they address their sovereigns as Tsar and Tsaritsa and pray to their Saints, but that felt purely aestethic. Yes, they're in fantasy Russia, but they may as well be anywhere else. They didn't have that way of thinking and talking that made me think "yes, this is a completely different world". 
 Overall it's a good start for a series and I'm hoping there will be more details about the setting in the next book. Plus, y'know, the Darkling. Okay, he's a douche, but I have a literary type and that type is manipulative assholes, so he's right up my alley. There was some initial squick because ew a hundred-year-old dude hitting on a teenager, but when I got to his backstory I totally understood why he did what he did, while at the same time hoping that... er, spoilers. Suffice to say that I was very happy when I figured out the meaning of the title, because that's one cool piece of foreshadowing.

I love books like these, where the girls aren't always girly girls. Why? Because this is how I grew up, being a tom boy. I never knew how to apply make up, how to pick out cute clothes or knew what normal girls did when they hung out. I liked to play night games, soccer and ride my bike pretending I was a ninja turtle or something like that. I connected with Charlie right away, though I have no brothers. I was able to commiserate with her struggles of what to do with makeup and clothes and how, in the our eyes, they looked unnatural on us. 
 Charlie's brothers are intense when it comes to protecting their sister. I really liked that. I also liked how Gage was her best friend, for the most part. He was the closest in age to her and they shared everything. No topic was off limits. Until. Until Charlie started to wonder if there was something wrong with her because she wasn't really much of a girl, she was one of the guys. Oh, poor Charlie! But hey, this just goes to show there is nothing wrong with a girl who loves sports, plays them too and finds a way to show a bit of her feminine side as well. 
 Charlie had that one girl who sort of planted herself in Charlie's life. She isn't a tomboy. She wears makeup, wears cute clothes and is what people think of when they imagine a teenage girl. It's a nice change, from going to having friends all boys to having a friend who can speak to her feminine side, to have someone to talk to about things a girl just doesn't want to talk about with a boy. I loved seeing Charlie grow and change, though not enough to change herself into a person she doesn't like, just into a person who is well rounded and comfortable with herself. 
 On the Fence was a fun read and definitely reread worthy.
