I'm pretty sure that if I had a chance to hangout with Libba Bray, we'd get along really well. She's clearly a smart feminist lady with a sense of fun and adventure and I've loved many of her books. 
 That being said, this one was a little more middle of the road for me. The story takes place at a female boarding school in England in the late 1800s and focuses on the eventual friendship formed by four girls (each with their own back-story baggage) as they recreate a magical "order" and research a fire that occurred at the school 24 years previous. While I loved some of the ideas that come up through the story (the awareness of a woman's place in that time period; grappling with the difficulties of discovering and appropriately using power; etc) I feel like the characters were a bit 2-dimensional. Sometimes like-able and sometimes despicable (just like real teenagers!) - it was hard to get a strong feel for any of them beyond their surface actions. I have hopes for further books in the series.

This one takes close concentration and effort. Mantel's writing here is so dense that you have to constantly pay attention to figure out who is speaking and being described. When in doubt, it's the protagonist, Cromwell. That being said, this is worth the effort. It is slow at times and the pacing does seem a bit too drawn out occasionally, but it's still highly worth the read. It not only defuses formerly-held beliefs you may have had about the reign of Henry VIII (Thomas More was not the sympathetic objector portrayed in "A Man for All Seasons" and he certainly was no saint), but it also presents an interesting portrait of a man who is somewhat in the shadows of history but was front and center at the time.

As far as entertainment, The Martian is a thrill ride. It's the sort of novel you feel like you've seen in a movie somewhere; it's a little Gravity/Apollo 13 meets Cast Away with sprinkles of Deep Impact, The Right Stuff, and other similar films. I'd say this means The Martian has a very promising future. Has someone bought the film rights yet? ... Checking ... Yep, Matt Damon is set to star. Figures. 
 The Martian was so entertaining I was tempted to give the novel a full five stars, but once you trim the thrills, The Martian is a bit thin. Still, it's good for what it is. The tension is high, but not over the top. At times it's predictable as action stories tend to be, but at other times the author surprises the reader. It's funny, but occasionally heartfelt. It's full of science babble, but not at the risk of losing the reader. It's a good mix. I liked that Watney doesn't take himself too seriously, but at the same time, I have to wonder how believable he is as a character. Stranded on Mars for hundreds of days, Watney lacks a moroseness and an introspective outlook I would expect. Now, I can accept Watney is unique. I can learn from a character who is different from me *BUT* I still can't quite believe him at all times. If Watney is so comical and witty, would he waste his time on this log? If he expects to die on Mars, wouldn't he find his time better spent writing a hilarious farce and burying it in the Martian sand for future astronauts to find; a farce that would detail how his people, the Martians, propagated their seeds throughout the universe before their planet died and how, after many millennia, each people would discover the Martian language: English. I don't know. I just can't see someone as clever as Watney wasting his time formulating pirate-ninjas and complaining about disco. It seems beneath him. 
 Really, I'm not complaining about Watney. He was a good character, certainly worth rooting for. And it was a good novel: entertaining and very well written. My only complaint is the dialogue meant to explain technical details to the reader. Sometimes it didn't give the reader the benefit of the doubt. I understand Watney doing it, because his intended audience is an unknown reader; but within dialogue at NASA and aboard Hermes, it stood out. These people know what they're doing. If the commander of a spacecraft orders something, she doesn't then need it explained back to her in simple terms. A minor irritation in an otherwise great novel. How great? Well, let's just say I'm not that thrilled about Matt Damon in the lead role, but I still put my money on the belief this is going to make one hell of a film.

I had mixed feelings about this book. From what I can tell, this book's plot seems to be a bit of a mash-up between Christina Rossetti's poem "Goblin Market" and a Goethe poem called "Der Erlkonig." It's been a while since I read "Goblin Market," but I feel like Jae-Jones does a good job of emulating its tone, especially at the beginning of the novel. The novel feels rich and lush, and abounds with sensuality infused with dark undercurrents. Its tone is creepy and a bit hedonistic. 
 This book has been compared to the movie "Labyrinth," but it is must slower moving and less adventurous than that, so I think the comparison may be a mistake. It has a bit of a fairy tale feel to it, and feels more like Rosamund Hodge's "Cruel Beauty" with it's dark sexuality, or even a little like Martine Leavitt's "Keturah and Lord Death," what with its prevailing sense of tragedy and loss.* 
 I loved the atmosphere and tone. As mentioned above, it both referenced and emulated "Goblin Market" which the Lit major in me appreciated. It was filled with very interesting dichotomies. There was a mix of desire and fear; passion and pain; love and hate. It was very rich and lush and the writing was beautiful. The characters were nuanced, and early on I was really enjoying it. I found the focus on music and composition to be very interesting as well, and loved the relationships between the protagonist and her siblings. 
 However, the plot really dragged at times, particularly in the second third of the book. There was just not enough happening and the characters were constantly repeating the same battles, both internally and externally. The protagonist was constantly questioning her self worth and desirability, the main couple were constantly fighting their connection/attraction to one another, etc. 
 I thought it was well written and that the author did a good job of portraying atmosphere and the character's inner turmoil, but it just lacked some in the plotting and pacing departments. I did like the way it was concluded, and think that the author has tons of potential. I think that there will be a lot of mixed opinions of this book. I enjoyed reading it, but I think it will be too slow for some readers, and might get passed over because of its similarity to several other books, but is worth the read just based on the writing and sense of atmosphere. 
 *It seems to be similar to Danielle L. Jesen's "Stolen Songbird" as well, but I haven't read that one yet. It also has similarities to "A Court of Thorns and Roses" by Sarah J. Maas, "The Star-Touched Queen" by Roshani Chokshi.

The ending didn't disappoint. And it was one of those that is both complete and satisfying. There is still a lot to look forward to but no huge cliffhanger until the next book. 
 And I loved how Kasie West subtly connected the two futures. Addison's choice has an effect on others but only to a certain degree. Some things happen as they were always meant to happen and other things happen but with slight variations. And with paragraphs alternating between each version of her future you appreciate the differences and observe the ripple effect. And all characters are present in both futures to varying degrees. I just thought the whole concept and execution was really neat. 
 And the writing was so much fun!! I loved her relationship with both boys. Her relationship with Trevor was a little more serious, whereas her relationship with Duke was a little more playful. There were a few LOL moments for me where Duke was involved. For instance: 
 "'That would bring out your eyes,' he says. 
 'How would that bring out my eyes?' 
 'Because your eyes are . . .' He trails off as I meet his gaze. 'Uh, brown. your eyes are brown. I could've sworn they were blue.' 
 'It's hard to keep track when you're looking into so many, isn't it?' 
 He narrows his eyes in confusion and I try not to laugh." 
 Note: her eyes really were blue but she was using light manipulation to change them. I also really liked Laila, her best friend. She was so lively and exciting. One of my favorite quotes from her was from one of their phone conversations: 
 "'Aw, I'm like a proud mother bird watching my daughter fly from the nest. Fly, little bird, fly. Oh no! Don't fall. No, that's the ground. Addie, watch out for the ground. Man, tough luck. You'd better come back home.' 
 I stick out my bottom lip. 'Was that supposed to be encouraging?' 
 'No, but it amused me. And I'm ready for you to come home.'" 
 Really, just amazing secondary characters all around. And Addison herself was a great lead character. She was so smart and interesting and had a really good voice for the delivery of this story. 
 My only complaint - and it's not even really a complaint - and I'm talking SO SMALL it shouldn't change your mind at all - but for the sake of an honest well-rounded review I will say I had a LITTLE difficulty remembering where the last story left off when each chapter began. But it only lasted a second. So pretend I didn't say anything :) 
 Ok I have to admit something here - this book contained what might be my favorite sentence read of all time: 
 "I stir around the last few Cheerios in my bowl, the effort required to fish them out one by one too hard to find on a Monday morning." 
 Does that say everything about me? I am an avid eater of cereal and adored this sentence. I can't really explain it except been there done that. It was so honest and unexpected and quirky and spoke to me. Ha. 
 Ok for reals now. This book is fantastic and you need to read it. Just do it. PEER PRESSURE. But really, please? You won't be disappointed!

As soon as I learned The Lotus Palace was a historical romance/mystery set in Ancient China, with actual Chinese people as main characters, I knew I HAD to read it. When you have read as much historical romance as I have, you don't find many new things. Even with the known trope - rich playboy falls for servant girl - I found the culture and setting so different that half the time I didn't know how characters would react to things. It made for a fascinating read. 
 The Pingkang Li is the City's pleasure quarter, full of beautiful, educated, sophisticated courtesans who compose poetry, act as hostesses in events and generally trade wits with scholars. It wasn't clear to me if selling their bodies was part of the bargain, but it seemed they had the liberty of choosing their own lovers. Yue-ying, our heroine, is the servant of a famous courtesan in the Lotus Palace. She's practical, hard working, tough and has a port-wine stain that mars her face. Bai Huang, the hero, is a rich, charming, extremely attractive, good for nothing scholar who has been "courting" Yue-ying's mistress for a while. But everything is not as it seems with Bai Huang - he's been exaggerating his reputation as a fool to spy for his father, who's a powerful government official. For a while, he's been noticing Yue-ying because she feels real to him as compared to the illusions of the Pingkang Li. 
 Yue-ying's past was horrific. I won't go into details because I don't want to give spoilers but although she doesn't dwell in the past, it's clear that it damaged her deeply. Bai Huang, for his part, hasn't had as charmed a life as you would expect, but it's mostly of his own doing. When he meets Yue-ying, he's desperately trying to redeem himself in the eyes of his father, who he disappointed terribly. 
 It takes a long time for Yue-ying to give in to the advances of Bai Huang. Practical creature that she is, she suspects his motives and it's not taken by his pretty face. She can't believe that a man like him - who could have any woman he wanted - would be interested in her, with her marked face, her situation in life and her past. But Huang crumbles her defenses slowly, with his love and persistence. Their relationship is not only about the physical but it's about trust and understanding. I was very touched when Huang acknowledged: 
 He had never trusted anyone else with the worst parts of himself. 
 The mystery was just somewhat disjointed with clues all over the place. Half the time I thought they were chasing red herrings and I didn't even recognize the murderer when he was unveiled. Definitely not the stronger part of the story. 
 I was fascinated by the cultural aspects of the book. I know next to nothing about Ancient China so I loved the descriptions of places, clothes, customs, etc. It amazed me how concerned people were with each other's privacy, to the point that they wouldn't share important thoughts or feelings because "you don't talk about those things." I was surprised by the way the final hurdle between Bai Huang and Yue-ying was overcome and it was only possible due to the differences in culture. 
 I'm definitely reading the next book - Constable Wu and Mingyu sound like a very intriguing couple. If you are looking for a different read, this book will definitely be for you!

It just seems no one can beat Dominique from The Chocolate Touch...anyways in this book especially it was good that we get the point of view of both Summer and Luc. They both have issues communicating with the other, and if I only had one of the POV's I would probably have hated the other person. When you read what they are thinking you are like of course, but then they don't express that as well as they should so the other person misunderstands and there are issues created. Without both of their thoughts you wouldn't really know what was going on with the other person. 
 Summer is used to people leaving her. Her parents never seemed to want to stick around, boyfriends always leave, or people just want her for her money. She is very insecure in a lot of ways, and she gets blackmailed by her dad to come to Paris and run the hotel he purchased for her. She gets draw away from her tiny island where she teaches the children and the people really love her (but even so she realizes that the kids will go away one day and she will lose them as well). She hates Paris since she was shipped off to boarding school there as a child. It was not a pleasant experience for her and she has nothing but bad memories there. 
 When she first meets Luc she mistakes him for a bellboy. She is so exhausted she almost passes out and Luc ends up carrying her up to her room. In her head she thinks how great he looks and maybe she can keep him. Maybe if she gives him a boat he will sail away into the sunset. So instead of saying all of that, she just offers him a boat without a reason which really makes him angry, with reason. It seems like she is just trying to buy him off and he is Luc! He doesn't need her money. 
 Luc has had a rough childhood as well. He and his dad busked in the metro for many years trying to make enough money for food and a roof over their heads. His mom ran off as soon as he was born. He has risen up from the streets to be an amazing chef in the hotel restaurant. Even though Summer annoys him, he still likes her. He sends her dessert after dessert, but because of her horrible upbringing where dessert was always withheld from her (while everyone else was able to eat it) she never eats them. She really does have issues, but then so does Luc. Of course everything works out eventually, but getting there could be frustrating. I didn't hate any of the characters, but man they could use some communication lessons. Summer always thinks the worst of Luc, even when he is trying to be nice. She always takes the worst possible meaning for the things he says and does. I was just like oh Summer, what am I going to do with you? Overall another great read.

"His Bloody Project" is the tale of Roderick Macrae, who murders three people. Roddy is the son of a crofter in Scotland (basically a serf), and is intelligent but has a hard life and a cruel and uncaring father. The first section of the book is by a modern day person who has "rediscovered" Roddy's manuscript, penned during the trial. The major part of the book is this manuscript, which poignantly describes his daily toil, relations with his family, and his family's run-in with the manipulative Lachlan Broad, one of Roddy's victims. This section is incredibly well written, describing in beautiful but melancholy terms Roddy's hard life. While you sympathize with Roddy, there are definitely a few red flags that make you question Roddy's morality and motives in the murders. 
 The final section is the trial, where some of Roddy's statements are questioned and you learn more about the state of the field of psychology at the time (Roddy's attorney has him declare himself to be not guilty by reason of insanity). This section is engaging - I especially enjoyed the inclusion of sections from newspapers reporting on the trial - but a little repetitive. I also would have like more explanation about why Roddy's lawyer is so passionate in his defense of Roddy. I can't imagine most attorneys of the time would have been so steadfast in defense of a client who has freely admitted to killing three people. "His Bloody Project" can be a tough read at times, and I didn't expect the murders to be related in quite such a graphic manner. But the characters are well developed, even minor secondary characters like the Smokes and Archibald Ross. The father is definitely an intriguing character, and Lachlan makes an excellent villain. 
 Burnet does a wonderful job setting the atmosphere, bringing you into the Scottish Highlands and the hard work but worthy life people found there. His use of some Scottish language was enjoyable and added more flavor to the book. (view spoiler)[I wish the ending had been a little less ambiguous. I think that Roddy did mean to kill Flora more than Lachlan, and would have liked a little more confirmation of this theory. But I understand why Burnet wanted to leave it to the reader - much like the jury - to form their own opinion. (hide spoiler)] 
 Overall, a very good piece of Scottish historical fiction/mystery.

So... this book was one of the rare few that have really pulled me in lately. In the beginning, it was anger and irritation. How could our protagonist repeatedly wish his child hadn't been born? How could he continuously insist that he would've preferred his child be aborted? How could he swear that if he could go back and change things, he wouldn't miss a beat? I'm so spoiled by the feel-good YA that is so popular recently that I didn't even realize that this is a very real reaction to a less than wonderful situation; 17 year old Ryden has become a teen father, and on the same day that his girlfriend and mother of his child, Meg, dies due to cancer. His dreams of going to UCLA on a soccer scholarship and going pro seem shattered; he's got to go to high school, attend regular soccer practices, work part time, and raise an infant as a single dad. This is not to say he had to go it alone; he had help from his mother (more on her later) and Alan, Meg's best friend. Regardless, it's no wonder he is resentful and bitter. 
 However, the book does show a great example of character development with Ryden. So I won't complain too much about that. 
 What I will complain about is this: Joni is a manic pixie dream girl. She has quirks and is different than the other girls and shows Ryden the better side of life. In the beginning, I found her to be incredibly childish and inappropriate. I hated that this would be his love interest. Over the course of the book, I didn't have her so much but let it be known that I still don't like her all that much. 
 I also didn't like Meg like I should've at the end; I think she was insane. She had unjust motives and was selfish. She was obsessive and she lied. So boo for her. 
 What I loved? The relationship between Ryden and his mother. She was there for him as a mother and a friend, whenever each was needed. She was a shoulder to cry and the foot when someone had to put their foot down. She was stern but supportive, kind and understanding, and really made me connect. 
 So the beginning of this book, I give a three. The end is a five. Averaged, this book deserves a 4 star rating.

 There are plenty of good and bad points to mention about this book, so right now I'm just going to say that in spite of those bad points, I really enjoyed this book. The characters are well-formed and the world is original. 
 Patrick Ness writes the book from Todd Hewitt's point of view. But aren't all books written from the main character's point of view? Well, yes, but The Knife of Never Letting Go is really written from his point of view. Todd is a mostly illeterate twelve(thirteen?)-year-old who grew up in a place where knowledge seems to be shunned. So the grammar, spelling, and everything else is exactly what you would expect such a character to be capable of. 
 That kind of writing might bother some people, but I got used to it pretty quickly. The next thing to note is the concept of Noise. It seems every character at the start of the book can hear each other's thoughts. The way Ness weaves this into the story is really interesting. There are also some parts where Noise is shown through big, blotchy fonts, which really emphasises the chaotic nature of Todd's world. 
 The spoilers start here! Beware! 
 So, the bad points. There are a few things in this book I take issue with for a number of reasons. Let's start with the fact that Todd never found out what the history of Prentisstown was until near the end of the book. Until then, he never knew what happened when it was time for somebody to 'become a man'. It's a mystery, and that's all well and good. 
 But here's my question: How is it that Todd doesn't know any of this when he hears the thoughts of everybody he lives with all the time? I know there are parts where he explains that you can't tell the truth from the lies in people's Noise and so on, but I still find it hard to believe. 
 The second problem I had was that, once I reached the end of the book, I still felt like the reason the Mayor was chasing after Todd hadn't really been revealed. The reaosn provided was that if they could make Todd into a killer, they could control anyone. So Todd was the last boy, and their army wouldn't be complete without him. I'm sorry, but that just doesn't strike me as realistic. Are we supposed to believe that Mayor Prentiss wants to send his army to the end of the planet to capture Todd because he's just a serious completionist? 
 My third problem is with Aaron. How frustrating is this guy? He just doesn't die! The problem here is not that Aaron isn't a good bad guy - he's a great bad guy. But for all the time he spends chasing them across New World, we never really find out if he's doing that as part of Mayor Prentiss's master plot or if he's doing it because he's mental. If Todd did kill Aaron, would Mayor Prentiss have won? Would Mayor Prentiss even have known? (I should mention that I haven't read the second in this series yet, so if this is answered there, I take it all back.) 
 And by this point, had we totally forgotten that Spackle Todd stabbed? If the point of the book was Todd trying to escape becoming a killer, didn't that ship kind of sail when he did this? The Spackle are shown to be sentient and intellegent beings, whether they speak or not, so shouldn't killing one of them count? 
 Okay, so now that that's all off my chest, I want to emphasise, again, that I did enjoy this book. Like I said before, the world was original and the characters were good. Todd was introduced as uneducated, easily frustrated, somewhat ignorant, but altogether good-hearted. These traits were consistently stuck to throughout the book. Equally well-developed is Viola, who is shown to be much smarter and calmer than Todd. And we learn that she's also pretty tough. 
 One of the most interesting things about this book is the way it almost changes genre as more of the world is revealed. In the first few chapters, I was quite convinced that this was a dystopian novel. But as it's revealed that they are all settlers on a new planet, and that they came her and gave up most of their technology voluntarily, it becomes more and more a science-fiction novel. By the end of the book, this world doesn't have a lot of traits that are dystopian at all. If a society voluntarily becomes a dystopia, is it still a dystopia? Something to think about. 
 The story was fast-paced, and after the first few chapters it became difficult to put down. I also want to mention that, in light of my criticisms, this is a children's book, and it's a good one. I will definitely be reading The Ask And The Answer at some point.

I feel a little bad about the two-star rating, because I don't want to give the wrong impression. This wasn't a bad book. This was, in fact, a fairly good book put into the hands of someone who just probably wasn't ever going to enjoy it. So, I didn't enjoy it. But that's okay. That doesn't always mean it's not a good book. I'll admit that some things are good for other people while still just not being my taste. Like spicey foods, or maybe skydiving. 
 Things I Liked 
 - Pretty good portrayal of depression. (The loss-of-identity, feeling kind of adrift, not knowing if the people you love are getting it part. Not the Oh-No-Willem-Left-Me part). 
 - That scene about falling-in-love vs. being-in-love. Cool sentiment. Good scene. 
 - Ms. Foley is awesome. 
 Things I Didn't Like 
 - Willem. At all. I actually really hated him. I didn't find him charming when he showed up, he didn't grow on me, I didn't understand why Allyson was so attached to the idea of him. 
 - Allyson, most of the time, although she had her moments. Part of my problem was that a lot of her motivation was Willem-based, and I didn't like him. 
 - I didn't think the day Allyson and Willem spent together was romantic. I thought it was full of weird bouts of jealousy and bad decisions (like getting lost in a foreign country). 
 - The whole "Lulu" thing. I felt like I would've been more on-board had she chosen to lie about her name, but instead Willem just never asked for it. Which leads to more confusion about how she thought it would be more than a one-night stand, when he wasn't interested in knowing her name. 
 - The whole tracking-Willem-down plot. I'm not opposed to plots about tracking down a lost almost-love you've only ever spent a day with - Serendipity is one of my all-time favorite movies. But I think the difference is that that was two-sided and always honest about being kind of absurd - and this was neither of those things. 
 - On that note: the one-sided-ness of the whole thing. I've got nothing against unrequited-love plots when the object of offection is at least likable, and they have some kind of relationship with the person who is in love with them. Willem is about 90% an asshole, and he and Allyson had an international one-night stand. Obsessing over him isn't love - it's obsession. 
 - Allyson's lack of ability to get along with any of the women around her. Hating one woman? Fine. Hating every single other woman in the book? Um, not okay. Even her supposed best-friend gets mostly hate. I don't get it. 
 Anyway, I wasn't a fan. But this was a well-written book, and I still love Gayle Forman's If I Stay and Where She Went, so I'm bound to pick up the next book of hers that doesn't include Allyson and Willem.

After Emily receives a daring list of things to do this summer from her best friend Sloane -- who, by the way, seems to be missing in action -- Emily's determined to accomplish everything on there, even if some of the tasks scare her. Skinny-dipping? Kissing a stranger? Could Sloane really be serious about this? Emily hopes that crossing off the items will provide an answer to where (and why) Sloane disappeared. But as summer continues on, Emily learns she can do so much more than what's on the list, and be exactly who she wants to be, minus Sloane. 
 Morgan Matson, like Emery Lord, is another auto-buy/auto-read author for me. Her books tend to be summer-themed, like Sarah Dessen, with strong friendships at the heart of the story. Though this friendship felt more one-sided to me throughout most of the book -- Emily's dependency on Sloane and debilitating shyness irked me in some cases, even after explanations were given -- it was still that friendship that propelled Emily's character growth in a natural way. Without Sloane's list, Emily would've sat at home, bored to tears. This list kicked her butt into gear and created a whirlwind, adventurous summer! 
 What was great about the list (I'm a huge fan of lists) is that even though it's definitely meant to bring Emily out of her shell and explore, it doesn't seem outrageous or forced. Emily starts off each chapter fully expecting to cross one thing off the list, and instead crosses off another. One instance in particular is her determination to cross off "steal something" and ends up "[sharing] some secrets in the dark." I loved that chapter. That chapter, I think, was Emily's big turning point for her character. 
 The cute romance on the side was unassuming, too. Frank Porter is understanding and kind, a genuinely good person. Their friendship blossoms wonderfully. Emily doesn't spend 2/3 of the book debating whether or not she likes him and if she should do anything about it, like many YA contemporaries seem to do. Let it fall into place naturally and the characters' actions will guide them! Thank you, Matson. Another reason you're an auto-buy! 
 I once made a List of Happy Things when I was in high school. It contained activities that made me happy, or things I'm sure would make me happy if I tried. Rolling down hills, finger-painting, baking cookies, that sort of thing. I'm pretty sure if I lived near an ocean, I'd add "skinny-dipping" to the list too. That's how Since You've Been Gone made me feel: happy.

There's another death, an apparent suicide but with clues that the same murderer has struck again . . . 
 I'm normally quite a fan of Scandinavian/Icelandic mysteries, but this one -- from Sweden -- was an exception. It wasn't out-and-out bad, but it bored me when it should have engrossed. I found Lackberg's attempts at wry characterization merely tedious -- Erica and Patrik are forever sucking in their stomachs, spending hours choosing their clothes before they meet, etc., which might be a pleasant running joke if you didn't have to wade through two or three pages of this gush every flipping time it happens. Again, Patrik's unpleasant, stupid boss has a very obvious hairpiece that -- oh the hilarity -- keeps flopping down to one side or the other. And so on. 
 The narrative isn't helped much by the translation. The translator, Steven T. Murray, is very well recognized and I've enjoyed his work elsewhere (under the pseudonym Reg Keeland he did the Stieg Larsson ones, for example, and they're if anything better than the originals), so I don't know what went wrong here. For example: 
 When she fixed her blue eyes on him he felt that he was seen. (p101) 
 He actually hadn't managed to look at the articles during work hours, but only because of a rebellious desire to make trouble. (p120) 
 She circled her finger round her nipples until they hardened and then purred, "Forgive me, that was stupid of me, Jan. . . ." (p239) 
 Once again, Axel felt the urge to rip open his chest and reveal what had been hiding there for all these years. To clear his conscience by pouring out the entire naked truth. But he took a deep breath and pushed back what was threatening to spill out. (p304) 
 Most remarkable of all, perhaps, are the potatoes that are put on to boil on page 210 and, by page 211, an hour and a half later, still haven't completely cooked. 
 The mystery itself is -- although I guessed various of its important elements before I should have -- a reasonably neat one. Unfortunately, the book has one of those godawful Reading Group Guides at the back, cleverly whipped up by someone in the Pegasus basement, no doubt. Part of it reads: 
 Camilla has been described as Sweden's own Agatha Christie, and the Christie-like provincial village of Fjallbacka gives credence to the comparison to Christie's "locked room" mystery formula. Yet The Ice Princess takes this formula to a new level. 
 The comparison to Christie is a bit of a stretch but isn't entirely inapt; this is certainly in the tradition of the classic mystery tale, although not especially cozy. But locked-room? Christie, although a few of her tales are locked-room, wasn't a major exponent of the style; while she and others active at the time had it as an occasional part of their repertoire, the classic writer whose name became synonymous with the locked-room tale was John Dickson Carr/Carter Dickson, not Christie. And, just to add to the "discussion note's" folly, The Ice Princess, far from taking the style "to a new level", isn't in any sense a locked-room mystery!

I would give this somewhere in the upper 3s to lower 4s. I guess the reviews I read said this book was so great that when I finally read it, I was a little underwhelmed. The story was good, the writing was good, and I did want to read more about what happened to the characters. But for some reason, even though I read every night, it seemed to take forever to get to the end of the book. 
 Plot: 
 I'm going to try to make this not too spoilerish, but it's hard.... Long story short, Haven, the heroine of the story, is sold to the DeMarcos, a wealthy family with ties to the mob. A slave her whole life, Haven finds that living with the DeMarcos gives her more freedom than she is used to. While she learns how to adjust to her new setting, she begins to get closer to the youngest DeMarco son, Carmine. As they get to know each other and grow closer, secrets come to light that could threaten their relationship and their lives as well. 
 Characters: 
 Haven is the heroine of the story. She comes from an incredibly abusive past, but because of her inherent goodness, she is one of those versatile people who can do well in any situation. 
 Carmine is the complete opposite. He drinks, he curses, he fights, he screws.... If it's bad, he does it. Those negative qualities are worsened by his extremely volatile temper. As we learn what caused him to be this way, we are supposed to realize that he's not bad; he's just misunderstood; all in all, he is more of an antihero than anything. One of the downsides to reading these kinds of books after you have children is that you think about what you would do if the hero tried to date your daughter. In this case, I'm pretty sure I'd whack him. Carmine was sometimes too abrasive, especially for someone who was supposed to love Haven so much. 
 Dr. DeMarco is the one who bought Haven. He seems torn in everything he does, especially when it comes to doing what's right and doing what his mafia family expects him to. They expect him to groom Carmine to enter the business; he knows that's not what Carmine's mother would have wanted, so he tries to find a way out of it. Dr. DeMarco has another son, Dominic, who is perky and friendly and pretty much too good to be true, but he really is. 
 The other characters include Carmine's best friend, Dia; ex-best friend, Nicholas (who would have actually been a better match for Haven); Dominic's girlfriend (Lisa maybe?); Carmine's aunt and uncle, Celia and Corrado; and several mafia figures, who are all pretty much interchangeable. 
 Writing: 
 Very well edited. (I love that in a book!) The language wasn't overly flowery, but it was very descriptive. There are a lot of Italian slang words, and a couple of them aren't explained, so you might want to keep Urban Dictionary open. Be prepared for lots of language and a little bit of not-too-detailed sex. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 This was a good book with an incredibly timely story. I read it right before the SuperBowl, and there were tons of news items and articles about human trafficking, so it did really increase my awareness of the subject. That's why I feel guilty when I say something just didn't click for me. It may have been my issues with Carmine. It may have been that it was a long book, and I'm a slow reader. It is a good enough book that I want to read the sequel; I'm just going to wait a while before I do.

"He's a good kid". 
 That may be my #1 pet peeve about parents. No matter what horrible act their offspring has committed, parents simply say "He's a good kid" instead of apologizing for raising a monster. (Replace "he" with "she" as appropriate.) 
 So we get a lot of "He's a good kid" in this book. For starters, the heartbroken father of a murdered 14 year old high school student finds it impossible to understand why anyone would want to harm his son because "He's a good kid". It doesn't take long for the reader to learn that Ben Rifkin was a vicious bully. That in no way excuses his murder, but suggests why someone might have had a problem with him. 
 The book's narrator, prosecutor Andy Barber, then begins to insist that his son Jacob cannot possibly be the coldhearted murderer who stabbed Ben to death, because "He's a good kid". His beloved wife, Laurie, says the same thing, despite some very convincing and disturbing evidence. So it must be a total coincidence that Jacob wrote stories for cutter sexual perversion websites, stories that basically described Ben's murder, right? He's a good kid, he can't do that! Jacob couldn't possibly torture animals, so let's just hide in the bedroom while we hear a cat howling in pain in our yard! No way, he's a good kid, someone else was torturing a cat in our yard. 
 It's an interesting perspective into the legal system - ultimately, no matter how skilled the prosecution or defense, a person's fate is held in the hands of 12 random people with no legal experience - and parental love. How well does any parent truly know their child? Andy and Laurie still see Jacob as a tiny baby sleeping on Andy's stomach, not a near-adult capable of stabbing a boy 3 times. Or killing neighborhood pets. 
 The book veers off into a "killing gene" or "bad seed" subplot that I did not feel was handled skillfully and was thus unnecessary to the overall story. Had this intriguing plot device been woven into the story properly, it would have added another dimension to it. Instead, it just made the book too long. 
 What infuriated me was Andy's sheer hypocrisy when dealing with his son. Andy deals with bereaved family members of murder victims and fights for justice, yet destroys evidence that implicates his son. I felt Andy was the worst villain in the story by a long shot. His manipulation leads to a truly ridiculous last-minute plot twist (view spoiler)[ that results in the murder of the wrong man, destroys another prosecutor's career, and leads to the senseless unsolved death of a teenage girl. (hide spoiler)]. 
 So while I did not like some of the events in the book, I enjoyed its brisk pace and the mystery at its center. It made me sit back and think for a while after reading the last chapter (view spoiler)[ Way to go, Laurie! Rot in hell, Jacob (hide spoiler)] which to me is the sign of a good book.

The Shack is one of those books that seems to be quite polarizing - people either love it or hate it. And honestly, I can see both sides. Personally, I am right down the middle on this one. 
 First off, let's talk about the story itself. We all know this is a tale of a man who, in the midst of his despair from a terrible tragedy, receives a note from God and ultimately, meets and becomes acquainted with God. Bam. That right there stirs up all kinds of controversy. From those who don't believe in God, to those who believe in a God that would never come face to face with a human, we all have our opinions on this idea. The fact that The Shack opens up the doors to have these conversations is, I think, the best part about this book. 
 Let me say it right now; I personally do not have an issue with the theological statement and the metaphors Young makes. In fact, I appreciate the uniqueness of this concept and his effort to put these themes into a fictional format. Our entire history has been handed down from generation through generation through stories. So, why not this as well? In addition, I liked that his focus was on having a relationship with God, rather than a specific religion and its set of rituals and practices. 
 "Who said anything about being a Christian? I'm not a Christian." 
 That all being said, this wasn't a particularly good novel. At first, I thought the language and wording choices were so simple so as to make it widely accessible and to let the themes shine through. I also thought it was possible that it dragged so slowly because I had seen the movie first and therefore knew what to expect. Wrong on both counts. 
 The writing itself is my biggest issue here. The characters were one-dimensional, their relationships were cliched, and the dialogue did not sound how people actually speak. Scenes that should have been nail-biters plodded along at the same slow pace as the rest of it. Descriptions were overwrought and long-winded. At 250 pages, this could have used some heavy handed editing to condense it and pack more of a punch. With a more skilled writer and more editing, this could have been so much more. 
 If you have some belief in God and want to go deeper, reading The Shack might be a perfect jumping off point for more questions and conversation. Otherwise, save yourself some time and see the movie instead.

 Twenty years ago, four year old Brian disappeared from the Arlington estate. Now, criminal journalist Griffin Hadley is writing a book that he hopes will cast a new light on the cold case. 
 However, Jarrett Arlington - Brian's grandfather - is the only one encouraging Griff's presence in Long Island. Family, staff, and friends are all set against his intrusion, including Pierce Mather, the Arlingtons' staunch lawyer. 
 When Griff begins to receive anonymous threats it becomes clear that his prying is making someone wary. Is finding out the truth about Brian's disappearance worth the expense of his own personal safety? 
 Lanyon's newest novel was one of my most anticipated reads for this year. It did not disappoint. While I enjoy his amateur sleuth stories, I liked that 'Stranger on the Shore' veered from that path and focused on an investigative journalist researching a cold case. It made for a different, and interesting, angle to the development of the mystery. 
 Atmosphere plays a vital role in the novel and envelops the reader, making the story all the more palpable. 'Stranger on the Shore' has a nice balance between hazy and vivid, giving the story a wonderful ambiance, but still maintaining a realism that kept me absorbed throughout. 
 I was notably drawn to the interactions between Griff and Pierce. In a different scenario, Pierce's hot and cold attitude toward Griff might have been jarring, but it fit perfectly within the context of the novel. Pierce had so many suspicions and stipulations, and it was interesting to see the conflict - and sexual tension - between him and Griff, who is adamant about writing the book on Brian's disappearance. It made for a great dynamic between the two characters from the start. 
 I liked that the focus of 'Stranger on the Shore' wasn't so much on uncovering what had happened to Brian, although Lanyon does not dismiss that significant factor of the novel. What I appreciated was how the mystery focused more on the how and why of the disappearance, and - of course - the culprit. Nothing was too straightforward, and I was always guessing and second guessing events, happy to be swept up in the intrigue. 
 There were aspects of the 'Stranger on the Shore' that, if handled poorly, could have come across as gimmicky. However, Lanyon managed them tactfully, threading speculation throughout the narrative, rather than choosing blatant ambiguity or shock value, which could have easily backfired and lessened the impact of the mystery. Lanyon's deft development of the story made for a well-written, engrossing read. 
 I am a huge fan of Lanyon's work, particularly of his novels. I wait in eager anticipation for the next and highly recommend 'Stranger on the Shore' to any avid mystery lover.

It's always hard to review books that I didn't finish. Mostly because there is a good reason that I didn't finish it. However, that's not the case with The Forbidden Stone. I wanted so badly to finish the book but when you find yourself dreading reading, you know it's time to move on. 
 The premise of the book is pretty solid. Four friends, Wade, Lily, Darrel, and Becca, uncover a secret message from Wade's Uncle Henry before his mysterious death. This message leads them to Germany where they attend his funeral with Wade's father. More clues are uncovered and the group begins to piece together what really happened to Uncle Henry. 
 I think I read approximately 150 pages of this book. It wasn't bad, it was just so slow. I never felt invested in the mystery or the characters. The book just was too unbelievable, even for fantasy. The book rests on the belief that the universe revolves around these kids and they are completely invincible. The shifting POV may confuse some young readers. In fact, the entire book felt too advanced for middle grade. Yet the themes and plot felt too immature for a YA audience. On the positive side, I liked that the father was included in the story. Too often books don't include parental figures and I thought this was a nice change of pace. Perhaps one day I will return to this series, for now it's staying on my "did not finish" list.

Ok, so I really enjoyed reading this book, but what did I think of it? I don't think this was a very good book at all and there was a lot that bothered me. It's just that this book has so much potential and with some tweaks this book could have been great. 
 Lara Jean is a really fun character to read about, in that she's very real. And to me, she's extremely relatable. She prefers staying in on the weekends and wearing PJs and doing scrapbooking and knitting. She's quirky. I like that. Out of the contemporary YA books I have read, I like Lara Jean the most in that she feels very real, as in, she is someone I could have known and gone to high school with. She's not all drinking and partying and like lol what up dog. Nor is she nerdy or gothy or edgy. She's not a stereotype, or a teenager on the page. She's a real person. 
 Let me describe the potential for this book then I'll talk about all my problems with this book. Lara Jean has lived in her older sister's shadow her whole life and she doesn't even realize it. Her sister is her rock and her foundation and her best friend, but now her sister has gone all the way to Scotland for college and Lara Jean has a chance to live her life. She doesn't have many friends (and that's a flaw I'll talk about later.) and she hasn't experienced a lot of living. This year could be her chance to change that. She always loves people who she knows she has no chance with bc she's afraid of commitment. (IS this bc her mother died, or she's been hurt before. This aspect of her could have been explored more.) 
 When the letters get sent out (by an obvious culprit and I don't know why it isn't obvious to her. She doesn't even suspect who it is and that's pretty dumb.) it could be her chance to explore life, live a little, become her own person, discover who she is and what is holding her back from love. Then she would meet the right guy and have an adventure all bc the letters were sent. That is the book I wanted. That is not the book I got. 
 Certain aspects of Lara Jean's character are not really explored very well. Why doesn't she have any female friends besides her sister and Chris? Why is she friends with Chris, best friends even? She seems very likable and it doesn't make sense that she doesn't have more friends. It needs to be explained why she doesn't want a real bf right now. What does she want to be when she grows up? What are her interests beyond her hobbies? What does she do? How does she do at school? 
 This book is trying so hard to be a coming of age story, but there needs to be like Lara Jean is X. Change and growth happen. Epiphany. Now Lara Jean is Y and it's so much better and happier. Bits and pieces of those steps were there but all mashed up and not clear. Maybe it's because this was book one. Idk. But I feel like even though Lara Jean feels very real and I like her very much, she is only half a person in some aspects. 
 And I know this is a romance more than a coming of age, but there is seriously no thought to Lara Jean's future or anything to do with it or Real things. Only sisters and love and boys. And I guess friends. And that is too bad, because this book also fails as a romance. I think more than anything it really fails as a romance. 
 So there are 5 letters sent out, but it's only really between two guys the whole book and I can't really discuss it at all with out at least light spoilers, so be warned. Anything super important though I'll put under a cut. 
 So Josh. Josh is confusing. He is one of Lara Jean's best friends actually I think, besides her sister, he is her best friend. But he is in love with her older sister and even though they broke up when she went to college, Lara jean knows Josh and Margot will get back together. So yeah, Lara Jean is crushing on her sister's (ex)boyfriend. And EVERYONE, the reader, Lara Jean, we all know that's wrong and cringe-worthy. Why do Josh and Lara jean have such great chemistry. I guess it's supposed to be friendship chemistry, but it really feels like they are supposed to be together, nevermind Margot.And then later in the book things get really weird and Josh becomes kind of a jerk and things fall apart. (view spoiler)[ Like out of no where he kisses her, and then she realizes she doesn't love him. LIke why is the whole book pushing them together and then suddenly it isn't? (hide spoiler)] Like there's one part that says she's more herself when she's with Josh. Is she or isn't she supposed to be with him. 
 And then Peter. He seems like he used to be a nice guy or deep down he is a nice guy, but then he has to keep up appearances or his attractiveness made him cocky. Why is he here? Why is he a love interest. He's pretty much a tool, even if he is super great with Lara Jean's younger sister. This guy has been dating the same girl for four years and he's obviously still in love with her. It gives no reason to why he would stop loving Genevieve and start liking Lara Jean. And then he does some questionable things at the end of the book. 
 Basically Josh and Peter are both wrong for her, but Josh seems a better match but at the end Peter seems a better match but there are all these obstacles and then the book ends. 
 It just, the characters and romances are not good and this just could have been such a better book. I still want to know what happens next though. I am sufficiently connected to want a happy ending. Or that coming of age story I wanted, since nothing is really resolved yet.

A truly remarkable book, this is that one book I've been ashamed to admit I hadn't yet read. When it came out I had just had my second child, then wrote a book the following year, two more books the following year, and another book the year after that, and then I spent the next while just catching up on everything I'd missed. This was always on the list, and it was extraordinary. The beautiful story of Aminata Diallo, her capture from her peaceful life in Africa, the brutal treatment she and thousands of men, women, and children endured, and the life she made for herself afterwards. Hill has done his research, and doesn't paint a black and white portrait where the white man is bad, Africans good. In the African village where Aminata lives, there are people born into slavery and they work as such within the village, though they are treated far better than the slaves who were brought to America. While her first placement in America is a nasty one, Aminata soon finds herself sold to a family who teaches her how to read and write, and those two skills change her life forever. This is a story of fierce determination, loyalty, love, the connections forced upon us and the loving connections we make, and a desperation to return to one's homeland. It brings home the reality of what was done so long ago, and it boggles the mind to think that human beings could ever treat other human beings in this manner. A true masterpiece that should be required reading everywhere. I thank Lawrence Hill from the bottom of my heart for this book.

My initial impulse was to give this 4 stars, but let's be honest. Once I got past the introduction (which was a bit dry for me), I stayed up all night reading the book. That should make it auto-receive 5 stars. 
 This was a great book, and I'm eager to read the rest of the series, which of course I don't have because I'm traveling. It was interesting and captivating. It's hard to believe this was written by a teenager (well, in some respects, anyway; there were points that were clearly very standardized, like the typical hangover and some of the relationship angst. At the same time, check out the description of a sunrise. I was just listening to someone point out how sunsets have become cliche, but Paolini manages to snag a new yet exact take on them. Well done.) 
 One of the biggest complaints I have is that we don't learn how old Eragon is until roughly 2/3 of the way through the novel. He could be 12 or 18. That's a pretty big gap, and something odd to leave hanging. The closest guess we have comes from his cousin, who is a few years older and about to be married. But hey, maybe the kid is a late bloomer. This is key in terms of timeline, like the fact that Bronn showed up 15 years ago. Was that before or after Eragon was born? (About the same time, it turns out.) 
 I also found Eragon's reaction to death a bit blase. Probably standard for fantasy, but still we're missing a basic human reaction. True, he is willing to slice and dice the human-like monsters, but the only insight we get is when he pukes a bit on seeing a massacre. Yet given the state of it, that seemed a bit weak; this was serious carnage. He does struggle a bit with ideals versus reality when his friend kills an unconscious man who had threatened them, and that's good, but mostly he feels idealized. 
 That said, this book has a lot of depth for a YA novel, and is definitely one I would recommend to my kids, if my daughter hadn't already beaten me too it. I'm eager to read the rest of the series. It left me with a few lingering suspicions on Eragon's parentage that I'm anxious to see resolved.

 I absolutely loved Kara's character. Kara was a strong, single mother completely dedicated to her young son Connor. She is a hard worker and stands up for her rights. Her idealism is infectious. Kara has been unlucky in love, and very hesitant to start a new relationship. 
 And what can I say about Reece? Reece made me sigh, made me swoon, and he made me dream. Aside from being just a little too perfect, I absolutely loved him. Loved his sense of responsibility, his sense of humor, and the way he protected his woman. And yes, he is hawt! 
 There's also a real thriller happening between all the love scenes. It's a great story and kept me on the edge of my seat. The investigative journalism part of the book seemed very realistic as well. Kara had to work through tons of paperwork to find her answers. It never ceases to amaze me how much research needs to go into a newspaper story.

 Oh, and Reece, you can get me hot and bothered anytime.

This book has received SO MUCH hype and I was thrilled when BookTube-A-Thon gave me an excuse to read it. While I did like it a lot, I didn't fall in love with it the way some people did. I think part of that may be due to the fact that I read it for a read-a-thon and therefore was more concerned with finishing it than savoring it. Because this is the book you need to savor. You need to luxuriate in the gorgeous writing and complex characters, and I didn't give myself the chance to fully appreciate the beauty of this book. 
 This was my first ever Victoria Schwab book, and I'd gone in with high expectations for the writing, as everyone raves about how beautiful it is. I will say, I was not disappointed in that regard, but I was surprised. It's not beautiful in the way I expected it to be. It's not lyrical and poetic and bursting with these artsy metaphors. Instead, Schwab wields words like a paintbrush, gracefully filling our minds with vivid images and sucking us into the story & characters. And I just think it is so funny that everyone talks about the beauty of this book when there is so much stabbing and shooting and killing. 
 Another thing that really makes Vicious stand out is the unique execution of a tired premise. At its core, Vicious is about two college kids who gain super powers. It's an idea that's been written countless times, right? Not like this. Schwab makes it feel fresh and new, like you've never read anything like it before. It was fascinating to see Victor and Eli, the two main characters, unravel how people develop these super powers, and even more interesting to read the ways they try to acquire powers themselves. My favorite part was, by far, the flashbacks to their college days as their mindsets and their relationship developed and changed. 
 Now, I don't think it's fair to discuss Vicious without mentioning the characters. It's kind of a daunting task, talking about these characters, because there is so much that could be said. Eli and Victor are complex and well-developed. Schwab brings the concept of heroes and villains into question, as well as intentions vs. actions. It's all kind of a giant mindfuck because you think you know who is the villain and who is the hero, but then your brain just gets completely scrambled because NOPE. You know who thinks they're the villain and who thinks they're the hero, but it's all so fantastically twisted. I have to say, I ended up really rooting for Victor, who is the protagonist. I didn't agree with all of his methods, and I didn't think he was a particularly great guy, but that's kind of the point. Humans are messy and selfish sometimes, but that doesn't make them evil. Victor was just kind of doing the best he could, in my opinion, and I love the fatherly role he begins to play for Sydney, a young girl he meets and adds to his team. 
 What prevented me from falling head over heels for this book, though, was the pacing. I found the novel to be a bit slow sometimes. I think a major part of that was all the jumping from character to character. There's a ton of perspective shifting and I understand why it was done, but it just got to be a bit exhausting sometimes. There were some parts that I just would have liked to stay in one person's head. 
 Vicious is such a complicated, intricate book, and even though I've written quite a bit already, I feel like I have not even come close to doing it justice. It is a dark, twisted book that will really make you think about the nature of humanity and right and wrong. It's truly a brilliant piece of literature and I now understand why everyone speaks so highly of it.

Elena Watkins is tired of her dad's paranoia. Moving every three months, never settling down or making friends, never able to experience a normal life . . . and then the dragons attack, she wakes up in a magical country, and she realizes "normal" will never define her life again. No one knows who was after her (or was it her father?) or why. Now she's struggling to fit into a world where the ordinary humans surrounding her might be dragons in disguise, and her own role might be bigger than anyone expects. 
 This book has a lot of solid parts, but it's also kind of jerky. The first bit is a thriller, with the abnormal home life devolving into an attack that leaves Elena all but dead . . . and then the plot just forgets about that and moves on. Elena's feelings for her father gets a few brief mentions but otherwise nobody brings up anything about that time, which felt really bizarre. The enemy doesn't appear to have been killed, so the lack of follow through was puzzling. Elena doesn't ask any questions about it. No one offers any answers. No one even offers to guard her against the possibility of future attacks. 
 Once we get past that, it's pretty definitely a YA fantasy/paranormal romance. There's one main romance (I can't honestly call it a love triangle yet) although this is hampered by Elena's emotions and will running one way and the plot clearly pointing her in another direction. I'm pretty sure the prophecy, for example, has a lot more to do with her romantic choices than anything else. 
 I did like Elena's female roommates. They're neat characters, and Sammy in particular was a lot of fun. I liked the dragon shapeshifters, the various types of dragons, and the various abilities. I wasn't at all fond of the whole "dragon personality completely changes when claimed by a human," which was disturbing to watch in action (even if it does clean up his character from jerk to decent guy). Especially since it's a given this is going to happen again with Blake. 
 It is pretty easy to spot the overall way things are going, though, which makes Elena's romance uninteresting and to my mind unimportant. (view spoiler)[ Elena is clearly the daughter of the late monarchs, with her "mother's" disappearance and its timeframe, and the prophecy about Blake, being some of the strongest evidence. Blake, equally clearly, is her Destined Soul Mate, so anything not involving him is basically doomed by Authorial Fiat, because the prophecy says the monarch's child will claim the Rubicon. Elena even has a PICTURE of her "mother", which she never bothers to bring out but would likely be instantly recognized by some of the older dragons who actually knew that dragon. (hide spoiler)] 
 I was also a bit annoyed that so many of the riddles present in the book are just reusing rather famous ones. Particularly Elena's last and hardest one. Given that it was part of a myth, the two pages devoted to her thinking it over had me wondering how she hadn't run into this before, since her father likes riddles and this is hardly a new one. 
 I'm torn about continuing this series. I would probably read more on Kindle Unlimited, but I don't think I like it enough to buy it outright (if this was in my library, it would get a rental). I feel like the story is dropping some interesting angles in favor of a love story it's too obviously telegraphing can't work anyway. On the other hand, the world was fun, and the dragons are by and large more fun, so I wouldn't mind seeing more of them. I rate this book Neutral.

Goodreads has been both a blessing and a curse to my reading life. I've discovered so many amazing books from the reviews of other readers, and my to-read list has grown substantially. However, this site has dramatically changed the way I visit libraries and bookstores. Whereas once I might've picked up a book based solely on its cover or description, now I can't grab a new book without researching it fully on Goodreads first. If it doesn't have many reviews, pass. Mostly negative reviews? Super pass. Had I used Goodreads while shopping at a blowout book sale at Barnes & Noble this week, I wouldn't have purchased Reluctantly Charmed. Too few reviews. And what a shame that would've been because this book was super charming. 
 Our main character, Kate McDaid, is a lowly advertising employee working in Dublin whose life is disrupted by her ancestor's will. Her great-great-great-something-or-other leaves her a series of Seven Steps from the Celtic Faeries she must share with the world over the course of seven weeks. What starts as a bit of a joke turns into a media frenzy as the world becomes obsessed with faeries. But as the steps progressively get less whimsical and more scary, Kate must decide whether she wants to continue publishing them - and what the consequences could be if she stops. 
 Kate McDaid (the modern-day one, of course) is such a likable protagonist and narrator. Her reactions feel real and relateable. As a reader, we feel her same doubt of the faeries in the beginning but just like Kate, we start to believe more as the story continues. She's funny and a little happy-go-lucky, but I found myself wanting her to succeed and laughing along with her when things didn't go according to plan. She's not the most flawed or technically-crafted character, but she's a fun character that you can't help but like. 
 Ellie O'Neill's biggest strength here is also the biggest weakness: this book is a lot of things at once. Mostly, it works: there's the romantic troubles a la Bridget Jones's Diary, some fantastical, magical elements similar to many of Sarah Addison Allen's novels, and a little bit of regular-person-turned-celebrity book themes, too. While this gave the story a really nice, entertaining mix, there were times that everything felt a little too rushed, especially near the end. O'Neill usually finds a way to blend so many genres, but when the blending fails, it feels forced and obvious. 
 I really didn't know what to expect when I picked up this book, but I was delightfully charmed and enchanted. This feels like a book that could have really taken off if the marketing had been stronger or a few a book bloggers had given it a read. I hope it gets more recognition.

Lehane saves his best for the last in his inconsistent yet enthralling Coughlin saga 
 This review contains no spoilers. 
 Intro 
 I will have to differ with the majority of reviewers and suggest World Gone By did not only end the trilogy on a high note but it was the best of the bunch. That is high praise coming from someone who felt Live by Night was one of Lehane's weaker efforts and did not have much hope from World Gone By. The Given Day was surely more ambitious but this is overall the better and more consistent of the two. 
 Plot 
 It's a direct sequel to Live By Night picking up ten years after its ending. Joe Coughlin is an enabler of sorts/behind the scenes facilitator for the mob and has to figure out whether there is any truth to the rumor that there is a hit out on him. 
 The changes from Live by Night are clear from the onset. Its pacing is a huge departure from the last two books and more reminiscent of the early Kenzie-Gennaro books, it's fast, visceral and relentless. The twists are less predictable or at the very least much better concealed by Lehane. There is not a single point in the book when it lost my attention and the only black mark against the plot might be the sheer familiarity of genre fans with some of its elements. The execution is excellent so it did not bother me and after all there isn't any truly groundbreaking way left to cover the gangster genre. 
 Writing 
 The writing is masterly, Lehane's vocabulary will put a lot of other best sellers to shame. His musings about morality and mistakes are thoughtful and profound yet they don't ever feel tacked on or come at the cost of slowing down the story. There are little touches of genius throughout the book. The way he doles out information on a mob doctor's past in snippets with a terrifying twist at the end is brilliant. A throwaway character that appears in one chapter and would be more of an expository device in other books become so much more interesting. His dialogues hit the mark capturing varying emotions with utmost ease; the intense callousness of mob bosses killing unsuspecting victims without a care in the world, the tenderness Coughlin feels for his son, the tension of a doomed courtship between Coughlin and his mistress. Lehane is firing on all cylinders and it's a joy to read. 
 Characters 
 The biggest change from Live By Night is the character of Joe Coughlin. I hated him in that; he came across as gullible and incompetent. That book wanted to portray him as a misunderstood outlaw doomed by destiny rather than his own choices; while this recognizes him as a man who tries to makes excuses about his own morality but ultimately struggles to buy into his own lies. This changes the whole tone of the book, it's much more bleak but arguably better for it. 
 While Coughlin's resurgence as a strong lead is a good sign what stands out are the supporting characters. They are impeccably crafted with King Lucias, a deranged mob boss and the aforementioned doctor being the best examples. They come with their own backstories and personality tics; though their page time is very low, they evoke strong reactions. 
 Verdict 
 If Live by Night was about hopes and aspirations of Joe Coughlin, World Gone By is essentially about his regrets regarding the choices he had made. A small change in approach completely changes the tone of the book, unravels greater depth in its protagonist and makes him much less likeable but more realistic in my view. If a reader can handle that he will do to well to check out this superbly crafted addition to Lehane's enviable oeuvre. Yes it does nothing new but what it does, it does damn near perfectly. My rating - 5/5. 
 P.S. It's a pity the worst book by some distance in the series (Live by Night) is the one that is being turned into a movie.

Jenna Blum has been writing short stories since she was 16. Several of them have been published. "Those who save us" is her first novel. The book has been on various bestseller lists and has been nominated for several awards. 
 For fifty years, Anna Schlemmer has refused to talk about her life in Germany during World War II. Her daughter, Trudy, was only three when she and her mother were liberated by an American soldier and went to live with him in Minnesota. Trudy's sole evidence of the past is an old photograph: a family portrait showing Anna, Trudy, and a Nazi officer, the Obersturmfuhrer of Buchenwald. Driven by the guilt of her heritage, Trudy, now a professor of German history, begins investigating the past and finally unearths the dramatic and heartbreaking truth of her mother's life. 
 The characters are put down very well, you really start to feel for them. Getting angry a bit at Anna for not telling her daughter more, but understanding too that she simply wants to forget what has happened. I found it very interesting to read a book from this perspective as most of WWII books are about survivors of camps, people in the resistance or people from other countries and how they got trough the war. I think it is very well put and gives a clear view what a human being will do to survive. 
 The book will be able to call for some negative feelings too though so you have to be able to really put things in the right place while reading.

 The writing is sooooo good. It's very literary- poetry is sprinkled throughout. John Keats - his life, his works are expertly woven throughout this story. This man can write.

Dan Brown writes like that one ninth-grade classmate we all had who, in freshman English class when we were assigned short stories, would try to vehemently impress everyone else by concocting an action-packed story with too much detail and complexity that we lose all sense of organization and concept. That's Dan Brown, from Digital Fortress to The Lost Symbol. All of his stories are intensely entertaining, but sometimes too much so, and they lose all sense of reality and feasibility. 
 Not to say I'm a master storyteller who could do better than Brown, but it's a bit problematic when you have readers literally rolling their eyes at how overblown everything in your story is. All of Brown's books fit into this category (especially his Robert Langdon adventures, which are too good to be true), but especially The Lost Symbol, which races from plot point to plot point without ever really explaining deeply into the characters' motivations or psyches. 
 Unsurprisingly, however, Brown's story starts off with a cliffhanger, like every single chapter in the book, with exemplary hero Robert Langdon being rushed into a chaotic scenario with an older mentor-figure whose life is at stake and a lesser-known sidekick woman scientist or equivalent who is unusually adept at codes, symbolism or science. The story begins and rushes off without any sign of slowing down. Except for the end of this book, in particular, which suddenly veered off the track and seemed to become a reflection of Dan Brown's own opinions on faith and religion rather than an adequate denouement. 
 Typical, I suppose; I shouldn't be surprised. But I wouldn't be all that annoyed with the story if Brown had only kept in the part about the chase and the hunt for the killer and all the adrenaline that goes with that. But too often Brown goes waxing poetic about science and faith and human curiosity. I can do without that lecture. 
 Plus, I wasn't even going to mention Brown's actual writing style, which really is reminiscent of high school kids trying to impress their teacher and classmates. His sentences are so short, choppy and dramatic that it makes some chapters a pain to read -- like the one in which Langdon has that thing happen to him toward the end? You know the one I'm talking about. That chapter was awful to read. On a serious note, though, Brown writes in that enticing way to keep readers interested and coming back, which is helpful when you're writing in this particular genre. But I could never get into it; it quite annoyed me, in fact.

 The Ghost of Graylock was such a pleasant surprise! I enjoy a good bone chilling ghost story and this one definitely delivered. Young Neil and Bree are staying the summer with their aunts in Hedston because their mother is having a hard time coping with their father having left them all to "follow his dream" of being an actor. Neil is our main character and though it never outright says it I believe he is 12 - as it was mentioned he's 4 years younger than his 16 year old sister Bree. 
 Neil is such an interesting young character, he is a thinker and its so fascinating to read how his mind works. He occasionally thinks about his mother's behavior over the past few months in response to their father leaving and he thinks about this new mom that they've been seeing as a "shadow person." He wanders if we all have a shadow person that is inside of us. I love how the author put this in because the way he works it out in his dead REALLY seems like how I would imagine a young teen thinking. 
 We get to the main plot because Neil likes to think of himself as a paranormal investigator, trying to emulate his favorite TV show Ghostly Investigators. So when he meets a local kid in town and hears about the closed mental hospital Graylock that is out in the woods and the ghost story tied to it - he simply must investigate and try to gather evidence. So off he goes to have a look, along with his sister, friend Wesley and his brother Eric. 
 While there, Neil and Bree have a close encounter and the tale takes off from there and the momentum barely slows down right up til the end. I thought because of how young the characters were that this wouldn't be as suspenseful as it was but I have to admit there were points where I really was on the edge of my seat. There is a great mystery aspect to the book where the kids are trying to figure out who the ghost is and why it is haunting Neil and Bree. I couldn't guess it right! - to me that's a good thing. 
 Seeing them work through the mystery and trying to figure it out along with them was a treat. I didn't figure it out until they did and I absolutely LOVED that. If you fancy a good quick ghost story this is for you - I devoured it in one night!

At the same time, I felt skeptical and worried that this book would be nothing more than a human and a ghost young adult love story. 
 I couldn't have been more wrong. 
 Love plays a predominant role in this novel. However, it's no teenage romance. Overwhelming loneliness, desperation, and incredible loss interweave through the story, creating an intriguing and hauntingly beautiful dynamic. 
 This book is more than a love story. The protagonists, Helen and James, must piece together the fragmented memories they have of their former lives (both Helen and James are deceased) in order to escape this eerie and desolate limbo they inhabit. 
 What's more is that Helen and James possess the bodies of two other individuals. The souls of these individuals, Billy and Jenny, abandoned their physical bodies, and Helen and James must face the tortured lives of those individuals. Billy's parents are no longer around, and while his older brother struggles to take care of him, both of the men face recovering alcohol and drug issues. Jenny's family is extremely religious, and Whitcomb does a phenomenal job of pointing out religious hypocrisy. 
 Though this book started a tad slowly for me, the tension quickly built and I found myself racing to see what happened. I wasn't disappointed. 
 Whitcomb's writing style is magnificent, the complexity of the story broaches a number of adult themes, and emotions aren't spared. This book is categorized as young adult, but it's far from any popular YA book I've read in the past number of years. The depth, love, grief, and heavy aching sensation of responsibility create a bold novel, and a truly satisfying conclusion.
I remember this being a really easy, fun, light, comical read - and I'm not a big 'chic lit' reader. Film was hilarious and re-watch movie.

From cultural stand point, this book was amazing. Lee put a lot research and study into her story. I felt like I could actually see Israel, the Mikva, and Jesus' prayer covering. I felt the social and political tensions as well. No other novel I have read set in the time period has made everything come to life so well from the standpoint of someone actually living then instead of now. 
 As to her topic, I applaud Lee on her courage. Few would dare to take a hated villain of history and show him as what he truly was, human. I have always believed that there was more to Iscariot's story than simply that he betrayed Jesus and I am glad to finally have read one possibility. 
 The only issue I had was that some of the events were changed. Either they happened to someone else or in a different place. This threw me off as knew how the stories were supposed to go. However, I understand that Lee needed to condense the story in order to, as she says in her author's note, get to the heart of the story.
