Second Grave... 
 Charley Is rudely awoken by Cookie, her best friend who, after a few minutes, tells her one of her friends is missing, so now Charley has to find her, as usual, because, you know, it is what she does. Meanwhile, Reyes, after escaping jail, tells Charley his body is nowhere to be seen... he hid it so the demons won't find Charley, but this stubborn girl refuses to let Reyes leave his body for good, so she starts looking for him despite Reyes disapproval. Yeah, that pretty much sums it up. 
 I liked this one very much and I don't give a rat ass if some people say Charley's attempt to be funny or sarcastic is getting old because to me it isn't. I love her personality because it reminds me of mine, and because despite all the stubbornness, the girl has balls and tries to make front to everything without giving up, and that's why she insisted on finding Reyes body so he wouldn't let it die, that is why she starts to investigate the case surrounding Cookie's friend, who is not the only one who has disappeared or the only one that went to a particular high school with some people who happen to be pretty much dead. Charley is persistent, which comes in handy when you try to search for papasito Reye's body... and also, apart from seeing death people and all, she is able to sense people's feelings, that's why she knows whenever someone is guilty or not... anyway. On Second Grave, Charley gets shot, kidnapped, shot again and punch in the face, and the funny thing is that she doesn't complain through all the book because someone has hit her, no, in fact, I think she acts flippantly about it, and that made me laugh because I know it is possible to think stupid thinks in serious situations, and that's normal. I did not find it annoying nor did I feel Jones was trying too hard to be funny, which I think is a natural thing for her... 
 Moving on. 
 Her relationship with Reyes has reached another level, and by this I mean it is freaking hot. I love it that Reyes tried to stop Charley from searching his body, and at the same time I think he gave her some hints this girl just waved as they passed her by, and not just him, but everyone around her. They said He hid the body from you, which means he hid it in the last place you'd look. That was pretty much obvious to me, Charley, ADD, Davidson. And it was painfully obvious Reyes body was at Charley's place when she went to pay Reyes fan number one a visit and saw a drawing of her building. Anyway, I assumed she was going to find out at the last moment, when she remembered a few things... but whatever... keep moving, Talia. 
 Reyes proved on this book how much he loves Charley. If you don't believe it, read Second Grave and pay extra attention to Reyes Fan, who has some pictures of him and in those pictures all you can see is Dutch written all over the place. Seriously, this guy spent an incredible amount of time thinking about her and AW, that is just too sweet. 
 There is other aspect I would like to talk about besides Reyes, Charley and the whole plot, and that's Charley's freaking father, who practically almost gets her killed only because he thought she would 'kick some ass' since she is not a normal human and she knows to throw a few punches here and there. Now, I don't care how logic this sounds, putting her daughter in danger without any kind of hands up is just wrong. Yeah, Charley moves faster and heals faster. She is stronger and stuff, but that doesn't mean you get to stab her in the back. Period. I found this situation a little bit upsetting because Charley forgets his father right away whilst I would have cut his head off and chewed it, then I would have thought about forgiving him, but that's just me and my sick head. 
 Over all, this book is AWESOME, and the ending is too good to be true; I loved Charley bounding Reyes to his body, and I loved Reyes getting pissed at her, since this only promise Reyes will be pretty upset on Third Grave, and I love bad guys getting upset... yay. 
 One thing I didn't love about this book was the solving on the main case. It was a bit incomplete to me, but meh, I don't care. 
 SO, yeah, I recommend Charley Davidson's series to everyone.

 In the end, I disliked the main character: she's supposed to be a young woman forced to grow up quickly, but from the get go she read exactly LIKE my mother.  Maeve's life is over-exaggerated -- for better or worse -- in bards' songs. Sure, she was a daring five-year-old when she chased after her father's prized bull. Yes, she learned how to use weapons against threatening beasts. And it's true she speaks her mind, in a witty, intelligent, and clever manner. But Maeve is a princess in first-century Ireland, and an independent, headstrong young woman is one to be feared or beaten down with a stick. She's determined to find solid ground to stand up for herself and her beliefs without angering her father, upsetting the land's most powerful druid, and crushing the druid's son, a healer and master with creatures. 
 Maeve, like King Arthur, is based on threads of fact but mostly of mythical fiction. Her frustrations are understandable, and the men in her life are equally supportive as well as manipulative, protective, and controlling. She can see right through them, and plays their game by speaking only the truth and pointing out inaccuracies and falsehoods. She wants to help her father defend the land -- thus her warrior skills -- but also wants to be a compassionate healer -- thus her lessons with the druid's son Odran. Maeve is a force of nature, admirable and wonderful to behold, and it was a joy reading her mind. 
 What I loved most about this book was what Friesner was able to accomplish with so little recorded historical information at the time. Truly, the tales that lasted from Iron Age Ireland are the tales sung by bards and centuries later recorded in manuscripts. Like the game "telephone," both in Maeve's experience as well as in research, only a grain of truth can be found in the poems. Even with little research, Friesner managed to concoct a beautiful and rich tale of love, friendship, and compassion in this tumultuous age. I loved the feast scenes -- so much laughter and joy -- and the moments Odran and Maeve spent in the hut caring for the animals. Every moment circled back to a previous, an endless loop of past events impacting the present, and it was fun to make the connections. Even the dark moments of sexist frustration and political intrigue were scattered with light, sarcastic commentary in Maeve's thoughts. 
 A fun read for anyone interested in ancient historical fiction, fierce young women, and awesome names you'll need a pronunciation guide to get anywhere close to its actual sound.

Gr9. I really think Mr. Zentner (Jeff if I may call him that) did a great job of identifying how grief can come upon us in mysterious ways. I tend to skim-summarize while I read, so I don't get all of the details, which may not be the best for reviewing, but I felt this book had a bunch of great themes soo.... I don't deal with grief. At all. I haven't gotten a single panic attack, but I also didn't lose three of my best friends. I'm also not great at sharing, so I don't get much experience with grief, and how others feel. Both the choice in POV, and the connections with others, and the 'Goodbye Days' that happened all helped me understand all of this in a non offensive, connectable ways. Anyways, on to the plot. Plot: Pretty good. I lost interest in a couple of parts, but overall, solidly written, with very little to no plot holes. The characters were well written, but I think Jessamine could've had a little more descriptions, and we (the readers) really could've had a bit more motivation to connect with her, and not only Carver. Also Eli's twin sister just kinda came off as super cold, which I guess can appeal to how some people deal with grief but not me? Anyhoo. The book was great, very enlightening, I actually met the author at a signing and he seemed super cool, so all in all, I'd advise y'all to read it!

I shouldn't be allowed to read classic children's literature. My brain simply doesn't appreciate its intended purpose - creativity, imagination, fantasy. Instead, I wonder, "What's the point here?" Sometimes, there is a point, but I think with Ronald Dahl, the focus is placed on the magic and if there happens to be a story in there somewhere in it..so be it. 
 I borrowed it from the library because it was on the most-commonly-banned-books-in-America shelf and I wondered how the author of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory could upset so many modest American readers? 
 I still don't know. Unless there is some upsetting symbolism that went way over my head and would be sure to go over the head of its intended audience, I don't understand how this book could offend anyone but mean, crusty old aunts who don't love and take care of their orphaned nephews. 
 That being said, I wish I loved this non-controversial story, but I didn't. I thought it was overly strange. Strange in a did-you-write-this-while-tripped-out-on-LCD? kind of way. Giant talking bugs. Living in a peach. Flying over the Atlantic Ocean with the help of string tied onto 501 seagulls via the giant silkworm and spider. Landing on the needle of the Empire State Building in New York. A ladybug marrying a police man (What the?). O.K then. 
 James was surrounded by mean, nasty aunts and now he's happy and living in a giant peach in New York City's Central Park. Wildly imaginative but famous through the ages? 
 To make sure it deserved its fame, I had my eight year old son read it (even though the word a** is in it twice. Why did Dahl do that?) and he liked it. He didn't love it. Not because it was strange but because like most things he reads, the characters are magical and the plot bizarre. For him, it seemed almost standard fare. When he finished, he handed it back to me and I asked, "Did you like it?" "Yeah." That's it. No buzz. No acting out parts of the story and certainly no regurgitating details from it like he does with some of his other books. 
 I guess we're just a bunch of fuddy-duddies around here because I found nothing extraordinary about James and the Giant Peach except it's eccentricity.

A story about family, the stories we tell ourselves to make the world make sense, and finding yourself. 
 Sydney has always been overshadowed by her older brother. At first because he was so good--charming and adventurous, smart and handsome. And then because he was crashing and burning, making mistake after mistake until he made the last one. 
 He drove drunk, and hit someone. 
 Now he's in jail, and Sydney is still overshadowed by him even so--their mother's whole attention focused on making the world make sense somehow. She's drowning in guilt for his crimes, since no one else seems to be feeling it. How can she make amends when her family seems to have erased the victim from their minds? 
 To save money, she transferred to public school, and she worries that the eyes on her know who her brother is. That she's being judged. And yet, the Chathams, a crazy, loving family whose drama and lives she gets caught up in, don't seem to judge her at all. Maybe finally she can find somewhere where she belongs. 
 A sweet story, hopeful but realistic. There are no easy fixes, no magical twists. But life, flawed as it is, is still wonderful. As she makes friends and finds herself, Sydney discovers love. Love in all its forms, strong enough to weather the trials of life. And though sometimes it is tested, in the end, things often come out okay. 
 A lovely read for people who like stories about family, and growing up, and self-discovery.

To get away from a life that seems to be falling apart, Ina travels to a remote mountain cabin to get away. While there she meets a supposedly sexy mountain man, ponders her next step in life, tries to get over her cheating boyfriend, and faces a little danger. The Goodreads description of this book promises big things, and I really looked forward to the story. Romance, mystery, suspense, and self-discovery. However, the characters and plot fall flat. 
 I was never able to really connect with Ina. She's a 23-year old college grad with a bright future ahead of her. And yet, because of the "mistake" she made her senior year (not sure how it was a mistake by any definition of the word), she lacks any motivation and direction. Also, she's kind of rude. When she isn't following the rules or getting called out on not-entirely-appropriate behavior, her response is to fling insults. The recipient of these spurts of misplaced anger is Adam, the owner of the cabins on this remote mountain. Now, Adam is super sexy, or so we're told. But I honestly had a hard time picturing that. Sure, he has muscles that would make any girl swoon, but a messy beard that is so unkempt that you can't even tell if he's smiling or not? Does he wash it? Is there food stuck in this beard of his? Don't get me wrong, I think guys with beards can be sexy. But when they're described as being messy, wild, and unkempt, my brain just can't reconcile the two. And Adam rants and whines and cries a little too much for my liking, especially when it comes to big, sexy mountain men. And yet these two seem to develop an instant attraction. I was never able to feel the chemistry, the whole relationship felt contrived. I just couldn't get behind it. 
 The story moves slowly, even though the book itself is a quick read. The reasons for both Ina and Adam fleeing to the mountain and/or their general distrust of people left much to be desired. Ina more so than Adam; he has suffered real heartache in his past. Even then, I feel as though his actions in the present are an overreaction. And all the while, there's a man lurking in the shadows, watching from afar, and somebody (perhaps the same man?) is stealing things. Call the police? Nope. Just ignore it and it will go away. Ina and Adam ignore it so well, that I even forgot about the aforementioned mystery. And then finally at 88% in (88%!), we get some excitement. Unfortunately, this also feels a bit forced and as if it was added as an afterthought. Overall, the plot drags, the characters are dull, and I just couldn't get lost in the story. 
 However, I think the idea behind the story was good, even if the execution wasn't. And for that reason I will check out another book by Ever McCormick. 
 (I received an ARC from NetGalley)

Soren's position at the Darest court is a joke. She was proclaimed Champion of the Rose, the protector of the Rathen kings--but there have been no Rathen kings in Darest for two hundred years. Her status as ignored non-entity abruptly changes when a blooming rose appears in the palace's magical garden, signaling the birth of a Rathen heir. Soren knows that the regents of Darest will do anything to maintain their position, and she needs to get to the heir before their agents do. (view spoiler)[But when Soren tracks down the heir, she finds not a baby, but a full-grown man. Strake was lost in time in the fae woods during a hunting party hundreds of years ago. Although he was just a minor prince in his own time, now he is the land's last hope. (hide spoiler)] Because the myths are right--only Rathen rule can avert the terrible doom that afflicts all of Darest. 
 Soren and (view spoiler)[Strake have an uneasy relationship, made harder by the Rose that twines through them. The first Rathen ruler created the Rose as a protection for the Rathens that would follow, but over the centuries it has gradually transformed from tool into something almost sentient. To protect the Rathen bloodline, it mind-controls Strake and Soren into sex, leaving her pregnant and each of them deeply traumatized and bitter about the other. The rape is utterly without details (in fact, I didn't realize what had happened until several pages later), but the characters deal with the emotional and physical aftereffects for the rest of the novel. 
 The Rose has other powers, too. With its magic, Soren is the only human who can sense the physical presence of the doom that stalks Darest. She, Strake, and the former regent's heir Aristide, work to halt Darest's decline and forstall the lethal magic that seeks Strake's death. They are beset with intrigue from neighboring countries and internal jockeying for power. 
 I liked Soren, although I wished I had a harder handle on her characterization. I think the trouble is that I'm used to characters falling into a category: scholarly, battle-hungry, fascinated by magic, family-oriented. Soren isn't particularly bookish, doesn't have combat training or inclination, can't do magic...mostly she rides her horse, works, and worries about Strake. Her internal workings are clear to the reader, but her outward seeming remained a bit opaque. Strake is pretty straightforward: smart, a bit snarly, dealing with a great deal of shock and trauma. Their romance comes kinda out of no-where, and was the only thing I didn't like about the book. The minor characters have charm and verve of their own--I was an avowed fan of Aspen from the very first. Aristide is the character I was most drawn to. He's so self-contained and perfect that the court calls him the Diamond, and stories of how he deals with those who cross him are legendary. At the start of the story I assumed he would be the villain, but his role is far more interesting. (hide spoiler)] 
 I really loved the magic in this book. It has a sort of dream-logic to it, and has an understated power, the kind where you only realize how impossible something is when you glance at it a second time. There's one scene, when Soren meets the fairy queen, that was particularly astounding. And I really liked that the story deals with the dark sides to ordained rule and magical tools in a really thoughtful manner. 
 Oh! And I nearly forgot to mention, because it's so casual and unremarked, that this is a completely queer universe. Everyone has lovers of either sex (although some people seem to have preferences) without it even needing a name, triads are as legal a relationship as couples, and both genders are perfectly equal in status and in roles. Love it! 
 The first five chapters are available to sample on goodreads or the author's website, but beware: they so intrigued me that I bought this book, and I am so frugal I buy a book once every five years. It is quickly, dangerously, enthralling.

If I could, I would give it 2.5 stars. This is the 2nd book by Mieville that I've read, Embassytown being the first. As with Embassytown, I am amazed by his word play and imagination, and there are passages that are so beautifully written that I reread them just to revel in them. But once again, I end up feeling very detached from the whole thing, other than perhaps feeling horror at the actions of Goss and Subby. I felt no emotional attachment to any of the characters and did not care what happened to them. The whole thing felt rather clever but cold. I mostly kept reading to see what would happen next, or what other kinds of weirdness Mieville would come up with. But at some point the weirdness felt forced, as if he were trying to create cause and effect connections between events that were supposed to have their own logic but in the end never did. It's as in his world building he never actually sat down to figure out the rules by which his novel would operate, but instead just sort of made it up as he went along, and when he found himself backed into a corner at the end, just made something up which made no sense and had no foundation in the preceding several hundred pages. It really makes one wonder if this book went under any kind of editing process at all. The last 150 pages or so were a real struggle to finish, and I only did finish them because I felt I had come that far, I might as well go on until the end. Only to get some heavy handed point about the irrefutable truth of the theory of evolution vs. those silly religious people who believe in outlandish things without any scientific proof. Yawn.

This was enjoyable, but would have been excellent had it been 100 pages shorter. Clever only lasts for so long until it begins to grate on your nerves. I enjoyed popping into alternate realities, and not the constant fight between brothers which, as I saw it, had no background and did not make that much sense. That said, I can totally see Martin Freeman playing Theo in the movie and I would love to see another novel based in the sky world.

 But boy did I love it!!! So much!!!! 
 My two bests friends and I are totally Jacque, Jen and Sally. I am totally Jen!!!! We both love us some good looking men and don't know when to shut the hell up!!!

I cannot even begin to find the right words to explain how much I adore this final book in the trilogy. After Anna and Etienne, I thought no other book could possibly compete, but I was so wrong. I adore Isla & Josh (and Lola & Cricket too), and I'm glad I got to be a part of their adventures. 
 What I love best about Stephanie Perkins as a writer is her outstanding ability to capture the voice of the MC. Every novel feels so different but equally lovable and charming. I also love that there are no good places in her novels to take a break. You won't put them down, because they are just so delicious. If you do try to step away, you'll find that all you are able to do is think about the novel and the characters until you cave in and start reading again. 
 Isla and Josh are fascinating characters, and I enjoyed reading about every little thing they did. I think they could have spent the whole novel cleaning and grocery shopping, and it still would have been interesting.

Reviving Izabel is the second book in J.A. Redmerski's In The Company of Killers series. As of 2013, the series includes: 
 #1-Killing Sarai 
 #2-Reviving Izabel 
 Reviving Izabel is a great sequel to Sarai's story in the first book which follows her escape from years of captivity with a notorious drug lord in Mexico. This story follows three main characters: Sarai/Izabel, Victor, and Fredrik who are all killers but all kill for different reasons. Sarai's motivation for killing is all about retribution, which I'm glad that this did not change from the first book. She is darker in her desire to settle scores with an edge of desperation that makes her impulsive, overconfident, and reckless. Since Victor's exit in Killing Sarai, Sarai/Izabel remains untrained and undisciplined, but yet she proceeds to act on her need to kill past/present villains. This story follows her experiences as she tries to live the life of an unskilled killer and the consequences that come along with that. Familiar faces come back into Sarai/Izabel's life, THANK GOD VICTOR! and Sarai/Izabel proves just how much she wants this life. As a reader, at times I felt she was full of herself, and her whiney attitude and behavior annoyed me to the point I was mentally asking Victor why he was sticking around, but I guess after everything she has been through and is willing to go through, she has the right to a bit of complaining. She is humbled over and over again by the consequences of the mistakes she makes along the way. "You can't learn to swim by reading it in a book...It is the best way, Sarai. To learn from your mistakes is to make them. Authentically. No amount of training, no rehearsed scenario is going to teach you better than the real thing." I enjoyed reading about her and Victor's relationship and Victor's own internal journey throughout this book. There is a plot twist/turn that had me blindsided WTF???? (I love that feeling by the way) and that's when my four-star enjoyment turned to five stars. It had me taking back any annoying thought I ever had about Sarai/Izabel. This girl is loyal to Victor and is deserving of a chance to work alongside him. 
 My favorite quotes: 
 "For a long time, I forget that he is an assassin, whose hands have taken many lives without thought or remorse or regret. I forget that I, too, am a killer, whose hands took a life just hours ago. Seems like we were made for each other, like two puzzle pieces that at first don't appear to fit, but eventually fall into place when looked at in the most unlikely of angles."
I'm not really sure how I feel about this book! It's Dragos and Pia so I love that, but I had some problems with it so it kept me from giving it 5 stars like the other Dragos and Pia stories.

Although I don't think I can really add anything new to a review on a classic novel such as the Hobbit. I will say that this has always been one of my favorite novels. There's something extraordinary about Tolkien's Middle Earth that has me coming back again and again. Part of it, I believe, is in the way that Tolkien writes. Making the reader feel as if they are experiencing the world and learning about it at the same time as the character's. I felt compelled after finishing The Hobbit to pick up The Lord of the Rings and then The Silmarillion after that. I know Tolkien was very interested in the nature of narrative and Fairy stories in general and it shows in this classic.

For people who don't already know: the hotel used in the movie actually exists. It's The Headlands Hotel, Newquay, England, and I've eaten there several times. 
 The staff are friendly and well aware of the relevant history. When I first spotted this book, it was on a clearance shelf at Barnes&Noble for about $6 and I thought it looked interesting but, knowing nothing about the author and money being always tight, I came home and added it to my Amazon WishList instead. Months later, I was thrilled to see it was available for free as part of my Kindle Unlimited loan subscription. This is the second time I've passed up 5-star reads on the B&N clearance shelf. The first was Tracy Chevalier's Remarkable Creatures. I am going to have to stop telling myself "no" there because most of those books are not marked down in their Kindle forms but full-price. 
 Anyway, "Slammerkin" did not disappoint. I read reviews for it that people didn't like it because they didn't like the main character, Mary Saunders. I guess reading as many murder mysteries and horror novels as I do, it never occurred to me that I had to like a character to enjoy a book. 
 Mary Saunders, until 90% of the way through the book, was a character I could empathize with, if not agree with her life choices. Keeping in mind the time period (1763-1764), she really had very few options as a young girl thrown out on the streets at 14 by her mother. True, it was "lust" for a red ribbon that got her there. Knowing young girls and their desire for bright, shiny new things, it was an extreme result. Given the times and the general low position women held not an unreasonable opening to a fictionalized account of a murky historical figure. As a young girl, Mary's young life and everything in it was a drab brown. She was simply reaching for a bit of color. 
 Anyone who can place themselves in the same time frame in the same set of circumstances as Mary found herself and say they wouldn't follow into prostitution as she did is far more sure of their convictions than I guess I am. Extreme poverty, hunger and simple human need force us to be people we might not otherwise become. 
 For fear of spoilers, I will leave my review of "Slammerkin" there. The last 10% took a turn I hope I would never take but the book remains a 5-star read and appears to be a plausible explanation of true events. History will never say, one way or the other, in regard to Mary Saunders. If you are a staunch religious reader who prefers more of a romantic slant to your historical fiction, skip this one - you won't find it here. If you're a woman who has ever, in her darker moments pondered her options and considered "what if I had to. . ." then you may find this an intriguingly dark read.

(Yes, I stole that from LBD. Cuz it works.) Yet, by the end of it, she makes it work for her, even while still playing soccer and keeping up her classes. 
 Things I liked about this adaptation-their names weren't recycled from the Austen original, various superfluous characters were toned down or left out, Megan's parents' relationship, and Margot. Oh, and how the entire Wickham-esque drama sorts itself out? LOVED. (view spoiler)[That her dad gets to stay on at the ranch and work, yet they don't have to worry about money? Dude didn't just throw money at the situation, he made it better. I squeeeed. (hide spoiler)]

 It's not some deep existential read-but it was a quick romp with some fun characters.

Every Heart a Doorway by Seanan McGuire is one of the novellas from Tor.com's new novella line. I particularly wanted to read it after hearing the description and favourable review from Alex on Galactic Suburbia and I'm glad I did. 
 I've read some Seanan McGuire short stories in the past, which have been varied in theme and tone etc, and her Mira Grant novels, which are more SF horror. As a result, I wasn't prepared for just how delightful Every Heart a Doorway would be. Not only is the premise and story interesting -- as you can probably tell from the blurb -- but the writing itself strikes a perfect balance between children's writing and writing about children's stories for an older audience. Not that portal fantasy stories are limited to kids' and YA books, but the kind referenced in Every Heart a Doorway mostly were. This makes it the perfect book for older and younger readers alike. 
 The story follows Nancy, a new student at the school for teens who have come back from portal worlds and wish they hadn't. She's an interesting choice of main character because she went to an Underworld, ruled by the Lord of the Dead, rather than the cheery fairyland type of place, like you might more commonly picture. She's a good character to ease the reader in with, because all the (mostly) girls went to very different places, so the fact that Nancy's is so unusual helps us keep that in mind. Also, Nancy is asexual, which in itself is unusual in a main character. I thought that presented and handled well, as was the trans character who played a key role and whose travels were complicated by his identity and vice versa. Also, the explanation for why more girls go through doors to other worlds is... depressingly logical. 
 The premise that I've mostly talked about so far is part of the world building rather than the story. The main plot properly starts shortly after Nancy arrives at school and other students start winding up dead. Naturally people suspect the newcomer, so Nancy becomes involved in trying to find the perpetrator with her new friends. The murder mystery was a bit dire, given the setting, but also served to underscore that portal travel and the events that can happen on the other side are serious business. 
 I loved Every Heart a Doorway and stayed up late reading until I had finished with it, unable to put it down. I highly recommend it to all fans of fantasy of all types. It's not exactly a portal fantasy story, but will definitely appeal to fans of that genre. Its also not a very long read, so if you're unsure, I suggest giving it a go anyway. I don't think you'll regret it.

I loved the way their relationship played out. Spencer didn't rush her, and he complied with her "glitches." 
 As far as the suspense part of the story, I really liked how the case evolved. I loved that Arizona saved herself. She got out of the situation herself. She was strong enough to fight back and win. And Spencer was just there for support. I loved that. 
 I would definitely recommend A Perfect Storm for those who want a sexy, action-packed romantic suspense.

I was initially curious about this novel because I enjoy stories built around playing with words and language as it's telling a story - and The Word Exchange definitely lived up to that. Anana works for a dictionary, and right from the beginning of the novel everyone is aware that this will be the last ever printing of the dictionary. It's a sort of the end of an era. All dictionaries are now online, and no one has the need for a print edition. After Anana's father disappears, she goes on an adventure that brings her into contact with other dying (or seemingly extinct) arts. 
 I really enjoyed reading this book because it had so much unique stuff in it. First of all, the language it uses is amazing. As they all work at a dictionary, naturally many of the characters not only have knowledge of obsolete or rare words, but they thoroughly enjoy using these words in their everyday conversations. The narrative also provided small doses of the history of a certain word, or how the word was used in a certain context, which was really interesting. 
 Besides the interesting use of language, the book also had a lovely representation of many historical artifacts, such as pneumatic tubes that characters used to contact each other. There was also things like secret meetings in old libraries - libraries joined by private membership only, because sadly all public libraries are closed - and even visits to archiving rooms. As Anana visited each location I was really happy with the descriptions of the settings and the general feeling I was getting from the story. 
 The storyline itself I found really interesting. Anana exists in this high-tech, fast paced world, but has an amazing appreciation of the older, more methodical way of life. As she searches for her father, these two worlds continuously collide and create friction for Anana, and I was definitely caught up in the story. 
 Unfortunately, though, the story at times was a bit slow to get through. There are some sections of theories about language and language development, some of the histories were a bit dense, and these I found a bit hard to follow. But at the same time, I don't think the book would have been as good without these parts. It needed these parts. Because this is a first person account, and the characters are recording their own stories, it's only reasonable that they go off on tangents and give a small discussion about certain words or terms, or the development of the language. I think I just found them a bit harder to get through because there's just so much stuff in them to process, and I would have to slow down my reading to be able to absorb it all. This is not a book that you can whip through in a couple of hours! 
 Finally, I was totally fascinated by this book because I can genuinely see it happening in real life. Many people are switching to digital instead of print, and this includes all reference materials like dictionaries and thesauruses. And the Word Flu is really intriguing. It replaces real words with made-up words, eventually rendering one unable to understand their own language. In The Word Exchange, as the characters are exposed to the Word Flu these strange words slowly start to creep into the narrative, and I really experienced what it was like to lose the ability to understand your own language - and to understand Anana's fear. It was so well done. 
 I loved this book because it is amazing to read. There are so many details put into the book, about words and definitions, the evolution of our own language, and the historical atmosphere it creates. Yet it's a totally believable, thriving world that Anana has to survive, and has a story that pulls you in. While I can't give full stars because of some of the heavy theory discussion and histories, this is a book I totally want to read again, to explore all the dusty corners for the details I know I missed. This was just a really interesting book, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who loves words!

Because she was chubby and wore thick glasses, and also because her sisters were always extremely mean to her. 
 This review was originally posted on (un)Conventional Bookviews

Futuristic America's only hope lies in the hands of the elite teen pilots of the secret new "Streaker" jets that may be able to defeat China's deadly drone force. Chase "Nyx" Harcourt is one of these pilots, a student at the United Star Academy, a school designed just to train teens to fly these planes.Flying as fast and high as she can is pretty much her only goal in life until mysterious encounters with a pilot from outside her academy propels her into the dangers of the real world. 
 I'm a fan of girl-warrior books in general, but frankly the whole idea of a handful of teenage pilots facing off against the entire military of another nation, not to mention a fleet of powerful drones, was a bit too far fetched for me. The simplicity of the concept and plot would work well for a younger teen audience if there wasn't an unfortunate amount of language and focus on (never explicit, but still) sex throughout the book. 
 There are things to like in this new dystopian YA, though: it's pretty much searingly fast-paced from beginning to end, and I did like Chase/Nyx as a character; her adrenaline-craving, belligerent side was contrasted nicely by her quieter friendship with her fellow pilot Pippin, though all her other relationships--I use the term loosely--were somewhat horrifying. 
 A broader picture of what this dystopian world looked like might have made Chase's harsher characteristics more understandable, as well as making the whole three-jets-against-the-world thing more believable. 
 This is not a new Ender's Game by a long stretch, but it is action-packed and exciting. I could see Breaking Sky working well with the video game crowd, or with fans of books like the Maze Runner.

This story wasn't for me. Many plots have been done over and over again but this one was almost too close to another more popular series I previously read, still different in its own way but not for me.

I was surprised at how close the plot in the book and the plot in the movie were. The film makers made very little changes. 
 That being said it is a shame they couldn't incorporate Beagle's writing. This is one of those rare books where reading the descriptions and exposition was just as wonderful as reading the dialogue and the action. The writing is so beautiful and the story so wonderful. And despite knowing that the book was written first, I was glad it was close to the movie. I don't think I could've liked it as much if it strayed that far from my childhood favourite.

5 stars!! 
 I read this book in one sitting, i stayed up til 4:30 am to finish it, and it was SO GOOD I can't believe i hadn't read it before. I loved the characters, and I could relate to Cath sooo much, BUT I WANNA FIND A LEVI. 
 It's a really good coming-of-age story, about a fangirl basically starting a new life as she starts college, but also tries to hold on to the good things in her past because she afraid of change. I loved her fanfiction writing, and the dynamic between Cath and Wren, and I loved Raegan and Levi was an amazing character. 
 I need more books like this!

"This is the story of how my parents split up." 
 Gasped. Out. Loud.

This book was so much better than Heir of Fire. 
 In this novel, Aelin is back at Riftfold from Wendlyn and things have changed dramatically since she was there. First, there are rebel killings happening almost everyday, and Chaol has gathered up a rebel force to rescue the prisoners (not unlike The Hunger Games), while Dorian is suffering with a Valg demon inside of him inside of the castle. Manon is at Morath with her Thirteen and Duke Perrington, and her character development in this book alone is fantastic! We also meet two new characters Lorcan and Elide, which have interesting side stories that I loved. Lysandra, a character from The Assassin's Blade, is a major character in this book and I loved her and Aelin's friendship. 
 The book was quite long, but it didn't feel like it dragged. The first part was interesting enough to keep me intrigued, especially Manon's point of view, and in the second half shit hit the fan and this series got real. It set up perfectly what was to come in Empire of Storms, although I do have a problem with (view spoiler)[the squad leaving Dorian-like, he just got his collar off and there is a very real possibility that the Valg demon is still somewhere inside him, or he can act on the Valg demon's thoughts, why are they leaving him when they are his only allies? (hide spoiler)] 
 However, I disliked what Maas did to Chaol's and Aelin's relationship. In the beginning of the book, already her and Chaol get off to a rocky start. First, he calls her a monster and blames her for the new situation in Ardalan, and in retaliation Aelin calls him an oathbreaker, traitor, and lair, which seemed very OOC for the both of them. It's safe to say the couple we loved in Crown of Midnight is no more, which I have learned to accept and have since embraced the Aelin/Rowan ship. However, I do wish that Maas kept their relationship platonic and didn't ruin their relationship just for the sake of making Aelin and Rowan the "superior" couple. 
 This book was overall really enjoyable, and I don't expect this series to be life-changing or have some ulterior message like Lord of the Rings or A Song of Ice and Fire. I'm expecting action, an interesting setting, and a good plot with some really great characters, and so far this series has definitely delivered. The people they were in Throne of Glass, are definitely not the same people who ended Queen of Shadows, and it's absolutely perfect. 
 Some favorite quotes: 
 "They joined hands. 
 So the world ended. 
 And the next one began." 
 "She was a wolf. She was death, devourer of the worlds." 
 "Dorian, we get to come back from this loss - from this darkness. We get to come back, and I came back for you." 
 "They were infinite. They were the beginning and the ending; they were eternity. The king standing before them gaped as the shield of flame died out to reveal Aelin and Dorian, hand in hand, glowing like newborn gods as their magic entwined."

I'd seen quite a bit of hype around this book so I was super excited to start it. I was a little put off by the fact that it sounded so much like Outlander (time travel and Scotland) and that it's marketed as "an Outlander for teens" but I still wanted to read Into the Dim. 
 First off, I love Outlander with very ounce of my being. Outlander means so much to me. So the fact that Into the Dim pretty much copied the concept of Outlander upsets me. It's so similar to Outlander and I couldn't stop comparing the two. Outlander is obviously, in my opinion, a million times better so I felt disappointed with Into the Dim. 
 I did like the writing though. It was really well written and I liked all the details. I also liked the characters. I think the characters will be even better in the second book.

I'm pretty sure I'll end up buying a finished copy of this book because the cover is beautiful and I'd really like to give it a second chance. I've loved Saga and Ms. Marvel so much that I've broken the promise I made to myself to only start a book when a series is completed. And as expected with those aforementioned graphic novels, I'm now all caught up and wondering if the author is sitting down and writing, or wasting time gallivanting about town. So, you know I made dang sure that this was a completed series before I started on this graphic novel. 
 This series has been labeled as a cross between Bambi and Cormac McCarthy's The Road. Well, I loved Bambi (though was traumatized), but did not love McCarthy's The Road, so was not sure how I'd feel about this story. 
 What's it about? A post-apocalptic world, where a pandemic that occured a decade ago resulted in a new breed of human/hybrid children. This is the story of one such child, Gus, who lives in isolation with his father. He has been warned not to ever, ever leave the woods. Well, we know how often kids listen to their parents about such warnings. 
 This graphic novel is wonderful. The author does a good job of world building, and the art is really good. I was swept along for the ride, and cannot wait to see what happens next. This is the first of six volumes, and I've already requested the rest of the series. I see some binge reading on my horizon.

It took me a couple of chapters to get into it, but when I did, I was IN -- as in I couldn't put it down. This book is like a "1984", with social commentary like "Fahrenheit 451", and a young adult version of the bones of "Blindness" by Jose Saramago. The message is spectacular! And the way Doctorow grabs onto a way to make security and freedom and the whole "war on terrorism" accessible to the teens who may be more concerned with their own lives, dramas, video games, etc., is awesome. I was infuriated so many times by the unfairness of what was occurring and the way the government just keeps saying it's "for your protection" or "we're making our country safe from terrorists". It's like, how far does that let us go? Does that make it okay to toss out the Constitution especially when the government is attacking its own citizens and setting up a Guantanamo Bay look-alike without trials, attorneys, rights, and WITH "persuasive methods" a.k.a. torture? 
 My only complaint about this book is the much too lengthy explanations into technology that passes beyond my understanding or care to understand. Just give me the basics, make it obvious that I would NOT want the government all over me with spy cams and what not, but the details about building a computer, about hacking into systems and making this secret -- again the DETAILS -- made it tough going at times. This info is vital, but in less bogging detail please. 
 p.s. Also awesome the second time around!!

This was so completely sweet. It reminded me of The Prince & Me meets A Prince for Christmas (with some obvious Kate Middleton inspiration). I wasn't sure about the story at the beginning, but ended up absolutely loving it. It's like a Hallmark movie where everyone's boyfriend is secretly a prince and there are all sorts of obstacles for a regular American girl to marry a European king. Obviously you know how it'll end, but the characters are what make these types of stories fun. And I really liked everyone in this book! If you're looking for inspirational fluff, this is the perfect story. 
 And this is actually one of the first Christian fiction books I've ever truly loved. The plot built around the characters' faith in a natural way instead of leaping across giant holes to shove it in. Plus, it felt inspiring instead of preachy. I'm definitely checking out this author's other books now!

So, when I read Bully (the first book to this series) I was almost horrified that I liked it. I mean, (view spoiler)[ the book was a romance and HEA between a girl and her high school bull (hence the title). (hide spoiler)] So, you understand my reservations with it, and the feminist in me hating myself for enjoying such a great but depreciating-at-times book. 
 Anyway, You'll notice that my review is marked five stars. Again, I am almost ashamed that I liked it, again, but damn, Penelope Douglas makes this book and these characters hard not to like and follow. Of course, she also makes you want to shake/strangle/ slap-them-in-the-face on many occasions too. And I must say, I enjoyed Until You even more that I enjoyed Bully. 
 So this is the part where I tell you some shit about the book, so it you don't want to know anything about it (I swear I will not spoil it that much) my advice would be to skip ahead. The characters in this book seemed to be even meaner to each other, which was the point, but there were occasions that I think the anger/frustration/not-hatred might have been taken too far. I understand, she was making the characters more realistic action/ reaction and shit. But damn it, when they just completely ripped into each other it was a little hard to read. The arrangement/characters would have gotten the book 3.5-4 stars, but holy mother of god, the ending was SO WORTH IT. 
 All of the anger, misery, and douchebaggery was totally worth reading, all because of the ending. Since reading the book yesterday (10 December 2013) I have read the ending six times over and would gladly do it again...and again and again. In my opinion, endings are almost the most important part of a book, if you have a lame ending/ one that makes no sense or it just...ends... then you don't have a great book. Penelope Douglas NAILED the ending. And I do mean nailed it. 
 SO all y'all who skipped to the end, I'll recap. Best fucking ending that she could have written. Five stars. Can't wait for Madoc's story!

** spoiler alert ** 
 First of all, I have to say that this book was not nearly as good as the first two. I rated those both 5 star reads, and they are some of my faves in YA dystopian. It almost felt like a different author at times, and that may have been the dual POV. 
 Dual POV--overall, I think I liked it. Tobias was very whiny, and I've read numerous reviews where people said he was like a different person in the first two books. But I wonder if that's really true. We never really got into his head until now...so maybe he has always been kind of whiny, but hid it well. But it was good to see his side of things, otherwise I may have hated him! 
 World Building--this was probably the best part of the book for me. I really wanted to know what was happening outside of Chicago, and it was actually a lot worse than I had imagined. The entire civilization was all about sorting people. This made sense, since that was the prime goal in the "experiments." It was such scary, flawed thinking, but also very believable to me. Actually, I saw a lot of similarities between Roth's world and our own. 
 Basic Plot--This is honestly the part that I had so much trouble with, as have many other readers. I was right up with the events in the story until the end. The ending just did not make sense. And I'm not just talking about Tris's death. I wasn't thrilled with her dying, but I can get over it, as I know that she was just being herself. Having to save everyone else is definitely her style. What bothered me was the whole thing between Evelyn and Tobias. I really feel that was too easy. If this book was to be taken seriously, (and therefore, take the idea of Tris's death seriously) it would have made more sense for him either having to erase her memory by force, or kill her outright. We have all these evil heads of society--Marcus, Evelyn, and David, and NOT ONE of them died at the end! I have trouble believing Marcus would have gone along with things as well. You'd think he'd have tried to kill Evelyn or Joanna or even Tobias after that meeting, and maybe force the issues a little more. None of that made sense to me. 
 Character development--I think the book was pretty strong in this, although not as much as the previous two. Tris is her usual smart,bad ass self, but she does learn a few things, as does Tobias. And really that's all the character development that really matters, everyone else is pretty fixed by now, and had their moments earlier. 
 Tris--Rock on, Tris! And RIP! I was sobbing when she died, I really didn't see that coming. I've heard lots of comments in that she really should have let Caleb just die. But I think it would have been a very different result. I don't think Caleb was brave enough to face down David and release the serum before dying. I really think Tris was the only one who could do that. And also, I really loved that even after everything with her and Caleb, when it came down to it, she could not sacrifice him to the wolves. And that is the ultimate strength in character. 
 Tobias--He frustrated me throughout the book ,but by the end I was okay with him. I'm not a die hard Four fan, so it wasn't a big deal to me. I felt really bad for him in the end, though. And I was frustrated that he didn't think of his plan with Evelyn sooner. OH, well. 
 I'm not going to go into my thoughts on all the other characters, except for maybe David. What a sleaze. And total idiot. That's all I have to say. lol 
 Now onto the hardest part--how did I come up with the 4 stars? 
 First of all, I really loved the read. I read it all in one day (partly because I was afraid I might get "spoiled" so I wanted to finish ASAP!)But I was really hooked with the story. 
 The ending is was made me consider giving this a 3 star. Not just Tris's death, but like I said before, it just didn't make sense. Roth is very brave. But I do think killing off her MC was a mistake. At least in the current ending we have now. It really just didn't fit. 
 But I loved this trilogy so much, and it felt like a telling of human nature, which had me hooked. I was with Roth until the very end, even with the choices she made. I think she is a brilliant writer, and wrote a fascinating story using a fascinating subject in shattered world. 
 I could not rate it 5 stars like the previous two, I just didn't feel it lived up to the conclusion we were all hoping for. But because of my enjoyment of the book itself while I was reading, I decided not to penalize it a star for a somewhat crappy ending. 
 But it seriously took me 2 days to sort through all my thoughts. 
 PHEW. You don't know how much this book has taken out of me! I feel like I've mostly got my thoughts all sorted, but I'm sure we'll all be talking and discussing this book for a long while! 
 And for the readers who really didn't like this book at all and gave it low ratings--I completely understand your frustration. I didn't have quite the same reading experience as you, but you have all made very valid points, and I think your opinions are important and valid as well. 
 Maybe this is what Roth was going for...she wanted us all to think a little bit and start some roaring discussions!

Never Never is the brain child of New York Times Bestselling authors Colleen Hoover and Tarryn Fisher. Both have different writing styles and types of novels so I was intrigued to read the product of their collaboration. Unfortunately, I was underwhelmed by this book, and even though this is part one I still expected more from it. 
 Never Never takes the reader on a mysterious journey with Charlie and Silas as they try to remember their pasts and their identities. Both awaken in the middle of their school day with no recollection of who they are, who their families are, or even what they look like. Bonded by their lack of memory, Charlie and Silas work together to investigate what happened to them, grasping at clues to try to uncover their past. 
 How odd to be made of flesh, balanced on bone, and filled with a soul you've never met. 
 Charlie is the defiant and independent female lead, much like Tarryn Fisher's other female leads. Silas is the school quarterback and the guy who was very much in love with Charlie. Or was he? The more they delve into who Charlie and Silas were, the more apparent it becomes that things weren't as they seemed. Both were keeping secrets. 
 Tarryn Fisher has written some of my all-time favorite books and Colleen Hoover's books introduced me to this wonderful book community that has become such a big part of my life. Having read both of these authors' books before, I didn't think the writing was at the same level as their past works, nor was the storytelling. 
 Never Never didn't capture my attention from the beginning like I had hoped. While I was definitely drawn to the mystery, I felt like much of the novel was Charlie and Silas coming up with more and more questions. Not much happened in this book apart from the characters running in circles searching for answers. While I understand that is is one a part of book, I was expecting to have a little bit more in terms of plot development after 140 pages. 
 Since this is considered a romance, I have to comment on Charlie and Silas's love story. I didn't feel the chemistry between Charlie and Silas. Charlie kept Silas at arm's length, always pushing him away, despite developing feelings for him. Given that, I didn't understand Silas's desire to want to make Charlie fall in love with him. This book just didn't make me feel much either way and because of that I can't rate it highly. 
 I really liked that the authors set the story in New Orleans. I visited NOLA in February 2014 and fell in love with the city. I loved that they incorporated the city's charming mystique, and I definitely think the setting will play a huge role in the next part of the series. 
 I rated this book on the merits of what I've been given. Even though I didn't love this book, I still want to read the next book so I can find out what happens next. 
 Note: The Never Never series is being billed a novellas series but it is more accurately a serial series. A novella comes with the expectation that it will have a distinct beginning, middle and end (a small story arc). In part one, there isn't a complete story arc. Never Never ends in the middle of a scene. Many have called it a cliffhanger but to me it is more of a to-be-continued ending.

 I used to imagine my toys as friends and it made me feel like I was never alone. Since I was home schooled, I liked the fact that I could just escape into a fantasy world with all of my imaginary friends. Definitely a touching story.

I know there are a lot of reviews saying that this book was not that good book because it was copied of from other books. To tell you honestly I dont really see what similarities they were seeing with other popular books.

Jace on the other hand was all perfect looking and everything (Angels or Nephilims are supposed to be good looking right?) but then he still has this attitude. As I have heard there are two more books after the city of ashes, city of glass and city of fallen angels and I just hope the next books wont disappoint me. ^_________________^

Loved loved loved this book!! 
 Seriously, Dex and perry should always be marooned somewhere with a bottle of Jack! Quite a few OMG moments and cannot wait to start the next one, in like 5 seconds :)

This was a re-read, and it was just as good the 2nd time through! Adventure, wit, humor, and dragons. What more could you want from a children's fantasy book? 
 Also, if you're looking for an introduction into the world of Middle Earth, this is an excellent place to start. Bilbo is one of my favorite fictional characters, and this story is so near and dear to my heart.

It was OK. I'd give it a middle-of-the-road 2.5 stars if I could. I was intrigued for the most part, but the format did wear a little thin at times, and felt a bit "gimmicky." It was presented as a series of interview transcripts and first-person accounts (log/diary entries), for those who are unaware. 
 I see a series is planned. Not sure if I'm interested in continuing--especially if the gimmick presentation stays the same.

I really enjoy Sarah J. Mass as an author and was really looking forward to this book. I thought it was definitely a departure from her other works, but still very enjoyable. There was a fairy tale aspect to this novel that I think readers will enjoy.

It's hard to say that this book is enjoyable because that doesn't feel like the right word. What this book is though is honest, genuine, and affecting. 
 It's the story of Melinda, a girl entering her freshman year of high school. She's an outcast, unwanted by her peers because she called the cops and broke up a big party at the end of the summer. 
 I enjoyed the way Anderson told the story and I was happy when Melinda finally spoke up about what really happened at that party. 
 The only thing that really disappointed me was that the book felt too short!

Somethings I felt Grace should have already known pre-screwed-up-ed-ness and that was a tad annoying. As were some of the cliches. Nonetheless, Ally Carter never fails to write an incredible story. Like the Gallagher Girls I think this will get better with each book.

I've been seeing a lot of hype around this book for a while and with the second one coming out I decided it was time to give this a go. I was expecting an emotional story by what I had seen around the blogosphere. And while this was a pleasant read, I failed to be wowed like so many others have. 
 Gigi is a nurse and a single mother. She develops a close relationship with a dying man who leaves her a farmhouse in his home town after passing. Taking the chance to restart her life in a different place and offer her daughter a better future, she picks up and move. But the first thing she encounters is the sheriff and the man that had been left in charge of the care of the farmhouse, who thinks she's nothing more than a gold digger. Add to that there are some strange happenings in town that amp up the danger and this could've all been a wonderful story. 
 Honestly, I never really cared for the characters. Gigi, for the most part, was levelheaded but at times she would act in a way that would annoy me and showed immaturity. And if I had to hear one more time a fight about how Jess was controlling her and not including her in decisions that she had a right to be, I was going to blow. I get it. He was walking all over her. He was a bit of a possessive ass. But the way she was handling it was like a bratty child stomping her foot in my opinion. So that got on my nerves once it happened one too many times. 
 My big issue with this book is more of the plot/pace. The way the story was developing, I kept feeling like there was something it was building up to, waiting for the other shoe to drop sort of speak. And I kept waiting, and waiting. And nothing was shacking things up. And nothing really ever did. We do get the final reveal on what's going on in town and that mystery is solved after a few dead bodies are found, but ... Was that it? It felt like the story is more about the every day of a relationship that starts off pretty early in the book and then it's all just about their normal fights instead of really having tension between or a good mystery around them. I needed one or the other for this to really take it to the next level, and sadly it didn't for me. 
 However, it was still enjoyable. Not a bad read, just definitely not what I had expected based on the reviews I've been seeing. And totally not what I kept anticipating as I was reading. I will probably continue the series though, because I do love a small town feel with a dash of mystery and I can't wait to see the author grow into her stories more. 
 On a side note, and I can usually overlook a lot when it comes to audiobooks, the audio of this is TERRIBLE. I could even hear several times the pages being turned! And the narration was just not what I wanted to hear. I ended up making the speed faster so I wouldn't have to suffer through the nuances of the narration (although I still heard the pages LOL). So this is one I definitely recommend as ebook or print.

I approached this particular book with no small measure of trepidation, since it takes place in the world of Louisa May Alcott's Little Women. This novel tells what befell the father of the March girls while he was off at war. It's so well done, so richly imagined, and well researched, that it feels to me like a welcome enlargement of my knowledge of that family I thought I knew so well already. I started reading it when I went to bed, and put it down, dazed, sometime after midnight. I recommend it, without reservations.
A perfect book, beginning to end. I read it again and again, and it's always fresh.

The Space Between the Stars by Anne Corlett is a dystopian novel that follows a few survivors after most of humanity (throughout the universe, no less) has been wiped out by a deadly virus. 
 Although the novel begins on a settled planet, moves to another planet, and then finally, to our planet earth, there is little science fiction. You have to take for granted elements of space travel and space colonies; they just happen, and truthfully, they are not really important. The whole thing could have taken place on earth without losing a thing. 
 Some interesting characters, some romance, some existential and theological ponderings. I think mainly this is a novel about Dorothy in Oz clicking those red shoes and saying--well, you know what she says. And home is not just a place, is it? 
 The Space Between the Stars wasn't what I expected, but it was entertaining. Did I find it "breathtakingly vivid"-- no, but since this is a debut novel, it might be interesting to see what Corlett comes up with next. 
 Read in February. Review scheduled for May 19.
