"Avatar: The Last Airbender" ended with peace being reestablished between the four elemental nations -- but there were still some dangling threads. "The Promise Part 1 (Avatar: The Last Airbender Book Four)" picks up where the series left off, and addresses the problems of restoring the Fire Nation to how it should be -- especially when not everyone agrees what that is. 
 Now that there is peace between the Fire Nation and Earth Kingdom, Zuko implements the "Harmony Restoration Movement" (named by Sokka) -- the Fire Nation will relocate colonists who have been living in the Earth kingdom for the past century. And while everyone is celebrating, Zuko also extracts a promise from Aang: if he ever becomes like his father, he wants Aang to kill him. 
 But after an assassination attempt, Zuko unexpectedly withdraws the Harmony Restoration Movement. It turns out to be a little more complicated than Zuko expected -- the Fire Nation citizens there have intermarried with the Earth Kingdom people, and don't want to be uprooted from their homes. Now not only must Aang and Zuko deal with colonials who don't want to leave, but also with "freedom fighters" who want the Fire Nation gone. 
 "The Promise Part 1 (Avatar: The Last Airbender Book Four)" is a story that I would love to see translated into an animated movie -- there's a feeling of warm, comfy familiarity in seeing all our old characters reunited again. It springs pretty seamlessly from the end of the TV series, showing where the characters have gone since and the troubles of a post-war world. 
 The primary problem is the story is very short, so sometimes it feels like the characters are flipping between emotions too fast -- Aang literally goes from zero to Avatar State and almost kills Zuko. Too fast! 
 However, it's otherwise a very solid story, with fire/ice battles and some fun comic relief from Sokka (the "oogies" he gets whenever he sees Aang and Katara kissing). And it revolves around a situation with no easy answers. Aang believes that the four nations must be distinct and some Earth people are violently opposed to the Fire Nation, but Zuko doesn't want to wreck the lives of the people who have become rooted in the Earth Kingdom. There's no "win" scenario. 
 Despite being the Fire Lord, Zuko is still morose and introverted -- partly because of his worries about becoming like his father, and partly because of his inexperience at ruling an entire nation. He simply doesn't know what to do, and it's eating him up. For some reason he doesn't go to Iroh for advice even though the old guy has never let him down before. 
 We also get some developments for other characters -- Aang and Katara are enjoying their new romance, although the "sweetie" thing is a bit cloying. But they get some nice moments here (Katara commanding a guard to not set her boyfriend on fire), and Toph is a pretty hard-nosed metalbending teacher. 
 "The Promise Part 1 (Avatar: The Last Airbender Book Four)" ends on a slight cliffhanger, leaving us wondering what will happen next for Zuko and Aang. It's going to be a long wait for the next part.

 "I'm saying that if I can't eat it, fuck it or kill it I have no interest in it."

Emmy meets Oliver again when they're both in high school. When they were just kids they were best friends, but Oliver was kidnapped by his father, and he vanished from Emmy's life--to be replaced by ever-more-constricting protective measures enforced by the frightened parents in the neighborhood. Emmy wants to be free to take risks and live her own life. Oliver's return might jeopardize her plans--but she can't turn her back on the boy who used to be her best friend. 
 This is a lovely, thoughtful coming of age book set in a peculiar situation: a teenager whose life was defined by the kidnapping of her best friend when they were both young is reunited with him. Because of the long separation, Emmy and Oliver are now totally different people who have to re-learn what it would mean to become friends again. 
 This isn't a YA romance, though I would definitely compare it to a Sarah Dessen or a Deb Caletti novel; it's a relationship novel, about the relationships between Emmy and her overprotective parents, Oliver and his terrified mother (I kind of love Benway for not making Oliver's mom the villain--even reading the story from Emmy's teenage POV, your heart just breaks for the poor woman), and, of course, the relationship between Emmy and Oliver. Emmy is able to reveal long-kept secrets to Oliver, because he's now an outsider. Oliver remembers what it was like to trust Emmy, and reveals secrets of his own that he can't make himself tell his traumatized mother. 
 If you like realistic YA fiction, this is a must-read.

I just love Jory. I can't get enough of him. I saw somewhere that Calmes is done writing about him, so I think I have only one more book to read, but I'm so not ready. 
 This time Calmes spends too much time with details of every day life as usual but for once, not everyone loves Jory. Okay 99% of the people do, but some people don't. At once point he even says to someone something like, "Everyone either loves me or hates me," and someone agrees with him. He does admit that women really love him. 
 And I get why. He's perfect. He's funny, he's interesting, he's adorable, he's helpful, he's good with kids and animals, he's creative, he works hard, he's easy going, and he's gay. What's not to love? 
 Well: I spent the first chapter laughing out loud. Seriously. One of my dogs got so annoyed she got up and went to sleep in another room. I love that almost everyone loves Jory but in that chapter I saw how exasperating he is to work with, how poor his social skills really are, and why some people can't handle him. He was almost Ssperger-ish but not. I think I'm going to go read that chapter again... I particularly love how Sam and Dane know exactly how to handle him, what he needs, and have to constantly tell other people to just chill and let Jory run with it. The scene near the end with the doctor was sad but hilarious, too. 
 The gay men in Jory's life just don't take no for an answer, either. And it gets old. There was just too much of "I love you Jory" "no you don't" "Yes I do, be with me" "no" "i'm better than Cage" "there's no one else for me" "let's be friends" "okay" "I love you Jory" "Please move your hand," etc. Jory tolerates WAY too much and he forgives WAY too many times. He gets irritated with their behavior but then gives in again. It's just ridiculous. 
 The plot was interesting but there was too much day to day stuff and character development and not enough of the plot itself. I wanted more action and suspense given that a huge portion of the plot revolved around mobsters. So the pacing was quite off. 
 But the characters were great as always and the action, when it occurred, was good. Calmes is good with danger. I was really worried the ending would just fizzle because I had fewer and fewer pages and nothing but sweetness was happening but then bam came the thriller endgame and it was good. I just love it when people are in danger and the ones that love them get all blubbery. It was good. 
 Four and a half stars but I'm wavering between rounding up or rounding down. 
 A Matter of Time was better and there really was too much repetition of everyone wanting Jory so I'm going with four stars for this one.

Great read, though the format may take some getting used to for some people. Don't except a straight forward, linear narrative. The larger story of the zombie war is told through a series of individual interviews that function as cross-sections of the war. Eventually all the vignettes link up to form a big picture, but they're a bit disjointed and sometimes the full impact doesn't hit you until a hundred pages later when you read one little detail mentioned in a different interview. 
 This is, at heart, an ethnography of war stories detailing humanity's first large scale war against something other than itself, and how it played out across a global scale. It's well-crafted, realistic, chilling, and startlingly introspective. Definitely worth your time.

4.5 stars 
 What I really wanted was not to be a burden to anyone. To be really and truly free. 
 Don't Breathe a Word was an incredibly touching and captivating read. It's one of those books that leaves me wondering and thinking long after I've finished it. 
 We have Joy Delamere, a girl who suffers from severe asthma and is in an unstable relationship with her boyfriend, Asher. She feels her family and Asher are suffocating her, not allowing her the freedom she wishes she could have in life. So, after a night in which Asher went too far in damaging Joy, she escapes into the streets of Seattle, where a homeless boy had offered her protection would she ever need it. She sets out to find him, hoping she could be saved from the suffocating life she had been living. 
 This book was such a breath of fresh air. It's raw and real, and the issues and problems explored in this book were dealt in a tender manner. Joy learns that living on the street isn't as freeing as she thought it would be. She suffers from drug dealers, rapists, thieves, and abusers. She lives in a ratty old shack, with the boy, Creed, and his gang, May and Santos. Together, they pitch in to bring in money somehow, bring in food from the garbage, protect each other from the street thugs out there. Their world is truly heartbreaking. Each teenager is running away from something, each with their own morbid history. We learn slowly why each one escaped their other lives and how they ended up homeless in the streets of Seattle. I loved Creed! He was protective (not overbearingly, though!), caring, understanding, determined. He had a dream to become a musician, and Joy was there to encourage him forward. I thought they were a perfectly complemented pairing. 
 Holly Cupala really wove this story into a beautiful one, and I was able to connect with Joy on some levels, in her pain and her imprisonment she feels. My only problem was that in the beginning, Joy appears to be a girl who doesn't know how to stand up for herself. She depends on other people to help her--like Asher, then later on Creed. But I got to watch her develop into a fierce and brave girl throughout the book, and I admired the strength she has towards the end. 
 So, overall, I loved it. Joy's voice was real, honest, and Holly Cupala doesn't sugarcoat the horrors of run-away life. I'll definitely be looking into her other books as well!

Graeme Simsion's novel doesn't sit right with me. There's something about it that makes me feel uneasy, slightly annoyed even when I read the pages. 
 I think it's the comedic tone of the quite serious subject. Don Tillman is an unusual man, he's completely set in his own ways and any changes to his schedule and daily rhythm make him feel stressed. Fueled by his best (and only) friends Gene and his wife Claudia, he starts looking for a wife. 
 He wants his future wife to be compatible to him though, so he creates a questionnaire and calls the project the Wife project. Anyone who answers the questions wrongly is stricken off as a suitable candidate. He then meets Rosie, who answers most of the questions wrongly but who he can't seem to shake off his mind. 
 I don't really understand his need to find a wife, if compatibility is such a strong thing for him. The ensuing "romance" between him and Rosie leaves me with even more question marks. What is it that makes this romantic? What does she see in him? 
 The comedic undertone I mentioned before brings about "hilarious" circumstances which I would have preferred to see as sad. I feel that Simsion is making light of Don's condition and somehow it doesn't sit right with me. 
 I have the second book: The Rosie Effect in my bookcase too, so I'll start reading in straightaway. I'm sure it'll only enlarge my feelings about the first book. I'm not going to end on a too negative note, because it's worth mentioning the novel is well-written and at times difficult to put down.

 I loved this book! I crave stories of powerful women like Milla Jovovich's Leeloo and Ultraviolet, Trinity from the Matrix, and Lara Croft, and Ash is exactly like them in terms of being awesome. The beginning gripped me by the throat and didn't let go. I rarely buy books by new-to-me authors because I've been burned so many times, but I made an exception in this case and I'm glad I did. The action was non-stop and the romance, especially at the beginning, was pretty hot. I also loved both characters, but especially Ash. She kicks ass. 
 The only things that prevented this from being a 5 star book for me happened in the last 10 pages. Or, actually, what didn't happen. The ending felt incredibly rushed and I didn't get a good sense of completion or satisfaction, which otherwise knocked a perfectly phenomenal book down an entire quarter of a star. 
 I didn't like the way the romance wrapped up, and I couldn't figure out what the hell had happened with the plot, especially the bad guy. It felt unfinished but not in the good way, in both cases. 
 (view spoiler)[First, the romance. 
 After her big revelation that she liked Rip even before the loyalty training, they should have had sex in her perspective where it is clear that the loyalty training has been broken by her telepathic battle. Otherwise, I'm afraid it's still in operation. I mean, she did just spend 30+ hours undergoing some technobabble reprogramming to reinstall the loyalty training, right? So just because she liked him before doesn't prove that she likes him of her own volition now, and that puts them on much more unequal footing than the power dynamic of the cadet/commander relationship they are skirting. 
 Also, having a a nice finale to a relationship is just necessary to feel good about it. If you spend a whole book waiting for the girl to ask the guy out, you want the end to have the girl ask the guy out (and him to say yes). If you're waiting for the kiss, you want the kiss. If marriage, you want the proposal. If your protagonists have already gone so far as to have sex but there was a question of a power struggle during it and there was lots of angst before/after about whether it was wrong, you want the ending to show them having sex with that resolved and it being 110% right, so that you can be confident it is a true HEA. 
 As a bonus, going out of the Institute to have sex would convince me that they are actually going to end up together and not get dragged apart by outside forces, like what happened at the 3/4 mark of the book. I'm just really not convinced they're going to end up together as written, seriously. 
 Okay, second, the actual plot. (!) 
 A lot of info was revealed at the end and not explained. I assume there will be a second book that will further shed light on the conspiracy, but I think a few crucial things should have been tied up right now. 
 Yes, it was weird that Trevast had some magical knowledge of the Illuminati - er, I mean, telepaths - and something in the stolen file triggered his memory. Or something. I would have liked a little more speculation as to how exactly that occurred, since it is so shocking to everyone that there is no list of Illuminati - I mean, telepaths - in the stolen documents. 
 But! More important! 
 What I really couldn't figure out was the bad guy, Jevan. Maybe I read too fast and skipped an important line. Essentially the jihadists - aka Sariceans - developed a spiffy new engine. Ash and co. were dispatched to steal the plans. Jevan couldn't wait for her to get back, and decided to kill off her whole team to get the plans first. (If Trevast was one of the people controlled by the Illuminati/telepaths, then that was a costly impatience because they just lost one of their sleeper agents. If he was a member of the Templars instead, we never got any indication from anywhere that they even exist, so I'm just pulling this idea from the air.) 
 After Jevan can't get the plans decrypted, he loses Ash to the United Nations - aka, the Coalition. He is still trying to get her back. A few days after her capture, the jihadists attack -- in their spiffy new engines. 
 And that is when I stop understanding. 
 Before the attack, Jevan wants to control the secret plans. Maybe they'll help him become the leader of the Illuminati. I don't know. But after the actual technology has been revealed to the entire UN, isn't the cat out of the bag? Maybe her stolen plans are actual schematic drawings for how to build your own engine, which would shortcut the development process for the UN. But won't the UN now spend 100% of its time trying to capture a working ship, and/or send another spy team to steal the plans a second time? If the UN gets the plans, it seems like Jevan's whole bargaining position is shot. Yet he still goes after Ash to get the plans decrypted, even after the attack. 
 A slight hint about why he wants them so bad - is he going to blackmail someone who is immune to his powers, who doesn't care that the secret has been revealed, and will give anything to get these schematics? - would have resolved this more clearly for me. 
 Also, after the attack, his bargaining position is a little more precarious because he needs to give the plans to someone quickly so that the UN can start building their own ships. Otherwise, the jihadists will press the advantage, destroy everything, and the UN will no longer exist. If the UN no longer exists, the Illuminati and Jevan have no one to influence. He loses big time. That can't happen. If he is already secretly a jihadist, then he already has the plans. What the heck. I cannot figure him out. 
 I am basing my understanding of his desires on the actions of Bayis, someone it is established that he or his minion is controlling, who immediately forces Ash to decrypt the plans once she is recaptured. If that's not Jevan's idea, then it would be nice if there were some way to sort out the telepathic orders from normal ones. Otherwise, it's just confusing. 
 Okay, this is a hell of a long tangent. I just feel like I was left with some mysteries that are not very interesting. They seem more like simple oversights, which could have been wrapped up in one "mwahaha" from the villain during his false triumph and one, "Hmm, we'll have to learn more about agent Trevast" line at the very end. Oh, and a hot sex scene away from the Institute to leave me with the warm fuzzies at the end, of course. :) 
 The real interesting questions, which I feel should drive the series, are: 
 Exactly how deep does that Illuminati/telepath conspiracy go? What are their true intentions? Is Ash & Co. going to be the ones to take it down, or will she discover that she's still a pawn (even though she's now immune to their controls)? Or will she even discover something redeeming about them? (hide spoiler)] 
 Overall, I seriously loved the book, which is why the high stars. It is really great! I intend to read the sequel, and I wonder if it will be more of Ash or one of her fellow anomalies. I love series books that follow a different couple in each book, but I think there may also be more to reveal in Ash & Rip's relationship, so I am good either way.

"We're all ghostwriters, my boy. And it's not just our memories. Our actions, too. We all think we're in control of our own lives, but really they're pre-ghostwritten by forces around us." 
 Ghostwritten begins in Okinawa, just one of ten sections that implants the reader into an already existing story that could work as a living, thriving, halfway point to an excellent book. Okinawa opens up to Tokyo. Tokyo opens up to Hong Kong, Hong Kong to an ancient Holy Mountain. We journey to America and Ireland, London and Petersburg. Each section boils in future importance, as if those characters' lives have been planned, or written. Discovery, vast connections via a system of likes and dislikes. We are categorized whether we like it or not. A jazz aficionado will go to night clubs and record stores, and mingle with similar like-minded people. Do it enough--in any city, no matter how large--and you may begin to notice similar faces and people, a pattern in that system. 
 One section deals with the transmigration of a spirit that possesses humans through contact. In a way, we are the spirit who transmits through differing characters and stories and landscapes. Aren't we a similar spirit reading this right now? You have to know someone intimately to be able to love them. So love at first sight is a contradiction in terms. Unless in that first sight there's some sort of mystical gigabyte downloading of information from one mind into the other. As if the reader must download this information, too. None of this happened. None of this really happened, Mitchell proposes at the climax of the most suspenseful and shocking scene in the book, as if Mitchell is winking at us with his own "in-joke" as if it were all just some mystery thriller, and wasn't it just that? Did we for some time believe it was actually real? Are we suckers? Is Mitchell that good of a writer? Or do we immediately possess or download a characters' mind? It's a little of both, I think. 
 For a moment I had an odd sensation of being in a story that someone was writing. 
 Ghostwritten merely forewarns that anything can happen at any time (sometimes, those events even get their start from a world away). Chance dictates that tomorrow could be the best day of your life. Or the worst. But there's only one way to find out. 
 did you know that... the universe is the shape of a donut, and that if you had a powerful enough telescope you would see the tip of your tail? 
 Do you care? 
 My only major gripe appears somewhere around Clear Island, where I began thinking, "Yet another story with a cast of characters I have to learn and appreciate. The end will be warranted, but here comes another 10 pages where I need to grow accustomed to even more strangers." Ghostwritten's ten sections are rarely unsatisfying, but they can leave you hanging just as things are getting good. Mitchell's novel is a valiant first effort that reaches for profundity instead of having it naturally evolve. It's desperate for answers. And the last section, Underground, acts only as a conciliatory prize as it circles back to Okinawa. After all, the major themes here, from interconnection, fate and chance, are all themes any other good book addresses. But Mitchell attempts to force upon the reader motives and tactics outright instead of letting them coalesce in the background, like any great book would do. We don't need to be told what answers to look for; those questions should be inherently written into the world.

This is a flawed entry into the Harry Potter canon, there are a number of things that contradict the previous seven books, but I did enjoy the book. It's a quick read, being all dialogue. The themes of family are very poignant and very touching. I liked the friendship between Albus and Scorpius and how the depiction of Slytherins and the Malfoys changed in regards to our characters even though there's still a prejudice against Slytherins as a whole in the Hogwarts student body, it was balanced very well. I also liked the depiction of Snape, I was never one of those readers who forgave Snape and thought of him as a hero immediately after his backstory was revealed, but after this, I like him much better as a character. I like Draco much better too, we certainly hear a lot more about his home life as a child, his struggles with his father, he's no longer just a bully, he's much more complex. My favourite part of the book is definitely Scorpius, he's smart, loyal, brave, optimistic. He's the Hermione to Albus's Harry. 
 Now onto the flaws. (view spoiler)[First of all, it was confirmed Harry can't speak Parseltongue anymore after that piece of Voldemort was destroyed--and they even talk about it in the play, but somehow he can still speak it when he needs to? Harry talks about being rid of Voldemort in his mind as well as "physically" (i.e. soul-wise), but that strains credibility for me. The magic system in the series have never been very rigorous (e.g. Portkeys, do they transport you at a specific time or just take the first person to touch it? Are there different incantations for the two functions?), but this is one of those things that you can't slide on. Nothing about the world building that's occurred up to now suggested that there was a psychological component to Harry being a Parselmouth! 
 Second, I simply cannot believe that Voldemort had a daughter with Bellatrix Lestrange. It just contradicts everything about the characterization of Voldemort. If it had turned out that Tom Riddle as a young man, perhaps while working at Borgin and Burkes, had an affair with someone we've never heard of before and this was his granddaughter or great-granddaughter I might have believed it, but the Dark Lord Voldemort does not view people as anything other than obstacles or disposable tools on his road to world domination. I can't believe that he would be interested in having sex with Bellatrix Lestrange. I mean what exactly did they say to convince him? Though now that I think about it, I'm wondering if we should believe Delphi's (Voldemort's daughter's) word--whether she's deluding even herself about where she came from, but then she is a Parselmouth, and she probably knows that Voldemort would be able to tell if she's lying, so.... 
 By the way, if Delphi was born in Malfoy Manor before the Battle of Hogwarts, and Voldemort had Harry's blood in him already, does that mean that Delphi and the Potters are related? (hide spoiler)] 
 Edit (Dec 14, 2016): This book is better seen as a sequel to the film series rather than the book series.

 One of the drawbacks of being a Stephen King fan is that I'm constantly looking for links to his other works since he loves to do that. As a result, it's difficult for me to read his stories for the sake of reading that particular story. I did that here. From the moment we met Richard Farris, my mind made him Randall Flagg, and I'm still not convinced that he wasn't.  Maybe Gwendy was just a link in a chain that led to a great disaster in the future. That being said, I'm now having fun pretending that the boy in Pescadero pushed the black button June 16, 1990. Wouldn't that be neat? Yeah, I know in 1984 RF said Gwendy would (view spoiler)[live a long life, sell a book at age 35 (which would be way after 1990), and die surrounded by friends (hide spoiler)], but this wouldn't be the first time Flagg/Walter/Marten/Ageless Stranger/Man in Black/Walkin' Dude/Covenant Man/Russell/Richard/Whoever lied. Even before he started to blow up, Sterling could not believe that Ethan picked her to ask out. Even before he hit a million followers, before his single started airing on the radio, before the concerts and the sold out tour destinations, Sterling knew she was so incredibly lucky to have Ethan Cross as her boyfriend. 
 Ethan and Sterling click in a way Sterling didn't think possible. As much as she loves performing culinary experiments and correcting egregious grammatical errors in signs, Sterling loves spending time with Ethan more. As great as hanging out with her friends is, hanging out with Ethan is better. 
 Then Ethan's music starts getting noticed and suddenly Ethan is a hot commodity thrown head-first in the world of fame and celebrity. Sterling, much to her initial dismay, is thrown in right beside him. 
 Ethan is getting compared to Michael Jackson and getting more famous by the second. Meanwhile Sterling finds herself appearing next to Ethan in countless tabloid photos, traveling around the country to catch his sold out shows, and even garnering a small following of her own. 
 Between her hot boyfriend, the sudden fame, and the free couture, Sterling should be living the dream. The only problem is Sterling is no longer sure whose dream it is in Now and Forever (2014) by Susane Colasanti. 
 Now and Forever is a bit like an exclusive trip behind the velvet rope; a look at exactly what being famous might mean. Unfortunately, unlike other titles in a similar ilk, this book fails to offer a nuanced picture instead focusing on the glitz and glamor. While Ethan does change as he gains fame throughout the story, the implications of that change or what caused it (privilege, growing up, celebrity in general) are never discussed anymore than Sterling's own relationship with her fame by association. 
 While this is a sweet romance, a lot of the story is spent on a bad relationship. Although this focus on the bad makes the second romance that much sweeter, it simultaneously raises questions about why the novel's plot focuses where it does for so long. 
 Like all of Colasanti's heroines, Sterling is adorably romantic. While her absorption in Ethan's world and identity are troubling, it is an issue that's addressed before the story ends. 
 Now and Forever is a must read for any readers who are super into the latest boy band or music in general. Bonus points for anyone who is a celebrity news junkie. 
 Possible Pairings: Take a Bow by Elizabeth Eulberg, Where She Went by Gayle Forman, Reunited by Hilary Weisman Graham, To All the Boys I've Loved Before by Jenny Han, Open Road Summer by Emery Lord, Being Friends With Boys by Terra Elan McVoy, Famous in Love by Rebecca Serle

The book, I'd Tell You I Love You But Then I'd Have to Kill You, is basically about a 15 year old girl named Cammie Morgan who goes to The Gallagher Academy For Exceptional Young Women. This all-girls school is technically a school for geniuses, but essentially it is a school for spies. Cammie, nicknamed 'The Chameleon' for her ability to stay hidden fairly well, is pretty much a normal spy school student except for the fact that her mom is headmistress. Cammie has many amazing spy-like abilities and really cool classes she gets to take. Returning to her sophomore year with her two best friends, Bex and Liz, made it all seem even better. But living behind the sheltered walls of The Gallagher Academy makes these students a lot different from other students, who, most of the time, don't understand them. So when the girls get a mission from Mr. Solomon in their covert operations class where they get to experience some of the outside world they jump right on it. Sadly, on their mission Bex and Liz get caught. But Cammie, being the Chameleon, manages to stay hidden. This point in the book is really where I thought the story began to pick up because Cammie met Josh. Josh was pretty much a normal boy who thought Cammie was just a noramal girl, so he talked to her. Although, when faced with this new challenge all her years of spy training couldn't prepare Cammie for this moment with this boy. After this point in the story Cammie starts to have secret meetings with Josh, and with advice from her new roommate, Macey McHenry, she is able to have success in starting up a relationship with him. 
 Overall, I liked this book. I thought it was pretty interesting, but it was also very light and simple. By this I mean there were no real surprise moments. It kept me interested enough to keep reading but I wasn't jumping out of my chair. There were a few interesting spy moments like when they went on missions or cracked codes, but I felt it was lacking action at some points. Some parts were, at times, predictable and it was a bit of an easier book than I thought it would be. But, I did feel like it was a good book choice for me. Although, it did lack some surprise moments, the book did have romance and a great amount of information on the characters throughout the novel. But, being the first book in the Gallagher Girls series, I would expect the other books to have more action and spy moments. So, I believe this novel, for most people, would be worth reading. I think people would enjoy this book if they were looking for a fairly simple book that is entertaining, and for the most part, lighthearted.

Very different from what I expected, but not in a bad way. Really I didn't know what to expect going in to Something More Than Night. It's certainly a departure from the style and substance of the Milkweed Triptych (which I highly recommend!). 
 I loved the style and character of this book. It's almost dripping with uniqueness which I thought was great. It's poured on a little heavy at times but you come to realize that it just serves to emphasize the plot and setting. 
 There is the temptation to get bogged down in the minutiae of the theological/ontological "laws" being thrown around, but you soon discover to just take it at face value and enjoy the ride, which is quite fun. Once you're fully immersed you can appreciate how interesting the world is in SMTN. 
 What keeps it from 5 stars is the necessity to gloss over a few plot points and how the plot is advanced in some parts of the novel. I was wondering where the tale would lead and was a little disappointed when characters literally just stated what comes next. Also the obtuse feeling you have sometimes while reading can be off-putting but if you stick with it, it grows on you. 
 The characters are great, and there are some touching moments. Bayliss is a blast from beginning to end, definitely my favorite, and the ending was satisfying and fitting. Worth a read!

Peter Pan was never a favorite character of mine growing up. Maybe it was because I never watched the movie, or because wars and battles weren't subjects that I found appealing in a fairy tale. As a child, I was enchanted by Snow White, and the Brother Grimm's tales of unfortunate kids and terrible witches. There weren't witches in Peter Pan! Or hungry wolves! All I ever knew about it was that it talked about a crazy kid that could fly, a bunch of orphaned children, and a crazy (and a bit stupid) captain with a hook for a hand. Oh! and a crocodile. 
 So, people might ask, what am I doing reading a retelling of a story I never cared for? I.... I don't know. All I can say in my favor is this: I don't regret it. Not one bit. This is one of those books that has you on the edge of your seat the entire time, and stays with you long after the last line is finished. Brom presents a story that really analyses the implications of the seemingly cute and candid happenings of "Peter Pan": The kidnapping of gullible children, the war between them and grownups with swords and guns, the fact that they can never grow, and the untold consequences for those who do, are all of them explored in "The Child Thief" and given new and incredible dimensions. 
 Without a doubt, the most intriguing character of all is Peter. He's the hero we're used to root for: the symbol of our wild and untamed side, the representation of everything that's good and playful. That is, of course, until we are faced with his dark side: the one that is so invested on his mission, so stuck in his ways and prejudices, that becomes blind to death and to the sacrifices others make for him. Who knew that an eternal boy could be so interesting? 
 And speaking of interesting characters, the Captain blew my mind, but I can't say anymore without marking this review with a big SPOILER tape on top of it. So let's speak about my other all-time favorite character: Nick. When we first meet him, he's running away from home with a bag full of provision and methamphetamines. The tenants of his house are drug dealers and Nick, blaming his mother for the abuse these people put him through, decides to go and make a life with the money he hopes to get in exchange for the stolen drugs. Unfortunately things don't go as planned, and he's in the process of getting his ass kicked when Peter makes an appearance and saves the day. 
 Nick is a fantastic character. We see him grow and confront his own demons while being the only "devil" that can see through Peter and his schemes. He doesn't always do the right thing, but who does? Being thrown into a world you know nothing about, with dangers that surpass your wildest expectations, and surrounded by a little kingdom that stands on the cult of a kid that, at the best of times, has little idea of what to do with himself, is no piece of cake. But Nick pulls it off and deals with trouble in a realistic way, showing the author's mastery with words and a great ability in terms of character developing. 
 Avalon and its mythology are also a strong point. The island is all that remains of a once world full with magic, and is now seriously threatened by "flesh eaters", or men that are determined to extinguish it by destroying its leader, the Lady. Peter wants them dead at all costs, using as his main weapon the disposition of the children he manages to transport to Avalon and turn into little killing machines, or "devils". 
 The climax of this war, and the end of the book, was the only part of the book that left me wanting more (and heartbroken, but I can't tell you why), and the reason I almost took a star out of the book. It felt like a rushed way to end it all: You build up the tension to eleven, set the stage for a battle of epic proportions, and deliver something good, but not incredible. (view spoiler)[(You also kill everyone I cared about, so by the end I couldn't care less about Peter and his epiphany) (hide spoiler)] However, this does not mean that the book is in any way, shape or form bad or not worthy of any fantasy fan's time and energy. (I'm giving it 5 stars!!) As you can probably tell I'm no expert when it comes to retellings of classic children's tales, but it seems to me that there aren't a lot of ways anyone could actualize Peter Pan better than Brom. It was a magical experience that will stay with me for a long time.

This isn't a thriller, despite what the mysterious cover and ominous (and somewhat obvious) title would have you believe. It instead is a slow-moving, methodical account of one elderly woman's struggles with dementia and her attempts to be taken seriously when it turns out that her friend Elizabeth is nowhere to be found. The book proceeds pretty much in real time, with the narrator, Maud, illustrating basically every part of her day and in doing so revealing the sad ways in which dementia changes how you live, and even somewhat who you are. 
 Nobody close to me has suffered from dementia, and I know very little about it. I can't really even remember any other portrayals of it in popular culture, or at least any in which it was the central focus of a story. Hence, I can't speak to how accurate Healey's writing is. However, I can say that it never felt like she was being flippant with her treatment of dementia. Maud comes across as a real human being, and her condition is never used to poke fun or portrayed in any way other than very matter-of-factly. Indeed, it was extremely sad reading Maud's thoughts about how she is perceived and the dismissive, mocking tone with which some talk to her, sometimes including her own daughter. The tendency of people to treat Maud as either someone who does not know anything and cannot think for herself, or someone who may as well be on their deathbed and must be treated with the utmost caution and gentleness, certainly rings true, and seeing the way that people navigate both sides of that spectrum as well as the response Maud has to those sides was very engaging. 
 I guess now is a good time to say that this is a book with two stories in it: one that deals with a woman who is losing her memory and looking for her friend, and one that deals with that woman in her childhood, looking for her sister. The flashbacks are presented with basically no segue, as each break in the main story leads directly in to a vivid recollection of Maud's life as a teenager in postwar England. This second story is notable because it is so normal: it doesn't have the unreliable narrator that you quickly get used to in the rest of the book, and instead tells a fairly straightforward story about her childhood in a very standard way. Indeed, the way that the stories are interleaved is rather jarring, and had the effect of acting as a kind of foothold throughout the novel; even if I was struggling to keep up with the disjointed style and emotional content of the story, I could always count on a flashback coming to ground me and allow me to learn a bit more about Maud herself as well as her family. I did often wonder, however, how Maud was able to have such clear memories of events from her distant past. It may be that this is a realistic portrayal of dementia; I just don't know. As someone who is generally not very interested in history, the descriptions of postwar England just passed right by without any kind of impact. However, it was engaging enough when taken as short intervals between episodes primarily due to the mystery angle. 
 As I said above, more than anything, this is a very slow book. Healey chooses to focus a great deal on Maud's day-to-day, which when combined with the sometimes circular path of Maud's memories and thoughts, results in a book where nothing much happens for a long time. Thus, this book worked better for me as a vehicle for exposing me to a disorder and perspective on life that I really had no knowledge of, than as a gripping read. 
 Healey does her best to make Maud a real, round character despite her difficulties, and while she succeeds for the most part, there are parts where the characterization takes a back seat to the central conceit of depicting someone with dementia as faithfully as possible. This resulted in somewhat of a not-quite-full experience when I was done. In fact, quite a few parts of the story contributed to that feeling. The ending is convenient and somewhat predictable, and really had no bearing on how much I enjoyed the book. Many parts of the plot were simply an excuse to spend more time in Maud's head or past, and it would've been nice to be able to think about the plot and engage with it as much as I engaged with the narration. Hence, I'm not sure I'd really recommend this book; I certainly don't regret reading it, and feel like it will be a fairly singular experience, but its faults are also fairly obvious. However, as I already mentioned, I did feel it was worthwhile, and I really flew through the last quarter or so. I'm excited to read more of Healey's works in the future, as I appreciated her ability to make this book so engaging and emotional without relying on plot twists or getting overly sentimental.

 New to the neighborhood, she meets an attractive, but very grumpy neighbor, Dallas. Even though he seems to genuinely like her boys, he doesn't seem to be very impressed with her. But Diana is determined to be the bigger person, especially when Dallas becomes her oldest nephew's baseball coach. When Diana and her boys needle their way into Dallas's life, can he be neighborly or will something develop a step further? 
 Wait For It was a very refreshing story. In the rush of romance novels dealing with instalove or fast and heavy relationships, Diane and Dallas develop and evolve their relationship over the course of the story. If you enjoy friends to lovers novels, then I really think this is a book for you. 
 The whole theme of this story is waiting. And while waiting isn't exactly the most romantic thing to do, it's real and responsible and it proves to your loved ones that they are worth it to start something on the right foot. I thought this was a great book. It tells two stories, alternating chapter about for the first part of the book. The first story describes the journey of the titular Sarah, a ten-year-old Jewish Parisian girl rounded up in July 1942 by French police doing the bidding of the Gestapo. It describes how she hides her brother from the police, and then her subsequent ordeal and fate (read the book for the rest). It describes the harrowing treatment that the French Jews were subjected to, notably in the "Velodrome d'Hiver" and old cycle track stadium. The second story, interwoven at first, and then taking over completely, takes place on the sixtieth anniversary of the round-up. It centers on Julia, an American journalist married to a Frenchman, researching the events of July 1942. Julia's research is at first general, and then particular, as she stumbles on a family coincidence related to Sarah and follows it to its end. The book keeps our interest all the way though, showing how the different generations of French people reacted to the 1942 events, and keeping us emotionally involved with both Sarah and Julia. It was great. Read it!

I was fascinated by the premise of this novel: a future London and Oxford governed by a mysterious order, where music has replaced the written word and people are unable to form memories. In some parts, the book almost delivered, with a wonderful sense of disorientation, some clever uses of language and an interesting insight into people thinking in a totally different way. I really enjoyed the middle third, where revelations, plots and romance come thick and fast. 
 On the other hand, by focusing her story on people with no memories, the author gave herself a bit of a problem. In the first third, when the narrator is suffering like everyone else, though his outlook on the world is intriguing, its hard to a)form any real emotional connection with him and b)gain any real understanding of this unusual world. And then in contrast, once he's (perhaps inevitably) learned to form memories again, there's little to make him stand out from any other hero in any other story. Overall, the first third was confusing and a bit of a chore to get through, and then the final third was rushed, somewhat generic and left more questions than answers. It was extremely unclear what the order were doing and why - was the loss of memories the whole point or an unfortunate side effect? How did they gain power? There was enough in the middle section to make me enjoy this overall, but I really felt I had to fight for that enjoyment. 
 Apart from the memory loss, the other notable thing about this book is the use it makes of music. At first glance, this is most noticeable in the way that musical terms like lento or piano are used in everyday speech and in the narration. I'm just about familiar enough with the terminology to have found that interesting rather than jarring. But the deeper, weirder part is that people sing directions to each other (seemingly without words) and sign sentiments (loss, sadness, respect etc) in solfege (do re mi fa so la to do). I love music and have sang in choirs, but I've always struggled when people talk about music telling a story or conveying emotion, and here, this concept is taken to extremes. I suspect you have to really love and understand choral/orchestral music and the underlying theory of it to properly enjoy and appreciate this novel. 
 One final thing that caught me by surprise but was rather appreciated - the central love story is between two teenage boys. It sometimes feels like "LGBT novel" is treated as a genre all or its own or at very least, made a huge fuss out of, so it was sweet to see this cropping up naturally in the midst of a literary-meets-fantasy novel of this type. The romance didn't blow me away, as I'd struggled to really connect with either character, but it was nicely done. That said, I did wonder whether a female character who was built up and then completely dropped from the plot was the original love interest or at least intended to have a more significant role, as her sudden disappearance was oddly jarring. 
 Overall, this is worth a read, if you can make yourself fight through the opening section and suspend disbelief sufficiently for the rest of it - particularly if you have a decent musical education. That said, I'm bemused by the Booker nomination. The author has to be applauded for trying something a bit different and for blurring the genre with the literary, but this was really not that outstanding.

Callihan did manage to surprise me, not by the murderer's identity, but with the motivating force behind the werewolf. By far, the banter between Daisy and Ian is the strength of this novel.
I don't remember being particularly impressed with this book. Of course, I read it over ten years ago.

I am not a fan of not finishing books, so it really takes a lot for me to do so. I'm often willing to suffer just a tiny bit to finish a book because there have been so many times in which the ending makes up for the rest of the book. 
 This was not one of those times in which I was willing to suffer.Perhaps I was in the wrong mood or it just wasn't for me because this has a fair amount of great reviews saying that it's a fun, light read. 
 I had never understood until this book what people meant in reviews when they said "it was cringeworthy." In the first twenty pages I didn't like Bailey or her attitude which was rude and annoying, she had already described her hair TWICE as "lana turner pinwheel curls," and I didn't like the first person POV. I decided to wait until page 40 to make my decision to DNF which is pretty early, but I have a million other things to read and decided this wasn't worth the time.

Oh wow, where do I even start. Okay, let's start with the one thing that I did like: when the novel does not veer into overwritten purple prose, it can be funny. I liked a MC snapping at someone who commented on the age difference in his relationship: "Hey, maybe he's not a cradle snatcher. Maybe I'm a grave robber." I liked this description of a club: "The dungeons and the make-out rooms were less an orgy than a queue." Oh, and I also liked that sex in the novel is somewhat more realistic than the romance average. 
 On to the disappointing stuff: I don't buy the MCs as a couple. I'm 200% down with the stated agenda of the novel (to show a kinky couple for which kinks are not stigmatized, and sex is the easiest part of the relationship), but the relationship didn't work for me. I don't buy their insta-love with "It was more than just sex!!!1" from second 1; I don't buy their level of schmoop (I know plenty of schmoopy dudes IRL, but the likelihood of both being schmoopy, and both being schmoopy in identical terms, is kinda slim); I don't buy the romance between people who are at such different stages in life, and the novel did little to convince me otherwise. Moreover, I specifically don't buy them as a kinky couple. Like, I'm as vanilla as they come, but there are very few things in the novel that I have not or would not do, and many of them do not even ping as kink per se. I'm fairly certain that blindfolds, light bondage and dirty talk had all been demoted to vanilla-hood, right? So, I had these moments of blinking disbelief when, say, the dom blindfolds the sub, and proceeds to have this crisis: "It turned me on a lot. God. I'm sick;" and if that wasn't enough, he keeps asking whether that was "really, honestly, completely okay?" Consent for each part of sex is important, I get it, but if it's something this benign, it looks very much like an overreaction.

 Only two bad points about this book: the diabolus ex machina which makes the ending feel a little forced, and the character of Red. Why, god, why does this book feel the need to go out of its way to insult a character because she *gasp* likes clothes and is stereotypically girly? [I'm guessing we're now headed into summer, but like yeahhhh... what are the longterm effects of things???] Do Darla and Alex have a kid? I need to know more! I don't want an actual novel though, because I feel like this one ended so nicely and I don't want to ruin what a great series this was. I just want to know what's going on in their world!

3.5 stars 
 First of all - OMG the great Noelle Stevenson (aka gingerhaze) drew this cover! I was fangirling before I even started reading the actual book! If you're not familiar with her work check out her Broship of the Ring stuff, it's pretty funny. 
 Okay, this is one of those books that caters to a very specific segment of the population - not a small one!, but still one with its own rules and history (yes, actual history, oh the things one could write about big name authors of today who were once fanfic writers - all the drama!). So, to be clear, you're either a part of fandom or you're not. It's not just being a fan - it's being an active fan and contributing to it, and it's not generational (the trouble that those poor fanboys/fangirls in the 60's had to go through to share their homoerotic fanart of Kirk and Spock! Let us have a moment of silence for their tireless dedication), it's just a _thing_ you're either into or you're not. It doesn't make you any better or any worse than anyone else, it's a hobby, like knitting, or having a life. 
 I've always been part of fandom - fandomS, actually, so many! And so many more to come, I'm sure! So I could identify a lot with what was going on in this book. I've read reviews where the main character is considered creepy and unhealthy - maybe she is, but she represents a pretty big chunk of the world's population. So, what I'm saying is: this book is not for everyone. 
 So, Cather (yes, that's her name - more on that later) is a BNF (big name fan) - she writes the most popular Simon Snow fanfic: tens of thousands of fans obsessively check for updates of her slash fanfic. And Cath is pretty happy with that, she likes that her life, her friends, are on the internet. She matters, she makes thousands of people happy or sad with each chapter she posts. 
 But now Cath and her twin sister Wren are going away to college, and Wren doesn't even want to be roommates with Cath, she thinks they should have their own separate lives. 
 Cath doesn't know how to cope, she's not good with this real life stuff. I think there will be a tendency to dismiss Cath's issues, but she seems to genuinely suffer from social anxiety and that is no joke. Add to that the fact that they're leaving their bipolar dad all by his lonesome, and he tends to do poorly without them, and Cath is a nervous wreck. 
 Reagan, her roommate is barely in their room, so at least she has that, but her rommate's boyfriend, Levi, is ALWAYS there! And what's his deal?! Why is he always so nice? Why does he smile so much? Why does he try to be friends with everyone? Isn't that exhausting? 
 All this, plus classes which turn out to be disappointing have Cath wanting to retreat from this so-called real life into her safe secluded fantasy world, where she makes the rules and everything makes sense. 
 Personally, though I identify with Cath, for me the best thing about this book wasn't all the fandom stuff, nor the cool references to fan culture, or even the romance. It was Cath's family that did it for me. 
 There's the dad, who has mental health issues, but he really tries so hard and he does the best he can and he really, really loves his girls and the reader can't help loving him and worrying about him, as well. 
 Cath's mother left on September 11 (yes, that September 11), when both Cath and her sister Wren were 8 years old. Cath and Wren, get it? Catherine? It's not cute. Their mother didn't want a baby, let alone two, so when she found out she was having twins she couldn't even be bothered with coming up with another name: she just split the one she had in mind in two. 
 And now Cath's mother wants another chance. Now that they learned to go on without her, now that they don't need her anymore - now she wants to try and be a mum - only not really, because she prefers to be called Laura, and not be there if she is actually needed. And Cath, with all the moving away to college + classes + roommate + new friends + estranged twin + cute boys! + the fandom demanding their next chapter, is understandably not up for that kind of drama. Trouble is, Wren is up to getting back with their mum. 
 The whole family dynamics was so, so strongly written, seriously powerful stuff - I cried, okay, this pic may as well be about me: 
 Only I don't like to use the C-word, it's just that my eyes get really sweaty, or I have to water my chin - I do not actually leak weakness water from my face holes. 
 But as I was saying, the whole family thing? Even if you're not part of any fandom, even if you don't even know what fandom is, the way Rowel wrote Cath's family is worth reading the book. 
 Also, Levi! Hurray for non-creepy, non-abusive, polite, genuinely nice love interests! They're so rare (despite Peeta's success!) - you may as well go ahead and read it just for the treat of not going through a book muttering, "Girl, you need to call the cops, I'm serious, girl. I mean, he'll probably still kill you and wear your skin as a coat, but at least the police will have a solid lead." 
 So go read it, fangirls, fanboys and... normal people, I guess.
Loved this one just as much as the first one. Can't wait to read the next book in the series.

She is inspired by her faith to use those powers for good, first by saving a rude classmate from drowning, and later stopping an armed robbery. In this volume, we are introduced to her nemesis, the Inventor. Most of the story is watching as Kamala slowly figures out who she is and how she can use her powers, all while still living under her strict parents roof and going to high school.

3.5 stars 
 Ugh I've been thinking about this book ever since I finished it. There were moments when I was really invested in the story, eager to know what was going to happen next. And then there were other moments when I was just... bored I guess? 
 It took me a lot of time to get into the story, due to a lot of world building, which is really rich and interesting when you get used to it though. But at first it just made the book really slow; plus I had trouble to connect with the main character. I started to wonder when and if I was ever going to enjoy this novel. 
 BUT after a hundred pages or so, finally it got better! There were new characters and awesome action scenes, I was shocked sometimes, but it was so addicting that I read the last hundred pages in one setting. All the characters introduced were well developed (even though I did have difficulties to remember who was who at first) and I really enjoyed the last part of the book. 
 Overall I liked it, and I'm really excited to see how things are going to evolve now. I already have the sequel, so I'll try to read it as soon as I can!

 This started strong, but lost me around page 300. I really began to feel like the characters were all one person, rather than individuals. I got sick of the self-indulgent rantings of each character and the bleak outlook of America based on a hyper liberal view point. 
 I found the characters to be devoid of real human emotion. If you believe that everyone goes around hating the masses and fantasizing about "f%*$ing" all day long, then sure, Freedom is packed with raw emotion! And, if you do those things, you must have a very high IQ, indeed! 
 The dialogue was done badly. Anytime a character laughed, it reminded me of bad texting or Facebook, "Ha, ha, ha!" Sometimes Franzen mixes it up and just writes, "Ha!" Oh, good job, Franzen! You wouldn't want to work on character development or anything like that! Oh, wait, Lalitha really likes to say, "Be that as it may". Of course, you pointed that out via Walter, so then I was watching for it. How tricky of you?! GAG! 
 The female characters are nearly worthless. Apparently, women are full of "female bullsh*it", but because we are so packed with FB, he only takes the time to make Patty a complete mess. Lalitha is very one dimensional, Connie is psychotic, and Jonathan's sister, is an evil slut in comparison to the male characters who are heroic and authentic. Even when the male characters have ulterior motives, we are made to believe that their motives are somehow better and more deserving than their female counterparts. 
 I had grown to like Walter's character until the move to DC where he immediately fell for Lalitha, who I found arrogant. We as readers are asked to believe that because Walter and Patty are having difficulties that he is suddenly fantasizing about Lalitha all day long? Somehow it's believable that a character like Walter wouldn't ask his assistant to find new housing when he is so very tempted by her? Come on! Patty is apparently so racked with guilt for sleeping with Richard four years prior that she remains married and living with Lalitha upstairs for years while Walter salivates over her? I found it incredibly unbelievable that Walter would tolerate having a temptation so near and that Patty wouldn't get over her guilt and just leave Walter and Lalitha to it. 
 Again and again we're reassured as readers that the characters are "intelligent". If by intelligent you mean lying, selfish, and over-educated, then yes, by all means, they are intelligent. 
 Overall, I am too moderate to fall under Freedom's leftist spell. I don't think that the New York Times is the end-all-be-all of American culture. I don't care for art films, bad garage bands, or folks who refer to their parents by their first names. It simply became too much to swallow without question.

Quite The Novel Idea ~ Words from the Clouds 
 I'm honestly not quite sure where to start with this one. I liked it. No... I more than liked it. But I also didn't LOVE it. It's somewhere in that icky grey area between like and love that makes books in said area really hard to rate and review. Overall I really liked it a lot. But I wanted to love it. And I just didn't. 
 I really loved the writing. It pulled me in immediately and though it had potential to get boring, it never did. The voice was on point and it kept my attention throughout and made the book very hard to put down. On top of that it was also funny, mostly becuase of the MC's personality, which I'll get to in a bit. But I love books that can make me laugh. So points for that. I also loved the story itself and how it could be quirky and silly one second and then really heartfelt and sweet the next. There were even a few times where it just straight-up hit me in the feels, just because it was so relatable to me in that moment. And I love stories like that. 
 But like always, characters are the most important part of a story for me. And the characters in this book did not disappoint. I loved them all because they were real and flawed and they made mistakes and they weren't perfect and none of them were stereotypes. I loved them all, even the ones I didn't like at first. Like the hippies that pull up to Hawthorn's house. (Her mom is a hippie by the way. Yeah. You probably guessed that since she named her daughter Hawthorn...) I didn't like them at first but they grew on me like they did for Hawthorn. Especially Sundog. I also liked Hawthorn's family, especially her brother Rushford. I loved the bond that they had. I also liked his friend Connor and I shipped him so hard with Hawthorn. But more on that later. 
 And of course I have to talk about our main character Hawthorn. She's such a unique character. She's weird and quirky and funny and relatable and I just loved her. I love that when a popular girl in her town goes missing, her first theory is that she's a werewolf and she just sticks with it. She totally runs with it and goes to look for the girl that turned into a werewolf. Because why not? And I related to her more than I thought I would because of how she was treated at school. I really felt for her. She felt real and she's far from perfect and she makes mistakes but she also grew so much throughout the book. And I just loved her. 
 But here comes the part where I tell you why I ended up liking this book a lot instead of loving it to pieces. First, I wasn't a big fan of Hawthorn's friend Emily. I thought she wasn't a very good friend and honestly Hawthorn deserves better. I'm also not a big fan of Enzo, which is problematic because he's the love interest. I just never really felt it. It didn't feel right to me at any point. Don't get me wrong, I liked Enzo's friendship with Hawthorn, but I just didn't get the romance. I really shipped her more with Connor. Right from the start. And I just wanted Hawthorn to ditch Enzo and go be adorably in love with Connor. But she did not. Which made me sad. I also kind of hoped there'd be more of a focus on the mystery aspect of the story? But there wasn't? That's probably just my expectations being slightly misguided though. So don't let that stop you from reading this book at all. 
 Overall, THE HUNDRED LIES OF LIZZIE LOVETT was heartfelt, sweet, quirky, funny, touching and very engaging. I do recommend it for fans of YA Contemporary. Especially if you like a contemporary with a mystery aspect. Also if you're into hippies. Then read this too. Because the flower-power is strong in this one. Now go forth and read this at your earliest convenience.

Three stories woven with common themes: Portugal, chimpanzees, grief, death, and a physical journey. 
 * 
 This book was a slow meditation - and looking at the reviews, I can see that many people just couldn't get past the plodding of the first story. Perhaps it was easier with the audiobook format. Following Tomas on his journey was a struggle - but that was the point. The second story with Dr. Eusebio took a fantastical bent, and included probably one of the most interesting philosophical soliloquies I've ever read, delivered by the doctor's wife, Maria, drawing distinct parallels between Jesus and the writing of Agatha Christie. The third story, truly a love story, was beautifully done and plucked my heartstrings. I wanted to take a roadtrip with this wonderful little chimp, Odo. 
 Beautifully done, with many thoughtful pieces throughout - this one will stay with me for a long while.

Let me start by saying what a fan I am of Courtney Milan. Just about any time I pick up something of hers, I feel like it's a given I am going to love it. Unfortunately, this book proved the exception to the rule. 
 This is the third book in the Brothers Sinister series and it focuses on Sebastian and Violet. You may remember Sebastian from the previous books as the controversial scientist who had society aghast with his lectures on reproduction and inherited traits. What we learn here is that none of those ideas actually belonged to him. In fact, all the theories came from Violet. Sebastian agreed to present them because no one would take the ideas seriously from a woman. 
 All the lies are wearing on Sebastian, however. And as the book begins, he has reached his breaking point. Despite the fact he has been in love with Violet all of his life, he ends their arrangement, refusing to keep up the charade any longer. He also decides to stop hiding his feelings for his long-time best friend. 
 I was good with the premise and I liked Sebastian fairly well. He is an affable guy whose charm has always hidden a sharp mind. He enjoys women, but he is no heartbreaker. He is kind and giving and has always held his heart aside for Violet. I liked his earnestness and devotion. Even more, I appreciated his patience and acceptance of Violet -and even his jerk of a brother. 
 Violet is where the story lost me. She has been through a lot, no doubt. I won't spoil the particulars of it, but I will concede the point. However, her coping mechanisms got in the way of any ability I had to relate to her. I couldn't stand how she belabored her unlovableness; how she thought so low of herself; how she pushed everyone away; how she treated Sebastian. Granted, these things improve as the story progresses, but frankly, I just didn't like her. I wasn't sure why Sebastian loved her so. Yes, she is brilliant, but she has been a shell of herself for years, and not even an outwardly sympathetic one. Perhaps other readers will be able see past this to her wounded soul, but until nearly the very end, I just didn't see how she was good enough for all he put up with. 
 It wasn't all bad. Like I said, I liked the hero and was pleasantly surprised in liking Violet's mother. I liked the shout out to the pioneering women of discovery who never got their just desserts; and that Courtney Milan didn't try to make a child for Violet the happy ending. But it was hard to love a romance where I didn't like the heroine. 
 Rating: B-/C+ 
 *ARC provided by author for review

Y'know, between Decoder Ring Theatre's Flying Squirrel and now Squirrel Girl, I'm starting to think there's some magical appeal to squirrel-themed superheroes. Some wacky, butt-kicking magical appeal. 
 Volume 1 of Unbeatable Squirrel Girl is a beautiful, beautiful romp of silliness from beginning to end. Ryan North's writing is snappy, quick witted, and very frequently ridiculous, and the art is purposefully cartoony in the best way possible. I think Erica Henderson might possibly be the only person capable of drawing facial expressions to match this wonderful nonsense. 
 And Squirrel Girl herself! Doreen Green is such a great addition to the lady superheroes in the modern forefront, precisely BECAUSE she's so ridiculous. Let's face it, female characters so often have to be the "straight man" of a group - in a genre that so often skews towards drama, ladyfolk don't generally get to be the designated comedic relief. But Squirrel Girl gets to be goofy and fun, largely because there are other female characters (namely her amazing roommate Nicole) who aren't as goofy. WE ALL WIN! 
 So yeah. Guys. Are you still not reading Squirrel Girl? Why are you not reading Squirrel Girl? You should be doing that RIGHT NOW.

 This Raging Light proves that the main character doesn't have to be an assassin, a vigilante, nor a queen to be badass. 
 Lucille's dad was admitted to a mental facility when she was younger, and ever since then her mother has never been the same. Now, even her mom is gone. On top of that, she has a baby sister to take care of, bills to pay, a best friend to worry about, and worse of all, a boy who has a girlfriend to fall in love with. 
 I gotta tell you, I felt like the tone and the way that this book was written felt different for me. It took me a while to get used to it, but once I did it didn't take me long to fall in love with the story. I can't ever imagine being put into Lucille's shoes, but I must tell you that she is the most badass main character I've read. 
 Like what Fred said, Lucille is someone who jumps and takes actions; who doesn't wait for things to happen. She's strong and brave at the same time, but she's also vulnerable because after all, she's just human. I'm glad that she learned to let others helped her in the novel, and that's one more thing that made her stronger. 
 I loved how this book was also about hidden angels. I loved the way that things progressed - how the characters grew as time passed. Even Wren, as little as 10, really stepped up. I loved how honest to book is, and how it made me feel. 
 I didn't like how things ended though. (view spoiler)[I want to know what happened to her mom, and what happens to her dad later on. Who will take care of them. What happened with Digby and Elain? (hide spoiler)] I felt like there were just to many things left unexplained. Maybe the author meant for it to be that way, but I definitely wasn't satisfied by it. 
 Still, I recommend this book. This Raging Light is definitely an amazing book about a teen who had to grow up too soon. A must-read.

I hadn't re-read this book in a while, and I'd forgotten just how wonderful it is. It's definitely one of my favorite Austen novels. Anne Elliot is a quieter but tremendously appealing heroine; we can empathize with her and feel what she feels. She is a sensitive person who experiences a great deal of emotion, both painful and pleasurable, yet is called upon to conceal most of it. I think there is a heightened sense of characters' feeling and emotions in general in Persuasion, compared to Austen's other novels. There are also much clearer and detailed physical descriptions of people and places, though I don't think Austen ever goes so far as to tell us what color hair someone has! 
 Another thing that particularly struck me on this reading is that Persuasion seems to contain a much larger number of happy and pleasant people--the Crofts, the Harvilles, the Musgroves, Mrs. Smith. The Crofts are some of the most charming characters in all of Austen, and probably the nicest example of a happy married couple in all her books. Even Lady Russell, though she can be regarded as an antagonist for the role her advice has played in Anne's initial unhappiness, is depicted as a woman of sense and kindness, who in spite of her shortcomings is still a true friend to Anne, and is willing to admit her misjudgment of both Captain Wentworth and Mr. Elliot.

I don't read many classics because i find them difficult to get into and boring-however there are exceptions to every rule and i can't express how much i love this one. Steinbeck's writing is incredible-his characters are so well developed that they practically jump off the pages. This novella proves a book doesn't have to be several hundred pages long to have substance and emotional impact. Truly a timeless, unforgettable and haunting tale. It doesn't matter how familiar you are with this story-it will still punch you in the heart every single time. Highly recommended.

Well, where to begin. I started this book this morning and while work did detract me from it momentarily, I was immediately glued to until it's finished afterwards. (I was actually going to make a lame pun about ripping right through this novel - haha. I do laugh at my own terrible jokes) 
 I would say this was more of a 4.5 but I definitely didn't want to drop it down to four stars. I was looking for a good book about Jack-the-Ripper(as his story has intrigued me lately and I seem to run into it everywhere so I took it as a sign) with good detective-work and a good ending. I can definitely say I got what I wanted. 
 The first chapter drew me in immediately (I remember actually saying "Oho~!" out loud) as it was in the perspective of Jack-the-Ripper. While I was terribly disappointed that this was the only chapter in his perspective, I can't say I was surprised either. 
 The rest of the story is told from the perspective of the 14-year old Carver Young. Carver himself is quite likable, though that's not to say some of his actions or stubborn-ness were grating sometimes. Around then I would remind myself he was 14 and was entitled to act that way. I also think it shows a lot about the author to keep his characteristics and actions (as well as limits) believable to his age. Part of me really did wish Carver's character was older but I enjoyed it nonetheless. Part of me also wished this took place in London but you can't have everything. I also enjoyed watching Carver grow and stand on his own. 
 I liked the other characters as well, they were complex and , Delia was a strong female character who kept Carver grounded. Hawking was an eccentric and powerful character. I enjoyed how he made Carver work for himself instead of leading him to the answers. Finn was also deeper and instrumental to Carver's growth. The adults were well written and all the different personalities made for an interesting read. Of course the Ripper made for a fine villain and was also incredibly complex. Even while writing this review I still think of the different facets of his character all that he truly did. 
 Ripper was a very smooth read and for me, a page-turner. Some reviews state how long the novel was but I didn't feel that it dragged on at all. Plus I honestly like a long book (even if I still finish it in a matter of hours). I didn't feel as if there was a large overabundance of unnecessary information and all the loose ends tied up quite nicely. I absolutely adored the ending and the twist was well thought out and executed admirably. There were definitely some hints of humor (view spoiler)[I certainly laughed when Finn stated that Roosevelt should run for President (hide spoiler)] but was overall a serious novel. 
 I came away from Ripper thinking many things and all of them good. I believe the strongest theme that came across to me was that you cannot expect to be handed whatever you want, you must work for it yourself. Second would be that the result is not what is as important, but the journey itself. What you learned, how it affected you and how it brought to that result is farm more important. 
 I definitely found Ripper to be a delightful take on Jack-the-Ripper's story.

 The castle and the girl-fights are hilarious to read, Maxon seems like a doll and the setting is fairy-tale-like.

 Overall, I'd say this trilogy was great. I hated and loved each character. The concept was very interesting. The different writing styles to convey emotions and things was awesome. The plot twists kept me guessing each time but I never quite fully figured them out. The only thing that slightly irked me was the being so in love after only three months at the age of 16. It was like a Romeo & Juliet kind of deal. I mean, I guess at that age you might feel like you're that much in love but it's not quite...I don't know, I'm rambling!

He was an instrument on Alex's happy ending with Sutton so I have a bit of an interest on who might catch this playboy's heart. Also it doesn't hurt that "playboy fell hard and added faithful on his dictionary" is one of my favorite trope, lol. 
 The insta-love or insta-attraction isn't much an okay thing for me but still cute. I didn't like that the somewhat-twist smacked my face on the early part of the book. Too early but I guess it was supposed to be that way or I'll be hating the female lead.
