This book was... absolutely terrible. I've heard such good things about this series, about how addictive and fun it is, and how great the characters and the world are. I feel like I must have read a different book than everyone else, because this book was so fucking boring. It took me forever to read, I hated the characters, and the world was so uninteresting and weird that I barely managed to finish this book. 
 To start, Mac was one of the most annoying and boring main characters I've read about in a long time. At the beginning of the book, she finds out her sister has been murdered while studying abroad in Ireland. The police investigation into her sister's murder goes nowhere, so Mac decides that she will go to Ireland herself to force the police to reopen her sister's case. The police refuse, so she decides to investigate on her own, hoping to discover evidence that will force the police to reconsider. From that point on Mac makes a series of weird and questionable decisions that lead her to discover the world of the fae and her role in it. The book is narrated by Mac of the future, recounting the events of her life, so there were a lot of instances where she would add comments that made her sound very juvenile and made the writing seem very choppy. Mac is characterized as being a girly-girl who likes fashion and the color pink, and she is also able to hold her own in a fight. I really appreciate the message that girls can be badass and also like traditionally girly things, but I thought the author tried way too hard to get that message across. Mac went off on long tangents in nearly every chapter to describe her nail polish color or her outfit, which got boring after the second time it happened, and every time after that I wanted to rip my hair out. I could not possibly give less of a fuck what shade of pink her nails were that day. 
 Another thing that drove me absolutely insane about Mac was how against cursing she was. On multiple occasions, she uses "petunia" instead of "ass," and to be completely fucking honest, it hurt my eyes. This book is basically erotica in some places, and the fact that Mac was so against cursing was just laughable. And annoying. Just use the real fucking word, holy shit! 
 Then we have Barrons. The entire point of his character was to be Mac's brooding and sexy, while also extremely douche-y, mentor to the world of the fae. He was such a one dimensional character that I forgot he existed a lot of the time he wasn't around, which is saying something because he and Mac were basically the only relevant characters in the entire book. He is characterized as being very mysterious, but literally the only reason we didn't know anything about him was that Mac NEVER ASKED HIM A SINGLE QUESTION ABOUT WHO OR WHAT HE WAS. Like, what the fuck. The only questions Mac ever asks him about his background are where he is from and whether or not the has any siblings. 
 And, of course, because we also need a pointless fae character to keep things interesting, we have V'lane, or whatever the fuck his stupid name is. I spent most of this book referring to him as Vlad in my head because me brain literally refused to remember a name that stupid. V'lane is a death-by-sex fae. Yes, you read that right. His fae power is making women want to have sex with him so badly that they die. They literally die. I can't with this book. 
 Every time Mac meets V'lane, she takes all of her clothes off in the middle of the street. Without realizing what she's doing. Seriously. 
 Not only were the characters all flaming piles of human garbage, the plot and world building were horrendous as well. Barrons and Mac's journal were used as plot devices to dump definition after useless definition on the reader in the most boring possible terms, with future Mac jumping in to add even more information that I didn't care about. The writing was choppy and the narration style did not work for me at all. I spent half this book wishing it was over and the other half rolling my eyes at how ridiculous everything was. Needless to say, I will not be continuing this series.

Clay meets the unusual requirements and he becomes the night shift. The customers at Mr. Penumbra's are unusual and Clay realizes that there is more to the bookstore than meets the eye.

In a supply closet at work. Of course that's not weird!) It's also interesting that it's about the power of both books and technology and how the two can be combined, something I think people don't realize is possible. (I've been told since I entered the library field that "libraries are dying" and "we have computers, who needs books" and "it's all electronic now" and yet I am still a librarian employed in a library.) One thing that bothered me, though, was that the first person narrator would think things, and then other characters would answer as though he had spoken, but the thought was never in quotation marks, indicating it had never been spoken out loud. It happened several times. 
 Three and a half stars, but I will round up because I kept thinking about it after I read it and I liked the characters to much.

The moment I started reading The Maze Runner, I was instantly beguiled. The beginning sparked curiosity and everything was already a mystery; how and why the Gladers got into the maze, how and why none of them remembers anything except for their names, who was in charge and what was the reason behind it, just everything was a mystery. I like how the questions are being answered gradually as you go further along the book. Every revelation is shocking and it was fun unraveling the mysteries along with the characters. I found the book so clever it quickly became one of my favorites. 
 I liked everything about the brilliant plot, I liked the characters especially Newt. And Thomas, too. I usually don't like main characters because oftentimes, their POVs are infuriating af. But Thomas must be one of the few main characters out there that didn't annoy the heck out of me. Thomas is smart, he isn't whiny and idiotic, he's very brave and he knows what to do most of the time so most Gladers rely on him (mad leadership skills y'all). He became useful for the Gladers, making much more progress in solving the maze than they had for years. Furthermore, our main character appears to be one of the biggest mysteries of the book, which makes him much more interesting. 
 The Maze Runner was an astounding and thrilling adventure. There are a lot more questions unanswered, and it will surely make you crave for more. Highly recommended to readers who love the dystopian genre and a book with detailed plot elements and fewer plotholes. There are slangs contained in the book though, some might be a little hard to grasp.

 Riddle me this: what can cause a woman to lose twenty years of her life every time she falls asleep? According to S. J. Watson, brain damage from a tragic accident. 
 I'm no scientist. When I was five I really wanted to be Sally Ride until I discovered knowledge of science was a big part of her job. So to be fair, I really know next to nothing about the intricacies of the human brain. But with a traumatic head injury, can you lose your memories every time you sleep? 
 That's the premise behind Watson's psychological thriller Before I Go to Sleep. Twenty-five years ago Christine was in a tragic accident. Ever since, when she wakes up from sleep she thinks she's still in her mid-twenties. 
 On a typical day, Christine wakes up next to her husband whom she does not know. Thinking she had a dirty one-night stand, she slinks into the adjoining bathroom only to look in the mirror and see a much older woman. When her husband wakes he fills her in on her accident, memory loss, and marriage to him. He heads to work while she lingers around the house, not recognizing a thing. 
 Until one day when Christine gets a phone call. A doctor calls to tell her he's been working with her for a few weeks and she has been recording lost memories in a journal. The rest of the book is comprised of Christine's journal full of pieces of memories, confusion, and her husband's lies. 
 Before I Go to Sleep is definitely a psychological thriller, but it's not an edge-of-your-seat kind of thriller. This doesn't mean it's not interesting. I turned into this amnesiac woman, confused and scared with what I was reading, wondering why my husband would withhold things from me. But this is definitely a mild thriller, not one where I ignored phone calls and turned off the latest episode of "Eureka" just so I could keep reading. 
 The part of this book that goes downhill is the ending. I won't give it away, though you will easily be able to figure it out on your own. Early on I pieced it together, but I was hoping my instincts were wrong. I wanted it to be more complicated. More interesting. More. . . something. But it wasn't. It is the ending you imagine and it's such a let down. 
 And the speech in the end? Come on. It's like when you watch an episode of "Monk" and you wonder why the killer confesses in the end when the stuff Monk says has no physical evidence. Is it a guilty conscious? Is it Monk's hypnotizing curly hair? Whatever it may be, the same type of ending happens here and I turned into a big ball of snark. The ending is just so stupid and nowhere near as interesting as the rest of the book. I wanted to be amazed in the end, but what I got was a Lifetime Movie spectacular. Good start, crappy ending.

Like what's up with werewolves and Captain Niall? (Maybe she did, but I finished the book at 3 am in the morning, so forgive me if I'm wrong.) 
 The characters were engaging. Especially Sophronia. She was so amusing and headstrong, and not at all ladylike with her boyish pursuits and wit. She's the kind of heroine I enjoy reading about in stories. I thought Dimity was a nice contrast, all girlish charm. But there's intelligence in that head of hers, and I can't wait for the next adventure. And Sidheag. She's a warrior, that girl. This trio just screams trouble. Together with Vieve and Soap, and I can practically hear the emergency alarms going off. 
 Okay, what I thought could be better was the plot. I thought it was lacking in substance. I don't think it lived up to the standards presented by these amazing characters. I mean, Carriger has me reading about these awesome girls with the skills to match their personalities, and then all she had them doing is looking for a prototype. Granted, it is the first book and there were somethings to explain about the school and so forth, but I kind of expected something MORE to happen. 
 Not to say that it was a bad plot. No, not at all. I especially liked the part with the cheese pie. I thought that was genius. Sophronia really sees opportunities after all. I don't think any of the other girls could have thought of something so clever. 
 In conclusion, I would say this was a worthwhile book. Great characters, good plot, interesting concepts. Sign me up for the next one.

Shutter Island is off the coast of Massachusetts, housing an asylum for the criminally insane. As a nasty summer storm brews up, U.S. Marshals Teddy Daniels and Chuck Aule cross over to the island to search for an escaped inmate. But Teddy knows that things are not as they seem on Shutter Island. 
 Ho-lee crap. It's been a while since a book has messed with my head this much. Just as I thought I knew what was going on, a new revelation would come along and knock all my theories out from under me. It all ultimately made sense and brought me deeper into this world, and I have to say that I loved it. I didn't really know what was going on until the very last few pages, and I find that even after I finished it, I'm sitting here thinking, "Well, maybe it still really wasn't what it seemed..." You'll see. I bet almost everyone is surprised by this ending. 
 The twists and turns were the big draw of this book for me, but I loved Lehane's style. This is the first book I've read of his, but it won't be my last. Shutter Island is set in 1954, and I love the way these marshals speak to each other and so quickly establish common ground through The War. Their speech, their mannerisms, it all fit together to make them feel like real people. 
 If I say anymore, I'll give something away, so I'll leave it at that. I highly, highly recommend this if you like your thrillers gritty and unpredictable.

In my mind, John Green did an excellent job in writing The Fault in Our Stars. This is the first book of his that I have read, but I am not unfamiliar with his brilliance, thanks to having heard much about him from friends as well as seeing a lot of quotes from his vlogs and books on various social networking sites. 
 Hazel Grace and Augustus are such likable characters. Granted, since they are both fighting or surviving having had cancer, it can be foreseen that there will be a sad ending to the book, but I did not expect the ending. Unlike many other novels about cancer, this features a protagonist with cancer - and, perhaps more surprisingly, the story is told in first person. Most other novels that I have read are not written in first person unless it is from the perspective of a family member or friend of someone who has cancer. 
 Hazel and Augustus, as well as the other people in the novel are all likable. There are no "bad guys" in this book, aside from cancer itself. The story flowed well, and I enjoyed the surprises that each twist in the road revealed. I would highly recommend this book to pretty much anyone, especially those who have a heart for teens, since John Green certainly cares about teens - this comes through in his novel, and also in the epilogue about Esther Grace, the girl who inspired the novel.

I know that not all YA needs to be edgy or told in first person present, but I just couldn't shake the feeling.) 
 The story begins in a small village as young Iolanthe is practicing her skills as an elemental mage. Prince Titus shows up and -- OMG!-- realizes she is the person he's been looking for, the one who can defeat the evil Bane. I was excited about this Harry Potter-ish idea, but then poor Iolanthe spends most of the rest of the book in hiding. I wished that she'd been given more exciting stuff to do than (view spoiler)[ disguise herself as a boy. That part of the book was amusing, and if you like those kind of breast-binding romance novel plots you'll love this, but I didn't find that it served much purpose to the story as a whole. (hide spoiler)] 
 The romance had its charming points, but I wished that the characters' feelings hadn't always been spelled out for me so explicitly. That darned omniscient voice was always telling me stuff like: "she never wanted to feel sympathy for him. But she did." Or: "She turned around ... willing herself to feel no sympathy for him. And not succeeding." Or: "the sharp feeling in his heart was not concern but a stab of envy." 
 The story world in The Burning Sky is one in which magical people and events exist alongside a non-magical world, like in Harry Potter. The non-magical part of the world was set in the Victorian Age, so the book had a historical fiction + fantasy vibe that I enjoyed. But I wished that the connection between the magical world and the human world had been more clearly explained. On the plus side, there were some scenes that were really well-done and memorable -- in particular, one in which Iolanthe is transformed while Titus is in danger. 
 Overall, I did find this an engaging read with a slightly draggy middle part. But I prefer my YA fantasy a little darker and more complex. Though this book wasn't a perfect fit for me, I can also see that a lot of people have really loved it, so if you're a fan of fantasy you should definitely give it a try!

 Okay time to get serious. Easy was an incredible, heart-pounding, intense romance book that I absolutely adored! I don't usually read the Acknowledgements in books. If I love the book, sometimes I do, and that was the case with Easy. I'd like to share one part because I thought it was amazing and really shows how much emotion went into the book: 
 I couldn't have written Easy without the help of my husband, Paul. The creation of good fiction begins with raw, honest emotions--whether the author is penning a story about a mouse who wants dessert, or a sprawling epic of Tsarist Russia. The subjects touched on in Easy come with an even deeper obligation to remain true to those emotions. Paul encouraged me constantly to fearlessly portray my love of hidden connections, and my belief that our close relationships with family, friends and lovers--any and all of those, if we're lucky--are capable of healing the trauma all of us experience in our lives. 
 Tammara Webber, author of Easy 
 Isn't that awesome? That's what I love about Easy. Tammara Webber put her heart and soul into this book and it really, really shows. This book is about love, rejection, loss, fear, trauma, and daring to fall in love again. It is so empowering in so many different ways. And Easy totally has me wanting to take some self-defense classes! 
 It was so easy to love all the characters in this book.  I made the mistake of starting this book later in the evening.. then I was so hooked that I was reading through the night. Soon it was 3:30am and it took every ounce of will power I had to put the book down and finally go to sleep! 
 Jacqueline and Lucas have such incredible chemistry! It's mouthwatering.. it's HOT! Girls, it is FREAKIN' HOT! This is a new adult book so things do get a little hot and heavy.. and it's awesome. But it's not all just sexy lust. Lucas and Jacqueline had a really sweet relationship. I love the phase where Jacqueline isn't sure if Lucas likes her. The "not knowing" is so much fun! And since Jacqueline has a crazy rapist guy stalking her, Lucas really gets to play the "knight in shining armour" role and he gets to rescue her a few times. Swoon! 
 Tammara, you are a freakin' mastermind genius! What I wouldn't give to read Easy from Lucas's point of view!

Excerpt from my full review at seattlebooks.tumblr.com: 
 Over turmeric curry and sauteed broccoli the other day, my friend told me about this great "new-old" film she'd seen called Me and You and Everyone We Know. It won a Sundance award for Best Vision or something, and Roger Ebert loved it, and the trailer made it difficult to pin down a plot or even a general feel, but what I liked was that it was a sort of one-woman project, written, directed, and featuring Miranda July. 
 Four days later, I stood in City Lights Books and picked up this short story collection without realizing the connection between the two. From the get-go, July's character development gripped me completely. Oftentimes characters are the least arresting part of literature (in my personal experience), taking a backseat to an intricate plot twist or phenomenal use of metaphors. 
 Here, July introduced me to women deeply flawed and terribly funny in an off-putting way. I don't know that, had these been real women, I would be able to stand being in the same room with them for more than an hour. At various intervals, they are falling asleep on the shoulders of unconscious men and lusting for underage students and teaching 80-year-olds how to swim across vast expanses of carpet. 
 This could very easily have been an unlikeable book, full of unlikeable people who do inexplicably awful things to each other. But July redeems her characters, baring their thoughts and neuroses in a way that makes them almost relatable and undeniably fascinating.

3.5 stars... Augh, give or take 1 star. 
 I'm torn in many directions on this one... in so many ways it was an excellent sci-fi novel; realistic ideas about long-term space travel, light-speed travel considerations, and 'island' biodiversity among others... sometimes delivered pedantically and sometimes in fascinating, life-or-death impact bottomline-ing. 
 The narrative conceit (the ship is creating a narrative, having never done so before and coming into something akin to consciousness as it/they does so) was either brilliant or terrible, depending on my mood and how one or another sentence struck me. Stilted info-dumping can be excused because it's a computer, it's trying to figure out what matters and what doesn't with a HUGE amount of data to sift through. On the other hand, how many times do we need the ship to tell us that all metaphor fails to tell the truth (we get it author; writing is hard!)? And as the narrative starts pinballing drunkenly around in the final chapters, we're to excuse the ship because this is the result of a million million decisions made of what to include, what word to use, what to omit over the course of decades... and too it reflects the physical actions of the ship in that moment/decade. 
 I loved the characters, Freya, her father, her mother Devi whom ship loves, her friends and various pillars of the community. The society is extremely well drawn in a sort of communal leadership performed via 'talking circles' as in tribal populations which works well until there is a crisis other than maintaining status quo through space. 
 But my biggest appreciation and complaint go to the observations about humans/humanity. When the ship is speaking, it makes sometimes brilliant observations. When ship is repeating inhabitants conversations about humanity, they do the same. However these are nearly always sweeping generalizations. And that is the problem. 
 "Why?" she asks Badim. "Why do they hate us so?" 
 He shrugs. He too is troubled. "People have ideas. They live in their ideas, do you understand? And those ideas, whatever they happen to be, make all the difference." 
 "But there's more than ideas," she protests. "This world." She gestures at the fading sunset. "It's not just our ideas." 
 "For some people it is. They don't have anything else, maybe, so they give everything they have to ideas." 
 She shakes her head, still upset. "I would hate that. I would hate to be that way." Underneath it all there is a disdain for these unenlightened humans that the author obviously shares. Ship's observations tell us all about Robinson's personal philosophy which seems to be something along the lines of 'if everyone would just chill out and let be, we'd be cool.' A lovely thought for the surfer high on pot, but when applied to complex situations like the post WWII Nuremburg trials or post apartheid South African reconciliations - which he directly refers to - they are demeaning and childishly oversimplifying the horror, pain and monumental effort to change hearts and minds that is necessitated in such cases. I know nothing of Robinson's personal history, but something tells me if he lost a child to genocidal violence or hate crimes or even the stupidity of a drunk driver, he would get a little mad. And just going surfing might not really do it. 
 And ship, as a seemingly enlightened entity by the end, should have realized as much. The only times progress in the tale occurred during strife were when characters stopped to listen and understand other's experiences rather than broadly generalizing or oversimplifying other's opinions which causes 'us-them' dynamics. The content is there for the author to see, so apparently he realizes it at some level. Why then does he continue to condescendingly drop sweeping generalizations about people and their motivations on us? or to blame those same people for holding onto past hurts and atrocities? I cannot fathom it. 
 So, overall I liked the tale, I even liked the ending, and I loved Freya. The story is sticking with me a week later. But so is the nagging bother about the author's inconsistencies between his message and true empathy for humanity.

Humanity has begun to colonize a new planet... and already there's a fight over it. When the people who took off early and landed there try to delay the landing of the corporation the government has allowed to settle the planet, there are deaths... which leads to a series of escalations on both sides that threatens to turn into full out war. James Holden and his crew are sent out to be mediators, but things start to go from bad to worse, because not only is there an alien ecology that nobody completely understands yet, there's also the relics of an alien race that seem to be waking up and putting everyone in danger. 
 The Expanse books have begun to have enough similarity to each other that it's really most effective to discuss them in terms of how they compare to the others. By now, the basics are pretty much the same, a crew of likable characters mostly seen through the eyes of Holden and a guest cast of new viewpoint characters, on some kind of adventure that may impact the future of all humanity. If you like them already, you'll probably be reading this, if not, you won't, so all that's left to say is if it's better or worse than the others. 
 Mostly, I think it's better. I still think that the second book might be the best of the lot, but if so, it's only by a narrow margin, because I liked this one a good deal more than the last or the first. The plot kept me guessing and impressively managed to raise the stakes as things kept going from bad to worse without seeming ridiculous about it. The viewpoint characters were mostly appealing (although a couple of times you wanted to smack some of them for following the instructions of mean-spirited short-sighted thugs instead of thinking for themselves), and there really is some cool sci-fi work being done about the potential clash of ecosystems and how people might be hurt by them even when traditional predator/prey relationships, or even viruses, aren't the issue. Some of the villains were just incomprehensibly villainous, but, although it's a fine line, I think they came down on the "love to hate" side rather than being ones that were too cartoonish to even take seriously (with the possible exception of one engineer). And the ending really put everything into a new perspective which I wasn't expecting and liked a lot. 
 So yes, there's no reason to stop reading here, even if it may be a bit formulaic (it is, after all, a series that seems designed to be a good TV series), it's thoroughly enjoyable and rises far above where you'd expect.

Oh, Tessa Dare. Once you were a guaranteed rollicking good read of the smoking hot historical romance variety... but for the past couple of years Dare's books have slanted increasingly saccharine and twee. I don't know why, but her books have been veering more and more towards the frothy Julia Quinn variety (and I used to love me some Julia Quinn before she leaned so hard into silly, breezy capers), and though they still have some heat, I find Dare's books don't really have much sizzle any more. Compared to the first Spindle Cove book, which also featured a strident heroine and war-wounded hero, TDD is a pale imitator and little more than fluffy confection. 
 And yet, sometimes empty literary calories are exactly what you want. I wish the characters had a little more depth instead of her relying so heavily on a Beauty & the Beast-type trope. And of all her books, this one felt like it was the most anachronistic in terms of how the characters spoke and interacted. Still, not an unpleasant way to while away an afternoon, but far from Dare's best and not altogether that memorable. Given how long I feel like it has been since her last book, I was expecting more from her and was hoping for a stronger start to her new series.

 Jane, along with Detective Thomas Moore, discover an almost identical crime committed two years ago. These books sucked me in and went straight to my heart, I felt for Katniss dearly and was engrossed in her struggles; however this book left me shattered. 
 I suppose what left me a little disappointed with the end of Mockingjay was that by the end of it all, after watching Katniss survive the Hunger Games which in themselves are twisted, then get sent back in; after watching her give up everything for her family for her sister, after watching her loose it all to win the war; Katniss is left destroyed. She is a shell of her former self. Her friendships are broken, her home destroyed, so many people dead. Katniss, a girl who from the very beginning has this amazing will to survive and an enormous heart is so broken by the end that she wants to die and her heart is shattered. 
 She's devastatingly broken and we hear about everything that brings her down in great detail; but her path to recovery is practically glossed over. I wanted to see more of Katniss's return to even the ghost of her former self that she seems to be left with by the epilogue, but instead I'm simply told that eventually she gets a little better and (SPOILER) that she and Peeta eventually end up finding themselves able to care about each other again. 
 I didn't want a happy ending and understanding what the book is really about I understand why it ends the way it does, and honestly it ends perfectly except that I wanted to see it; I wanted more details of Katniss, the girl who was on fire. The girl who is burned to ash and then things get a little better, not a phoenix rising, but a flicker of hope, just a little something that everything she'd been through was worth something to her; but we don't get to see it. We get graphic details about all the things that suck the life from her but barely any about what little spark remains. If I could have had just a little more romance there at the end, just been able to see that connection between Katniss and Peeta returned to them this book would have been perfect, but in my opinion it is lacking that. 
 I would still suggest reading all three books because seeing Katniss change and become this power that truly does the right thing is moving and I cheered and cried for her along the way; but I wish I had known more to expect when I got into them because they left me utterly devastated.

I'm hesitant when choosing to read YA books in this genre because I have found its been quite a hit and miss proposition for me probably because I am somewhat older than the target audience. Therefore I usually rely on the premise and world building to capture my imagination and draw me into the story rather than the characters. For me, The Iron King did just that. 
 Julie Kagawa may have drawn heavily on the Labyrinth (directed by Jim Henson), Caroll's Alice in Wonderland and Shakespeares Midsummers Night Dream for inspiration but she has woven the threads to create a fresh and engaging tale of adventure and magic. The premise is not exactly original, but there are magical and physical duels, clues to follow and a destined (if a little too pat) romance that entertains and intrigues. 
 However its the creation of the iron fey that is inspired and makes the story stand out. I love the idea and that it makes such perfect sense. 
 Megan is a little too shallow for my tastes, she isn't as resourceful as I had hoped she would be and some of the conflicts rely on her being too obtuse to see the obvious. Despite that, she is likeable and surrounded by such a fun and creative group of characters, I wasn't as irritated as I might have been. 
 The writing is excellent, Kagawa vividly describes the fey world and its inhabitants with carefully crafted detail by showing what her characters see and experience. It was easy to immerse myself in the NeverNever with its familiar yet unique landscape. 
 The Iron King is an entertaining YA fantasy with an engaging twiat of tradition. I am glad I have The Iron Daughter to hand to continue the story of the Iron Fey.

Look at that cover. Look at that title. How can a book that looks and sounds so awful be so completely fantastic? This book completely blew my mind. I loved every word, every scene, every chapter. Stephanie Perkins might just be my new favorite contemporary author. 
 Anna wants to be a movie critic. She wants to date Toph, the cute rocker boy who works at the movie theatre with her. She wants to have fun with her best friend, Bridgette. But all that comes tumbling down when her father sends her to the School of America in Paris (SOAP). Thus, Anna's French adventure begins! 
 Anna was a fabulous protagonist. I really, really loved her. She was so quirky and different. She was also a hilarious and relatable narrator. What I loved most about her was that she always redeemed herself. She has flaws, yes, and she acknowledges that and tries to fix things. I never grew tired of Anna's voice or her story. 
 The other characters were just as great! Rashmi was probably my favorite out of all of Anna's friends. I loved how real she was and how she never let anyone know her problems. Josh and Meredith were fun as well. Amanda... Oh goodness, I hated her. Stephanie Perkins truly knows how to write wonderful characters that I feel emotions for. 
 And that brings me to... you guessed it, Etienne St. Clair. The absolute heartthrob of every reader, I'm sure. I, personally, did love him, but not a ton. He has flaws, which I completely admire, and sometimes those flaws get the better of him. He has a great sense of humor and I would love to have him as a best friend. But I didn't absolutely love him. I don't know how to phrase it... I loved him, but I didn't love him. 
 The romance and sexual tension was incredible. The angst and fury and confusion, it was all so real. That's what I really love about contemporaries. They feel real. This book was filled with so much angst, I wanted to rip my own hair out while reading this. Luckily, the plot was fast and always super fun. I never got tired of reading it. There were so many twists in this book! I would read a scene and then exclaim something, causing my friends to throw me a questioning look. 
 I loved this book. Loved, loved, loved. It was so mushy and gushy and frustrating and absolutely adorable. 
 I would recommend this to all readers, even those who aren't fans of mushiness. Anna and the French Kiss is a phenomenal debut that combines friendship, romance, drama and a dash of French culture; a perfect read for any reader. 
 5 keys. Without a single doubt. I'm wondering whether I should start Lola right now or take a break from Perkins to absorb Anna's awesomeness.

Oh, how much I regret for having seen the movie before reading the book. But hey, it's an accident, I didn't know "Cloud Atlas" the movie was an adaptation of a novel after quite some time. The movie is definitely not bad. Yet, the laziness inside me keeps blaming it for the delay to read the book. 
 It is a great read. 
 Can't believe it took, let's see, almost 3 years for me to actually get over page 10. The book is hard to break in, that's without a doubt. But the effort is worth it. 
 Remember "One thousand and one nights"? Try reading backward from the last story to the first one and you will have a general idea of the structure of "Cloud Atlas." 
 Six stories are blended together, literally and figuratively. Adam Ewing's story is the first book. Imagine opening the middle page of that journal, then arrange Robert Frobisher's letters in between. Repeat the process with Timothy Cavendish's adventure, then with Sonmi-451's, then with Zachary's. Content-wise, the characters of each story all accidentally stumbled upon the writings of the characters of the previous one, Frobisher with Ewing's, Rey with Frobisher's, Timonthy with a book on Rey, Sonmi-451 with a movie made out of Timonthy's autobiography, and Zachary with the digitized memory of Sonmi-451. I think the structure is ingenious. 
 But there is more. Are all story tellers are being truthful? As Zachary's son questioned? As Timonthy criticized? In this way, "Cloud Atlas" is being quite post modern indeed, reminding me of "The name of the Roses" or "If on a winter's night a traveler." 
 Characters are connected, reincarnated. World seems to change but not change. It remains the same in some ways, those repeated themes related to life and human nature, though I don't find the meanings that spectacular compared to the book's format. The writing is indeed a feast of wonders. There are really six stories, separate stories with such different voices, languages, grammar, word usage. (But again, it could be hard to digest). 
 You may have got this from other reviews, but Sonmi-451 story is quite touching, and so is Frobisher's (or maybe I'm so biased and in love with Ben Wishaw's acting...). These are the two sad stories among all, perhaps the sadness makes them great.

It took me awhile to get to the final book for the Hunger Games trilogy. Having been a huge fan of the first two books, I just didn't want it to end... and secondly, I was slightly fearing disappointment as there was some consensus that the series deteriorated with each book. While there was not much I could do about it ending, I remained hopeful the latter would not be the case, but alas I felt Mockingjay was a fairly steep drop-off from the first two books. 
 While the whole return to the Hunger Games in Catching Fire was gimmick-y, I still fell hard for it. And while I don't relish the killing of children for sport (okay, maybe a little), I knew Collins could not pull it out a third time. So, without a Hunger Games, quite a bit of the magic was lost. Additionally, the creativity and "can't flip the pages fast enough" suspense of the arena was replaced by what I felt was repetitive, somewhat dull, "damsel-in-distress"-oriented action sequences. Also, sorely missing was the camaraderie amongst the main characters -- or at least those who made it this far and/or weren't tossed to the sidelines. The previously charismatic Katniss was downright mopey (not that I can blame her!) and the guys kind of lost their spark as well, particularly Gale even with (or perhaps due to) increased presence in this volume. 
 It's not that I didn't like it, I just didn't love it... and that makes me pout a bit like Katniss does when Gale and Peeta commiserate on her personality. I was really quite into it and optimistic but it just got sluggish in the middle/later half where it seemed like Collins was struggling to figure out how to end it, but with a surprise twist or two. The post-battle action end sequence and even the tacked-on epilogue won me back, tho probably a bit too little, a bit too late. 
 I gave the first book 5 stars, the second book 4.5 stars (with the round-up to 5)... Mockingjay gets 3.5 stars and while I am tempted to round-up to 4 stars out of goodwill for the entire series, the odds were just not in its favor for Mockingjay... a reluctant round-down to 3 stars.
I might like this series better than the Sookie Stackhouse books!

After the death of her miserly cousin, Antony North, Millicent Boarder fakes her own death and assumes his identity in order to ensure her mother and two sisters are properly cared for rather than face the poorhouse as they have once before. Mr North was quite wealthy with numerous properties and on a trip to visit one of her new estates, she comes across a Duke and his sister who have had a carriage accident. They make fast friends and Millicent is quickly swept up into the Ton. 
 But the success of her switching her gender as well as her identity has left Millicent with a new problem. Now she's finally become a man, she's found one of her own to love. But revealing her identity could see her hanged for her crimes and her family lose everything. 
 This was a fun read. Millicent is feisty and funny and I loved her as Mr North. I would have given this five stars if it wasn't for the way the love story developed at the end. That part fell a little flat for me, but otherwise it was a quick and easy read. 
 4 Stars.
It was OK but not great. started skimming which isn't the best sign.

What an engaging story! This is a book that is written in a very conversational tone, which makes it very easy to get through. The story told is sort of simplistic, yet it's very complex at the same time. I absolutely love stories that appear so simple yet hide their depth, so this one was right up my alley. There is also a fantastical element to the story, yet it's very much just a realistic tale of a young girl growing up in New York in the '70s. All of the characters came to life and had personalities of their own. How 'A Wrinkle in Time' was woven into the story was fantastic. It was one of my favourite books as a child, and I still enjoy it, so I loved how it was a big part of the story. 
 It's hard to describe this book, but it was just very enjoyable to experience. I feel like all the words were chosen very specifically, and the whole story is very strictly written to add up to one specific point. I loved trying to figure out what story Miranda was trying to tell, and who she was addressing the story to. Conclusion: this was a really charming story that will appeal to all ages.

Normally this isn't the type of book I'd read (i.e.: anything with "after the death of so and so" in the blurb), but I was too curious about the diary. It turned out to be a very intriguing read, with an unexpected twist in the end. 
 Tamara starts off as an unbearably obnoxious character, so much so that it took some optimism to get through her awful attitude at the earlier chapters, but she eventually grows and turns this into a satisfying, yet ironic story.
Really enjoyed this one :)

I always enjoy Kristan Higgins' stories despite the fact that they are written in first person POV. That usually turns me off - it actually works for her books. As usual, this book caught me and wouldn't let me go until the end. 
 While Harper started off as an annoying person, I did enjoy her relationship with Father Bruce. Also, her proposal to her boyfriend, Dennis, along with her list of things to do related to him, was really funny. 
 The flashbacks/memories really gave you insight into what happened between Harper and Nick. I loved that Nick started calling her wife from the first time he met her. 
 Both the hero and heroine made mistakes during their relationship and marriage, which is obvious during the flashbacks. 
 There were several times in which I did get teary during the reading of this book. It's a shame that she had a limited relationship with her father and her stepmother. Harper did go overboard on 'taking care' of her stepsister, but her realization of this seemed kind of quick. 
 Harper did grow throughout the book and realized some of her mistakes - related to her relationship with Nick, as well as her relationships with her father, stepmother and stepsister. 
 Definitely liked this book.

I was so looking forward to this, and it was very satisfying! It's no Knife of Never Letting Go, but then again, what is? 
 The setting is the hook here, a group of high school friends who live in a sort of Buffyverse, but they are the "normal" kids, not the kids who go around fighting vampires and demons and stuff. It's funny and sincere. 
 If anything, I would have liked more -- both more in terms of a longer book, and even more of a contrast between the kids with a supernatural calling and the more mundane-seeming lives of the other kids.

You can also see this review on my blog, Maybe Books Will Be Our Always! There is also currently a GIVEAWAY for the book!! 
 This books took a second for me to really get into, but once I did, I couldn't put it down. As the story began to develop, I became more and more intrigued by it. I really love Amber Argyle's writing style, story telling, and world building. Lets also talk about that cover! It's stunning! 
 This book follows the perspective of Ilyenna, clanmistress of the Shyle. When the Tryans had attacked friends of the Shyle, they send their men to help. When they come back, with both men from both tribes injured, the Shyle people are overwhelmed. One day, when the Tryans attack again, Ilyenna is severly injured. Fairies come upon her, heal her, and ask her to be their queen. But, there is a catch. In order to be queen, she will have to forfeit her humanity. When she decides to be part of her life a little longer, she is enslaved by the Tyrans. This story follows her, her fight to stop the Darrien's advances towards her, and her fight to save the her people and herself. 
 The overall pace of this story was fantastic. It didn't go too slow nor too fast. Also, what's really great about this story is that it is action packed. There wasn't a second that something wasn't happening. There is a lot of violence in this book, however. That aspect didn't really bother me, but if you don't necessarily like a lot of violence in books, I would say go in with caution. 
 The characters were well created and they were just amazing. I absolutely loved how strong and caring Ilyenna is. I love Rone too! He is so sweet and nice! How could you not?!? I was in constant awe on how much Ilyenna helped others no matter how badly they may of treated her, and how Rone would always put Ilyenna before himself. I just absolutely love the relationship between the two! 
 This overall was a fantastic read! I have completely fallen in love with Amber Argyle's writing and will definitely be checking out the rest of this series and her other books as well!

I greatly enjoyed this novel! I read this book in less than twenty-four hours (and it would have been far less if cleaning, eating and sleeping were not required). 
 I adored the main character, Charlie! She was willing to do anything for those she loves - her friends and family members, especially her younger sister, Angeline. 
 Charlie is loyal, brave, determine, hard working, intelligent and kind - she demonstrates this when she rescues someone who has tormented her for much of her life. 
 As admirable and relateable as Charlie is, she still was flawed. She was far too curious for her own good. I liked that unlike many YA novels, she wasn't boy crazy and seemed to have common sense (though I suspect many of my fellow reviewers will disagree with this but I don't believe she made poor decisions). 
 I found the novel's plot to be intriguing! I was pleasantly surprised by the growth experienced by several characters; but was even more shocked by the secrets held by so many. 
 I loved the novel's setting - a medieval style dystopian city. 
 Unlike many YA series novels, 'The Pledge' did not end in an abrupt cliff hanger ending. In fact, it would work well as a stand alone, though I am thrilled to know there is a sequel which I can't wait to read! 
 I highly recommend this book! While I wish I had read this novel when I was in grade 6 or 7, I still enjoyed it just as much as an adult in my mid-twenties.
A totally sick understory, which in my opinion, leaves us a victim that we don't give a shit about. I loved how Eve was giving the murderer advice on how to escape maximum penalty.

This book was strange. It might be more meaningful to someone who has struggled with an eating disorder/ had close friends who have (but I think Wintergirls does a much better job at handling the topic.) 
 The idea seemed cool--a character turning into one of the 4 Horsemen, but I feel like the author didn't really add anything to the mythology to make it interesting. Because, really, what do Famine, War, Pestilence and...Death do? They make life suck. How am I supposed to sympathize with that? 
 I think this would have made a much better short story.

Eh. The Finishing School and YA seems to be Carriger's sweet spot even if she started out writing adult romances. This one reminded me of her adult books - good start with interesting premise and fun characters. But the dialogue tries to be a little too clever, and towards the end, it was really dragging. Spare me the possibly meaningful banter and just give me more action and werecreatures and a resolution already! This does seem to me like a book I'd put in the "new adult" territory. There's some discussion of taking a character taking a lover, a lot of coy comments about nudity as werecreatures shift back and forth, and a lot of slow burn but stylized flirtation that younger teens probably wouldn't be so into, but for the 17+ could be fun to read about. I'll probably still try to read the next one just because I enjoy the characters.

This is Schwab's slightly earlier work, but it still proves that she knows what she's doing. This book was brilliantly plotted, unique, and pulls a little on your heartstrings. 
 It plays on the idea of "going somewhere after you die" but in a completely new way. The structure of the Archive and everything involved is something I've never seen before. Mackenzie is dealing with her own losses, her grandfather and her brother. Her brother affects her the most, and we see how her desire to see him again in the Archive then affects her ability to do her job, and even her relationships. 
 What I love about Schwab is her fantastic characters. Mackenzie aside, Owen and Wesley play important roles. Wesley is a sweetheart, and with Owen there's this wonderful "who is he? what's he doing?" curiosity about him. No matter who these characters end up being, they're still done right. Roland, too, is a character who doesn't get as much page time but he's one of those you really want to meet in real life. 
 It took me a few chapters to really get into it. The way it's written (flashback and present) seems a little incomprehensible until a certain point, but then everything becomes clear.

This series and these books just suck you right in from the beginning! This is the story of Rider and Harmony. I was curious as to how Tillie Cole was going to get me to like Rider when the majority of us hated him at the end of the last book. But guess what, she accomplished it! And while I did warm up to Rider and found forgiveness in my heart, Flame will forever be my favorite character in this series. And that is because he is the most broken off them all and Maddie saved him! 
 It is very hard to review this book without giving away spoilers......so, on that note, just believe me when I say this is a series definitely worth reading! 
 Warning: there are definitely many triggers for people in this book so be prepared for that.

oh. my. gosh. 
 The sweetest game. The sweetest couple. The sweetest family. The sweetest story. The sweetest ending.

It wasn't uncalled for, I have the same fears too. Which is why I always say, I am not getting married. But who am I kidding? Eventually I would have to fall in love and have my own family too right? I hope I find my perfect one, the one who will be the perfect mess with me. The game changer for me. And the sweetest addition to my life. It freaks me out a little to know that humans can be capable of loving this much. Too much at times. 
 This book of romance, struggles and life story is so relatable. I assure you, you will love this book. Just like me.

Do not read unless you've read the rest of the series! 
 I loved it. I hated it. 
 It was the ending that annoyed me to the point that I was left feeling utterly deflated. Disappointment City. 
 I was always a Dorian lover, there was always something so 'off' about Kiyo. But I never thought him possible of keeping the identity of the twins' father from Genie. 
 I don't know, it was the way the ending fell together, in a haphazard glueing of pieces, like 'and then... and then... and then...' 
 What we all really wanted was to see Dorian's reaction when she told him right? And we were left hanging! 
 That said, it was a superb book, despite the lacklustre and throttle-worthy ending. 
 I always think it's a hard task, to bring a series to a close, and often if said series has been wildly popular than it will never satisfy the reader. 
 Dorian forever! 
 ^.^

The Age of Miracles was one of those stories that's objectively amazing but subjectively unremarkable. I get why this is a good book. Really, I do. Karen Thompson Walker wrote a great story with wonderfully insightful prose. As far as storytelling goes, The Age of Miracles knocks it out of the park. The problem was that it was a story that I just personally didn't like. Basically this is the perfect summation of the age of theory of "it's not you, it's me." 
 The Age of Miracles is the story of a 12 year old girl named Julia and her family as they navigate complex interworking's of their relationships as well as contend with the end of the world. It's a coming of age, family drama set amongst the backdrop of the apocalypse. The Earth's rotation has begun to slow down thus setting off a chain reaction of events that causes the entire human race to either adapt or die off. Here's the thing: The Age of Miracles is a family drama first and an apocalypse story second. So we don't particularly see the world fracture or see incredibly devastating natural disasters. We do see a gradual change and how people learn to adapt and cope with the fact that the world is dying. Realistically, the world might only be around for another few years at this rate. It's a very interesting concept to see people continue on in the face of their own destruction in mostly the same ways they would continue on if it wasn't the end of the world. The dichotomy of seeing normal adolescent tragedy coupled with the apocalypse is what makes this a truly great story. 
 Seeing the story told through the eyes of a young girl just entering into puberty is an interesting angle. I think it's fair to liken Julia's budding understanding of growing up and the world around her to Scout's in To Kill a Mockingbird. Both have a similar soulfulness to them where we as readers experience the heartbreak inherent in everyday life being seen for the first time through a child's eyes. We get to see how everything starts to deteriorate for the first time, whether it's relationships, health, or the very world around them. It's in the first acceptance of this decay that the first heartbreak happens in the process of coming of age. The apocalypse shines a peculiar light on the normal coming of age tale and at the same time shows just how universal some things are regardless of whether it's the end of the world or not. 
 Overall, the prose and soulfulness of The Age of Miracles was really something quite thought provoking. Objectively speaking, this was a great book and I would definitely recommend it to others. The only reason this isn't getting five stars from me is because it's not necessarily a story that I particularly liked. There's a difference between thinking something is good and liking it too. But, like I said before, this is more of a "me" problem. I'm the weirdo who reads entirely too many books that could be considered "werewolf porn" so what do I know, really?

The ideas and commentary make this an awesome book. Asimov uses parallel universes to transfer energy and wraps the idea in mystery, crisis, and aliens. There are three stories with completely different perspectives that piece the entire story together. The second part that focuses on the aliens is slow and difficutlt to visualize at first but as it starts to make sense it gets interesting. I liked the commentaries on epistemic arrogance, social motivations, and sexuality. These commentaries occur in a way that strengthens the story instead of appearing as tangents for the author to insert speeches. As is typical for Asimov, there isn't much action because the story revolves around the ideas. However, unlike his later addons to Robots and Foundation, this book doesn't devolve into a bunch of circuitous dialogue. The ideas drive the story. The far out sci-fi aspects can be supported by theories that are still current today. Very well done. Great science fiction.

I was really disappointed with this book. The story was good but this book was so boring! Also I think the characters weren't developed well, the books didn't give me enough to really like, love or hate any of these characters. In the end I didn't care who Cassia chose, I just wanted to finish this so I can move on to another book. This had a lot of potential too for a great story, but this wasn't for me!

I was so much happier this time around reading Room for Just a Little Bit More!! 
 I'm super excited that Brody & Kacie FINALLY got the happy ending they deserved...and a "little bit" more!!

It was *okay*; I just don't think Dorian's motivations/feelings were in any way properly explained and that peeved me big time. Way better than the new movie version, however; the ending of the book is MUCH better and I'm happy that the completely sappy romance at the end of the movie was not in the book. Although, I guess, the filmmakers put that in because they didn't feel book-Dorian's motivations were explained either!

The Dark-Hunters series is one that I'm always saying I'll catch up on. I read the first, and fell in love with Sherrilyn Kenyon's story telling. When the opportunity to review the newest addition to this much loved series arose, I said sure because according to most readers this is a series you don't have to read in order. Thank goodness they were telling the truth. I had no problems figuring out the workings of the world in which the Dark-Hunters and Were-Hunters reside, and suffered only mild confusion when it came to boss guy Acheron and the peculiar Nick. I'm not sure if reading previous books would help clear that up or not because both guys seem to harbor many secrets along with a mutual dislike of each other. 
 I was immediately engrossed by the story of Dev and Sam. Dev is a shapeshifter who works at his family owned bar as a bouncer. He has experienced more than his fair share of grief during his longer than average life. Sam is a former Amazonian warrior (Very cool!) who made a deal that she'd get to take revenge on those that killed her family in exchange for becoming a Dark-Hunter. Living with the constant pain of the loss she felt so many years ago, she never expected to be happy again. Unable to even touch others because of her empath abilities coupled with her Dark-Hunter responsibilities, she has resigned to living the life of a loner. Then she meets Dev who is a closed book to her, and she can't seem to fight the attraction. She is falling for him and he for her, but unfortunately this is against the rules. That isn't enough to stop these two from a few forbidden kisses and more. Of course a paranormal romance isn't complete without bad guys trying to stir up trouble. There is plenty of trouble making, along with a healthy dose of romance and sizzling chemistry between the two main characters. 
 After finishing No Mercy the first thought that occurred was why the heck haven't I read books 2-18. Author, Sherrilyn Kenyon, has such an amazing ability to create fascinating plots weaved with greek mythology, and super hot couples. I've also found my newest book boyfriend, Ethon. I truly hope he is featured more prominently in future novels because I think I might be in love 
 Dev is a super sweet and likable guy. He has lost so many people that are close to him, but isn't nearly as jaded as one would expect. Sam comes off all kick your ass biker chick in leather, but has a kind heart under the tough exterior. They are a perfect match. Things progress quickly between the lovely couple this book focuses on, but this is something I've come to expect and accept in this genre. Only complaint was the ending seemed rush. We spent all this time building up to this super battle only to have it over before this reader was ready. No Mercy is still a fascinating and enjoyable read, but the execution of the ending could have been paced better. 
 This is a series all paranormal romance fans need to check out. Of course I might just be the last PNR fan to experience the fabulousness that is Sherrilyn Kenyon.

In this second book about Anna Dressed in Blood, Cas discovers that Anna hasn't quite moved on as he had expected. Instead, she is trapped in hell. 
 He sees her suffering and feels compelled to save her from the grim fate she doesn't deserve. Cas becomes consumed by his desire to help Anna. With the help of his friends, Thomas and Carmel, they learn about a secret, sacred Order. The members are not too thrilled about helping Cas. Some of them are downright nasty. 
 But Cas is persistent and determined to help Anna no matter the cost. Can he succeed? Will he rescue her from hell and free the lost souls that are trapped where they don't belong? 
 This story is beautifully written and engrossing. I felt like I was right there with Cas and his friends as they embark on a mission to try and save Anna. My only criticism is that I find it hard to believe that teenagers would be permitted to spend nights away from their home and fly off to another country on their own. Cas and Thomas, okay. but Carmel? Doesn't she have parents to answer to? That seemed a bit unrealistic but certainly not enough to ruin the story. I truly enjoyed the "Anna" series and look forward to reading more books by the very talented Kendare Blake. 
 Oh, and for those of you who read the first book and are just dying to know, Cas finally tried Saskatoon jam and actually likes it! :-)

I absolutely adored this book so freaking much. 
 And yes, it made me cry a lot.

When I was in middle school a friend recommended Mercedes Lackey's The Last Herald-Mage trilogy to me and while I found them reasonably entertaining, I already thought (and this is saying something, if it's coming from a 13 yr old) that the protagonist was kind of a drama queen. So much moaning about his pain and how singular his pain was! I was curious about Lackey's other books but I never really got around to any of them (disclaimer: I'm pretty sure I've read at least one or two other Lackey books but I literally can't remember which ones) and looking back, that was a mistake because I clearly missed my enjoyment window for these books. 
 I have to cut the author some slack for first book awkwardness but Talia is the Mary Sue of my adolescent fiction dreams: (view spoiler)[young teenager who is oppressed by her incredibly strict conservative family is rescued by a MAGICAL HORSE who whisks her away to a big city where she's the most chosen-est of the special chosen ones! Her suffering and culture shock is gently nursed by all the important people who all become her bffs! Literally everyone loves her (except the villains, natch) because her magical abilities make her a super-wise therapist* at the tender age of 15! 
 *I also have reservations about Talia's liberal use of her empathy powers to "soothe" people without telling them. I get that you wanna help people, girl, but that's a terribly grey area you're going into. (hide spoiler)] Had I read this series as a middle schooler I would have loved Talia (I'm not immune to overblown magical fantasies, okay) but as an older reader I had much less patience for her special snowflake status. 
 This book also has a weird thing about telling, not showing? A vast amount of the action happens off-screen and people's emotions are all delineated in the straightforward fashion that you usually get beaten out of you in your earliest creative writing classes. I almost felt like I was reading a first draft rather than a finished product and I didn't expect that from such a beloved author so I have to assume that this might be due to the fact that it's one of her earliest works. 
 It was a bittersweet nostalgia trip, in the end. I'm a little sad for younger me who would have torn through a lot of Lackey's books but I'm not terribly upset that I missed out on what seems to be mediocre writing.

I think that I probably didn't like this as much as I expected because I watched the movie first, and I watched the movie as a child, so I kind of built it up in my head, so by the time I got to the book, I was kind of let down. And this was a very long sentence. Overall, I enjoyed the book!

You know, despite the half-naked guy on the cover and the innuendo in the name of the book, it's really not all about sex. Yes, there's adult content, but not that much. The main focus is developing the relationship, and the various problems going on in the Psy-Changelings world, what with the Psy still being emotionless bastards. 
 This book follows Faith. She's an F-Psy, a forseerer, meaning she gets visions of future events. She's the best F-Psy in the world and worth billions. But recently, her visions have taken a dark turn, showing her murders. She wants to figure out why her visions have suddenly changed and why she feels emotions in them. She decided to do to Sascha, one of the few Psy who isn't connected to the PsyNet or the Council, as she's part of a Changeling pack. And on her way to the secret meeting, she meets Vaughn, a pack member and Jaguar who's more in touch with his animal side than most Changelings. 
 And I gotta say, I kinda liked this one more than the last. It had more humor in it. I mean, who would have thought dark, brooding Vaughn had a sense of humor. But he does. And his relationship with Faith is less dominating. He constantly pushes her, but he does it to help her. This book had less Neanderthal-ness than Slave to Sensation as well. The guys are still really protective but in a more supportive way. 
 The writing and pace of the novel was good. The plot regarding the killer was good and the one with the council, great. We got to know more about the world and about Psy in particular. We found out about the Silence conditioning and some of the safeguards built-in to it to prevent people from breaking Silence. It was interesting to come across an emotionless Psy who slowly comes to feel and develop romantic feeling for someone, as well as normal feelings, like whether she likes coffee with milk or without, since Psy don't actually like or dislike things. 
 Overall, I liked getting more into the Psy-Changeling world. We're still pretty disconnected from humans but that will probably change as the series moves along. I'm very interesting to know more.

I like how much emphasis there was on cake. I was just devastated that it turns out they don't bake it from scratch but actually use a cake mix! THE CAKE IS A LIE 
 I stayed up to 2am finishing Insurgent, because I found it terribly difficult to put it down. This didn't feel like a 'filler' book, which makes me so happy! John Hughes movies are all the rage. Kids everywhere are firing up Atari games. Billy Idol and Cyndi Lauper songs are blasting in dance clubs. To the average person in the 1980s, this may appear par for the course but in Ernest Cline's sci-fi novel Ready Player One, we're no longer in the 1980s, we're in the year 2044 and the most obnoxious decade of the 20th century is back in a big way! 
 The whole world is up shit creek without a paddle. People are living in crude skyscrapers constructed from stacked mobile homes, crime is at an all time high and the economy is in the toilet. The only escape from this dreary existence is a massive online RPG network dubbed the OASIS. Players strap on a visor giving them full 360 degree vision of a computer generated world in which they design their own avatar and live out a much more pleasant existence. 
 The game's creator, James Halliday, passed away a few years prior and before doing so, hid a prize deep inside the game. Halliday decided that whoever could claim the elusive prize would gain controlling interest in his company and inherit his unbelievable $240 billion fortune (that's billion with a b). Knowing that everyone on earth would be gunning for it, Halliday did his damndest to make uncovering his "easter egg" as challenging as possible. One would have to both know his life story inside out and be a true scholar of the 1980s. Well, unless you're a giant soulless corporation like IOI (Innovative Online Industries) with its sights set on complete market domination. 
 For years IOI have been sending out their army of hunters, desperate to uncover the location of the egg. Fortunately for the OASIS community, IOI haven't made headway in their search. It isn't until a young player named Wade Watts from the stacks in Oklahoma City uncovers the Copper Key - the first step in the search for the egg - that things really begin to heat up. Can Wade complete the quest before IOI claim the prize or will another ambitious player step up to the plate and nab the billion dollar crown? 
 Despite being born in 1984, I'm not quite a student of the 80s. I was six years old when the calendar turned over to 1990 and the following ten years really crafted my sense of humor and fascination with pop culture. Put on an old episode of the CG TV show ReBoot or Pixar's first Toy Story to really get the nostalgia drug following through my veins. While I was worried that the majority of the references within Cline's Ready Player One would sail over my head, thankfully I had enough crap jammed into that "useless-knowledge" part of my brain reserved for Saturday morning cartoon shows, WWF wrestling, Ghostbusters and Top 40 radio to get me by. 
 While the book took a little too long to get going for my taste, once Wade (or Parzival) grabbed that Copper Key, Cline pushed down on the pedal and took this Delorean of a novel to 88mph. In looking around at several other reviews, it's hard to believe people haven't praised the dialogue nearly as much as I feel it's deserved. While Cline isn't doing anything special per se, it should be noted that everything just feels so natural. I'm going to really miss these characters. 
 Bottom line, this is a really fun book. I welcome the person who takes a crack at recreating the ultimate 90s nostalgia trip where all the characters wear flannel shirts, watch Boy Meets World and obsess over Kevin Smith movies.

The author contacted me on Goodreads after seeing my review of The Walled City. Her book is nothing like the other, but it was still an interesting ride. 
 Cleavesham is a small town with the usual small town cliques and the usual small town drama. Everyone is related to everyone else, it seems. Even our main character is related, through marriage to other kids in her class. The book starts out with a dead body, bled out on the floor of Emily's family's shop. That's pretty shocking, how did it get there? What is even happening? Of course the book takes the back in time route to get you to that point. 
 The first scene that makes sense is Emily at the park with her little sister, and four girls from her class have kidnapped a small boy and are basically torturing him. It paints a very real picture of who these girls are and how they feel about consequences and other people's feelings. They're extremely sadistic, having broken some of the boy's bones in an attempt to try to make him bite off the head of a live bird. Emily is unable to stop them, despite having misgivings about the entire thing. At this moment a newcomer, Jack, fumbles upon the scene and stops it. 
 It's hard to get past that scene. It's a hard read. I almost set the book down forever. It's torture to the nth degree. The descriptions are not nice, and the characters involved have no redeemable qualities. Even once surpassing that, the book is mainly mystery. The girls involved in the torture begin to die one by one, and the newcomer is of course to blame. Emily tries her hardest to convince everyone that Jack is innocent, falling in love with him in the process, even though it becomes clearer as the story continues that Jack may not be everything he says he is. In fact, Jack may be a mental patient of some sort. Yet, even armed with that information, and the possible ramifications, Emily is still hopelessly in love with the guy. 
 I wasn't sure if I was going to like the book even though I do really like dark mysteries. And this was one that fell into a similar vein as the books written by Kate Karyus Quinn. Certainly there was less supernatural junk going on, but people were dying left and right and everything was confusing until the end. I almost stopped reading again when Emily almost drowns herself in a vat of jam by being an idiot. The book had been going nowhwere up until that point, but that reveal at the end was so satisfying. It's just a wonderful ball of awesome that cements everything together. The stuff about Jack afterwards was a little meh. If only the scenes were backwards, it would have let the book off on a strong note. Still, the ending moved the book's rating up a whole lot. 
 So, all in all, this book is a little bit gross, a little bit weird, and extremely satisfying.

I started reading this book and I found the beginning quite slow and the world building confusing and not very well explained. I decided to check out other reviews to see if it got better and was worth reading when I came across all the controversy surrounding this book. 
 That alone almost made me want to stop reading altogether but I decided to continue and finish it so I could form an honest opinion for myself. 
 I did enjoy the book, more than I thought I would after all the negativity. However, I feel it could have been a much better book and tend to agree with most of the criticisms surrounding it. 
 Firstly, some of the names, that of the main character in particular, really put me off because every time someone used America's name it made me cringe. Your lead character's name is arguably one of the most important decisions in a book and I just didn't like the choice at all, especially the fact her second name was some weird homage to her profession. It felt overdone and frankly silly but by the middle of the book I could overlook it mostly because I enjoyed the plot. 
 I think the idea behind the book was pretty solid and I did like the progression and felt the pacing and overall story was done well. 
 Unfortunately, most of the characters were cliche and one dimensional and some of the dialogue was cheesy and out of place but, again, I enjoyed the story enough to ignore that for the most part. 
 I don't like the love triangle. I thought I'd prefer America/Aspen but frankly Aspen seems to just want to win America once he realizes she may have feelings for Maxon. He messes her about too much for me to ever root for him seriously. 
 Maxon I liked but he's a pretty forgettable love interest when compared to other popular YA male characters. I'd like to see more depth to his character in the next book and I'd also like his opinions to be formed more on what he feels he should do than what his opinion becomes once he's spoken to America. 
 I did like America's interactions with Maxon, though I felt she sometimes was a little over the top in how she expressed herself to him when being raised as she was she probably would've been wise enough to not voice every negative thought she has about Maxon/the royals/the country to his face. It just seemed a tad unbelievable that she'd have no filter and no mind for discretion. It would have felt more natural if their relationship had progressed to that instead of being that right away. 
 Overall, I wish I could have given it a better rating but there were too many little things that should've been improved before it was published, particularly the world building which is a huge thing when using a future setting in YA fiction. This would've been 2.5 stars if I could've given it but I rounded it up purely based on the potential the plot has and how much I really did enjoy the premise of it.

I feel a little disappointing by this installment in The Selection series. The first book totally surpassed all my expectations and I could fully understand the hype, but this book? Not so much! I found myself getting bored with the repetitive will they/won't they nature of the book and noticing so many dislikable qualities in all the main characters that led to an inevitable loss of empathy with the story and their plights. 
 America, the female protagonist and through whose eyes we view this fantastical world, seemed like a self-obsessed individual with an impetuous and often immature nature. Her reactions to the events in the palace she is housed in are often rash and seriously misjudged. Her previous low placement in the caste system hierarchy governing this world made me presume her to become an advocate for her people and a strong leader for future change. Instead, she spent much of her time lamenting her individual woes and forgetting that there were larger pressing issues. I can only hope she matures as the series continues. 
 Prince Maxon also acted rather sketchily in some places and the explanations he gave for his sleazy actions were unjustified, in my opinion. It was in his actions that I felt most disappointed. America behaved poorly, but she never actually betrayed who she was. As a reader, she allowed me to hope for her future redemption, but in Maxon's case, I felt like he became just another stereotypical 'guy' with his brains placed somewhere other than his head. 
 The first portion of the book provided little forward motion in the plot other than a continuation of the intricacies of the love triangle plot concerning America, Prince Maxon and childhood sweetheart, Aspen and held little interest for me. From about the midway point the story really improved and there were many unforeseen moments I enjoyed reading of. I preferred the more action-driven parts of the story rather than the parts concerning court intrigue that I found a little monotonous in areas. 
 The ending was a strong one and has really heightened my interest in the series and I am looking forward into continuing with this, despite everything, guilty little pleasure of mine.
