Just when you thought Elizabeth Scott was getting to be predictable...along comes LIVING DEAD GIRL. To clarify, I love, love, love Elizabeth Scott. I have happily read and gushed about her first three books: Bloom, Perfect You, and Stealing Heaven. 
 If I had just a handful of words to describe Living Dead Girl, they'd be: powerful, haunting, and unputdownable. 
 It is the story of a girl caught in a nightmare. "Alice." A girl who at the age of ten was reborn. 
 Get up. 
 Those were the first words I ever heard. 
 Open my eyes, see a girl, black and blue all over, dried blood along her thies. Red brown stains smeared across the hairless juncture between. 
 "Get up and take a bath, Alice," the man in the blue shirt said, and Alice did. 
 I did. 
 That's how I was born. Naked, hairless, covered in blood like all babies. 
 Named, bathed, and then taken out into the world. (20) 
 Kidnapped by a pedophile during a class field trip, Alice has endured the unthinkable for five years. Now she's fifteen, five foot seven, and a hundred pounds. Her time is running out, she knows this, she wasn't the first Alice. But it is in how she lives--her world, her thoughts, her decisions--that will haunt you most of all. Suspenseful, dark, and very chilling. Definitely not for everyone. But if you can go to the dark side, if you can walk in her shoes for a bit, it is really something. 
 Scott's writing is incredible. If I were in charge of handing out awards, one would be heading her way. Her book is amazingly haunting. It just resonates with feeling, emotion. The mood might be dark. The ending bittersweet, but oh-what-a-book. 
 In previous posts, I've compared Elizabeth Scott to Sarah Dessen. She may not realize it, but that is high praise, very high praise coming from me. Some people may think that Stephenie Meyer is the "perfect" writer. But for me, Sarah Dessen, has always provided the most satisfying of reads. But with her fourth novel, Living Dead Girl, new comparisons must be made. Alice Sebold. Nancy Werlin. Gail Giles. Laura Wiess.

My passionate opinions of Divergent notwithstanding, my decision to read Insurgent by Veronica Roth was more out of spontaneity and convenience, and less out of curiosity. Oftentimes it is the latter that compels me to read books, especially sequels of books that I did not particularly enjoy. Nonetheless, although I did not particularly enjoy Divergent, I picked Insurgent hoping that it would be an improvement, however marginal, to its predecessor. 
 It is noteworthy that Insurgent is the first audiobook I have listened and completed. The crux of my Insurgent audiobook experience: I enjoyed it. More specifically, I enjoyed listening to the audiobook. I'm traditionally a paperback or ebook reader, but, to my surprise, I loved listening to the story. I think I now understand the beauty of aural storytelling. Usually my attention span, especially when the information is conveyed aurally, is short-lived, but Emma Galvin was a fantastic narrator that held my interest effortlessly. However, this experience taught me something about myself: how critical I am of something depends on its medium. I am more critical of books than I am of TV shows and movies. Audiobooks, it seems, fall into the latter. With that said, I believe I would have enjoyed Insurgent much less if I had read it as a paperbook/ebook. But am I complaining that I enjoyed something more than I should have? Absolutely not. 
 Although the state of the world and conception of factions divided by our personalities is nonsensical and beyond salvaging, I picked up Insurgent for the story alone. After all, I detected potential in the narrative and its development when I was reading Divergent. There were also undertones of revolution (and you and I know that I'm a big sucker for those), and perhaps Insurgent would have provided some insight as to why and how the factions were formed. So, was there a revolution and does Insurgent attempt to save its big worldbuilding flaw? Yes and, well, not at all. 
 Following the catastrophic aftermath of Divergent, Chicago as Tris knows it is thrown into chaos and the perpetrators remain at large. More importantly, Chicago is prepared for an uprising now that the faction responsible has been ousted. Herein is the potential that I hoped for - perhaps Roth would provide us a lesson on the necessity of revolution, that rebellion is not necessarily a violent thing drenched in blood but can be achieved through collective action. When introducing the 'underground resistance', Roth is partway there. The unexpected would-be heroes are poised to strike, ready for action, and are interestingly the group that most of Chicago has overlooked thus far. Though this bears some symbolic connotations (as it should), my optimism for this book quickly began to falter. 
 Contrary to what people may believe, rebellion is possible without violence, and it is called civil resistance. It is a very simple idea, but it is a complex process, particularly when the oppressors are violent. Understandably, in the context of Insurgent, where traitors are armed to the teeth and are killing people left, right and center (which makes no sense, but let's let it slide anyway), at face value civil resistance does not seem like a viable option. The important idea, however, is that there is a power in collective action. Rather than ask the hard questions about rebellion and revolution - especially in its challenges - any thematic potential in Insurgent is forsaken. But, my criticisms of Insurgent aren't its should have's and ought to have been's. 
 Here is my biggest gripe: Insurgent trivializes revolution, and that is something more harmful than people give credit. 'Rebellion', in Insurgent, is a shoot 'em up mission spearheaded by fumbling teenagers who have no idea what they are doing and only succeed out of sheer luck and because it conveniences the plot. What is the purpose of their rebellion? To kill or destroy the leader. But to what end and what of the consequences after? God knows, but if you do, please CC your theories to Roth and I. The very idea that revolution is merely taking down an autocratic leader is more than ludicrous; it is naive. 
 "But CW, this is just an entertaining book! It doesn't really matter!" Well actually, it does matter. Other than The Hunger Games (which I wasn't fond of either, but I will admit that it handled its themes better), the Divergent series is the other most accessible young adult book out there that touches on these themes. Insurgent ignores the social and political implications of an uprising. Actually, there is nothing social or political about it at all. Rather than show that revolution can lead to positive change at a cost and why it is necessary (because, you know, if you are going to write a dystopia you need a degree of social commentary), Insurgent instead presents revolution as something that is 'action-packed' that lacks meaning, purpose, and depth. To me, Insurgent has included revolution without any understanding of the term or its social significance. 
 History is filled with revolution, some absolutely horrific, some peaceful, most necessary. More importantly, even today, revolution is important. Movements like 'Black Lives Matter' and the 2014 Hong Kong Protests are inherently tied to ideas of revolution. With the shuddering amount of police brutality occurring in the United States where people are actually being killed, should someone suggest we resolve this Insurgent style? (Note: I am not insinuating Roth's personal and political values are reflected in her portrayal of revolution.) The tragedy is that the idea of revolution - which is about power of the people and collective action - has been clumsily and thoughtlessly tossed around as a tool to make a book 'action-packed'. 
 All of that aside, there is a lot of almost going to happen and not a lot of things that actually happen. It seems that the purpose of Insurgent is to build up to the finale - and with the lack of development of characters and lack of action, it shows. It is possible that Insurgent has fallen victim to second book syndrome. On character development and overall story which have already been discussed ad nauseam - meh. If there was one thing I didn't mind too much, it was the relationship development between Four and Tris. They certainly argue more in this installment, but isn't that a part of relationships? Interestingly in Insurgent, most of their arguments stem from a conflict in ideology or belief in how to do things. Therefore, I didn't see their bickering as a detriment to the book - I'd say that it helped me understand Four and Tris's characters more. 
 However, the fault is that Insurgent fails to be an engaging book. When you have readers who are curious about the development of the story but are tentative in their investment, Insurgent would not be the kind of book that would renew interest. If anything, Insurgent has confirmed that this series is something I can give up half-way, and, sad to say, that would not be a loss.

I was so excited to read Eve, from the moment I started seeing it in IMM posts around the book blog community. It sounded like such a great book, so I quickly snagged the Kindle version as soon as it was released! 
 I really liked the story with this one, the idea of a Plague (The Stand is one of my all time favorite books, so I loved a different take on the survivors of the great plague!) The dystopian society that Anna Carey has created is well thought out. 
 The main characters are great, although flawed. I liked Arden a lot, although I'm still struggling to put my finger on why. Eve did scrap at me a bit, I didn't always love her naivety, especially considering she had memories of "before" the plague... that just didn't add up for me! (One particular scene with a television set REALLY brings this to mind!) Caleb was great, as were the boys in his dugout for the most part. 
 The relationship between Caleb and Eve happened a bit too fast for me, and it felt slightly forced. But I was able to look past that as the plot wasn't really centered around the romance, at least not in my opinion. 
 I think the biggest struggle for me was the timing of this book. They aren't very far removed from the plague and all of the characters have vivid memories of "before", yet they seem so clueless as to life before, not remembering televisions or "love"... that just didn't add up for me. 
 In the end, this book has some excellent moments and shows a lot of promise. If you can bring yourself to look beyond a few major flaws you can really enjoy this book! And the ending? It definitely left me wanting to read the next (planned) installment of this series.

Talk about an awesome read. I happened to really like this one a lot. The connection between the two characters was steaming. Malcolm Saint was that alpha ass type of guy that will change whether he admits it or not for the right girl. 
 Rachel is after the story to save her dying magazine company. And that story is Saint. At least it starts off that way. Then he keeps surprising her and makes her fall hard. 
 The story kept my attention. It has some funny parts. Lots of awe and swoon moments. I am dying for July to come when I can read the next one. 
 Def recommend this one!

Probably a 2.5 ... I wanted to like this book - I really did. But the things that bothered me about it, didn't make up for the things that I liked. 
 In The Look of Love we meet Chloe, who's just had one hell of a night. Her ex-husband has attacked her and when she fled, ending up in a ditch in her crappy car. Along comes Chase Sullivan, who can't help but rescue the beautiful, curvy woman. 
 Chase is a photographer who's traveled the world, slept with tons of women, never settling down. Their immediate attraction is a given. 
 He convinces her to spend the night at his brother's winery instead of a motel and the story moves quickly from there. 
 This is a story of instant love. 
 And I think what bothered me most, was that I just didn't buy it. Her ex-husband had stifled her and controlled her for 10 years and she is making a life for herself but none of that matters once she meets Chase. 
 Chase is one of those "she is MINE" kind of guys... at least that's the impression I got. I have a hard time believing that this playboy, yes I called him a playboy based on his own description of himself, suddenly and instantly changes his outlook on relationship based on meeting this girl. The guy who has basically decided he's not going to settle down is three days in to knowing Chloe and is declaring 
 "I love you. Always. Forever." 
 fine fine fine... 
 I guess that's to be expected in a story like this, but then, something happened at about 80% in. Chloe, our dear heroine, has trust issues. I guess the best way to prove you trust someone is this ... 
 "I want you to tie me up." 
 aaaaaanyway - I'm going to mention one other thing that irritated the crap out of me. WORD REPETITION. 
 I get that it was the author's intent, but I never want to see the word lovely as an adjective again. 50 instances of the word were in this book, but that didn't surpass the 73 instances of the word love. And to think that these two only knew each other less than a week... 
 I will say this, I was told that the second book is much better, so I'll come back to this series to check out Marcus's story and hopefully I'll enjoy it much more than I did this one. 
 I think if you're looking for a light series about sexy, hunky guys... this might be for you. If you're willing to look past all the things that irritated me of course.

 Favorite quote: "...a crying that cannot be diluted by a brave deed or a kind word, but only by someone holding you as your shoulders shake and your tears run down your face.."

I don't know, this is a super solid read, but I didn't swoon. I was concerned about the amount of time the two main characters were logging on the subway as they traveled across New York over the course of a day. A romance told over a single day, between a teen boy and a girl he meets in a record store. The girl, though, is facing deportation with her family. This is her last day and last chance to try to prevent the USCIS from sending her and her family back to Jamaica.

I found this book confusing for most of the story. Despite it saying so in the blurb I was surprised to find that Gottie was traveling through actual wormholes and spent a large proportion of the book wondering if it was just a result of her grief or if she was actually time travelling. I came into the story expecting to read about a cute romance with a side of learning to grieve and grow. Which I got. Although I hadn't expected to encounter actual real wormholes and quite a lot of mathematics (most of which went right over my head). 
 That being said, I did enjoy the story. It was cute and the characters were realistic. Being half Dutch, I found that I recognised some of the German, such as Oma (grandmother) and Opa (grandfather) both of which I called my Dutch grandparents, which helped me to understand the story and feel a deeper connection with the characters. 
 However, I felt like it took me a while to get into the story and it got the point where I really just wanted to be finished - but that was probably more about me being in a slump and less about the book itself. The only reason that this book has three stars rather than four is because I am determined to stop giving every book I love (but not to the point that it is my most favourite story ever) five stars and that means that this book, falling under the really liked but not loved category, gets a three. 
 I recommend this story for anyone who wants a cute summery read but is prepared to have a bit of science-fiction squished inbetween the Aww moments.

This book took me on an emotional rollercoaster of feelings that I never want to get off. Especially considering this is the first time we've had a story finale by Sarah J Maas. I didn't know what to expect! Is she a Stephanie Meyer, where everyone gets a wee bruise and comes out alive? Is she a George RR Martin, who enjoys killing every single character with no remorse? Or is she a JK Rowling, who kills characters we know and like, but in a way that totally makes sense for the story? 
 Well, I won't tell you, but I will tell you that you should read this book to find out. 
 First off, Feyre is incredible. In the first book of this series, A Court of Thorns and Roses, Feyre is a meek human, docile, willing to do whatever Tamlin tells her to do, all in the name of love. When I first read it, I fell in love with Tamlin, and loved the way that Tam and Feyre loved each other. They were so great together, Tamlin so protective over here. Then A Court of Mist and Fury comes along, and Feyre changes. The whole story is Feyre changing and growing as a character; she comes alive. Now, in A Court of Wings and Ruin, Feyre using all of that growth and character development to be the strongest female lead I may have ever run across. She is daring, brave, strong, and so incredibly kind. She doesn't let Rhys, or anyone really, walk all over here. She stands up for what she believes in, and refuses to back down from what she thinks is right. I would not want to be on the battering ram end up her wrath. The way that she is able to manipulate the Spring Court and learn their secrets is absolutely beautifully written. I *almost* started to feel bad for Tamlin.... 
 There are twists and turns to this story, at every single point. Some are a bit expected, but some of them shocked the heck out of me. Sarah J Maas is incredible at making us feel on thing, only to reveal later that we were completely wrong. Here's a spoiler for the first two books, if you haven't read them yet (and if you haven't, what are you doing here?). Did anyone honestly expect to hate Tamlin as much as they did at the end of ACOMAF? I didn't. I thought Tamlin was the best book boyfriend ever! But going back, he's overprotective in a bad way, red flags all over the place, horrible temper. Her writing style makes Feyre seem so real. I never had the thought "Feyre, you're so stupid, can't you see what's happening" because we see EXACTLY what Feyre sees. And her interpretations on what she's seeing is logical, I don't find myself questioning anything. Until a twist is revealed, the webs start to get more tangled, and you're like, yeah, that makes sense! 
 The relationships in this story feel so real, but they also feel mature and safe. None of the characters are abusive towards their mates or partners. Sometimes they keep secrets from each other, but only because they're keeping these secrets for good reasons. When a character gets mad at another character, they fight, talk it out, act reasonable and are able to get over it because their family is so closely knit. 
 Since this is the last book in this story (but there will be additional stories in the universe!), the main conflict with Hybern gets resolved. There are no cliffhangers here. But there are a few loose ends that don't get tied up, which are hopefully going to be the basis of these additional stories that will be published. It does NOT take away from the ending of this story though. I feel satisfied and satiated, only left with that longing feeling of wanting to live inside this story forever. 
 My only concern about this book is that it is listed as a "teen and young adult fantasy", and I do not agree with that. There are some explicit intimate scenes that might be inappropriate for a young teenager. A Court of Thorns and Roses might be able to squeak by as a YA story, but the rest of them are definitely not. 
 I laughed, I cried, I sobbed, I threw my kindle across the room, I cheered, I did it all. This really is a masterful ending to an incredible story, and I highly recommend that you finish this series with a bang and read this book. In one sitting, if possible!

Wow, I'd forgotten just how good Stephen King is when he's good. This is miles away better than either film adaptation. Carrie seems so real, and your skin crawls at the humiliation she is forced to endure both at home and at school. Stephen King has a very specific command of language, and you can tell that each word of the text is picked with clean precision. At times, I thought the characterization bordered on becoming cartooning, but this criticism was often countered by surprising moments of depth from various characters that both provided welcome insight into the complex nature of bullying as well as some interesting departure from stereotype. Carrie is King's first published novel, and there is certainly nothing to indicate that here. A worthy showing from the master or horror in his prime.

I have been marathoning the wonderful Percy Jackson series after reading it five years ago. I wasn't too excited to read The Sea of Monsters to be honest. It was my least favorite book in the series. I have heard from many people the second book in the Percy Jackson series is their also least favorite. 
 However, after rereading The Sea of Monsters, I am pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed it. I actually enjoyed Sea of Monsters more than The Lightning Thief. 
 The beginning is a little slow and I won't lie, Percy kind of annoyed me. If you've read The Percy Jackson and Heroes of Olympus series you know that Percy is known for having strange misfit friends and being extremely loyal (often to a fault) to them. In the beginning, Percy is friends with Tyson, a fellow classmate that is homeless and picked up as a "community project" by his school. So pretty much a charity case. 
 My problem with their relationship was that it felt like Percy merely tolerated Tyson despite claiming heatedly to be his friend. The problems I had with Percy particularly escalated when (view spoiler)[ Percy finds out Tyson is a child of Poseidon and his brother (hide spoiler)]. At this point, Percy is struggling to even tolerate Tyson because of how he is received by the other characters, especially Annabeth. 
 There is nothing wrong with tolerance but my issue was that Percy was embarrassed by Tyson's presence, but he was more embarrassed that people knew he was embarrassed. I understand Percy's ambivalence was bred from guilt, but still, as the reader, being constantly reminded of Percy's loyalty and his implied title of defender of the misfits was pretty annoying to me. Maybe I am reading into much into this, but I felt like it was border line self righteous. 
 I understand that he is quite literally a flawed hero, and I commend Rick Riordan for not being afraid to show us this but I couldn't help but find Percy's indecision between embarrassment of being associated with Tyson and his embarrassment of people knowing this to be a little on the hypocritical side. However, this left a lot of chance for personal growth and by the end of the novel, Percy's character development is phenomenal, and a lot of his character maturation has to do with Tyson. 
 When Percy and Annabeth go on their quest to save Grover and retrieve the Golden Fleece, they encounter many enemies and(Luke and his minions) and monsters, and monster minions who work for Luke. Long story short, Percy and Annabeth get in a lot of sticky situations. Now you would expect Annabeth to wile their way out of these dilemmas, but it was actually Percy who came up with many plans that involved knowledge of Greek mythology that inspired cunning escapes. 
 For example, (view spoiler)[ Percy clearns Chiron's name when he tosses the drachma onto the ground where it hits the puddle and he gets into contact with Camp Halfblood while Luke unaware of the audience behind him admits to poisoning Thalia's pine tree and framing Chiron. (hide spoiler)] I was quite impressed by Percy's resourcefulness, which for some reason, I don't remember him being this smart from the first time I read the series. He even beat wise girl, so score for Percy. 
 Despite my minor issues with Percy at the beginning, I loved this book. This was a great marathon. I learned so much more about Percy's character, including both flaws and strengths, and I guess that allowed me to see him in a more real light. I really got to appreciate the complexity and depth that is Percy Jackson. 
 I even learned to appreciate Luke more. Maybe I am going soft or Rick Riordan created a very good "villain," (probably the second one) but I actually sympathized with Luke...even when he was a scum bucket. I can understand the motives. He is an interesting character that I want to see more of, especially when he is around Annabeth. 
 To conclude, Sea of Monsters is a great sequel with so much action, great character dynamics, amazing character development, plot twists, and of course humor that will leave you hanging onto every word. And that cliffhanger...damn. I mean sure I already read the book once, but it's been six years. If you haven't read (or reread) the Percy Jackson books, then what are you waiting for? 
 Go and read them right now before Ares curses you.

I KNOW my emotional response to this book. I liked it, so three stars it has to get. But why? What is it that has prevented me from giving it more? 
 Please read the above book summary. I am not going to repeat all of that. I assume you know that this book is based on the two real-life Grimke sisters that fought for the Abolitionist and Women's Rights movement in the 1830s and 1840s. 
 The book is well researched. It has an excellent epilogue that in detail specifies what is and is not fictional. Many of the characters really did exist and they are woven into the fictional events. It is the fictional story that gives me trouble. In reality Sarah Grimke was given a personal slave when she was eleven, Hetty (of ten years), but this slave soon died. Here she lives on and is used by the author to show us the horrors of slave life in Charleston, South Carolina. It is this fictional story that doesn't ring true to me. There are cups of tea on roof tops, things like that, which create a feel good story that people so love...... but which didn't work for me. 
 And I will not talk of the ending; how realistic is that? 
 The theme of slave quilting is pretty too. Too pretty? Too sweet? Is it a gimmick to tie the story together? 
 Slavery is bad. Of course, but there is no discussion of why so many people refused to abandon it. Nothing of the economic basis for slavery in the South is discussed. Am I too much of a non-fiction book lover for this? Should I give up on historical fiction completely? 
 The narration by Jenna Lamia who voices Sarah's story and Adepero Oduye who speaks Hetty's, the slave girl's story, are distinct. I like how each uses their own appropriate vocabularies. Sarah is genteel, clearly from the upper crust, the slave owning class; her speech and choice of words well reflect this. Hetty's is exactly as expected, that of a slave's, with a diction that matches. Each uses a language that seems genuine. BUT at the end of the novel, when both are middle-aged woman, they still sound like teenagers. This, along with the author's feel good touch, had me thinking this was more a young adult novel than a serious one for adults.

Well what a turn around. I was honestly thinking that maybe this trilogy wasn't for me when I finished A Darker Shade of Magic but I am happy that I didn't give it up. 
 I had real issues reading the aforementioned as an audiobook so for this one I decided to read the physical book and it made a world of difference. I will admit that at some points I did want to hear what it sounded like aloud so I did look up the audiobook then but the overall production never inspired me to continue the book fully in that format. I will say that Micheal Kramer, who was voicing Kell, was really good surprisingly. I enjoyed him way more than I did Kate Reading's portrayal of Lila. Kate's inflections were just all over the place and she made Lila sound too young for her personality. I kept wishing that Lila would sound a bit more grown and sassy so that I could stop envisioning her as a 15 year old girl . 
 The purpose of this book was to grow our current characters and learn more about them as well as introduce new characters. Of the new ones introduced I loved Alucard and Hastra the most. Hastra for his loyalty to Kell and Alucard because he is a silver tongued, funny, dangerous, loyal and sexy pirate. You see both of these characters in conjunction to sections link with a main character. So Hastra with Kell's chapters and Alucard in Lila's in the beginning. Eventually Alucard gets sections to himself and I loved reading his thoughts and learning more about his background. Hastra doesn't get his own sections but you do learn a lot about him in his conversations with Kell. 
 Along with character growth, we see a lot of relationships develop in both good and bad ways. My favourite relationship from the first book was always the bond of brotherhood and love between Rhy and Kell. It was so beautiful in the first book that you only get to see its beauty grow through trial and tribulation in the second book. I loved how you got to see their dynamic shift and grow and not just between them but with the entire family. I really wanted to see more of Rhy's parents in this book and I got it but not in the way I wanted. It was one of the most crushing things about this book. All you need to do is read pages 491-493 to understand and experience the heartbreak and the anger felt by Kell. This is actually the part you should also listen to in the audiobook. Michael really puts so much feeling into the dialogue here that you can't help but want to stand up and yell "PREACH!!!". I did just that and I was never more happy to be in my room :). 
 Lila and Alucard's relationship was equally as dynamic. It was a mix of double speak and flirtation that developed into a mutual trust. A considerable accomplishment considering that Lila is not winning many, if any, BFF awards in her lifetime. Alucard is very mysterious at the beginning but we learn about him and the ties that bind him as we go. Eventually some of those ties are exposed and are tested as well which makes him more integral than I would have first thought. LOL reminds you of any Lanstov pup y'all might remember from another popular series *wink*. The way that the relationships in general intermingle is what keeps you reading because a lot the 'action' doesn't happen until your in the last third of the book. 
 Speaking of the above mentioned action, it is a lot of fun and reminds me a lot of 'bending' which is a term coined from the Avatar: The Last Airbender series. If you've never seen the show, then watch any episode of that to get a visual idea of what elemental manipulation looks like and then come back to the book. Even though the 'action' doesn't start till near the end, it is still only a background item to all the machinations happening between the characters. Oh and this of course is not including all of the drama caused by none other than Delilah Bard. You don't need epic shoot outs for you to become fully invested in this book and for the pace to keep moving. A lot of little things kept the momentum and I appreciate the skill it takes to do that. 
 I know I didn't get into individual character break downs here but I feel that if I were to do that for this book it would give too much away. However I do want to take the time to express that I think that Lila Bard is one bad mutha#*%$. I mean at one point I honestly thought she was going to go all Darth Vader on us. That girl is crazy. 
 As I am writing this I have already started A Conjuring of Light and its already insane. I mean I am literally trying not to status update every reaction per page but it is sooooo hard not to. I mean Vicky is throwing everything in the blender here at the beginning and I am 10,000% sure she hasn't hit the frappe button yet. LOL I AM DOOMED :) 
 Alrighty Book Peeps don't forget to check out my other reviews on The Reading Experience and I will see you in the comments. 
 Jo

Gin's at it again, though to be fair she tried really hard to lead a 'peaceful'(ish) life. Sadly after two bozos find it thrilling to try and rob the Pork Pit, well things escalate to the point where she doesn't a choice. Not if she wants to live. And get revenge. 
 Interestingly enough Detective "Clean Cut" Donovan Caine is the character I had the most issues with. I understand he has morals, integrity, yadda yadda. Okay fine. How in the name of daisies did he last as long as he did in Ashland? I can not, for the life of me, fathom of it! To be honest I spent a good deal of the book wondering if he was too good to be true. I kept waiting for the other foot to drop so to speak. I suppose the fact he was rigidly righteous and unrelenting was the other shoe. 
 I felt bad for Gin, but also rather annoyed. She knows Donovan won't change, just as he knows she can't change her past (or present). The two of them are playing at a possible future together. I liked Owen better. He was a reasonable guy. He understood that not everyone, especially for someone who went through the hell Gin went through, can remain spotless. 
 Estep's wit and verve are in full swing, with Gin just as smart-ass as I remembered her. I like that about Gin, she doesn't let the situation crack her. Its a trend in urban fantasy heroines I really appreciate--makes it much more believable when they're surviving brutal physical violence. Sophie, the goth dwarf who works with Gin, was her usual taciturn self. I think for her it was as close to a relief as she would allow that Gin didn't just become Suzy Homemaker. Fletcher wanted a more peaceful life for Gin, but I doubt even he expected her to just let things rest when innocent folks are in trouble. Or when given information about Mab that could help to avenge her family. 
 The third book, Venom, is due out at the end of September and the fourth book, Tangled Threads, is due out May 2011. I suppose, if I have to wait, I will. But honestly I want Gin back quickly; there just isn't enough assassins in my reading diet right now.

This one was really close to five stars. Really close. There are just a few nitpicky things I can say that's wrong with it, but first, the good stuff: 
 -The narrator, Lupe dy Cazaril, is flawed and tormented, but still a good man. He is very likeable and sympathetic, and (view spoiler)[I love that he got a good ending in this book. (hide spoiler)] 
 -The setting and worldbuilding and religion-building, even, were exceptionally well done. I could see the geography of this fictional place in my mind as I read. I could see the people that Cazaril saw, and I believed that they worshipped the Five Gods. This fictitious religion made more sense to me than a lot of factual religion, in some ways. Even the names of things and the politics made perfect sense. 
 -The secondary characters are well-fleshed and also believable, though not all of them are likeable, of course. There's got to be an antagonist to the protagonist, after all. The antagonists here are also believable, apart from the (view spoiler)[purely paranormal aspect of one of them. (hide spoiler)] 
 -Iselle. I love Iselle. She is a strong, intelligent, powerful leader at the ripe old age of 16. She is hell on wheels, bound and determined to save her family and her country without sacrificing herself to the curse. Wonderfully written and I always applaud strong female characters. 
 -The writing is superbly done. Clear and concise but also aesthetically pleasing, Bujold's prose is not bloated or purple or flowery without reason. It's very direct and understandable, but loses none of its style by being so. 
 The one fault I found with this book was the excessive amount of religious philosophizing that seems to be a major pastime for the characters. Their religion seems more real and immediate to them than real life religions are, but we don't need to dwell on it for a good 15% of the book. Once we understand the tenets and practices of it, and Cazaril's role, we don't need to sit in a character's head thinking about it for pages and pages. 
 That was a minor detraction, though, and as I said, this was close to a five star read for me. I don't know if I'll pick up the next book in the series, as it doesn't feature Cazaril, and I don't know that I'd want to visit Chalion without him. But this volume is definitely worth reading, even as a stand-alone. 
 TL;DR: Adult (and not in a yucky way, but not for kids) Fantasy lovers everywhere should give this one a try. It's very good.

Wow!! Its just so wow! Amazing! Where was I all these years and missed the treasure trove of Georgette Heyer books? I absolutely loved Frederica. I lived within the book and when I was not reading it, its incredible characters stayed with me! I don't know whether it has yet been attempted, but Frederica should be made into a motion picture! The characters of Frederica Meriville And the Marquis Vernon Alverstoke are very unique and likeable, especially The Marquis! For all his selfishness, absurdities and immovability for taking efforts to please anyone he is just so so loveable when he just annoys by failing to recognize his own nieces and nephews and when he gets bored and especially with the assumed weak memory! The best part of him is how he copes with the barging of all the Merrivilles in his life and is rather enjoying it! The incident of creation of 'The Baluchistan Hound' is one of my favourite parts of the book! His matter of fact behaviour, the calm he possesses in adverse situations and the way he puts himself out to be of use to Frederica is what touches the heart. He is, until now my favourite Georgette Heyer hero! In fact I took more of his fancy,than perhaps of Fredrica! Frederica on the other hand is a very strong, determined, focused and selfless girl going to extents beyond her reach for her family! A very confident and loving character adored by her younger siblings, though not by all of them all the time! The other characters right from Felix to Jessamy to Charles Trevor to Lady Elizabeth are people who you can't help but love and Lady Buxted just gets on your nerves while her son is just as annoying! 
 Overall, I just never wanted the book to come to an end! It broke my heart! 
 Georgette Heyer was a genius beyond comparison. There is not one part in her books which one may find unrealistic or blotchy or not in the flow; everything just properly falls into place beautifully and creates an canvas which one shall never forget. Perfect period details. Frederica goes to become one of the most loved books owned by me and with which I will never part! Must Read

"At the fourth flight Lila did something unexpected. She stopped to wait for me, and when I reached her she gave me her hand. This gesture changed everything between us forever." p. 22 
 It took me so long to finish this novel, that when I turned the last page, I immediately went back to the beginning. I wasn't sure how this wonderful story had started. I had totally forgotten the prologue - but it all made more sense now that I had finished the whole book. 
 This is the first volume of a trilogy. The third volume was part of the Tournament of Books and I don't think I had heard anything about Ferrante until the list came out for the TOB. I will be getting to the other volumes - Ferrante is a masterful storyteller. 
 I took awhile before I could follow the storyline. I know nothing about Naples, Italy, also very little about Italian culture and there were a lot of characters. However the narrator Elena and her friend Lila are compelling people. Elena tells a good story and her friend is fascinating. I kept reading so I would know what happened to Lila, her family and the neighborhood. Once again, I have found a writer who shows me a world foreign to me, but worth knowing. I am glad that I got to see Elena's world through her eyes. I am looking forward to seeing what happens next.

Definitely in my top ten favorite books. Wonderful storytelling and some of the most relatable characters I've read. I identify with pretty much all of the characters in a lot of ways as well as the situations. My first time living on campus in college is so similar to Cath's; her thoughts, her feelings, making friends, finding love, sharing the same major, just SO MUCH of Cath's experience is my experience, which makes me love this story even more. I graduated from college just last year and Fangirl really took me back, will always take me back every time I reread (it's happening). Such humor, such heart, such everything. I have SO MANY tabs sticking out of this book for all my favorite moments; they're EVERYWHERE!

It was interesting to read this 15 years after it was published. Bryson includes so much commentary about how humans have impacted the environment, and makes so many predictions, that I found myself sometimes looking into how his concerns played out (since we have google now, and everything). I liked his casual, funny writing style, his combination of recounting experience with local history, and his honesty. This book does not make me want to hike the Appalachian Trail.
The Foxman family may be my new favourite dysfunctional family. Read this and laugh, cry, and feel right along side them. Great read!

In some ways, I am still surprised every time I pick up a new Tamora Pierce book. I keep expecting to get the same style of writing in Song of the Lioness and, like most authors, she does not remain stagnant. 
 I say this because Mastiff feels like more of a break than usual from her earlier works. Overall, this series has been very different (and, unlike the Daughter of the Lioness duology, quite good), but the pacing still felt a bit off to me. I kept waiting for things to happen that took an appallingly long time to occur. 
 That being said, I have like Beka Cooper from the beginning and I really do think this trilogy is a welcome addition to the Tortallan stories. Other than pacing, my one quibble is with character. Someone behaves a certain way and it was jarringly out of character to me. Which is odd, because Pierce is usually really REALLY good with characters in character. So this slip was doubly disappointing. 
 Realistically, if you've made it this far with Pierce's books, you'll appreciate Mastiff. It's a master storyteller doing what she does best.

Highly anticipated books like this always scare me. What happens if the author can't take the pressure of writing such an anticipated story and it falls flat? What if it doesn't go the way I WANT it to go? There are no guarantees and I was both extremely excited and extremely scared to start reading. 
 Another fear of mine was the fact that knowing this book had the big Ghost reveal, this story would be centered around the Psy. In the past, the psy-only books have not been my favorites. They lack some of the intensity that the changelings bring to the world. 
 I shouldn't have worried. I was hooked from the very first line. I wrote my review with names in it and then have changed them to HERO and HEROINE in case people don't want to know. 
 There are some series that always have a tough leader, a guy that makes those sometimes ruthless decisions that go against most morals. He may seem heartless but there is always a purpose to his actions. The last one I remember that caught my interest as much was Jonas from the Breeds series by Lora Leigh. But after that, it's been the HERO. The HERO, who should be psy and Silent, but has so much bottled up passion he could melt you at his feet. The HERO, who is ruthless in the pursuit of what he wants and won't leave anything or anyone who gets in his path standing. 
 Then focus all that intensity on the woman he loves. OMG!!!!! Ms. Singh, I am in awe of what you've done with this story. From all the layers to the HERO we get to unfold, to the story of his one true love. This is a second chance at love story. The girl he fell in love with as a kid and was taken from him. Brutally. The one he's been searching for since. For such a hard shell on the exterior, I couldn't help but melt at the softness inside of him. 
 The HERO is, in one word, INTENSE. There's so much he has learned to keep bottled up and as that shell cracks and all that intensity spills out..... Be prepared to fall in love. Changelings have nothing on the HERO. 
 The HEROINE was also perfect for him. The perfect balance to his intensity. Nurturing, soft, but strong at the core. Able to stand on her own. Able to fight for her man. Able to heal him. 
 Then there's the Ghost. On this subject, I'm keeping my mouth shut. However, I will say that I found the big reveal a bit....anticlimactic. After waiting to find out who the Ghost is for so long, I was expecting bombs going off, cities collapsing and the Ghost riding in on some white horse to save the race. I don't know. I wanted something epic. Instead, we find out as almost an afterthought. And that's all I'm going to say. No more. 
 Nalini Singh's writing has the ability to paint a picture in my mind. Beautifully crafted words that flow and let the imagination run wild. And for the span of time it took me to read this book, I was living it. 
 I wish I could give this book 10 Stars! Every single page of this book is packed with intensity. It's enthralling, all consuming, and mind blowing. Yes, I was thoroughly blown away! This will be one I want to re-read and hold dear.

I started this with some trepidation, because humor based on gender stereotypes is rarely my thing. It sounded fun though, so I gave it a try -- and it turned out to be a lot of fun, as well as sweet and unexpectedly wise. 
 Johnny is a really good guy, who somehow rarely gets credit for his stellar qualities from women. The traits that other men love in him, like being good at sports and able to fix junker cars, always seem to lead women to one conclusion: "asshole. " They rarely notice that he's considerate, generous, warm-hearted, chivalrous and at least makes an effort to remember to put the seat back down. 
 When Johnny meets a woman who seems like she might just possibly like him, he's determined not to mess it up this time. And seeking advice from pretty much anyone who'll give it, he performs a make-over, becoming "John" (because "y" ending names are too little-boyish) who likes wine instead of beer and opera instead of sports. What happens next is partially incredibly obvious and partially a real surprise. 
 This is a light story -- lighthearted, lightly characterized, lightly over-the-top. The beginning description of Johnny's adolescence, in his first-person narrative, made me feel like I was reading YA -- and actually I think young adults could love this story. (There's some swearing but no graphic sex.) It's very funny in a wry sort of way, and though there is some ridiculous situational humor, it's not what entirely drives the book: in one memorable scene, John takes his date to an opera that turns out to be put on by a farm family in a hayloft, but they just go with it and have a really good time. 
 I think what I liked best about the story is that it's essentially non-judgmental. Although Johnny's "manly," low-brow tastes are embraced, he discovers he actually likes some of the new things he's tried -- but more importantly, he discovers that "things like who loves sports and who loves GH (General Hospital) and who loves both... none of that stuff mattered so long as, somehow, you saw down into the essence of the other person and they saw you." 
 It's hard to categorize this book: it's not traditional romance, not exactly YA, certainly not realistic fiction. Its most obvious category is humor. But I think romance readers will also enjoy it; I certainly did.

2.25 stars. I was definitely anticipating this book, but I can't really remember why. I thought that I liked Red Queen quite a bit (I gave it 4 stars here, but left no comments in my review), but a year later I could remember absolutely nothing about it, and I had to read a recap before starting this book. 
 A lot of my thoughts while reading Glass Sword were colored by The Hunger Games, as I think this was definitely a sort of Hunger Games-wannabe. Mare, the main character, felt the weight of the world, but I wasn't exactly sure why she was feeling all the pressure. There were a lot of people who were more important than her that should have been feeling that weight, yet she was self-centered enough to think that everything ever was her responsibility. I think that was my main problem, was that I didn't buy Mare's angst. And she had a lot of it. There were no light-hearted moments, and there definitely could of been. 
 I liked the supporting characters a lot, but they were all wrapped up in the haze of Mare's self-centeredness that they didn't shine through as much as they could have. 
 Also, I found the writing style consistently... weird, I guess, is the right word. It was written in first person present tense (which is probably why I was reminded of Hunger Games), and it took me out of the story. It's a matter of personal preference, but I am not a huge fan of present tense writing. There were also quite a few instances where things might have been better left unsaid (and let the reader infer what was going on). There was one instance where Mare thought, "By now, I should know better than to lie. But a lie is what they need to carry on, and if my deceit saves even one of them, it is worth the cost to my soul," but the whole chapter had been telegraphing this idea, so by the time I read that line, I just rolled my eyes.

 Then, of course, there's the originality - it's definitely, as others have said, an amalgam of lot's of other futuristic/dystopian/fantasy books (specifically, the Red Rising trilogy), but I don't think that would have bothered me all that much if the execution had been better. A book that leaves you feeling all kind of things. Feelings of tingling, shivers, satisfaction and in awe. 
 THE PLOT 
 Maybe Someday is a book about a a girl who faced feelings of betrayal after finding out that the two closest people to her had cheated on her, lied to her and deceived her for the past two years of her life. Feeling that she's lost everything, her best friend, boyfriend and apartment, Sydney finds nowhere to go but stand in the pouring rain crying at how her life had turned up side down in a blink of an eye. She isn't as alone as she thought she was when she finds herself sleeping on her neighbour's couch. Since that night, Sydney's life takes a turn of moving on, learning how to trust and love again only to find moments of guilt, shame, moments of intense want and need. Sydney fights the urge not to do what her boyfriend and best friend once did to her. Does she fail? 
 THE CHARACTERS 
 The characters in this book are amazingly written. The way Sydney and Ridge fall in love through writing music and playing of the guitar had me fall in love with the love they had for each other. The guilt and shame that came with loving each other had me want to tell Ridge the wise words of Johnny Depp 
 If you love two people at the same time, choose the second. Because if you really loved the first one, you wouldn't have fallen for the second. 
 The characters in the book brought me moments of pain, laughter, feelings of angst and sympathy. I was easily able to connect to the characters. 
 THE WRITING 
 I loved how this book was written from both the point of view of Ridge and Sydney. There were moments I really wanted to know what the other was thinking or feeling and Colleen Hoover was able to do that. She gave me the satisfaction of being able to read both their minds, to feel what they're both feeling and wanting. If this book was written from Sydney's POV only I think I wouldn't have enjoyed it as much as I do now. 
 I love, love, love this book. Thank you Colleen for writing such an amazing piece.

 Since the 1300s Timbuktu in central Mali has been a center of learning. The city sits at the southern edge of the Sahara Desert and on the banks of the Niger River. 
 This made it popular crossroads for people from many cultures to meet. There were many universities here and intellectual debate was popular. The city became known for its Islamic scholarship. Thousands of manuscripts were written and studied here. Some of them were elaborately decorated. 
 But there have been periods of invasion and anti-intellectualism too. During these times the manuscripts were hidden around the region. By the time of the European invasions, the existence of the manuscripts was not known to outsiders. That led to quotes like these: 
 "Perhaps in the future, there will be some African history to teach. But at present there is none. There is only the history of Europeans in Africa. The rest is darkness." 
 -- British historian Hugh Trevor-Roper 1963 
 After Mali won its independence efforts were made to start collecting the manuscripts in Timbuktu again. Abdel Kader Haidara's father spent his life collecting manuscripts. In his will he chose Abdel to carry on his work but he wasn't interested. Ten years passed before a library in Timbuktu convinced him to start buying manuscripts again. He was so successful that by the early 21st century there were 45 libraries in Timbuktu with manuscript collections. Then Al Qaeda came. 
 The librarians knew that the manuscripts would be a target. After all, they were written in a very progressive Islamic area. There were manuscripts with sexual advice and rulings on how to treat women fairly. They decided that it was time for the manuscripts to hide again. 
 It was a big job. There were around 350,000 fragile manuscripts in city in 2012. How do you get them somewhere safe when travel is restricted? 
 I really enjoyed the part of this book that was about the manuscripts. About half of it though was about the history of the Islamist uprising in Mali. That drug for me. There was kidnapping and crime and torture but I wanted to know about the manuscripts. 
 This book shows the importance of honoring the history of the a place. I like reading about Henry Louis Gates' trip to Mali and his reaction to seeing the manuscripts. He had always been told that black people didn't have a historical culture or anything to be proud of in their past. Seeing these works of scholarship and art made by black people touched him deeply.

I still really enjoyed it though, and I'm looking forward to reading the sequel.

This book...I'm still trying to wrap my mind around it. It is beautifully written, and Suma has a unique voice. After finishing it, I'm still not sure what it was that I read. There is not a Eureka! moment where everything clicks into place...instead, you are as confused as you were when you first started getting into the story. 
 I kept expecting it to be an elaborate dream - as does the Chloe one point in the book. I was waiting for Chloe to wake up in a psych ward somewhere. But it does not turn out to be a dream. Chloe and Ruby are interesting characters. They are both damaged, flawed human beings connected by a sisterly love that borders on obsession. Ruby is an indelible force; a tempest of a character. On the surface, besides being attractive, she doesn't have a lot going for her - but, as her sister points out, she is the woman every man wants to be with and every girl wants to be. The word no is not used on her. She can release a horde of balloons with secret messages written on them, and then have those messages acted on. She is the only woman who can deny the forces of life and death. 
 Chloe, in comparison, is a pale shade next to her sister. Throughout the story it is commented on that she resembles Ruby more and more, not just in looks but in attitude as well. This is the highest compliment that can be paid to Chloe. She wants nothing more than to shine in her sister's eyes and have her love. She understands Ruby like no one else; she is the only one who truly has Ruby's love. Yet, she pushes against the restraints that Ruby suddenly puts on her - she ignores curfew, she ignores her advise to stay away from a boy, she ignores the rule about not leaving town...and all with disastrous results. What does become apparent throughout the novel is that like Nick from The Great Gatsby, Chloe is an unreliable narrator - everything is through her POV which is almost borderline crazy. 
 Soma's writing makes it almost impossible to put this book down. You must keep flipping the pages, trying to make sense of this nonsensical situation. How can a dead girl be alive? How can one girl control so much with her will? Who is Ruby? Who is Chloe? And what importance does the drowned village of Olive play? 
 Imaginary Girls is viewed through a murky lens...as if you were swimming underwater and trying to peer into the depths. The more you try to see, the less you really do. It is as if the water of the reservoir has not only flooded the sleepy town in the Catskills but has started leaching into the pages. It is, in short, a work of art. It is like nothing you have ever read...and while your questions won't be answered, you know that the story couldn't end any other way.

This is my second time reading this book. And oh. My heart is broken all over again. But damn it. This sequel is so perfect. I cannot. It is amazing. But it is also the most painful one to read, and some things make me angry, yet I can't help but love it so much. I'm thrilled that I finally got to re-read this book. So, so happy that I have been accepted for an eARC of The Winner's Kiss, which I will be reading next. I'm so excited to finally get to read it, after waiting so long. But I'm also so very nervous about the heartbreak. 
 I'm unsure what I should say about this book this time. It has been just over a year since I first read it. And I haven't been able to stop thinking about it. I hadn't really forgotten anything, except for the look of Roshar. Whom I adore. But yeah. I really loved reading this book for the second time. Though it still breaks my heart. There is so much hurt. So many lies. No love at all. It hurts my heart. Yet this book is so well written and so interesting and I love all the characters so much. I can't help but love it the most. 
 This book takes place after the ending of book one. Kestrel is engaged. And oh, how I loved reading about it. Because I hated it so much, lol. The prince was such an interesting character, though. I loved how he was in love with someone else, though it was so heartbreaking too. I loved how he and Kestrel slowly became friends. I liked him. I'm glad there wasn't even a hint of a love triangle. There never is in this series. Just so you know. Not much romance in this, but no triangle either. Just a little bit drama. 
 And ahh. All the drama. I really cannot stand drama. But I couldn't help but love it in this book. Because I understood it all so well. Though, well, I'm still angry with Arin. For how he threw away the knife. Ugh. I will never get over it, lol. For how he didn't understand things. But I'm also angry with Kestrel, for lying so much. Yet I can't be angry with her for long. Because I understood her the most. She had so much to lose. And oh, how she broke my heart. She risked so much. She did so much. She is the sweetest girl. 
 I must say that the ending of this book is still my favorite thing. It is so brutal. So amazingly written. I loved every moment. Well, except for that Arin moment, hmph. It still bothers me, lol. But Kestrel. The scene with her dad. I cannot. It was heartbreaking. I do not forgive him. I just don't. I'm so curious to read about it in book three. I hope it will be epic. But yeah. I still don't forgive him. So mean. But oh, how it was interesting to read about. So many dead people in this book. And interesting things happen. 
 I don't know what to say. The writing is all kinds of stunning. The plot is exciting. I love the difference between the people in this world. I loved getting to know some of the other people too, like Roshar. He was awesome. And I want more of him in the next book. There are so many characters in this one. A little bit of Ronan and Jess. I loved them both in the first book. In this one, not so much. I hated how they both treated Kestrel. I just can't stand it. I'm sorry. But I am not happy with Jess at all. Hmph. 
 I cannot deal with how amazing this book is. And how heartbreaking too. So many bad things happen. Especially that ending. There are so many lies. But the truth is just under the surface of those lies. And it hurt my heart. They both love each other so much. Sniffs. Book three must be amazing. It must. But anyway. I can't say more about this stunning book. Just that I love it the most. And I adore Marie. And I cannot wait to read whatever she writes next. I'm so glad I re-read this book right now. Read it. Now.

I really loved this book. I like the era in which it was set. I also like Margaret Atwood's writing when it is not set in the future. One of my favorite books of the calendar year, even if it was read in January.

This is quite the disturbing little story. I'm a big fan of sour candy, have been since I was a kid, but I'll never be able to eat one again without thinking about this story. Well done Mr. Burke. The dynamic between the kid and the main character was perfect, and I'm left wondering if the kid really knew the depths of what he was a part of. The sheer hopelessness and desperation of the main character was palpable. Very enjoyable read.

VAIN by Fisher Amelie is a beautiful story about redemption and finding love and home in an unlikely place. 
 "No one can know sincere happiness, Sophie, without first having known sorrow. One can never appreciate the enormity and rareness of such a fiery bliss without seeing misery, however unfair that may be." 
 The pacing was perfect although, the beginning was a bit redundant trying to make a point. It was a bit heavy handed in the "moral of the story" and I felt the first few chapters there was a lot of telling me how everyone looked, telling me what they did and telling me what to feel. To the point I really did hate the MC but I think it worked for the story because you needed to hate Sophie so that she could change. 
 I am very forgiving of Indie reads (like I mentioned before) and I am inclined to agree with the 5 star rating this novel has on Amazon. 
 Part of the story reminded me of the movie "Out of Africa" with it's vivid description of Africa and the epic love story that blooms in a devastated country. Only with a happy ending. :) 
 This book is shelved in the adult fiction but I really think this would be a good Young Adult to New Adult read as well. Beautiful story, moving prose...well done Ms. Amelie!

Ok... let's just push pause for a minute here! Hard Bitten is the fourth installment of the Chicagoland Vampires series. I was impressed at how well-crafted this urban crime mystery story was. It was really a lot of fun to play detective with Merit and follow clues using your gut instinct. However, I think this whole book can be boiled down to one main event right at the end. 
 O MY GOSH! WHAT IS THIS!? I'M SHOCKED! 
 Before we get into that ending let's talk about the rest of the story first. Merit is still finding her place as a woman and vampire and thus becoming someone she never thought she would be. There's something to be said about rolling with the punches but Merit goes beyond that and is thriving. While Merit does kick a fair amount of ass she also has a vulnerable side. It's so amazing to have a heroine with good self-esteem. She consistently makes good decisions and has a sense of integrity that is remarkably kind. All of these attributes make me adore her even more. Even when she's making decisions that usually would bother me (IE: holding Ethan at arm's length for self-preservation) she doesn't annoy me in the slightest. Perhaps it's because she's not doing it just to be stubborn for the sake of being stubborn. She has well thought out reasons for making these decisions. 
 On a side note, I just realized one thing that seems to be completely lacking in this series. I haven't been able to find one instance of sexism anywhere. The main character is a woman and no one bats an eye at it. She not a strong "woman" she's a strong person who also happens to be a woman. Personally, I love the distinction. No one tells her she can't do something because she's a woman. None of the men try to "protect" her because she doesn't need it. Is Ethan protective of her? Yes, but that doesn't make him stop her from doing her job. I'm not sure why it took so long for me to catch on to the feminism that's inherently a part of this series but now that I'm aware of it, I LOVE it. 
 Also, the humor still remains. There are really great one liners in here. Before I get into that ENDING I'll just quote one of the lines that made me laugh to prove my point... 
 This time, my voice was softer. "Give me something to go on, here. What kind of black magic are we talking? Elphaba, Wicked Witch of the West-type stuff or Slytherin-type stuff?" 
 OK... THAT FREAKING ENDING! This will all be in a spoiler so I can just speak can just speak candidly. (view spoiler)[ Ethan and Merit are finally getting back on track with their epic romance and then boom... ETHAN GETS KILLED BY CELINA WHILE SAVING MERIT'S LIFE! What. In. The. Actual. Fuck? While I appreciate the mic-drop ballsyness of it, I just can't get over how bonkers it is. Obviously Ethan's not going to stay dead since he's in all the rest of the series but I'm not sure how that's getting fixed. I have some theories though. Gabriel did share that vision with Merit where she saw green eyes that were like Ethan's but also not so perhaps what that means is that he will come back but in a new body? Maybe it's something Mallory will be involved with? She did go on a ghost hunt with Simon so maybe there could be some magic to bring his soul back or something. Speaking of which, I don't like Simon. Not sure if that's because I'm just suspicious of everyone or if he will actually be a black hat in the future. I don't know, I just think I'm feeling black magic vibes from him. I had a feeling the mayor was up to something. Everything just kept circling back to him so often that it started to feel like the proverbial smoking gun. Maybe he's a dark sorcerer or maybe he's a fairy? We learned that the fairies hate humans and only hate vamps slightly less. Who knows? I doubt it's the last we will see of him. Also, I'm glad Merit got to stake Celina. I hope she doesn't get brought back too. Ugh... I'm over her. (hide spoiler)] 
 OK now I'm on to Drink Deep so see how this whole mess in the ending is going to get sorted out. It's probably going to be insane!

A fun book that is reasonably well written. Hunger Games meets Gladiator. Combines sci-fi elements with ancient Rome (weird, but it seemed to work hard.) The first book definitely sets up the trilogy while still feeling like a complete book by itself. I will definitely read the others in the series when I get a chance. I had only two complaints which happen to be spoilerish (view spoiler)[ Within the first sentence they introduce Eo, the main character's wife, it's obvious she's going to die. I was curious to read this book, because for the most part, Luke is absent or mentioned in passing in the Journey to The Force Awakens books so far. He's not visibly in the trailer and mystery surrounds his role in the upcoming movie. So I looked forward to getting some hints or clarification through this book.

 Well, honestly, all this book did was confuse me further. A character from Aftermath shows up. A villain I don't recognize with a staff that can take on a light saber does too. And a young character whom I gather from the epilogue plays some role in the movie pops in to say hello. 
 Looking forward to clarification from the movie.
