3/5 I liked some aspects, but the rest needs a lot of work. 
 Before I begin my review, I'd like to say that when you read a book, it's probably not best to immediately write a review on it rambling on about how amazing this book is and how everyone in the world MUST read it. Honestly, most of the time, you just get over the phase of obsession with the book (eventually) and you can see it more clearly for what it really is and begin to see its flaws. Therefore, your opinion on a book can often change - especially after you read other books. My opinion on this book has certainly changed over time - I've long passed the stage of blind obsession and after reading many other books I've finally created my real review of this book: 
 This book was a little different and I don't really think it fits fully into the YA genre for the following reasons: 
 Firstly: 
 > The way that Hazel and Augustus think is NOT the same as your everyday teenager so they aren't very relatable to the majority. They are, like somebody else said "they're like 60 year olds trapped in teenagers bodies" the way that they talk and think is nothing at all like a normal teenager and everything they say seems to have been planned out perfectly - oh and another thing, quote: "Hazel and Augustus are the same person" their personalities are exactly the same they are pretty much a male and female version of each other. 
 > It's about 2 teens who have cancer, so it might be a little tough to understand how they're feeling if you don't have cancer but if you do have a good sense of empathy you'll be able to put yourself in their shoes and it really does give an insight as to what it's like having cancer. 
 > If you do have a good sense of empathy (or an overbearing sense of empathy like me) you will not enjoy reading this book because you will cry A LOT. 
 > For the older teens who'll be able to understand it better: their philosophy on life, death and terminal cancer is quite interesting. In that sense, however, this book is probably better for adults or older teens. 
 So, to sum things up: 
 It was well written. The storyline engaged me and it was a page-turner. It also opened my eyes up to their philosophies on life and death and helped me understand cancer more. I guess we kind of pity people with cancer and think "hey this person deserves something more than people who don't have cancer" and "this person is super brave for having cancer" but really, they're just being themselves, dealing with the issues they have and they're no different than you or me. HOWEVER,the characters and the way they talk and think just let me down a lot because it's utterly UNREALISTIC and cliched due to how perfectly planned everything is. Overall, the ideas addressed in this novel are interesting and thought-provoking although maybe it would have been better if the main characters were two professors because it honestly won't work out any other way... but that's just my opinion.

 The Duke and I 
 is the first novel in Julia Quinn's Bridgerton family series. It features Daphne Bridgerton and Simon Basset's story. 
 Daphne Bridgerton is the eldest girl in the Bridgerton family of eight. She wants to get married and have a family more than anything. Her problem is that all the eligible men view her as normal. Then she met Simon, Duke of Hastings, and her brother's best friend. Simon had troubled and unhappy childhood, as his father had rejected him due to his speech impediment. He just came home from traveling the world and was not prepared for the attention his new title brought to his personal life as ambitious, marriage-minded mothers flocked to his side to introduce their debutante daughters. Set not to marry and have children, Simon went to Daphne and comes up with an idea of faking their interest to each other to keep women and men at bay. It actually worked. Until one of them fell in love... 
 When I started this book, I didn't really know what to expect. And then after reading a few chapters, I felt glued to the pages. I'm thrilled to say that it left a big happy satisfied smile on my face. 
 Daphne is such a strong heroine and a perfect match for Simon. I loved how she helped him see how he is a better person than his father. As for Simon, I admired him. Despite his past, he was able to become a better person. I loved how comfortable they were with each other from the beginning. Not exactly love at first sight, but something that develops into much more than what he should feel for his best friend's sister. With his past, it takes someone really special to deal with a guy like Simon. Let's face it - he's got issues. But Daphne is the perfect woman for the job. 
 Julia Quinn sure knows how to use her words! And just as in her past works, the banter between these two is incredible. The dialogue between them is fun and witty, their relationship development is strong, and the chemistry between the two of them is fabulous. 
 All in all, 
 The Duke and I 
 is a wonderful, engaging, emotional, utterly enjoyable, and unforgettable romance that you will surely enjoy. Definitely recommended for historical lovers.

Look Again caught my eye at the grocery store and I tossed it in my cart on a whim. I haven't done that in a long time - all my books come in the smiling Amazon box. The premise was intriguing and the last book I read by Scottoline was "can't put it down" good, so I couldn't pass it up. 
 The book was good overall, and lived up to my expectations. The pacing is expertly crafted so that in quieter moments in the story, the story flows while Ellen's panicked moments, the writing is clipped and frantic to set the mood. That's a real strength of Scottoline's writing and makes her books (at least the two I've read) so good. 
 The premise, that an adoptive mother sees what appears to be *her son's* picture on the missing child mailer and then has to struggle with what to do with her suspicions, is a scarily realistic scenario. It lends itself well not only to the thrill of mystery solving, but also allows for a thorough exploration of parenthood. Particularly motherhood. 
 There are some weaknesses. I don't care for how the child is written, there's a lot of shouting and giggling from the character. He just didn't come alive for me. I felt the parts he was directly in dragged. 
 There is *a lot* going on in this story. It did seem to fit together in the end, but I think the story could have been simpler. And for the love of Pete, there is no reason to throw in a romance! 
 It wrapped up too neatly at the end, with far too many convenient occurrences. That was pretty annoying. I hate when authors cheat themselves out of the corner they wrote themselves into. 
 Overall though, this book gave me exactly what I was looking for. It was a page turner and I couldn't wait to see how it turned out.

I haven't been this happy since Desiree Hartsock accepted Chris Siegfried's proposal in the most dramatic season finale of The Bachelorette ever. Just Kidding. But seriously, I don't mean to be a total fangirl or to sound like I'm 16 years old - but I really can't imagine a better night than sitting down with some wine to watch The Bachelorette finale or reading Kiera Cass' The Selection series. Okay, hopefully the wine graduated me to at least 21. Right? 
 So if it isn't clear, I LOVED every flipping second of THE ELITE. From the first chapter I was captivated and couldn't put it down until the very last page. And now I'm staring at the expected publication for book #3 in a stupor - May 2014?!?!? I didn't even know there was a 3rd book until I read this one, now I find out I have to wait almost an entire year??? 
 URGH! Okay so other than my frustration that I have to wait until 2014 to get my happily ever after with what I anticipate to be a TON of frustration along the way, I cannot say enough amazing things about this book. Actually, this is going to be the strangest series of compliments ever - in that they sound like I'm complaining about everything when really Kiera Cass knows exactly what she's doing. 
 America is enfuriating - but perfect in her own obnoxiously stubborn, blinders up, nearsighted way! She gets so caught up in every little thing that Maxon says or does and blows it completely out of proportion, but you know what??? She also CARES! Like, a lot. About Illea, the caste system, the monarchy's role, the responsibility she's undertaking if she marries Maxon, everything. I finally opened my eyes and realized that while I might not agree with the way America approaches things or how stressfully long it takes her to give Maxon an answer, at least she doesn't just get caught up in the "winning" aspect of the selection process and blindly barrel forward without considering what she's saying yes to. 
 Aspen. I kept waiting for him to do something that would allow me to say, SEE AMERICA??? He's not the one! Let him get caught kissing a maid or be oblivious to the importance of America's potential role in the country's future, something! But Kiera Cass wouldn't listen! She just kept writing this great guy that was supportive and understanding, patient and good. And finally, finally, I got it. Because it's not that big a deal if America picks Maxon over Aspen if he's really a jerk. It's only a sign of how true her feelings are if she has two great options and picks Maxon. So yah, I was wrong about that too. 
 And Maxon? He's not perfect and he's sometimes just a guy needing to be loved or cared for or paid attention to, but he's also endearing and sweet and he has greatness inside of him and he's just smart and quiet enough to know he has to be patient and calculating about how he approaches it. And I fell more in love with him by the minute. (Even the novella #0.5 that I complained about because I thought it added nothing to the overall story and if anything just made America look worse in her selfishness, I now realize had its own purpose in allowing the reader to see who Maxon is and why, just in case we were as blind as America at the beginning of this book.) 
 I had missed these kisses, so quiet, so sure. I knew that, in my whole life, if I married Aspen or someone else, no one would ever make me feel this way. It wasn't like I made his world better. It was like I was his world. It wasn't some explosion; it wasn't fireworks. It was a fire, burning slowly from the inside out. 
 We really didn't see that much of Aspen or Maxon in THE ELITE; a lot of the book was America's struggles, but honestly, I didn't feel like I was lacking for anything! Kiera Cass is building something epic and she's doing it one book at a time. I loved the world, the depth of the dystopian society Kiera Cass has created, and the seamless way she interweaves the dystopian world with the romantic journey and keeps everything in perfect balance. 
 I couldn't be more excited about THE ONE and will most likely be foaming at the mouth by the time it arrives!

Spell Bound is an amazing climatic conclusion to Hawkins's series and it did not disappoint in the slightest. The characters are also just as awesome as before, I loved seeing their dynamics and I simply loved their personalities which always shone beautifully through in both the drastic situations and the "relaxed" ones.  The characterization was even better than the previous books where it reached the point that you could understand their thinking even though you couldn't always predict their actions. This is why the ending was so great because it answers all of your questions about the characters you've grown to love and/or hate, tying all the loose ends together while making sure no one is forgotten. But you don't just find your answers about the characters; all your misunderstandings and unanswered questions towards the plot are put right and you'll look back thinking "oh I hadn't even realised that was important" or "that was so subtle and incredibly clever".

She is the kind of heroine that you can not only look to but relate to, and with her snarky comments you can't help but love. She's heroic without realising it and since you read the story from her POV it really only hits when other people talk about her. 
 Anyway this series has captured my undying attention from the get go with its enigmatic characters and thrilling plot, and the ending even as bitter sweet as it was left me with a smile on my face. Sure the series wasn't perfect but up until the last page I had no ground-breaking complaints, and my only complaint was that it was the last page! Even the death(s) I felt were done well and I almost feel bad because I know I shouldn't have presumed otherwise but this was a huge surprise. It was pulled off by the way the surviving characters dealt with everything, and the death(s) turned out honourable so I had new respect for the character(s). 
 The Hex Hall series are light and quirky reads combined with a lot of action and mystery through the plot and its characters. The main plot of this book - the "fill-in boyfriend" plot - was executed well enough. While mostly predictable, fake relationships turning real will always hold my attention. The chemistry between Gia and Hayden was written really well and I couldn't help but smile at some of their interactions. I thought that their flirting and the ups and downs of their story felt real and convincing. This isn't the part of the story I have a problem with. 
 The reason why this is a three-star rating and not anything higher is because of some of the other things that the author tried to do that I did not think were as successful. I wasn't the biggest fan of all of the girl versus girl drama. It seemed that Jules was written solely for the part of villain and, because of that, I enjoyed the book so much less when she was present. I think that this sort of thing is absolutely a reality in high school; however, even these "real life villains" have more to them. Sure, Jules has a relationship with her mom that isn't perfect but we never really delve into this, never recieve any information that will give her substance. The betrayal that the friends felt when they found out about real Bradley and fill-in Bradley and the entire lie was enough of a catalyst for this plot - it could have done without the "Jules is evil" thing. 
 Additionally, I can appreciate the commentary on social media gratification and obsession that West presented here but, again, it was just too surface-level. If there is going to be this huge conflict between Gia and her brother and herself about how she is the person that he presented in his film then, ideally, we would have seen that person throughout the book. Sure, Gia tweeted a few times and there were some small references to social media but, when it comes down to it, I didn't buy into this subplot. After all, this whole fill-in boyfriend thing started when Gia wanted to prove her friends wrong in real life - she was looking for approval from them in the flesh, not from them online. I can kind of see how this subplot is justified but I just wanted it to be fleshed out a lot more. 
 Finally, and this is just a little thing, I actually just wanted to see more of Bradley! There is some back story to their relationship but I wanted more. I think it could have been interesting to have one last confrontation between the two after her lies get exposed. 
 I liked Gia's growth as a character. I liked how she realized that, maybe, her friendships just had to start changing as she moved onto new things in her life. Bec was a gem and her and Bradley's mom was just lovely. Gia's parents could have been explored more but, overall, I think West presented a solid portrait of what this family is like. This was a very quick and entertaining read that I probably read too much into instead of just enjoying such a cute fake relationship plot!

 Let me say this before anything else, I am not disappointed with this last installment of The Girl of Fire and Thorns. I did, however, have issues with it. 
 Firstly, I found it so hard to get back into Rae Carson's world. Sure, I know the main characters Elisa and Hector, but the secondary ones? I was thisclose to forgetting them completely. Plus, there was no recap of any sort, and because of that, I didn't enjoy it as much as I wanted to. All I could remember from the second book was the last few chapters - that Hector was abducted, and that Elisa was determined to rescue him. That's it. 
 Next, in the first few chapters of this installment, there was no Hector-Elisa moment. So, yeah... it was kind of dull for me - having no romantic scenes whatsoever. I think that is my main issue with the first few chapters of this book. There were, however, a few chapters told in Hector's POV. So, those made it a little better. 
 But everything just got a whole lot better, more interesting, more romantic, once they got Hector back... 
 Hector. Hector. Hector. What can I say about him that hasn't been said already? Hector is truly a knight in shining armor. He puts others before himself. He is respected. He's very protective of Elisa. Everything about him is just so... masculine. He's everything I want in a fantasy hero. But probably, my favorite character I the slave child Mula. She's a new character, but I was immediately drawn to her. Her childlike honesty and innocence is just so refreshing and comedic at times. She blurts out what goes into her head. 
 The story in general is very similar to an Indiana Jones movie - scorpions, traps, all those other things. It's safe to say that if you like those adventure stories, then you would enjoy this one. 
 Honestly, I found the story dull for the first half. I kept putting it down. But, like I said, everything got better once Hector joined Elisa's adventure. With that, the second book is still the best for me. 
 I expected more romance here because the second book was romance-abundant. And it annoys me that my expectations weren't met. Elisa and Hectors chemistry in the second book was really great, and so I was expecting more... um... one on one action. But the book focused more on their journey rather than on the romance. This is not to say that there's no romance at all. There was. I just expected more kissing and loving and romancing. 
 The writing, however, was exceptionally good. And the setting was interesting, having a Hispanic touch. All in all, it's good enough, just not what I expected it to be.

Barnes is leading us by the nose basically from the opening pages and I love how cluelessly oblivious I was to it all. It is still just as funny, clever, and I'm once again in awe of this amazing female lead and how strong this story is without a requiring a romance element to distract, provide angst or to flip the pages in anticipation of.  And it's not that my mind is blown any less by the writing or the events, it's just that hindsight and perspective and understanding has left me with more questions than I had the first time. Or rather, questions I hadn't been able to formulate in my excitement over the ending, too overwhelmed by it all, whereas now.. now I'm thinking, hmm. And I hope it's questions that have yet-to-be-revealed answers and not convenient loopholes or coincidences. 
 Seeing as I have THE LONG GAME in my possession as I type this, I have hopes that the sequel delivers these particulars to me. But also.. I'm just excited to finally have more of Tess and the gang. 
 Merged review: 
 "This thriller YA is Scandal meets Veronica Mars." 
 Um, you had me at Veronica Mars. You would've had me sooner, marketing folks, however I've never seen a moment of Scandal but I'm now thinking maybe I should get on that pronto stat. 
 This book was everything I never knew I wanted. Well okay, I've always wanted these things but it's rare they all come together in such an incredible kick ass fun clever heartbreaking twisted way. What does THE FIXER have that makes it so awesome, you ask? Let me tell you. 
 - a badass independent intelligent heroine who is taken from the only life she's known and forced to adapt to something new and unknown, and manages to do it mostly on her own. Tess knows who she is, what she stands for as an individual, and never struggles with that awareness. 
 - a brilliant cast of very different characters, with their own strengths and weaknesses and secrets. half of whom are supporting Tess and half of whom are working against her. 
 - a tightly paced thrilling plot that will keep you guessing, and likely guessing wrong, to the very end. 
 - heartbreakingly emotional scenes that nearly made me cry (but not of the romantic variety). 
 --> there is NO LOVE ANGST HERE people. no love triangle, no love interests, and only the slightest bit of flirting -- and it's not even acknowledged by our leading lady. Tess doesn't need a boy. and Barnes doesn't need that extra drama to fuel her characters, or her plot, and this book is wicked strong as a result. 
 ---> for once we have a book where young people, who have just met, have no interest in jumping each other. they just want to stay alive and take down the masterminds behind a government conspiracy. you know, as one does in highschool. 
 - politics! American ones. very detailed and complex but still very interesting, and not too hard to follow, even for an ignorant Canadian like myself. 
 - humour. I was literally laughing out loud on MULTIPLE occasions (Asher, always Asher). 
 - an excellent ending that wraps up enough to satisfy but also reveals so much that is still unclear, setting up a sequel brilliantly. 
 - if the YA classification is putting you off, I'm here to reassure you that this did not feel YA; it was a very adult mystery that just happened to involve teens. 
 - in. tense. seriously intense. I had no idea how serious and large this book would feel. epic. 
 - twists. this book is more tangled than the cord of my iPod's earbuds. but unlike my headphones I LOVED this tangled web. 
 And I can't wait to get caught up in more in next year's sequel THE LONG GAME. This was my very first read by Barnes but it certainly won't be my last.

 Rating: 2 of 5 
 I'm really disappointed with this book. It's cheesy and I have a hard time with the characterization. There's also a bit of an over dramatic flare throughout the whole thing that I'm just not getting on board with. SJM places a lot of importance on her main characters and I have a hard time taking them seriously half the time. 
 I understand what this book is trying to say and I really appreciate that message. I like the idea of moving past a first love, one that's controlling and manipulative. In this way, I really like the book. I love the idea of that because it's something you rarely see in novels. People change and love can be an awful thing when it forces you to endure abuse. 
 But on that note, I have to speak about the things that I didn't like. 
 Feyre was the main problem I had with this book. I liked her self discovery and the way she realized she had value as a person. Even so, I couldn't stand her anger and her over reactions at things that didn't warrant such a thing. When Rhysand didn't tell her that they were mates and she stormed off, leaving him in the dirt. What the fuck? You don't do that to someone you love, no matter how angry. He nearly died. This selfishness is shown throughout the book a million other times. And Rhys just forgives it. If it were him doing such a thing, I'm sure Feyre would think about it multiple times until it drove her crazy and she blew up about it, saying it was unforgivable. She needs to get a fucking grip. 
 Another thing I realized I didn't really like is the way SJM structures her sentences. She adds a lot of dashes, and maybe that's because of the first person point of view, but it really started to get on my nerves. Every pages there are sentences with dashes in them. I flipped through and it's rare to find one without them, but this one is just me. 
 I hate to do it, but this book suffers from a major case of special snowflake syndrome. Like, it wasn't enough Feyre turned into a Fae, but she got all of the powers of the High Lords as well. Marries the most powerful High Lord (that, of course, was her mate). Has the most powerful friends. She is literally the only person that can stop the cauldron. The list is endless. 
 Then, the enemy that they were fighting doesn't appear until the last pages of the book. And when he does, it doesn't feel like a a real fight. It all felt very fake to me. The king wasn't trying to kill them, really. Everyone was just standing around. And of course, of fucking course, Feyre's sisters are turned into Fae. They had to get love interests somehow. Talk about convenient. 
 Tamlin, for some reason, became the absolute worst person possible. Everyone seems to be suffering from some sort of PTSD because he is not at all like himself. There is no way what happened with the ending should have happened at all. 
 I'm sorry. I really am. I thought this book was going to be good, given how much I liked the first one. 
 Still, I did like the relationship that Feyre and Rhysand had, no matter how much I despise how it all clicked into place. It is the healthiest relationship I have read. I liked the sex scenes and the build up to their lasting relationship. But after they were together, it became cheesy and love soaked. 
 I don't know, guys. Read this if you want. I don't know what else to say.

 And when I say 'crazy supernatural things', I mean exactly that, emphasis on the crazy part. I loved the supernatural salad here; while we've all heard of werewolves and vampires (these days, who hasn't?), the Shadow-Warriors and Mixens... well, I've never read book with them in it. 
 After I've successfully gone quite some way without gushing, the gushing shall commence. I'm sorry, but why is it that fictional men are always hotter than the guys I know? That's hardly fair. And Fated didn't disappoint there. Even thinking about Lucas right now, weeks after I read the book, I still get the tingles. He and Evie have that whole starcrossed lovers thing going on, and I guess that helps his image, since you can't help but think of him as a bad boy on a certain level. And then Alderson tops it off with a kiss scene (not saying who with, though!) so hot, I almost had to go take a cold shower afterwards. And I read adult about as much as I read YA; I'm used to steamy. I wasn't expecting that scene though, and to have that dumoed on me like that... 
 Anyway *cough* yes, great read. Like I said in the Hunting Lila review, I do believe I have found my new favorite author - and I have no doubts I'll be running to the bookstore for the continuation of Fated.

Sadness isn't strong enough, grief doesn't feel right. It feels like I was cut open and then taped together. Anytime someone mentions this book, my tape falls away uselessly and it hurts all over again. 
 I never wrote a review after I first finished reading it because it all hurt too badly. I didn't want to warn anyone away from this book because I didn't want to be the only one feeling this way. 
 But tonight, I'm trying to read Sometimes It Lasts by [author:Abbi Glines|4872191. I love Abbi and all of her books. She's an amazing author who tells fabulous stories. She's never broken my trust. I can safely read her books without feeling like at any moment I'm going to feel completely powerless to the hurt Taking Chances caused me. Much like poetry or opera, this is a book you want to study first. Picking it up to read for pleasure, with no preparation, is probably not fun at all. It's excruciatingly long and prosaic in many places. It's unbearably sexist and didactic, one long trigger warning for rape and slut-shaming. It was written as a guide to behavior, making it kind of repulsive from a modern standpoint. 
 Read in context, though, this book is incredible, even revolutionary. The little feminist glimpses are strangely compelling. I'm studying its historical impact as my senior thesis, and boy was there a lot of historical impact! Beyond that, and outside my research purview, the author was a remarkable individual. He seems to have been totally committed to didactic fiction, but wrote a practically-pornographic novel. He was a marketing genius of his time, but was totally clueless about why people read his book. 
 From my Banned Books Week review: 
 The reason Pamela was a big deal, and the reason I'm writing a 20-page history thesis about it, is that the public related to this novel in a whole new way. It was about a lower-class woman, written as if it were a compilation of letters she had written to her parents in distress. People who read this book felt along with Pamela. Both men and women were astonished at the magic Richardson was working, to make each of them feel like a young servant woman suffering improper advances. They listened to her heartache, they recognized that real people did suffer similar distress, and they heard Pamela's explicit arguments that her soul was worth just as much as anyone else's. This book helped blow the dam open, and turned novels into the mass media items they are today. It's been argued that the development of the novel established the most important precursor to human rights laws: The recognition that other people have inner lives like yours. That's what people were trying to ban.

Title: Ironskin 
 Author: Tina Connolly 
 Genre: Fantasy retelling 
 Setting: An England after the Great War, but not the England we know. 
 Reason for Reading: I read a review for a later book in the same series (h/t +John DeNardo) and it looked interesting. 
 Finished In: Days - I couldn't stop - I gobbled it up! 
 Pages: 305 
 Copyright Date: 2012 
 Cover: The cover art is gorgeous and shows a woman wearing an iron mask and a silver dress. She's standing in the moonlight. 
 First lines: "The moor was grey, battlefield grey. It had been five years since the last fey was seen, but out here Jane could almost imagine the Great War still raged on." 
 Themes: Jane Eyre (this is a loose retelling), fey, children, beauty. 
 Best part: It's really hard to choose just one. This book has a lot going on. 
 Worst part: The cover copy! The cover art is gorgeous but the copy is all wrong. For one thing, the cover review says it's a retelling of Beauty and the Beast, which is not at all true since it's a retelling of Jane Eyre. (Characters mentioning the fairy tale does not make it a BatB retelling, okay? No father in sight, no bargain, no roses, no Beauty living a new decadent life in an empty house, no pining Beast - I could go on and on but my point here is, I'm sorry but Ann Aguirre is just WRONG. ) For another thing, the cover blurb includes a major spoiler which is not revealed in the book until more than 100 pages in. Seriously, whoever was in charge of the cover text deserves 100 lashes with a wet noodle and they had best not be showing their face around here. 
 Imaginary Theme Song: That's a tough one because there is very little music in the book. I might go with something creepy and atmospheric like this: http://music.zoekeating.com/album/int... 
 Grade: A. 
 Recommended for: Any fans of Jane Eyre or alternate history. 
 Related Reads: Jenna Starborn by Sharon Shinn and The Eyre Affair by Jasper Fforde. I didn't love either of those books but they are the other sf/f Jane Eyre retellings that I know. Also, The Fire Rose by Mercedes Lackey, which is one of my favorite retellings. 
 I think this is an interesting and haunting book. It's impressive as a debut. Although the ending was extremely satisfying it left a lot of questions open (in a good way). I'm curious to see what will happen with the rest of the trilogy. 
 I liked the way this book explored themes such as, what is beauty? What is normal and should we try to be normal? How do we decide what is best for children? For such an engrossing and quick read it went the distance in terms of interesting questions. 
 I recommend it highly.

 "I'm going to kiss you now, Evie, and when I do, it's going to mean that you're mine. I don't care how far away from each other we are. You. Are. Mine. I'll wait for you. And I want you to wait for me." 
 Eight years later, Evie is now working as a housekeeper at the hotel, while part timing in catering.  "How many people do you think walk into their apartment at the end of the day, small and simple as it may be, and look around and feel like one of the luckiest people in the world?" 
 She had never heard from Leo again since the day he left, she wondered all these years what happened to him. I love all the flashback of Evie and Leo's childhood together. The answer finally came when a strange man albeit a handsome one was stalking her and after confronting him his motive, she was told that he is Jake, a friend of Leo, who had passed away during an accident.

Things move quite fast between them and they soon fell head over hells in love with each other. This might sounds like such a lame insta love, but when I read it, I don't feel that way at all. Everything just seems so natural between these two.

Jake appears mysterious at time that keep you guessing and unable to put the book down. What is his deal? What is his connection with Leo? Should we trust him when he explain about his ex-girlfriend?  There's more that I want to say and gush about, but I'm afraid is gonna be rather spoilerish. But I am in no way talking about the ultimate spoiler (the reason of Leo's disappearance). Here goes

"Shhhhhh, shhhhhh, says the sea, but I don't believe her." 
 Hi I was a literal puddle of tears after I finished this one last night. I went in expecting it to be good (because Stiefvater is bae) but I didn't realize HOW good until I actually started it. I listened to this as an audiobook, ps. and I do recommend you do that. The narration was really good and I didn't think it took away from the story at all. The narrators didn't try to really mimic other voices, but made them different enough that you knew who was talking. Anyway, this is a story about people who love horses and the horses that love them back. 
 This one just had so much goodness to it. If you like Stiefvater's writing style in The Raven Boys, then you will enjoy her writing in this one as well. I find her writing to be very unique to her character's voices and I think that Puck and Sean were just beautifully constructed. They were two halves of the same whole while still being their own individual selves. I think I really liked that neither of them wanted to leave the island because I don't like stories where someone gives up what they want for the other person. They both had end goals that were complimentary, which is nice (and rare in real life, but shhhh). 
 I loved the world building in this. It had enough fantasy elements to keep me interested, but also grounded enough in reality that I could picture it all very easily. I liked that everyone was aware of the "magic" surrounding the island and came all over to see it, but didn't necessarily try to take it away from the island. I also liked that it felt like the sea itself was a character in this story because I think too often people forget that you have to treat the elements with respect or they will come back to haunt you for the rest of your days. 
 "You leave nothing to assumption," Dory Maud says. "You swallow her with your eyes. I'm surprised there's any of her left for the rest of us to see." 
 THE CHARACTERS WERE JUST SO GOOD. Even the side characters served a purpose in this and weren't just sounding boards for Puck and Sean. I also liked that Puck and Sean had some overlapping story arcs but that they also had their own direction and path to take. I think what I liked most is that Puck wasn't doing this just to say she could do it and it didn't become an "issue" book even though other characters tried to make it that way. She was just trying to do the best she could under the circumstances to keep her way of life. As I said in my status updates: Puck is bae. Sean is bae. They were both just GREAT characters. I hope you all get to know them soon. 
 "I didn't know," I start truthfully, "that it was the hard way when I started on it." 
 Best Stiefvater book? Best Stiefvater book! This one has the delicacy and intrinsic nature of The Raven Cycle but with more romance and horses. And Puck. And Sean. So there's that too. PS I CRIED AT THE END. Does that surprise you? It doesn't surprise me.

(I tested it, asked my husband, "Do you know who Mr. Darcy is?" The answer was no. Which is surprising, since I watch the movie at least once a quarter. Or at least every time I pick up a P&P remake. It took everything in me not to put down this book and put in the movie this time around. 
 And there you have my review. Sort of. The modernization was good enough. It centered around the dog show arena and of course the rich and...not-so-rich. The book included plenty of Darcy, and Elizabeth moments, many of which avid fans will recoginize either from the book or by the movie. In fact, many of the key phrases from the book were utilized here. Elizabeth, true to the original, was a master of misunderstanding Darcy, but in this version it was almost to a fault. In fact, I think that both the pride and the prejudice fell to Elizabeth most strongly in this rendition. Mr. Darcy was constantly putting his foot in his mouth, and more than once I felt that Elizabeth's responses and disdain were uncalled for. I got a bit frusterated with her refusal to hear Donovan Darcy out, and if I were him, I most certainly would have given up on trying after so long. Mr. Darcy was charming and compassionate and understanding. He was apparently quite handsome, although for some reason I had a hard time picturing this particular Darcy in my head. 
 The dog shows, while the common ground between Elizabeth and Darcy in this book, were really a rather small part of this novel. I did enjoy the the bits that were there, but I think when I requested the book part of me had actually hoped on a few funny scenes and dog antics, but other than a scene of a dog peeing on beautiful carpet there really wasn't any thing like that. I guess they were show dogs, and were trained to absolute perfection. 
 While I guess I didn't LOVE, love this book, I still always enjoy an Elizabeth and Darcy rendition, in its (at this point) many varieties. I love the different interpretations of the brooding, overly-handsome Darcy, and Elizabeth's fumbling of the relationship. If you're an Austin fan, and enjoy modernizations, I see now reason why you wouldn't enjoy this novel.

This one was right at a 4.5 for me. I'd never heard of Tarryn Fisher, but I've loved just about everything I've read of Colleen Hoover's, and Never Never was no exception. It is a novella, but its 140 pages pack so much mystery and suspense, you'll actually welcome the relief that comes with the end of the book. 
 Plot: 
 In the middle of school one day, Charlie and Silas are terrified when they realize they can't remember anything or anyone. They know that before they lost their memories, they were a couple, so they decide to team up and try to figure out what happened to them. As they work together, they learn what kind of people they were and find out that their relationship wasn't always a loving one. At the same time, they see the qualities that drew them to each other in the first place. 
 Characters: 
 Silas is a jock (although he doesn't remember it) and an artist (a photographer who finds beauty in unexpected places). Charlie's very strong-willed and OCD. Apparently she was also a mean girl. What's really entertaining is the fact that the amnesia seems to have made both of them better people. I liked Charlie okay, but Silas was definitely my favorite of the two. The way he reacted to some of the situations he found himself in was hilarious. 
 Writing: 
 There were a few typos here and there, but who cares? It's Colleen Hoover! Never Never includes all of the qualities that make her books so incredible: great character interactions, a witty sense of humor, an untraditional romance, lots of secrets, some personal tragedy, and a plot that will make you want to read until you can't keep your eyes open anymore. There is lots of language, and there are some sexual references, but nothing too graphic. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 There's a HUGE cliffhanger, which is a bummer since there are jillions of unanswered questions. Some of the other reviewers said the less you know going in, the better. I'd definitely have to agree. My own little piece of advice is to avoid trying to predict what happens and just read the story. Once you start moving from scene to scene, you realize that nothing is as it seems, and it pretty much stays that way throughout the book.

 The Unbearable Book Club for Unsinkable Girls is a book that is really unexpected. What starts out as a cute story about four girls from completely different worlds being forced together through summer reading turns into something so much more. 
 This book is really more of a coming of age story focused on our narrator, Adrienne Haus. "A" is a girl who finds herself without her best (and only) friend for an entire summer because of a knee injury that prevents her from going on an outdoor excursion. As she mopes around the house and dreads this stupid book club her mother started, she finds herself identifying with the characters in her summer reading books, and these characters begin teaching her more and more about herself. 
 The other girls in this book club are very distinct (and somewhat cliche). CeeCee is your typical "A-List" girl who hides her problems behind her pretty face and outgoing personality. Jill is adopted from China and already has her life for the next 10 years planned out to the day. And Wallis is a mysterious new girl who skipped two grades. The four of them, who would not have interacted otherwise, find themselves thrown together for an interesting summer. 
 I am a firm believer in writers being intentional with every detail in their story. And somewhere I feel like Jill got lost in translation. I kind of feel like she was just thrown in the story because four is better than three. But in my opinion, Jill's presence in this novel doesn't add anything to the story. She was just someone who happened to be around. 
 I can tell you, I did enjoy this novel. But I can also tell you that if the summer club was centered around movies or cooking, I probably wouldn't have liked it all that much. I think the fact that this novel focuses so much on literature is the reason why the story developed into one that I liked. The five works of literature discussed in this novel (The Yellow Wallpaper, Frankenstein, The Left Hand of Darkness, The House on Mango Street, and The Awakening) really allowed for some dynamic MC development that would not have been able to be conveyed otherwise. I appreciate Ms. Schumacher's incorporation of these major works of literature into her characters lives. It really appealed to the booklover in me! 
 Surrounding the bookclub plot is the coming of age story, which mostly has to do with self-acceptance what the lack of a father means for Adrienne's place in the world. This becomes one of those subplots that seems more "thrown in for character development and growth" than anything else--if this were removed, it wouldn't affect the story at all. But Adrienne does find a way to define herself in her small town world, and she learns some valuable lessons about friendships and mother-daughter relationships along the way, and this is mostly because of Wallis. Out of the other three girls in this story, Wallis is the most dynamic and most crucial to the story, and she ended up being my favorite character. There is just something loveable about her to readers (and to A's mom) that the other girls don't quite understand. 
 I must say, the ending has a complete shock (which surprises me coming from a YA contemporary), but Ms. Schumacher sets up a beautiful open-ended Epilogue to her cute cute contemporary YA. Overall, I found this book to be enjoyable for lovers of literature like myself.

I had not really heard much about Night Owls until I received a copy from Bungle with a few other books. I was drawn to it immediately due to the cover being simple, yet bold and dramatic. My copy was a proof copy, and for promotion the publisher had single words put onto the covers, my word was Love, you can see the cover here. 
 I went into reading Night Owls with no idea what to expect, not only was this a new book for me, but also a new author. Once I began reading it was quite clear that I would love this book. Night Owls is a book that you can read without worrying over missing out on some bit of important information, without keeping an eye open for hidden agendas or plots. It's doesn't make you think or try to hard to concentrate, its just basic, and I know that sounds like its coming across as a 'boring book', trust me it's not. Reading Night Owls was a breath of fresh air, it was relaxing and stress free, the perfect book to read to get out of reading slumps, or for a quick, uncomplicated read. 
 Night Owls follows Beatrix, as she attempts to get into a medical examination part of the university, to draw cadavers, and enter them into a competition. After a disastrous first meeting, Beatrix makes her way home and bumps into Jack, another person on the night owl bus. After a while this couple strike up an easy friendship, learning about each others secrets and reasons for being on the night bus. 
 As thier friendship develops into something more, Beatrix learns more about Jack than most people know, and he slowly lets her in, showing her his family secret. 
 Night Owls was a quick read for me, and I could not read the pages fast enough. Beatrix was an interesting character for me, she is strong and determined to do these drawings, even though it physically makes her sick when it's over. Yet she also has a very caring side, this is only seen more when she meets Jack's relative, which is connected to a big family secret. Rather than it putting her off Jack, Beatrix embraces it with open arms, and when it all falls around her Beatrix uses this to help her for her competition. 
 Jack was someone who I thought was nothing but trouble, but the more we get to know him the more we see why he goes around spraying graffiti at night. This graffiti is also linked to the covers, and I think it was a fantastic idea from the publisher to market the book this way, even down to the different designs. 
 Final Verdict 
 Night Owls is the perfect uncomplicated read, but one that also makes you feel things and become emotionally invested in the characters.

Rivers of London, Ben Aaronovitch (Gollancz) 
 magic policeman 
 hunting the streets of London 
 won't need your map, mate 
 Right from the start, Peter Grant's narratorial voice makes itself comfy in your reader's brain and settles down for what turns out to be a rollicking good criminal case in the magical underbelly of London. It's been hailed as what happens if Harry Potter became a policeman, and you know what? It really does have the same sort of laid-back, magic-is-just-another-part-of-the-fabric-of-society tone that JK Rowling managed with the Muggle and magical worlds of Harry Potter. 
 Aaronovitch has a methodical approach to setting scenes and gives the reader a detailed tour of London and surrounds. In the beginning this was a fantastic opportunity to really visualize the places Peter Grant moved through, but ... well, by the middle to end of the book I was tiring of the almost excruciating detail given to streets and buildings. It worked well to set up the story and seriously establish an authentic London, but once the story gathered its momentum the layers of detail just seemed to slow everything down. 
 I enjoyed the characters of this book: they were a mix of familiar and new. I'm assuming Aaronovitch is building up his magical world for future books, which is a very good thing in my mind. I'd like to see a continuity unfold as Peter Grant gathers more experience in future books. The exploration of London's (and Britain's) river 'gods' was pretty unique and worked well alongside the more macabre criminal case. 
 The only drawback, apart from too much detail given to the streets and statues and ephemera of London, was the main character's all-too-sudden expertise with magic. As the story opens, Peter Grant is just your regular under-performing police rookie, just about to be assigned to a desk job. A chance encounter with a charismatic ghost leads him to the magical police - which works well. However, Grant uses his rudimentary knowledge of science to really make leaps and bounds in his apprenticeship. His 'master', Inspector Nightingale seems to be happy to let Grant do all the hard magical work. That didn't ring true to me. The case is quite dangerous and for most of the novel, the police (including Nightingale) are clueless about who is responsible; so when opportunities arise for some magical investigation (such as trying to raise ghosts in a graveyard) I couldn't really reconcile the idea that Nightingale would let his apprentice do the spells. 
 Anyway, that's just a gripe. I really recommend this book to those hordes of Harry Potter fans, and even to the fans of Harry Dresden. Aaronovitch is quintessentially British and his hero, Peter Grant, is equally so.

A crisp, interesting look at terrorism and its effects on the victims and the perpetrators. The interesting part about the book is how it is structured--it starts with the bomb and only afterwards do we see the shattered remnants of people's lives. Mahajan's prose hammers in the theme of being like the bomb on multiple levels (at times this can get a little heavy-handed, but for the most part, is really heartbreakingly clever). 
 The story starts with three boys--the Khurana brothers and their Muslim best friend, Mansoor--going to pick up the Khuranas' television at the electronics repair stand. The brothers perish in the blast, but Mansoor survives the blast, running away in the confusion, sustaining a serious wrist injury that comes back to haunt him in adulthood. 
 We see the Khuranas cope in their own way, and how the Ahmeds deal with the blast. Mansoor eventually studies abroad in the US and returns to India once his wrists start acting up again, and the memories still haunt the two families. For Mansoor's part, he tries to get involved in an activist group challenging harmful attitudes against Muslims and advocating rights for suspected terrorists. There he meets Ayub, a young man of a more humble background who initially is the most vocal advocate for nonviolent resistance. But human emotions get the better of Ayub, who becomes involved in a seedy world, and brings those issues out into the open. 
 I really enjoyed this book, and I can see why it's getting rave reviews. I'd rate this a 4.5 (a half star off because I think the ending is a little rushed). Mahajan is a gifted writer, and I hope to read more of his future works (and now I'm off to hunt for his previous novel).

 "She's passed the fear barrier, and she'd lived, and she'd discovered not certain death, s she'd imagined, nut impossible splendor. What other beautiful things had fear been hiding from her? What else has the curse long kept her from discovering? For the first time in a long time. She wanted to find out." 
 A Semi-Definitive List of Worst Nightmares is a hilarious and inspiring take on fear, growth, and battling your inner demons. Esther Solar is cursed. Her family has been cursed by Death to succumb to their greatest fears. For her father that's agoraphobia, her mother bad luck, and her twin brother Eugene it's the dark. But Esther doesn't know her greatest fear, and she's in no hurry to find out, that's why she keeps a list of all her "worst nightmares". But a surprising reunion with her childhood friend Jonah Smallwood leads Esther down a path to confront her fears in an attempt to try and stop her family curse before it consumes them all. 
 Things I Liked 
 I absolutely LOVED the fun and humor in this book! You might not expect a book about your worst fears to be so light-hearted, but I found myself smiling or laughing in almost every chapter. Esther, Eugene, and Jonah all have a jovial sarcastic personality. Even though they all are dealing with their fears and anxieties, they maintain really snarky humor that I loved. 
 I really liked the inclusion of little mini-lists that were observations or facts about a certain situation from Esther. I thought they worked really well in the story, they added more information and context - especially regarding her grandfather Reginald. 
 Jonah Smallwood is a treat. He's so charming and suave and devil-may-care. I really liked him (even though I got mad at points). I loved that he wanted to do special effects makeup - it's a truly unique artform, and I loved that we got to see a character pursue art in a different way. I love how relentless and charismatic he is, it's so easy to follow these adventures he and Esther are on, because he is such an effervescent personality. 
 I really liked how Death/The Man Who Would Become Death were personified in the story, through Reg's stories. It really made this abstract concept/curse more grounded and gave a depth and history to the story and their family. 
 The writing in the story was so easy to fall into. The story had this grand adventure feeling. It was so lively, humorous, and fun, when it easily could have felt formulaic or repetitive with the fear-a-week method Esther and Jonah used. 
 Things I Didn't Like 
 I would have liked to see more of Hephzibah, Esther and Eugene's best friend. I felt like I didn't really get to know her, therefore I didn't care about her relationships with either Eugene or Esther. 
 A Semi-Definitive List of Worst Nightmares is a story of finding the strength to battle your demons, both real and imaginary. I loved the humor and the joy I had while reading. I like that we get to see the characters trying to fight their fears in different ways - facing them head on, talking to each other, talking to a therapist - it was nice to show that growth comes in many different forms. This was a great story that was filled with fantastic characters and large personality. 
 *Trigger warnings for: suicide, self harm, and abuse

Wither is haunting, beautiful, sinister, and at times, even disturbing. I actually devoured it in one sitting, which was surprising, because there were a couple of things that actually turned me off about the novel. Nonetheless, something kept me going until the wee hours of the morning, just to know what happens at the end of it all. I even had a bizarre sister-wife dream of my own after finishing! 
 The world Lauren DeStefano has created is scary in the fact that it seems so plausible. Genetic engineering happens already today, girls are snatched off the streets and sold in today's society. Though, if I'm being perfectly honest, if a third World War did break out, I don't know if I'd believe America would be the last place standing. (China has my vote!) 
 Rhine as the main character wasn't irritating, though I almost felt a lack of...something. Emotion maybe? Her pull in either direction wasn't strong enough, her hatred wasn't fierce enough, she wasn't as sympathetic as I expected, and she wasn't as determined as I wanted. She had elements of all these traits, enough for me to like her and sympathize with her, but not enough for me to admire her. I wanted more of a forbidden romance out of her and Gabriel - more than a couple of stolen kisses. Though I did like the bit about him hiding June Beans in her breakfast, and the fact that they actually talked. A conversation is so rare in young adult romances these days! 
 However, as usual, I'm in love with the secondary characters. Especially the sister-wives. I loved the deep relationship between all of the girls, the strange combination of being sisters and friends and wives. I enjoyed Jenna's character, though I wish we'd seen more of her. I loved little Cecily, though she was one of the parts that disturbed me the most. The whole concept of a thirteen-year-old being completely obsessed with marriage, sex, and pregnancy is a little nauseating. I tried to get in the mindset that, really, in their society, she's pretty much ready for it, given their lifespan is so short, but my modern sensibilities just wanted to grab a black marker and black it all out. I can also understand why Rhine could become so easily frustrated with her, but I also found myself wanting to tell her to lay off, the Cecily is only a child. By the end of the novel, I'm so drawn to Cecily and totally scared for her that I hope she makes appearances in the rest of the series. I need to know what happens to that poor, vivacious little redhead. 
 As for the men of the story, I appreciated all three for what they were. Gabriel is the (obviously) gorgeous servant who connects with Rhine over the simple desperation of being trapped. I can't wait to find out more about him, because I felt he was a little bland in this one. Linden was also incredibly sympathetic. I was left at the end really wishing that, you know, someone had told him the truth. He's such a naive, sweet man, he deserves to know the truth about the people he loves. I appreciate that he never forces himself on any of his wives, and that he was actually so head-over-heels in love with his first wife. It made him extremely likable. His father on the other hand? Total creepster! I foresee him being a huge problem in the series - or at least I hope so, because he's such a fantastic antagonist. 
 As mentioned, there were a couple of things I didn't quite like about Wither. The pacing was a major one. Even though I read it in one day, it just felt so, so, so slow. Like nothing was really happening until the last couple of pages. I've been wondering if it's a deliberate choice though, to reflect the monotonous lives of the sister-wives, stuck in an endless, unbreakable routine inside the mansion. If it was, I understand it, but I could've used a few little pick-me-up scenes to keep the ball rolling. I also didn't like the repetitiveness of a couple of things. Saying over and over where she hid Gabriel's handkerchief, repeatedly letting us know exactly what ages men and women die. Little details, certainly, but when they're repeated every couple of chapters, it starts feeling a little redundant. 
 However, the ending was so deliciously hopeful, I'm begging for more! I can't wait to see what comes next in Rhine's life. Do they make it out ok? Are they hunted? Is a cure discovered? I am definitely looking forward to an amp up in the action and romance in the sequel!

 I don't know exactly where to start, so I'll just choose out of a random hat (joke intended): 
 Writing 
 Okay, so the writing in this book was bubbly and intoxicating. The pace and voice was so consistent. I honestly loved it. The descriptions -- of which there were so many, and they were amazing -- reminded me of a butterfly: they were light, fluttery, and powdering, yet just glided through. Everything was magical and mechanic, and I really liked it. To me, it was so imaginative and immersive. So, just to clarify, the descriptive language was something I loved. 
 Characters 
 I didn't hate or absolutely love any of the characters in Caraval. 
 We have Scarlett, the female protagonist, who is not quite Mary Sue, but not particularly special either. She is self-sacrificial, and not especially wise, intelligent, gorgeous, or talented (not that she has to be, personally speaking, I suppose). To be completely honest, she reminded me precisely of a mix between Elsa and Anna, and Rapunzel from Tangled. Most of her planning in consequential situations boiled down to "if you let so-and-so go, then I'll do blank-and-blank willingly"(this is where Rapunzel comes in). Then we have her cold, practical nature born from the abuse or neglect of her childhood (she even says "you can't marry someone you just met!"). That would be Elsa. Then finally, we have her headstrong, romantically curious nature, which would be Anna. I didn't love Scarlett by any means, but she wasn't completely helpless or boy-crazy, which I appreciate. Plus, I can understand where many of her motives are born from, even if I cannot imagine myself doing the same. I mean, the only man she's had in her life has been her father, and she doesn't seem to have any friends. She is utterly drawn to a new, vibrant world, overwhelmed and seduced by it. It would make sense that she is simplistic in some aspects, because she's just understanding them (if I'm playing Devil's Advocate here). A cool touch: she has synesthesia, which adds a little more color (literally!) to her. 
 The main male is Julian. Strangely enough, we didn't really get to see his personality brew too much throughout the book. I think he was pretty well layered, however, being a little arrogant, but not as a resting state, but instead a defense. He was actually quite sweet in some parts...? I wish Garber had devoted just a little more time to letting their relationship culture. 
 The Plot 
 Okay, sometimes I need to take a book at face value: if it wanted to be the type of book that did the types of things this book did, then should I let it? That is the question folks. 
 Basically, it was magic-based... sort of. It had magical-ish stuff, but what is real? What is not? 
 What did she eat? Anything? 
 I liked it at a "this is a book who is doing this particular book's thing, and it wants to end with doing what it did" level. 
 Basically, to not spoiler, it was what it said. 
 Some points were fantastic. It was enchanted and magical, with fey-type tricks borrowing from all different types of culture from Celtic to Lewis Carrol. While a little untethered at times, at many points I was totally captivated. 
 However, at the end, it sort of flatlined into this stagnant trope that resolved with what I would consider almost a Scooby-Doo type ending. I didn't really understand the means, and it seemed like a handful of physiological and psychological damage and actual danger for the unnecessary end explanation. 
 Another thing I enjoyed what the fact that it was imperfect, not a tidy loop. Scarlett made some mistakes and there were wrong turns on her end. On the other hand, however, I believe the author could have balanced them a little better. At a few points I was just wishing she would figure something out wholly. Maybe more riddles? More leads that actually turned up? It was just messy sometimes. 
 All in all, all the real conflicts were completed in a hardy, sacrificial way, instead of sharp or cunningly. Then again, I'm a Slytherclaw (that's a Slytherin-Ravenclaw hybrid, in case you don't know me, which obviously you don't), so I crave conning, intelligent methods in the first place (and all places, really). What about you? Is it acceptable? 
 In the end, however, we did not learn enough. The world was flipped and I was given very few tools or leads. Nonetheless, I can definitely say the book was immersive, captivating, and intriguing. I want the other book. If only there hadn't been such clashing within the narrative's prospects and just a generally lackluster, if not nettling, ending.

 I don't know if I've ever said this, but China Mieville is one of my favorite sci-fi authors, so when this one popped up on NetGalley, I had to take a chance. Mieville and YA? I'm so there! The beginning of this book moves slowly, in a way I think all Mieville novels do, but the ponderousness of it makes even more sense when you realize Railsea is an homage to Moby Dick (a book I loathed in high school). Sham is a boy who doesn't know quite what he wants, doesn't even know his own feelings on most subjects, except for salvage. He's fascinated by ancient relics of times gone by, times when gigantic, whale-sized moles weren't out there trying to kill everyone and everything. As someone who worshiped the BBC's Walking with Dinosaurs, this new world of huge mammalian predators fascinated me. I got the feeling early on that this was going to be Sham's coming of age tale, and y'all know how much I like coming of age tales. When Sham and the other crew find a dead train fallen off the rails, he finds a memory disk full of incomprehensible pictures-including one of a lone rail, unheard of in the tangle of the railsea. Soon, Sham and his captain, Naphi, along with the crew of the Medes, are off to Manihiki City in search of a special kind of salvage: alt-salvage. 
 When we reach Manihiki City, Sham immediately goes off to find the children pictured on his found disk. The results of this search are Caldera and Dero Shroake, and that picture disk belonged to their now-deceased father. Actually, Caldera and Dero lived with two fathers and one mother, a kind of polyamorous triad, and this information is presented in the most blase way. I like that Mieville felt the need to make gay/alternative relationships and parenting something so normal so far in the future. I like inclusion, and I like the Shroake siblings, too. Sham is, however, nothing if not indecisive, and misses his chance to adventure with them. He also meets a boy called Robalson, who claims to be a pirate and turns out to not be a liar. Whether he wanted to or not, Sham and his rescued bat, Daybe, go on a pirate adventure. This is also the part where the POV shifts from Sham to everyone else. I think this, the second quarter of the novel, is much more interesting than the first. The story starts to pick up, you start to learn more about Sham, Captain Naphi, the Shoakes, the railsea in general. The language remains as it has been, which can sometimes be hard to understand, but it had a nice literary feel to it. 
 The story eventually splits into three, following the Shroake siblings, Sham and his pirates, and Captain Naphi on the Medes. It's also here that the narrator becomes almost its own entity, with Mieville giving the narrator its own chapters and making the narrator seem omniscient. It's a trend of older novels to address the reader directly, something I saw a lot in my high school's American Literature class, and it usually bugs me. Not here though, maybe because we're following three stories now, and the separate narrator chapters helped me keep them straight. Things are moving quickly now, and we're learning more and more of the stories, more about the pasts of the characters. The thing about this novel is that it moved so slowly sometimes that I got frustrated, but I never stopped reading or was even tempted to stop reading. I wanted to know how Sham's, and the Shroakes', stories ended, and they do end. Magnificently. 
 So, in short, this one is a little slow, a little weird with the dialect and style of writing, but it's very Mieville to me. The story is twisty and intriguing and different, despite being an homage. Come for the futuristic, dystopian train society, stay for the giant, man-eating moles!

I'm one of thousands of North American students who read TKAM in high school and like its narrator adored and placed Atticus Finch on a pedestal of triumphing over age old prejudice. 
 But neither myself nor Jean Louise are children anymore and "Go Set a Watchman" brings us to 1950's Alabama. There has been a world war, her beloved older brother Jem is dead, and the lovable Dill is traveling the world, and Maycomb's white citizens are struggling with the federal courts and the NAACP. Where Atticus sits on this issue shocks us all because we're no longer children and the idols of our childhood become mere humans as we grow older. By the end of this book,neither Jean Louise nor I are naive young children anymore. 
 Are there problems with this book? Yes, it's an unfinished manuscript and choppy writing and lack of smooth transitions to childhood memories are missing finesse. The ending is also a wobbly resolution. Does it change the way I feel about TKAM? Definitely not! I'm extremely glad that the editor pushed Harper Lee to tell us about 1930's Maycomb or else we may never have heard the name Harper Lee or Atticus Finch.

This story follows Sloane, a 17 year old girl who has been thrown into a zombie apocalypse. Now the story takes place a few days later where Sloane is surviving with five other teenagers in their old high school.

 "The vomiting seems to be her way of expressing her feelings towards Ford."

Most of the people you see going to work today are LARPing an incredibly boring RPG called "professionalism" that requires them to alter their vocabulary, posture, eating habits, facial expressions - every detail all the way down to what they allow themselves to find funny. 
 Okay, this ostensibly a graphic novel about a girl (high school) who plays a MMORPG called Coarsegold. 
 But in reality is a lecture about poverty in China and the economic and class differences between middle-class American teens and impoverished Chinese teens who have no workers' rights or health care. 
 I was rather disappointed. I was hoping for more plot and less lecture, and instead this was heavy on lecture and rather light on plot. 
 THE GOOD: 
 - Chubby female heroine. Shown as natural, respected, without self-esteem issues or any kind of weight-related weirdness. Probably the best and most life-affirming thing is seeing her kneeling over the tub with her shirt off in order to dye her hair red. It's amazing and world-changing to see fat girls and fat women portrayed in this kind of normal, everyday, things-are-okay kind of way without it being The Fat Best Friend, The Goofy Sidekick, or The Girl Who No One Loves and Feels Like Trash About Her Size. Instead, Doctorow is offering us a completely normal and un-self-conscious MC who is going about her normal life, unconcerned with I Am Fat, I Hate Myself, Why Do No Boys Love Me? or some shit. A+ 
 - Excellent art, drawings, and great understanding of not only MMORPGs but of high school and interpersonal relationships within family and without. 
 THE BAD: 
 - It's simply a lecture. A call to action, a "learning tool," a device to promote activism and call attention to the plight of teens who are forced to work from a young age in countries where there's no such thing as health insurance or workers' rights. 
 While I think that this is a noble and important cause to call attention to, it doesn't really make for great fiction, instead coming off as a PSA. The author has a clear agenda and doesn't even make an attempt to hide it. *shrug* This just kills my interest in the book. 
 A much, much better book that dealt with some of these same issues but was super-subtle as well as incredibly entertaining was Neal Stephenson's Reamde, an AMAZING knock-your-socks off novel that also dealt with stuff like the issues of MMORPG and the differences between Americans, Chinese and Russians when it comes to governments and human rights. I'd highly recommend it to anyone on earth. 
 I can't say the same about this. 
 Tl;dr - Well constructed graphic novel with an obvious and overwhelming "message" about human rights. Might be of interest to teenagers who play MMORPGs, however no one is going to read this and NOT feel preached to... Doctorow is just coming on too strong here. I appreciate what he's trying to do, but this doesn't make good fiction.

 Once again, Khaled Hosseini has written a very powerful, emotionally impactful novel, this one tracing the paths of two siblings who were separated one day in 1952 and the many, many different people who connected them, entire families part of the story of Pari and Abdullah. The kind of novel that had me staying up late on several nights, wanting to read more.

Morgan Stockhour is a resident of Interment, an island that has been separated from Earth and now floats above it in the sky. Internment possesses the ideal conditions of a Utopian society until the shocking murder of a young girl leaves everyone feeling unsafe. 
 'You have all heard the warnings about the edge. We have been told its winds are a song that will hypnotize us, and by the time we awaken from the trance, it will be too late.' 
 The warnings to not peer over the edge, to look down on Earth's people, have been drilled into all residents since before anyone can remember. Those that chance this danger are known as Jumpers and Morgan's brother Lex is counted among the few to have survived, except he is now blind. Here lies my first issue. We end up meeting another of these 'Jumpers', a young girl, yet she ends up with a mind that isn't "quite right" (something sounding a lot like epilepsy). No reasoning behind the differences in their injuries is given. But you'd think an island floating in the sky would have severe winds especially near the edge and you wouldn't be able to be anywhere close to it. 
 The world-building is spent mostly on the culture of these people, rather than explaining the actual reasoning behind why an island just randomly detached from Earth and floated to a still livable position in the sky and not straight out into space. But basically the way the society works is there's the evil group of leaders, a King and Queen, that seek to control all aspects of the residents lives including arranged marriages from birth. And then it goes off on a typical tangent with the evil plot being discovered and the subsequent plan to escape/overthrow those evil doers. It was hard to get a feel for the time period this is set in. The society seemed technologically advanced yet had the feel of a medieval type era with its arranged marriages and King/Queen rulers. But you would think it'd have to be set in a distant past since one would expect the people on Earth to fly up and make contact with the 'island people', no? 
 The slow, meandering pace of the introduction was an interesting first look into this strange society and could have worked were it not for the continued slow, meandering pace even after the murder mystery aspect was introduced. Even during moments when you would expect a certain level of excitement or tension were made inexplicably dull. Unfortunately, what could have been an interesting dystopian tale turned very predictable and far from original.

I really enjoyed this book. To me, it was about family and personal identity.

His marriage with Jolene isn't going too well, but they have to pretend it is alright in front of their two children, Betsy (12) and Lulu (4). When Jolene's military life shoves itself to the top of her priority list, Michael and the girls must learn to cope with less of their mom around. 
 I liked this story because I felt the casting of characters was very diverse. I am confident that almost anyone that reads this book can relate to someone in the story and come out of it with something learned. Jolene was realistic and down to earth, while Michael was selfish and afraid. The children were emotional, confused, and selfish. Even the neighbours had a part in the story, through Jolene's best friend Tami and her son Seth. 
 Family is the #1 theme, whether it is your nuclear family, extended family, or military family. The point of the story isn't to separate them, but to combine them into one large family. Instead of seeing divisions, a person should see continuity and togetherness. I think that is the real point of the novel. 
 The emotions in this book were a rollercoaster. I found myself experiencing almost all emotions at one point or another. Many people say John Green's "The Fault in Our Stars" is the saddest book they have ever read, but I didn't cry for that one. I cried for this one. Why? The emotions are more real. They are raw, uncensored, and aren't sugarcoated in the least.

"You'll have to forgive me. I'm a refugee from the past, and like other refugees I go over the customs and habits of being I've left or been forced to leave behind me, and it seems just as quaint from here, and I am just as obsessive about it. -- So. More Waiting. -- Waiting is also a place: it is wherever you wait. For me it's this room. I am blank, here, between parantheses. Between other people." 
 The Handmaid's Tale is an interesting case. It feels well thought out and hastily written all at once. The writing is excellent for a chapter or two and then monotonous for the next five. I often felt like I was going nowhere with this book, this weird story - all to realise I'd just read 150 pages. Why this book failed to impress me is a bit of a mystery to be honest, but I do have a few clues as to why that would be. 
 What this novel doesn't try to hide is it's objective: to shock you and to make you think. In a dystopian society where women have no rights, are treated poorly and where they are made to do ugly things against their will (there is a slight promise of resistance, don't worry) this seems like an easy enough thing to accomplish. And I do think it succeeds - if you get the whole premise of the book to begin with. 
 Because here's the thing: I had no idea what was going on most of the time. You're following a first-person perspective and she doesn't care to explain most of the things to you in this world she lives in. You're just thrown in to this story, and if I hadn't known what this story was about I would've been even more confused. And the truth is, even though by the end of the novel I was on track and felt like I understood (mostly) everything, I still didn't get enough. I've seen people praise Atwood and this novel for the world-building even with the lack of actual plot but this is what I don't seem to understand. What world-building? Am I honestly going to have to just believe that a fairly intelligent and liberal society could just change like that in a matter of a few years? The U.S. above all (What I mean by this is that the whole rest of the world would just watch idly by whilst something like this would happen? That Japanese tourists would just take pictures??). 
 I felt that as interesting and horrifying as the setting of this book is it only just scratched the potential it actually had. Maybe this just relates to the way the story is told, and I won't get more into that as I would feel it spoils an important part of this story. And as much as I could complain, I didn't dislike the story. There were redeeming factors, such as glimpses of what the fricking heck actually happened, snippets of great prose, and the ending (referring to the Historical Notes). So I would still recommend The Handmaid's Tale. Just beware the "no-plot-zone".
