 What makes high fantasy so enjoyable to me is also what makes it difficult to review. It's so dense, and so much happens, yet, as others have pointed out, so little happens. This novel is no different in that it doesn't have a central plot (other than the overarching threat of war between each kingdom) so much as it has lesser, character-driven plots that eventually converge into the whole. In the background we have political intrigue and war, but the foreground introduces the characters, whose stories eventually begin to converge near the end. Because of this structure, the plot itself is still shrouded in some mystery. You might wonder, for instance, what Jezal's chapter about the poker game has to do with the plot. Well, it doesn't. But it serves to provide a detailed introduction into the type of person he is and what motivates him. 
 Abercrombie's strength, which I first noticed when I broke my Abercrombie cherry on Half a King, is characterization. His skill in writing multiple POVs, each with a distinct voice, is flawless. I did not find that any of the voices blended together. In fact, so skilled is he that there was a moment in which I was reading a chapter written from Jezal's POV and another character entered the scene. That character was not named or described, but I immediately knew who she was when she spoke because each character's voice is so strong. 
 He introduces a motley bunch here, most of which defy categorization. The murderous and notorious Northman. The pompous, pampered, womanizing nobleman seeking to advance his career with the contest. The commoner who rose above his station, but is still judged for his common roots. The mysterious, strict, but wise, magi (by far my favorite of the lot). The tortured who becomes the torturer. The clever, bawdy woman who doesn't play by society's rules and doesn't care what you think of her. The former slave who seeks to impose vengeance on the world for what they have stolen from her. 
 But they all have more depth than my simple labels can give them. Just when you think you have a character figured out, they do, say, or think something that makes you question your notions of who they are. Everyone is a shade of grey, everyone has flaws. Dark characters have some good, and good characters have some bad. What I really liked is how many of the "bad" characters (Glotka, Jezal, Logen) were striving to be better. And good characters, like West, had moments of weakness that almost completely changed how I viewed them. So strong, and so ambiguous are his characters that some I didn't think I would like for anything other than their brutality were winning me over by the end of the book. 
 As with Half a King, Abercrombie writes women who are in every way equal to the men, be it in wit, strength, or just will. They are equally flawed, as well. Ardee perhaps drinks a little too much, and though she has a clever mind and wit, she sometimes does not know when to stay silent. Oddly, she also doesn't know when to speak up, either. (view spoiler)[I was surprised that after her confrontation with her brother, she was not honest with Glotka about what happened to her. Of course, he isn't stupid, so he knew exactly what happened, but her excuses seemed like a moment of weakness to me. (hide spoiler)] Ferro, my least favorite character, is strong, like a machine, but she is so blinded by her need for vengeance that she just doesn't think, and she blindly walks into dangerous situations that threaten her plans. 
 Then there was the band of Named Men, still somewhat enigmatic. I enjoyed their chapters the least, but I think that's because I was already attached to other characters when they were finally introduced. I imagine their story will converge with many others in Book 2. However, one of the most touching moments in the book for me came in one of their chapters, when they paid tribute to a fallen comrade. They are nothing if not loyal to each other. 
 Their chapters, along with Glotka's, introduced a theme I noticed here and in Half a King: how friendship can warm an icy heart and melt away the bitterness of the world. 
 With an author this accomplished, it's almost pointless to mention the world-building, which, as expected, is top notch. Unlike some novels, my copy contained no map, but it's no matter. I built one in my head based on the descriptions provided in the book; that is, the novel is detailed enough that I have a good idea of where every land is relative to the other, the types of people who inhabit that land, and even what its terrain looks like. 
 As with any good fantasy, many aspects of this world mirror our own. It contains castes, cliques, a commentary about the link between money and power, and even racism and nationalism. He doesn't present these themes in a polemic way, however; rather, these themes occur organically within the context of a character's individual chapter. For instance, Ferro, a dark-skinned character, refers to others as "Pinks," a word she delivers with such disdain and venom, it's clear the word is meant as an epithet. 
 Abercrombie is known, at this point, as lord of the grimdark novel, so I was expecting something much darker, bloodier, and violent. It had bloody and violent moments, don't get me wrong, but it was not nearly as bad as I was expecting. But it isn't all dark! There were many moments of unexpected humor and sarcasm.

I like this book but the more I think about it the more problems I realized it had. 
 So this is the story of Caymen Meyers, a really poor girl who falls for a really rich guy. Now why do I feel like I've heard this story before? That's right, because it's overdone! But back to the review. That whole rich-guy, poor-girl, thing was where my first of problem began. If the rich talk bad about the poor then they are A-holes and horrible, selfish, shallow, and just plain rude human beings. If the poor talk bad of the rich then that's OK because they are the underdog. The one's who have nothing so it's perfectly OK to hate those who do. Um, NO! It's not OK either way. Caymens mother completely discriminates! And she's a hypocrite too! She wants nothing to do with Xander, in spite of having never had a single conversation with him, for the sole reason that he has money! Then she goes and talks bout how rich people are horrible and they judge and they they are better than everyone. 
 Another things that got to me was the amount of insta-love. I mean sure they hang out and do a whole bunch of stuff before confessing their undying love for one another but it still felt rushed. They had no reason to hang out or see each other in the first place. Xander goes into her doll shop one time to buy a doll and another to pick something up for his grandmother. The next day he is waiting outside her shop ready to walk her to school. Uh, what? Do they even know each other? They have had two conversations. TWO! Two short and meaningless conversations. They exchanged a joke or two but that's it. Why would Xander bring hot chocolate to a person who he had two encounters with? Why are they acting like they are BFF's? That is not enough! 
 I know I just talked about how I felt the romance was rushed but I also think it was drawn out. The whole problem could have been fixed and they could have been together sooner if Caymen had just asked Xander about his 'girlfriend'. Just go up to him and ask, "hey is that your girlfriend with you in this picture?". And if you are afraid then bring it up casually: "You girlfriend looks nice in this picture," and see his reaction. It's that simple! 
 Now my biggest problem was the end. I did not see that coming and while that is usually the sign of good plot twist this time it was just too random. I didn't see it coming because it came completely out of the freakin' blue! Right out of left field! No one could have seen that coming! It's like the author just really wanted to add a plot twist and decided to add that in the last forty pages just to throw people off. But it wasn't the fact that there was a twist that pissed me off, it was what the twist implied. This meant that Caymen's mom was the biggest selfish, self centered A-hole in the entire book. Not only does this mean that she made her daughter live a life of poverty in which she had to give up her life to make a living but also goes against the entire moral of the story that love can cross boundaries and overcome everything. I feel like the book would have done so much better without that BS plot twist and that totally unfinished ending. 
 Now that I have completely criticized the book and pointed out many of it's great defects let me point out some of the good. 
 A thing I liked was the main character Caymen. In spite of it all she was actually a pretty likable person. She was funny and relatable and I loved who she would think one thing and say another because I feel like we all edit what we want to say so it comes out nicer. Though I think she should be a bit more confident I really liked her. Xander wanted to punch sometimes but I guess he was OK. Caymen's mom I wanted to run over and over and over and over again.

 I picked up this series for a bargain price at a Borders closing and I'm not sure how long it would've taken me to check it out, if at all, if I hadn't. And let me say I'm glad I did. 
 Alexandra Sabian is an Enforcer with the Federal Bureau of Preternatural Investigations (FBPI) who is working on cases that seem to be the work of a serial killer who is beheading, defanging and shoving crosses through vampires hearts. Varik Baudelaire is pulled out of retirement by his former boss, Damian Alberez, and, as the newly reinstated Director of Special Operations at the FBPI, is charged with working with Alex, his former trainee and fiance, to solve the case. For Alex, these killings bring back memories of another from over forty years ago, that of her father, Bernard Sabian. It was his murder that brought the formerly hidden vampire population out in the open, allowing vampires to freely live among humans. 
 Major players in the book are a bigoted sheriff, Harvey Manser; a human lieutenant in the Jefferson PD named Tasha Lockwood who is the liaison between human law enforcement and the FBPI; Emily Sabian, Alex's mom; and Stephen Sabian, Alex's brother and owner of a blood bar named the Crimson Swan. 
 I liked most of the characters a lot, although one character's actions bugged me (view spoiler)[Tasha really annoyed me. I thought she'd end up being a great character who'd bridge the divide between vamps and humans in the law enforcement community, and that she might be a good friend for Alex. However, she became quite bigoted towards vamps for what I thought were fairly poor reasons and her decision to give evidence to one of the bad guys ticked me off, though I can understand why she got pissed at the vampires for keeping her out of the loop. I guess I was just hoping for more from this character. (hide spoiler)]. I thought Stephen's refusal to accept Varik's return to Alex's life with anything short of malice was great. It's how I'd imagine a brother would act towards someone who hurt his sister so much, and he was a great character and I love the way he and Alex interacted and I hope he has more of a role in future books. And her mom? She has more secrets than the U.S. government, some of which are revealed, the rest of which I can't wait to find out. 
 As for Varik, he's a terrific romantic interest for Alex, but this is definitely not a book that's heavy on the romance. Though he lets Alex know in no uncertain terms that he's never stopped loving her and wants her back, he doesn't come off as wimpy or needy, as he very well could have. Despite what happened in his past, he's a sympathetic character who's very likeable, even if he has no qualms about intimidating humans. And he's super patient about Stephen's blatant hatred for him. That's not to say there aren't a few things I'd like to change about him. The hair down to his waist? Blech. A techno ringtone? Really? And don't get me started on the Corvette. He's an awesome character but it sounds like he walked off the cover of a 1980s romance novel. 
 Alex was written as a strong lead who's passionate about her job and whose family is the most important thing to her. Yet she's also, and I really hate this word but am using it anyway, fairly vulnerable. That doesn't mean she's a pushover or bursts into tears at every turn, but things do affect her and the death of her father continues to haunt her. She doesn't just fall into Varik's arms and admits throughout she's not sure she can trust him, yet she's able to admit when she may have been wrong in judging him after something fairly serious happens. And what happens to Alex on the last couple of pages ticked me off (view spoiler)[I thought it was completely unfair of the FBPI to launch an investigation into all of her past cases, particularly when the penalty for being found guilty of corruption is death. (hide spoiler)], but I'm sure it will be dealt with in the sequel. My one complaint about her is that fact that she calls her father "daddy." I have to grit my teeth when I hear adults do this and it's not any less grating having a fictional character do it. 
 Although the murderer was fairly easy to guess after they were introduced, it wasn't a last minute reveal and there was a lot of action that followed his outing. There was also more going on than just the murder of the vampires and though more than one plotline can get confusing or muddle the story, all of the plots were well written and converged nicely. Holmes also threw in a couple of surprises which were not easy to guess, and one completely threw me for a loop and had my jaw hanging when I read it. Trust me, it's a good one! 
 I loved that, while there vampires are the main characters in the story, this isn't a vampire book per se, but is more of a mystery with vampires. 
 I'm really looking forward to reading the next book in the series, Blood Secrets.

 Well I've had this book on my shelf for years now. I just always put it off despite the rave reviews, and that's just how I operate with really popular books - the hype makes me put off reading them till later. I finally picked it up because of tumblr. I was browsing the fandom and the people on tumblr just make the most beautiful edits and graphics I've ever seen and the love they have for these characters is insane. So I started reading it, and I've heard from so many people say that it starts out confusing and is really slow. Personally, I enjoyed it from the beginning. I just really loved this, and I have never LOVED a paranormal book like this ever. 
 On with the review! 
 Characters: 
 This has never happened but I love each and every character so equally in this book. Blue Sargent is an interesting, likeable MC. I thought she would be another MPDG, but I was wrong and I ended up empathizing with her a lot more. I liked how independent she was. I especially enjoyed her relationship with each Raven boy. Gansey, Ronan, Adam, and Noah. My lovely Raven boys. I love them. I can't choose! Maybe personally for me -- I'm a Gansey girl, but damn all four of them are so unique. Stiefvater really gave them very different personalities from each other, but you can also see how they do relate to each other. You see why they are friends. Stiefvater wrote the characters in a way where we see so many aspects of themselves which I really appreciated. Gansey on superficial level is the All American rich boy who has it all, but is fascinated with death and ley lines. I don't want to go further with the characters because I think the magic of this book is reading it on your own and falling in love with each character as the story keeps going. 
 Plot: 
 I feel like the synopsis is very misleading. It makes it seem like a love story, and there's hardly any which I really really liked. I love that focus was on the plot on trying to find Glendower and the ley line. It's utterly fascinating and I looked up alot of this information on google and it's based on legend and there are actual ley lines if you're interested. It's so good, and there are interesting reveals. It's honestly the best paranormal plot I've ever read in YA. 
 Writing: .5 
 From an objective standpoint, I can see why ALOT of people say that this is a slow to start book with confusing plot/writing style in the beginning. Personally, I enjoyed not knowing. It made me read faster in the beginning because I was desperate to find out what's going on. I think this was Stiefvater's purpose. It has this atmospheric mysterious feel to it. The best that I can compare it to is like watching a very complex television show like Fringe or maybe Lost. You think what's the point to all this and then it comes together with purpose. Everything connects and you want to reread it by the end because you want to look for all the clues. 
 Bonus! SO MANY GOOD QUOTES TOO. 
 Feels/Romance: .5 
 My feels came from my love for the Raven Boys' friendship with each other and Blue's relationship with each one of them. I wasn't squealing, but I feel so deeply attached to these characters and I was crying at the end because I just wanted to hug them all and find a solution for them. 
 Ending: .5 
 I only took .5 away because it was bit abrupt, and cliffhanger. UGH. Can't wait to read The Dream Thieves, but I think I'll wait unitl the 3rd books comes out. 
 Overall Enjoyment: 
 I enjoyed every single second of reading this. I was hypnotized every time I did pick up the book and read it. JUST READ IT 
 Rereadability: OH YEAH. I will for sure because I want mark all my favorite quotes. 
 Final Rating: 4.75 stars --

This is another instance where it's daunting to write a review because the novel is well-known and loved by millions of people. As a Sci-Fi/Fantasy reader, it's embarrassing that I've only read this once, and I've waited 'till 2016 to read this. I'm glad that I can finally say that I've read this. I've finally read and enjoyed one of the most influential books of the sci-fi genre. 
 I understand all the buzz regarding this novel. This is the first time in my whole life that I laughed out loud while reading a novel. I've never believed that a novel could be humorous enough to make me elicit more than a giggle or a smile. This novel changed my perception of humor novels in general. I finally have faith in that genre, and an even stronger desire to read more important Sci-Fi novels. 
 I don't see the need to make a short summary of the novel. You can find other reviews that did that. I'm writing this review to express my feelings toward the novel, and the journey that I had with it. Speaking of journey, it was a damn short one. I honestly hate gigantic novels, but it's always fulfilling to finish one if the book is great. This book I can consider amazing, but too short. 
 Aside from the humor, I enjoyed the wittiness of the novel and the author himself. The ideas he incorporated in the novel are vital for the readers to understand. It may be a humor novel, but it's more than that as a whole. 
 The characters are funny and well-developed. The main ones managed to make me laugh. Ford reminds me of Sheldon Cooper from The Big Bang Theory, and Arthur as Leonard Hofstadter. This is like a classic Big Bang theory episode, or maybe The Big Bang theory is a modern Hitchhiker. 
 The plot is not that complex, but it is interesting. I'm always interested to read about other planets in the galaxy, even if it's just fiction. I like to imagine that there are hundreds or thousands of worlds out there in the galaxy. Funny thing that the Earth blew up in this novel. Funnier that they considered Earth as a funny name in the beginning. 
 All the ideologies Adams incorporated here are interesting to me. How some animals are superior and manipulated us, or how the Earth was all a project of some aliens. It's funny and vastly interesting. I can't wait to read the other books in the series.

 Moment of Fate by Karen Stivali is book 5 in the Moments in Time series, and it is an amazing romance. To say I loved this book, would not express just how much, I adored the characters and their story. If you have not read the other books in this series, you can read this story as a standalone, but I would highly recommend you reading all the books, they are all amazing. I have to also mention, did you see that cover? Yummy! 
 The MC in this book are Bryan Dane and Oliver Newcastle. When the book starts Bryan experiences a shock and it causes him to change some of his behaviours, one of which is sleeping with anyone who is willing. Bryan is a bit of a male tramp. Which is why he self-imposes a year long celibacy vow. A year, to focus on himself, his studies, his band, and his friends - no sex. One year. How hard (pun intended) could it be? Enter, Oliver to the scene. 
 Oliver has come to NYC to spend the summer in an intensive summer program, while he simultaneously explores his sexuality and blogs the experience as, Oliver Unabridged. The two first see each other on campus by chance in the elevator and then Oliver leaves his journal behind where Bryan is working. Bryan, opens the journal trying to find out who is belongs to when he sees the information about Oliver and the website name for the blog. Bryan starts reading, Oliver Unabridged without knowing who is writing it, and he is immediatly hooked on the realness and openness of the author. 
 The two meet again, after Bryan's band plays one night and Bryan inadvertently eats something he is allergic to, Oliver is there and he helps him through the allergic reaction and then ends up staying with him to make sure Bryan is okay. Its during the allergic reaction that Bryan realizes, the Oliver he is talking to and the Oliver he has been reading about, are one in the same. 
 The story quickly takes off from here as the two start really getting to know each other, spending almost all their time together, and people think of them as a couple. Bryan, who has sworn off anything to do with relatioships baulks at the comments and Oliver acts as if they don't affect him one way or another. Bryan becomes Oliver's mentor in everything but sex. That is until a movie at a friends house gets them both so ramped up they end up in Bryan's apartment watching porn together and getting off. That moment is the beginning of the end for Bryan and his celibacy. 
 These two are so hot together. But remember, Oliver is all but a virgin when it comes to being with a man. So, lucky Bryan gets to experience all his firsts with him! From mutual masturbation, to hand jobs, frotting, blow jobs, and more...trust me, Bryan doesn't mind, but he holds back some... 
 These two carry on like this and all is well, until Oliver has a date. Bryan, can't understand why its bothering him so much, he doesn't want a boyfriend. When he finds out Oliver is taking his date to the Bar where Bryan will be playing, Bryan is forced fo start confronting his feelings. 
 "I'd be feeling something. That was for sure. I'd be feeling like a possessive fucking idiot standing on stage watching their date play out." 
 When Oliver shows up on his doorstep after the date, Bryan finally admits his desire for Oliver, he stops holding back. 
 "Is that what you think? That I don't want you? Because wanting doesn't even begin to cover how I feel about you. Crave. Need. I don't think a word exists that explains how much I want you." 
 But even a great friendship and hot as hell passion can't make Bryan forget his past, his hurt, his fear of being hurt again. So when its time to either man up and admit he has feelings for Oliver or let him go...he gets scared, he pushes Oliver away, convinced Oliver is just confusing his first sexual encounters with a man, for love. 
 "He stared at me with love. And it scared the hell out of me because I was pretty sure I stared back with the same expression on my own face." 
 It's at this point in the book that I want to reach into it and slap Bryan upside the head. But, I also understand he is scared, he has been hurt, he doesn't want to go through it again. Sometimes though...you have to take a chance, sometimes the chance of pain is worth it when you get that elusive happily ever after. 
 So, during a chance moment of Fate when these two see each other a month or so after going their separate ways. Bryan takes that chance and leaps hoping Oliver catches him... 
 "I was already so head over heels in love with you I was too stupid and scared shitless to even realize what was going on. Jesus, Oliver. I miss you. I need you... I love you." 
 Will these two get their HEA or are they forever meant to be just a simple moment in time? 
 5 Stars --

Review brought to you by OBS staff member Annabell Cadiz 
 Synopsis: "Every single lifetime, I'll choose you. Just as you have chosen me. Forever." 
 Luce would die for Daniel. And she has. Over and over again. Throughout time, Luce and Daniel have found each other, only to be painfully torn apart: Luce dead, Daniel left broken and alone. But perhaps it doesn't need to be that way. . . . 
 Luce is certain that something--or someone--in a past life can help her in her present one. So she begins the most important journey of this lifetime . . . going back eternities to witness firsthand her romances with Daniel . . . and finally unlock the key to making their love last. 
 Cam and the legions of angels and Outcasts are desperate to catch Luce, but none are as frantic as Daniel. He chases Luce through their shared pasts, terrified of what might happen if she rewrites history. 
 Because their romance for the ages could go up in flames . . . forever. 
 Review: I have never truly fallen in love with Luce or the story behind the Fallen Series. There just always seemed to be something missing within the plot and the books have a tendency to drag out far longer than I would like. 
 Passion is not an exception to that. The book essentially begins where Torment had left off. Luce is traveling through the Announcers to locate her past lives. She wants to know more about what she had gone through with Daniel and to better understand what the curse over them is exactly. The overall story does help to fill in missing aspects from the previous two novels. The origin and reason of the curse is fleshed out practically until the end. 
 Luce spends pretty much the entire novel venturing into her past lives. Half way through the book I was tired of reading about them and skipped a huge chunk on the novel. Even then, I was still able to fully understand the curse and the reason for it. The good stuff doesn't really happen until about page 261 but even then I skimmed over some pages. The chapters just drag out too much and Luce reaches her lessons agonizingly slow. So much of what happens could have been condensed and still would have worked. 
 Luce did manage to grow up some as she journeys through her past lives and being away from Daniel and her friends helped to let Luce come to her choice on her own. She was a little stronger in this installment and matures in wisdom through being able to inhabit some of her past lives. 
 Some of the chapters are also narrated from Daniel's perspective as he attempts to locate Luce. Readers gain more incite to what Daniel had to go through choosing Luce over Heaven. Daniel wasn't always so closed off and guarded. Readers also get to better understand his relationship with Cam and how Cam fell from grace. 
 Other than the chapters seeming far too long (therefore increasing Luce's ability to whine and make stupid choices at times), Passion has other flaws. The pacing is, most of the time, slow. The plot is pretty flat until closer toward the end when the story reveals how the curse came to happen. Daniel conveniently forgetting about his past lives was a bit annoying. In a way I understand, he didn't want to remember always suffering through having to watch Luce die, he just wanted to remember the good. But I still found that a bit out of place. Bill was an extremely irritating character. You find out who he is closer to the end and that makes sense as to why he is so dislikeable but he distracts from liking the story. Lucifer is far too predictable which rather bored me by the time he reveals himself to Luce. Much of the other characters weren't much in the story and I missed them. They are as much apart of Daniel and Luce's story as Daniel and Luce and the story felt strange without them. 
 The final two chapters set the stage quite well for the final installment, Rapture. I am curious to know how this series ends and if Luce and Daniel are finally freed from their curse. I just hope the pacing and fluidity of the story is much better than it's predecessors.

1870. Charles Dickens is dead. He leaves behind a struggling publisher, a bereaved public, and an unfinished novel. The Mystery of Edwin Drood promised to be Dickens' masterpiece, equally adored and misunderstood, and revolved around the question of whether the young hero was murdered or in hiding. Now the mystery will never be solved; the novel is only half written. 
 Or is it? 
 It falls to James Osgood, Dickens' American publisher, to find out the truth. Along the way, he must fight opiate dealers, cutthroat publishers, and Dickens' close friends' diverging opinions about the possible endings to Drood. What he discovers is intriguing: could Drood's missing ending hold the key to a real-life murder mystery? 
 The novel is intriguing, a literary thriller written by a master of suspense. Pearl does an excellent job of incorporating period details without ever slowing the pace. There were facts that I didn't know. Did you know that Dickens offered to tell Queen Victoria the ending of Drood? Or that Dickens was stalked by a female admirer? Or that an American tax collector blackmailed the Dickens staff? 
 The book is divided into six installments (the same number of installments as Drood had at the time of Dickens' death) and they flip from the present (after his death) and past (while Dickens is on a book tour in America). At times, the structure can be confusing; after one or two of the flashbacks, I had difficulty remembering exactly what had happened in the previous section regarding the present day action. Overall, though, that structure heightened the suspense and revealed Dickens the man and how much the public craved his writings. 
 I enjoyed the characters, especially Dickens' publisher James Osgood (a historical figure) and Tom Branagan (a fictional character) who acts as Dickens porter on his last American tour. Most of all, I enjoyed learning more about the time period and exploring the possibility of what might have been the ending of the author's last novel. Edwin Drood may be an unsolved mystery, but The Last Dickens' ending is satisfying.

Izzie's life as been anything but simple. She lives with her grandmother--whose condition isn't always as stable as it should be--and works so that they have money; but it's what her life and one that she doesn't want to give up. Unfortunately, her social worker, Barbara and her grandmother have been planning something that will change Izzie's life forever. Suddenly she's moving to Emerald Cove--which is the exact opposite of Harborside--to live with her uncle (a state senator) and his family. And it's there, in Emerald Cove and at Emerald Prep that Izzie will truly have to fight to fit in--and there are a few residents who will do anything they can to sabotage her. 
 So, I did like Isabelle (Izzie) better than Mirabelle (Mira) in Belles. Why? Because unlike Mira, Izzie is well and truly determined to remain true to herself and when she's challenged, she'll do everything she can to meet it and rise above it. Also, she's still modest despite everything--she really wants to do good (both with her new family and at school). On the other hand, you have Mira who really seems to get stepped on by both Savannah (her 'best' friend) and her boyfriend as well. On the upside, Mira really starts to speak up for herself towards the end and I'm hoping that she continues to improve in Winter White. Then there's Brayden who is really growing on me; he knew Izzie before she moved to Emerald Cove and well, he's a nice guy--you'll see what I mean. I also really liked Hayden, Mira's older brother, who Izzie feels that she can talk to. And yes, it's a bit confusing at times to have one boy named Brayden and another named Hayden--there were a few moments when I had to look at my notes to remember who was who. 
 There are definitely some not-so-great decisions made in Belles by Mira and Izzie that were a bit difficult for me to read--mainly because I like it best when characters stand up for themselves--but one has to expect some cattiness when it comes to the rich. (Gossip Girl, anyone?) Also, it does start off a little slow for my tastes, but things definitely start to pick up once Izzie gets to her uncle's house--and it alternates between what Izzie is up to and what Mira is up to although it's written in third person. Having said that, I really did end up enjoying Belles and I'm definitely going to be looking forward to Winter White later this year! If you're a fan of Gossip Girl, then I'd recommend this to you (or if you like books along those lines).

For the first middle grade novel to be reviewed on my blog, this was a fantastic choice! It clearly had promise, and on that it absolutely delivered. I was definitely pleasantly surprised by this one. 
 This is a wonderfully written novel. With middle grade, I think it's very important to have a narrative voice that a younger reader can connect to. This was absolutely present with the main character and narrator, Jack. His narrative voice is so friendly and easy to follow, especially at the beginning, and I think it is perfect for younger readers. At the same time though, it did not feel juvenile at all. As an older teenager reading an MG novel, I did not feel spoken down to, or like it was too young for me. That can be a hard balance for MG authors to find, but I think Peter Lerangis has done an excellent job writing in a voice that can appeal to people of any age. 
 If I had to describe this novel in two words, I'd say action-packed. There is always something happening. This is the perfect book for a reader who gets bored quickly because there is no time to get bored. It jumps from some wild event to a daring escape to an unbelievable rescue, and so on. This was done extremely well because while it is definitely exciting and always moving, the transition is still there. It moves at a fast pace but not at the expense of important information. This is another area in which I feel Lerangis' experience in this field really comes through. You cannot dispute that he knows how to write for his audience. 
 While the plot was certainly the highlight of the novel, you can't forget the characters. The main character, Jack, is smart, entertaining, and, what I especially enjoyed: skeptical. When he is told a bunch of wild, unimaginable things about himself, he doesn't just accept them; he thinks the man who told him is absolutely nuts and tries to run away. He thinks logically, which in a story with such wild happenings, helps make a lot of things more understandable. As for the friends he makes, Cass, Marco, and Aly; they're all a little strange and they each have their quirks that sometimes make you want to grab them by the shoulders and shake them, but these things make them feel like real 13 year olds. What real 13 year old doesn't have some annoying quirk or habit? You really grow to enjoy them despite the occasionally irritating behaviour, because really, it's normal. 
 Overall this was a fun, exciting novel for my first foray into middle grade fiction on the blog and I loved the mythology/history aspect! Can't wait to see which wonder they tackle next! I will absolutely be keeping my eye out for the next novel in the series. 
 4 stars!

 Before I get on to the review. Let's start out with a very important fact about me: 
 My first tattoo was dedicated to my love of music. It's my lifeblood, so I went into these book very expectant. Now, let's kick things off with my thoughts on The Hum and the Shiver. 
 wenty-year-old Bronwyn Hyatt returns to Cloud County, Tennessee after a horrifying experience in Iraq brings her back to the States a war hero. She returns to her home a place she both dreads and loves, a place she has a deep connection to. Bronwyn is a Tufa, and they are at the apex of their magical strength, which manifests in music, when they're home. The Tufa are an enigmatic ethnic group living in the mountains, believed to have been there when the first white settlers stumbled into the area. They're called everything from black to Native American. However, no one knows for sure who they are or where they come from. Bronwyn is a pure-blood Tufa and one of the "First Daughters," women who carry the songs of the Tufa through the generations. Even though Tufa men sing the songs, as well, the First Daughters are the most powerful and most important of the Tufa. Despite this, Bronwyn is a bit of black sheep among her kind. She was rebellious as a child, eventually leaving the safety of the Tufa land for the military. She returns a rebellious woman who is insistent of honoring her heritage while embracing the change that seems to be coming for them. On top of this change, signals of death are in the air, leaving the Tufa on high alert because the signs point to the Hyatt family. 
 This book also follows an uninspired reporter named Don Swayback who has lived away from the Tufa for years, but he is part Tufa. With Bronwyn's return, which he reports on for the small paper he works for, he feels something awakening in him as he begins to embrace more of his heritage. That chance encounter stirs something in him. Being part Tufa means he may or may not have the capacity for the magic as explained by this passage: 
 "Anyway, we need to talk about blood. You got more Tufa in you than you realize. It ain't always about quantity: you can have a man ninety-five percent pureblood, but if that missing five percent is the part that lets him ride the wind, he ain't a true Tufa. You know about riding the night wind?" Don shook his head."You will, I reckon. I hope. One night you'll go outside, look up at the sky, and either hear the hum or feel the shiver. If it's the shiver ... well, you're still kin and I love you, but it means you'll never be a real Tufa. If it's the hum, though, you'll feel the stirrin' of your wings." 
 I should briefly point out that in this book the term "the hum and the shiver" is used frequently and in many beautifully poetic ways. It can be used to express many different things in the Tufa life. 
 Don't think you're going to get just a flowery book about music and magic. There's politics at play among the Tufa. While many believe them to be one people, they are actually two separate and equally power factions of people who don't like each other much and seem to be vying for power. Don's story can seem a little disjointed from the rest of the book until you keep in mind there is a power struggle going on. Also, there's much prejudice that the Tufa deal with, especially with the state trooper that patrols the area whose role isn't much more than to be your standard racist villain. There's also a few villains among their own including a man named Dwayne Gitterman, an ex-boyfriend of Bronwyn's, who has "burned" the music out of him through his own evil. While he's more interesting as a villain for this, he isn't much better a villain than the state trooper except for his Tufa connection. There's also that looming violence that Bronwyn dealt with in Iraq, which thankfully isn't fully explored, mainly because Bronwyn insists on not revisiting that part of her ordeal. There's some mention of violence against women, even a scene where one man sort of describes how he could carry out a rape against Bronwyn (he's really not that stupid, though), but he does do some other violent things. This is redneck country, expect some ugliness is what I'm saying-in language and actions. It's totally in keeping with the setting of such a story, but it may offend some. 
 I will admit in explaining the Tufa at points I think Bledsoe was trying to be as plain as possible for clarity's sake, but instead those passages started to feel redundant and had me asking, "What can't the Tufa do? Can one Superman punch someone into the sun? Asking for a friend." On their own land, they hold a lot of power. Some people may even ask why would the Tufa even ever leave their lands with that in mind, but just because something is the "best" thing for you doesn't mean that your heart doesn't long to see things, to see the outside world, to have new experiences, even if that means weakening yourself or facing the unknown to do it. People run from their heritage all the time. That's part of why Bronwyn left and she is hardly the first Tufa to leave, even in her family, but she found the need to be home greater than her need for something different. Bronwyn as a character left me conflicted. She was selfish and selfless, and maybe that describes most of us. However, so many of her actions that seemed selfless also seemed to really further her own selfish actions. Despite the terror she's been through, though, she is still a twenty-year-old woman barely out of girlhood and it shows. She's strong, weak, self, sexual, and a million other things, and despite this, we need rounded female characters that don't just embody our idea of what a heroine of a story should be. 
 The love interests of the story come in two forms. One is a older teenaged boy (which may squick some people because he is like seventeen), Terry-Joe Gitterman, the brother of Bronwyn's former boyfriend, and a pastor ten years Bronwyn's senior named Craig. Tufa don't have religion per se. That's not to say they don't believe in God, but they have their own beliefs and they are very private about them. So, giving Bronwyn a Christian love interest was intriguing. Both provided different angles to Bronwyn's idea of love and sex, and in the end I really thought Bledsoe did something unique where this love triangle was concerned. While I did think Bledsoe played it a little safe with Craig, doing much to make him so likable despite him not really being someone the Tufa would open up to, I did like that Bledsoe presented Christianity not as something that should be about brimstone and fire but as about your actions and what you do to help your fellow man without their being some burdened placed on the actions because "God is watching!" In other words, Craig did things because he knew they were the right thing to do, and he didn't condemn those he helped because they might not believe as he did. I only say he played it safe because there were moments when he did have the Christianity be so "in your face" and then back away from it instead of leading to more challenging conversations. 
 About halfway through the book, I stopped listening to the narration. My reasoning for this is because Card's voice reminded me too much of the lady who co-narrated the novel, Wreckage (and that book annoyed me, so she faced a prejudiced in me getting to really enjoy her narration) and didn't fit how I think Bronwyn-young, yet old all at the same time-would sound like, which came off too flighty and just didn't feel right. Also, Card wasn't really singing the verses in the book more than chanting them when I was looking to hear some twangy, bluegrass type music for the Tufa songs. As for Rudnicki, his voice was so deep that it distracted me. I love deep-voiced narrators both male and female, but his voice actually lulled me and made me miss bits of the story because it was easy to get caught up in his voice, which is very musical in nature compared to Card's. Don't let my thoughts on the narration deter you from listening to it, though, if you're considering the audiobooks. Fun fact: Card attributes Rudnicki for much of her training. 
 I would be lying if I said that part of my ratings and feeling on these books come from many reasons aside from just the story itself. I connected with the story as a southerner and knowing how small towns can be with their secrets and their "haints." Secondly, and the larger reason I started this series, is that I love books that combine music and magic in inventive ways. As a musician, I could relate too well to so many lines in this books about the hum and the shiver. My instructor was one of those people who believed you had people who played music and then you had people who music was so much a part of them that to rip music from their soul would surely kill them. She always said proudly that music was in my soul, and she still brags to this day about me being the youngest child she's ever taken as a piano student because she "saw" something in me. I played a few other instruments, but the piano is my Magda (what Bronwyn calls her mandolin and most treasured instrument). In a way, she believed much of what this books believed, but in a much more realistic way. And I can name a few musicians that can touch me in a way that feels like something short of magic. This book does a beautiful job of capturing that feeling, the emotions and stories that music can capture in them.

This should have been so much more badass and dangerous and heartbreaking than it was.

 And don't get me started on my main bad bitch Ventress. My beautiful, bald, angry, impersonal queen of the dark side. What have they done to you?

 I'm disappointed yo. There's no reason for this not to have been amazing.

This was a very intricately researched story of a woman condemned to be executed for murder in 1830s Iceland (though it feels quite medieval at times, which I imagine is quite accurate). You may well smell the manure, scratch at the lice, and shiver in the cold as you read this (I'm sure I did). However, I found the character interactions to be just as chilly as their environs. While the final 50 pages were quite moving, it took me a long time to get into the story. I found the odd shifts between first- and third-person jarring, and there wasn't quite enough of a plot to pull me through the story (I fell asleep half-way through a chapter at least three times this past week while reading before bed). That said, there is some nice prose here and enough way-of-life details to fulfill your "Icelandic historical fiction needs" for quite a while...

The Hundred Oaks series is one I have been invested in from the very beginning so getting the chance to snag Defending Taylor early for review was something I didn't expect, so you know I made a start on this as soon as possible. 
 Taylor makes the decision to take the blame for something, to ensure her boyfriend would get to keep his scholarship, assuming her Dads position would mean she would get a lenient punishment. What she wasn't expecting was to be kicked out of school and be forced to go to Hundred Oaks, her rival school. Attending a new school isn't something Taylor planned on, and she finds it hard to fit in and settle, especially with the animosity of school rivalry. Her effort to join the soccer team seems futile, when she is he only committed one, and the rest are happy to let their star player take over practice, if you could call it that, and refuse to accept her help. 
 Taylor wants so much to keep it all secret, to protect Ben, even if it means sacrificing her own future. She finds it hard to open up and share why she was expelled from school, but with the help of her counselor and some prompts she begins to open up to Ezra, but can she tell him the whole truth. 
 Defending Taylor was a book I found hard to put down. I love how easy it is to fall into this world and get to meet new characters, and catch up with old friends from Racing Savannah. Defending Taylor is a book that really makes you think about how far you would go to save someone you love, and how far is too far when it starts to impact your future? 
 Taylor isn't perfect, and she makes silly mistakes, but to me that makes her human enabling the reader to make a connection with her. I liked how her relationship with Ezra wasn't rushed, even though they did have some history together. 
 Final Verdict 
 Defending Taylor was a book that I could not get enough of. I really enjoyed reading this one and I'm looking forward to see what comes next in this series.

Twenty-seven year old Libby Mason is in pursuit of an ideal man. In her eyes, this means rich, distinguished and successful, a man who can ultimately cater to her coveted uber-fabulous lifestyle. In the past, her interactions with men turned into confirmed disasters, but she is determined to find "The One". 
 When the benevolent and handsome Nick comes along, Libby is convinced that she will not fall hard this time around, particularly since he is broke as a joke. Nick is to only satisfy her sexual needs, and to provide fun companionship. So why can't she stop thinking about him? 
 As she rapidly grows fonder of Nick, he cuts her off when he realizes that she is in too deep. Libby turns to her best friend Jules for comfort and advice. The solution? Girl's Night. Ow! On their night out on the town, Libby meets Ed McMahon, a loaded and very eligible bachelor. 
 Ed is the complete opposite of Nick. He's older, cornier, snobbier and not to mention the worst lay of her life. But, he dotes on her, making Libby feel like the ultimate princess for a change. 
 When he proposes, she finally sees herself living in a lap of luxury, dreams of being the wife of a successful businessman finally coming to fruition. But as expected, she comes to learn that social status isn't all its cracked up to be, especially when there is no love. 
 The ending is sort of predictable, but overall the story is a great one.

 I felt really frustrated throughout the book, in the beginning because it was kind of depressing and disgusting while it was new, then, because nothing was happening (the woman just drove by the city visiting useless side characters adding shit to the story). When the mystery finally unraveled, I was once again frustrated, because it was rushed and unsatisfactory. No thrill in the ending whatsoever.

 Im so glad that I finally had the chance to pick up Hollow City. I was wanting, no, craving to know what happened in this thrilling trilogy. Ransom Riggs is such an amazing author. Ive said this about a couple other authors, but honestly, I think that Ransom is just so much better than the others. 
 Hollow City was so well thought out and everything had so much depth to it. The characters all had a unique background, and all the areas even had a great deal of description and deal. 
 I had so many different emotions for each of the characters. They were all so different, and well written. Of course one of my favourites were Jacob with Bronwyn as a close second. Jacob always took charge when he needed to, if he didnt want to. Sure, he may not have had the best ideas, or played out his plans correctly, but it still showed how much he cared for all the peculiars. And Bronwyn, oh wow, Bronwyn cared so much for everyone. Every single little character, no matter how big their part in the novel was, she cared about them. She never wanted someone to get hurt for no reason. She wanted to protect everyone, and save everyone whenever it was possible. I have nothing but respect for Bronwyn, it doesnt matter that shes just a written character. I feel as though, if everyone acted like Bronwyn, there wouldnt be as many problems in the world as there are... Im getting off track. 
 If there was one thing that I didnt enjoy as much as the other parts, it would be the romantic relationship between Jacob and Emma. It was obvious that they cared deeply for each other and would do anything to protect each other, but I feel that it didnt fit that well with the rest of the story. Perhaps in a different novel it would work better for me. I loved both characters, and some of the parts with the two of them together were /super/ cute. They couldve been relationship goals, if it had been in a different setting.

So, there were some things I did like about this book. First off, a romance set in semi-sort-of Ancient Greece was cool and not something I have seen done before. I enjoyed the sassiness of the heroine and her amusing internal voice. I could sympathize with how Cat's traumatic childhood would make her reluctant to form lasting relationships with others. I wanted to learn more about her crazy family and why she made her escape as a child. All good stuff. 
 That hero, though. Gah. 
 Some of the time, Griffin was an okay guy and I liked him and his sarcastic sense of humor. Then he'd turn into this high-handed, incredibly jealous He-Man type and I wanted to punch him as much as Cat did at the beginning of the book. Like, okay dude, you don't get to kidnap a lady and then get all bent out of shape when she seems reluctant to be a card-carrying member of your bro-posse. Nor do you have the right to force her to make a binding promise to never leave you (something which carries weight in this world of magic). Or turn into a giant green rage monster when your chosen lady spends time with your male best friends. Not attractive qualities, sir. 
 You know a romance book is not for you when you much prefer the side male characters to the main hero (I'd totally read a book featuring someone like Kato. Or, you know, Kato himself). I'll probably read the next book when it comes out in January, since I've become invested in this world and the story, but I would much prefer if that aspect of the plot were to take center stage over the romance.

THE ART OF SINNING by Sabrina Jeffries is a fabulous and exciting start to her new Sinful Suitors historical romance series. I loved everything about this sinfully sexy novel, from the humorous and affectionate secondary characters to the intriguing subplots and the steamy and sweet love scenes. Jeremy Keane is one hot, bad boy of an American blond artist, and his love interest Lady Yvette is an independent, striking brunette, a Juno of a goddess and a Circe of temptation, with an unusual hobby of collecting street cant for dictionaries. 
 Jeremy left America and his responsibilities to his family business in order to avoid his feelings and memories of both his wife who died in childbirth and his stillborn child. He came to England to find a model for his latest, controversial work of art. When he sees Yvette at a ball, he knows she's the one. He's powerfully attracted to her at the same time, but he believes that he has an empty heart and that Yvette deserves better and more from a man. 
 The attraction goes both ways. Yvette has a weakness for flirtatious rogues, but she's been burned in the past and doesn't want to get involved with a man who can't make and keep promises. She doesn't want to fall in love with Jeremy, because she's afraid he'll break her heart. Yet, she can't ignore her longing for him. He is sexy and naughty and talks a little dirty when they're alone, but underneath his roguish facade he's a gentleman with integrity. 
 Jeremy and Yvette both have to overcome the hurts of their past to fall in love and have a future together. I loved their intelligent and witty banter, strength of character, and passionate pairing. And I loved that Jeremy isn't the caveman type of alpha male and doesn't have a possessive and violent nature. He's not the kind of man that resolves conflict by beating up other men and challenging them to duels. He's soulful and smarter than that. 
 So far, THE ART OF SINNING is my favorite Sabrina Jeffries' historical romance, and smoldering alpha male Jeremy Keane is my favorite of her heroes. I look forward to reading more novels in this sinfully sexy, promising new series.

I really liked Lions of Al-Rassan, nice world construction, fun plot arc, and solid main characters but I did have a few issues with it. 
 Sentence structure, oh man. The sentences have a feel of "writing how you talk" and it's a little awkward at times. They either drag on or just have a really strange construction to them. But I think the reason that they stand out to me so much is because I do the same thing when writing. It just led to me having to re-read sentences to figure out what the actual point of it was. 
 Character wise there was a lot of them. Maybe if I hadn't taken a few days off from reading it wouldn't have been so bad but there are some really big jumps to new narratives of characters we know nothing about and aren't mentioned for a long time so I'm not invested in trying to remember their name or title is. Thus forgetting who they are when they re-appear. 
 The author also does this things, which is a very common writing technique mind you, that annoys me. He avoids proper names to drag out the mystery of who is either hurt/dead/sneaking around. It works in some cases but in others I just find it tiring. One POV is enough, but it pull it out for three different character POVs it's just too much. 
 I'm better at writing about things I don't like instead of the things I do like about a book :/

"Those who don't build must burn... There's some of it in all of us" 
 The premise was relevant, chilling and scary in fact -- because I am reading an actual book that focused on a setting that destroys them and treat them as a taboo. The book "predicted" the takeover of television and mass media in written literature and this gave it a timeless grade to it. 
 However, the story felt short and the last several pages were a bit underwhelming. I felt that the storyline didn't progress in the same rate as the first two parts. I also thought that the characters and scenes can be fleshed out more (like for Clarisse, Mildred and even Faber's part), but instead we got more of Montag's inner thought. Apparently though, Bradbury thought that letting Clarisse live is a great idea (he got it from the movie adaptation that didn't follow most of the book's element) and he eventually employed it on the stage adaptation of the book. Last complaint will be that setting didn't feel futuristic enough (especially for his writing time), but I guess it's good too because we had more focus on the story and (a bit of) the characters. 
 This is still definitely a classic and I have to give Bradbury a break with all these as the book was written 50 years ago! Recommended for that and for being a quick read.

Like most Old West legends, the story of Hugh Glass is rife with speculation, exaggeration, and outright fiction, but the facts are just as unbelievable. That Glass, a fur trader and hunter, was viciously attacked and mauled by a grizzly bear is true. That he was near death and not expected to survive is true. That John Fitzgerald and Jim Bridger were left to watch over him and give him a proper Christian burial is true. That the two sons of bitches left Glass alone to die, stealing his rifle and knife, is true. That Glass survived and embarked upon a bloodthirsty quest for revenge is true. 
 Everything else, of course, is speculation. And Michael Punke, in his novel "The Revenant", speculates wonderfully. 
 Punke's unenviable job of piecing together a fictionalized account of the real-life Hugh Glass was nevertheless fruitful. Where information couldn't be found from primary or secondary sources or from the plethora of existing works about Glass and the American Fur Trade, Punke simply "filled in the gaps" with a novelist's imagination, albeit an educated imagination borne from much research as a historian. 
 Did I mention that "The Revenant" is Punke's first novel? 
 Having written only historical nonfiction prior to "The Revenant", Punke's prose stands with the best of writers of western fiction. Clearly, fans of Louis L'Amour, Zane Grey, Stephen Crane, and Jack London will find a kindred spirit in Punke. He writes lovingly of the beauty of nature while not betraying the sheer terror and lack of compassion nature has for humans. 
 The grizzly attack, which happens early in the novel, is graphic and intense, but it is, of course, not the only scene of wanton violence. There are surprise Indian raids that result in high body counts, and there is Glass's hunt for the two men who wronged him, only one of whom probably deserved killing. 
 I haven't seen the recent film version of "The Revenant", starring Leonardo DiCaprio, although I'm sure it's excellent. 
 I can't say much more about Punke's novel without probably giving away too many spoilers, so I'll keep it short. Fans of westerns shouldn't pass this one up.

I'm so excited to have found this book and its author, Rae Carson. I was hankering for a quality fantasy, and didn't even know it until I started reading. There are so many good things about this book, the first of which is that it actually has an ending! Yay, no cliff hanger! 
 The world and magic that Carson creates is unique and unlike those typical of fantasy. Elisa, the main character, and her people are dark-skinned people from lands of desert and jungle. Their enemies are the evil, animalistic, light-skinned barbarians to the north. Carson's system of magic centers around something called godstones. Each century God chooses a person to fulfill some divine purpose and marks that person as His own by placing a faceted jewel, the godstone, in his/her navel. The stone is a living presence, pulsing heat whenver the chosen prays or feels comfort and turning icy in warning of any danger. Elisa's enemies use these stones to wield some kind of sorcery, and as this century's chosen, she may be the only one able to combat their magic and save her people. This combination of religious-based magic and multicultural characters/society made for a really interesting read, something totally different from the fantasy I'm used to reading. 
 I tore right through the book in just two days. The plot is well-paced and totally unpredictable (another thing that was exciting about this book). I always enjoy a good girl-with-swords plot featuring a strong female character who knows how to wage war and win fights, and Elisa and Carson provided. 
 Oh, but one small little rant. I saw that a lot of reviews were calling this Divergent for the fantasy genre. Ummmm...definitely no! It's not that at all! I don't even really understand how they're coming to that conclusion. Yeah there's a war...and a young heroine who can fight...but that's true of many YA fantasy novels, many of which were written before Hunger Games (I'm thinking all of Tamora Pierce's novels). So, no, just, no.

The idea behind A Shade of Vampire is pretty catchy and kept me reading through to the end. A vampire prince who goes under a sleeping spell to escape vampirism, and a girl kidnapped to be his personal toy once he wakes up--but who he falls in love with instead. The island they live on, their government, and they way they live, all had me wanting to find out more about this coven of vampires. I was interested in learning more about Derek as well, and in seeing where his relationship with Sofia would lead. Despite the insta-love factor, I was rooting for them to be together, even when an unexpected variable was thrown into the picture. What can I say? I'm a sucker for tortured souls. 
 But while the ideas behind the story were catchy, I couldn't help but be disappointed in the way things unfolded. The great ideas were all there, but I couldn't shake the feeling that the story wasn't yet finished. The biggest factor in this is the pacing. The story begins at a pace that gives us detailed descriptions of what happens through Sofia's eyes at almost every moment of the day. Then somewhere in the last half of the book it suddenly skips days, then weeks at a time, hurriedly glossing over what could have been some of the more interesting parts of the story (Sofia's training sessions) in just a few pages. After that, it slows down again and settles back into the every moment descriptions, but the time in the story no longer computes with the time frame in your mind. The book is short--just under 150 pages, which I read it in about 4 hours. And with Bella Forrest's descriptive writing, I think there could definitely have been more of the story told, while keeping the same pace throughout the entire book. 
 Other little things were bothersome, such as some of the more predictable moments, and a few overused cliches. It is a story that can suck you in if you let it, and it does have some very bright moments. There is a seriously awesome part where Sofia tells Derek to stop feeling sorry for himself because he's not the victim. I almost cheered when she said that, because it's something I sometimes wish I could say to so many characters from other books. Overall, I think this is the type of book you would pick up if you have some free time and want a quick read.

 As I read this, two other books kept coming to mind -- A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry and Want Not by Jonathan Miles. Rather than unequivocally recommending this book, I'll note that if you liked A Fine Balance and Want Not, you'll probably like this.

How the mighty have fallen. On the night before her wedding, Parastrata Ava makes a major mistake that throws the merchant spaceship crewes of Parastrata and AEther into chaos. Left to freeze to death, Ava begins freeing herself the only way she knows how - by "fixes". 
 Salvage stands out in many ways from the pack. Although sci-fi, don't go in expecting uprises against governments or battle scenes. Instead, it unfurls slowly, taking the time to explore a new location and way of life, but moving on to something else before you can get bored. Also, it's a stand-alone novel, though in the hands of a different author it could've been dragged out to a trilogy and stuffed with filler. Thankfully, this 520-page tome is self-contained, and though theoretically there could be other stories set in this world worth telling, Ava's seems done for now, and that feels right. Another rare thing in its favour is that I actually cheered for Ava's romance with Rushil. 
 Alexandra Duncan depicts beautiful, dangerous settings with colour and depth. From the austere life on merchant ships, to house-boating in Haiti, to the humidity of the Salt, and to a more luxurious life in Mumbai... But as much as Ava may wish for independence, she can't make it alone. If Perpetue, Rushil, and Soraya have taught her anything, it's that sometimes you can rely on the kindness of strangers. Ava does seem rather too stupid to live when she has to be rescued in each new location, but by the final chapter she seems capable, and maybe even confident. 
 Salvage is not just a pretty cover - there's also an extraordinary story inside.

When I finished The Girl Who Played with Fire, I wrote the following paragraph in my Goodreads review:

 One thing that was a bit odd is the epilogue -- it reads as more of a second climax than a typically mundane they-all-lived-happily-ever-after epilogue.

I have been so excited and anxiously awaiting this new release and initial book in Raine Miller's new Blackstone Dynasty Series, and it has definitely been well worth the wait. This is such a sweet, passionate, and super sexy romance, and the charming wealthy billionaire Caleb Blackstone is impossible not to fall in love with! 
 Caleb Blackstone has everything any man could ever want and more. He is handsome, wealthy, and very successful in running his family's empire. Although he has it all, he questions the one thing he is missing - a woman to keep his attention and worth building a future with. Until he meets her... and then he just knows he's found the one. Brooke Casterley is undeniably beautiful, but she carries a sadness with her stemming from her tragic past in which she is fighting to overcome and rebuild anew. The attraction between Brooke and Caleb is instantaneous and seems to come so naturally to them both, but they come from two different worlds. Could Brooke be strong enough to survive in a world like Caleb's? Could she find the courage to open up to love again? 
 Caleb and Brooke's relationship has several qualities that genuinely melt my heart every time I find them in a romance. One of these qualities is a mutual respect - for both their needs and their boundaries - and the other is adoration. Caleb knew that Brooke had a lot to overcome, and he respected her needs by being so incredibly patient and cautious with her every step of the way. Caleb was so smitten and completely adored Brooke as he continued to convey his confidence in his love for her. He was so incredibly caring and accepting of her insecurities, and in turn this gave Brooke the ability to overcome her barriers and return her love to him. They both nurtured each other's souls, and it was very beautiful to watch them blossom and grow together! 
 This is where Miller's incredible writing talent comes into play for me. She has the ability not only to craft very unique stories with multiple layers, but characters who seem to grab my attention and make me feel. Whether the characters themselves know it or not throughout their stories in which she writes, I love how she creates strong, genuine, and truly caring alpha males and compliments them with heroines who also exude their own confidence and strength. Her characters seem to be more realistic and intriguing as they evolve together and transition throughout the stories she tells. It's almost a dance that Miller orchestrates with such a perfect pace as the slow burning passion becomes such a beautiful love story! 
 There are also hidden mysteries, pasts, and connections within this story, some of which are revealed and some that look to be revealed in future books in this series. I really enjoyed meeting the Blackstone family and am definitely looking forward to seeing more of them. Caleb's sister, Winter, and his friend, Jacob's, story will be next in Filthy Lies which is expected in February of 2017!

 I felt like this book was a mix of Divergent and Six of Crows. 
 Why do I compare this to Divergent? Well, we find ourselves with a divided society. The people of Loom are divided in Guilds, and they must take two tests before joining them. If they do not pass these tests, they are sentenced to death. 
 The five guilds are: 
 *Harvesters - We don't see them through this book (or not that I can remember), but these are the people who supply raw materials to the other guilds. 
 *Alchemists - They create the Chimeras, they seem to be the only guild that's not under the Dragon's control, they're far from the others - territory wise - 
 *Rivets - They work in the mines and the refining process. 
 *Ravens - From what I understood, they seem to be the ones who do all the transportation. 
 *Revolvers- They make GUNS AND EXPLOSIONS! 
 The people from the Guilds live in Loom, which is the place where the Dragon King has taken control; while the Dragons live in Nova. Our main setting for this book is Loom, while it seems like the second book will have Nova as it's main setting. 
 Why do I compare this to Six of Crows? First, I love books where the author can pull off multiple POVs! There are various scenes that reminded me of this book, mainly because our main characters are doing a break-out from a very secured jail. THIS SCREAMED SIX OF CROWS TO ME! - Our characters are very unique, each one has very different characteristics and somehow they all fit and work well together (Although there's some very rough hate at first.) 
 The first 100-ish pages of the book seemed a bit slow to me. It can't be easy to build a world and at the same time involve some action in it, so this is understandable. At first it was so difficult for me to understand the world, like I said... we have two lands and five guilds (also, the Dragons are divided in three houses). 
 We have various main characters, but I'd say Arianna is the "main of the mains" haha. She is such a bad-ass female character! She hates Dragons - which you'll find out why in the book - but it's surprising when she finds herself trusting Cvareh, who wants to overthrow the King and work with her to do so. 
 We also have the lovely Florence, she was my favorite character! I wanted to ship her with Arianna, I don't know why, but they seemed to have that kind of chemistry that lovers have. Arianna openly identifies herself as a bisexual, we're told multiple times that she was in love with a woman - who's now dead - so this definitely made me ship her with Florence more. But don't get too excited, I think Florence is going to be sent to the sister-zone! Also, there seems to be some love/hate romance going on with Cvareh and I don't know how to react to this. Author ELISE KOVA, DO NOT TOY WITH MY FEELINGS OK. 
 Before wrapping-up my review, here are my favorite quotes from the book: 
 "Adulthood just meant finding the variety of crazy that resonated the most with you and doing it until you died or it killed you - whichever came first." 
 Our characters go outside of what they were "told to do", Arianna and Florence do not want to be part of a Guild just because they were told to. They want to do bigger things, and be themselves while they do it. Cvareh is part of the lowest ranked Dragon house, and he wants to prove to be more than that. This is something our three characters have in common, which is why I love that quote so much. 
 "Fighting for an ideal meant nothing if the people it was meant to benefit died in the process." 
 The book was greatly built to leave us with the perfect opening for a rebellion in the second book, with that being said I CANNOT WAIT to get my hands on that second book! 
 The Alchemist of Loom comes out in January 10, 2017 while the second book comes out in April 2017! (WHAAAAT! YES!)

 Reading Order

 Review 
 It's beautiful to have Lucien and Sophie back together again and also awarded with a back story of Dylan and Kara. 
 I have always loved Lucien and his ALPHA caveman ways with Sophie but it was a pleasant surprise to see that "hulking" man have more tender moments. 
 Then we meet Dylan (Matthew) in this story who is on the run from something - he instantly gets the "Ding-Dong Dance" syndrome over Kara. We have commitment issues, sex, angst, lies, sex, love, sex, heart-break and did I mention HOT STEAMY SEX? 
 This was a fast read that grabs your attention and keeps it flowing with all the action that is happening. The only problem I had with the book is how the POV would change without any warning - at times I found it hard to distinguish what was happening to who 
 We all remember Kara from the prior books as Sophie's friend who is still healing from being left at the alter. She travels to Ibiza with Sophie to open a store in one of Lucien's new sex clubs. She just wants a summer to work, relax and heal without the drama and lies of any men in her life. 
 Dylan Day (Matthew) is on the run from something but we are left in the dark through most of the book. Something happened to him back home in the States which made him pack a bag and start a new life in Ibiza. He tries to remain hidden from women and runs into Lucien who gives him a job of managing the new club. 
 Kara is first very skeptical of Dylan and feels that he is one big lie and she doesn't fall into his trap of being suave. But things change and the sexual tension between the two just keep getting hotter and hotter. The romance between them is beautiful and the sex is even more. Dylan is falling in love but knows that he will lose Kara when she finds out he has been lying to everyone. 
 But like any romance novel, there always comes a time when the shit hits the fan and hearts will break. Are the lies bad enough that Kara will never forgive Dylan? What are the secrets he is keeping? 
 The biggest question, though, is will there be a "Happily Ever After"? 
 Wrap Up 
 Well, the story between Sophie and Lucien finally comes to an end and they experience a love like no other. While Dylan and Kara find a love built on lies but these lies are only on the surface.....what is inside never was a lie. 
 But is this enough?

MONUMENT 14 was not a book I exactly had on my radar. In fact, when I read the synopsis for this book, my first thought was of a kids' show from New Zealand called The Tribe - kids orphaned by an apocalyptic event who mostly inhabit a mall in Wellington. But that's beside the point. Besides, they dress up in funny outfits and face paint and are in a "tribe". Still, beside the point. Emmy Laybourne's book was not on my radar until a fateful tweet landed this one in my hands, and what can I say? I was pleasantly surprised. 
 Following Dean, a young guy thrown into the apocalypse a few years into the future while on the school bus with several other kids, MONUMENT 14 follows - you guessed it - 14 kids living in Monument, Colorado as their bus crashes into a superstore in the middle of a hailstorm. Their driver leaves to find help and never returns, but things quickly begin to spiral out of control. Freak earthquakes, chemical weapons spills, choking black clouds of gas... 
 I am going to admit it. My favorite part of this book was finding out what bad would befall these children. Giant hailstones! Massive earthquakes! Extreme sadness! Chemical weapons than alter minds and bodies! Okay, some of it was a bit unbelievable. The chemical weapons especially. But Laybourne totally packs a punch with the bad things that happens to these kids, and that is not the least of it. 
 I enjoyed the honesty of this book. From Dean's voice, which sounded almost like an ADHD-addled kid (very boy-esque), to the mental state of victims of trauma, it felt very real. At the same time, this was an issue I had. The book focused too much on the problems these kids experienced, from finding out how to survive in this brave new world to simple stuff. We find out about lice, making breakfast daily, tearing down walls. I wanted more plot, more suspense, more intrigue and action. Or zombies. Zombies would have been nice, or at least more of the last 100 pages. 
 One of my fave young adult books is LIFE AS WE KNEW IT by Susan Beth Pfeffer. While it comes close to matching the compelling nature of Pfeffer's work, a post-apocalyptic story about a family trying to survive the aftermath of a catastrophic worldwide disaster, it doesn't match the level. There is something off about this, but don't get me wrong, I really enjoyed it. It will just take a certain reader who enjoys the nuances of survival and doesn't need a plot to drag them through. There is a story here, but it's slow building, laden with tiny details about life and living and children and teens and the world. 
 My suggestion? Check this one out, but only if you go into it not expecting extreme action wall to wall, or zombies like I might have kind of thought looking at the cover... There are pseudo-zombies, but they're not eating brains. Think the Rage virus from 28 Days Later, except with more bloody boils and sterility issues.

 Amani has respect for the desert and a longing to explore. She's a coward who runs. She's selfish. She's stubborn.
